0.title: Jeremiah: The Weeping Prophet
0.overview:
Jeremiah is the book of a man who was sent to tell his own nation that it was finished, and to keep telling them for forty years while they laughed at him, beat him, tried him for his life and threw him into a pit. It is also the book in which God promises a new covenant (a new binding bond with his people), a righteous King from David's line, and a day when he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (31:34). Judgment and hope run side by side through all fifty-two chapters, and both come from the same God.

Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a village a few miles from Jerusalem. The word of the LORD came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BC, and he was still prophesying when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, and after it (1:1-3). He lived through the last five kings of Judah: Josiah, the reforming king; Shallum, carried off to Egypt after three months (22:11; 2 Kgs 23:31-34); Jehoiakim, who cut up and burned Jeremiah's scroll column by column (36:23); Coniah, hurled into exile (22:24-26); and Zedekiah, who asked Jeremiah for a word from God in secret and never had the courage to obey it.

Assyria collapsed, and Babylon rose in its place and defeated Egypt at Carchemish about 605 BC (46:2). Judah's kings tried to survive by playing the great powers against each other. Jeremiah's message was that the real threat was not Babylon but the LORD, whom they had abandoned, and that Babylon was the rod in his hand. These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years (25:11). The seventy years are most simply counted from about 605 BC to the first return about 538 BC; some count from the temple's fall in 586 to its rebuilding in 516. Daniel read the number and prayed (Dan. 9:2).

The charge against Judah is set out in the second chapter: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (2:13). They worshipped other gods on every high hill, oppressed the poor, and assumed that the temple would protect them anyway (7:4). Underneath all of it lay a problem no reform could reach: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (17:9).

Jeremiah did not want the job, and God answered his protest with a promise: Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you (1:8). His commission was to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10): four words of demolition and two of building, and the building words come last. He was told not to marry (16:2), so that his lonely life became a sign of the coming ruin. He was put in the stocks (20:2), arrested as a deserter (37:13), and lowered into a cistern where he sank in the mud (38:6). After the city fell he was taken to Egypt against his will (43:6-7). The book never tells us how he died.

Jeremiah lets us see inside his own heart. He argues with God, curses the day he was born, and tries to stop preaching, and finds he cannot: the word is a burning fire shut up in my bones (20:9). Yet the same man says your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (15:16). His prayers teach every weary servant of God that honesty with God is not unbelief, and that faithfulness is measured by obedience, not by results.

The book is not arranged in date order. Chapter 1 is the call. Chapters 2-25 are mainly warnings to Judah: sermons, visions, acted parables and Jeremiah's own anguished prayers. Chapters 26-29 show him in conflict with priests and false prophets, and include his letter to the exiles. Chapters 30-33 are a book of comfort (30:2). Chapters 34-45 tell the story of the siege, the fall of Jerusalem and the chaos after it. Chapters 46-51 are oracles against the nations, ending with the fall of Babylon (51:64). Chapter 52 is a historical appendix.

Who wrote the book down? Baruch son of Neriah was Jeremiah’s scribe and friend, who wrote at his dictation and read the scroll in the temple (ch. 36); he went with Jeremiah to Egypt (43:6). The Greek translation of Jeremiah is about an eighth shorter and arranges the oracles against the nations differently; both forms were known among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Hebrew text, followed by the ESV, is most likely the fuller edition that Jeremiah and Baruch completed (36:32).

Through all of it runs one conviction: God's word will be done. I am watching over my word to perform it (1:12). His word is like fire and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (23:29). When the king burned the scroll, God simply had it written again, with more added (36:32). What God says about judgment happens, and what God says about mercy happens too.

And the mercy is astonishing. To the exiles God says, I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (29:11), spoken to people who would spend seventy years far from home. It was a promise to a community, not of an easy life, and many who heard it died in Babylon; yet for everyone in Christ the same God works all things for good (Rom 8:28). With Babylon's army at the walls, Jeremiah buys a field in his home village as a sign that the land has a future (32:15), and prays, Nothing is too hard for you (32:17). The last verses of the book show a king of David's line brought out of prison to eat at the king's table every day of his life (52:31-34): a small light left burning for David's house.

That light leads to Christ. Jeremiah promised a righteous Branch for David, whose name would be The LORD is our righteousness (23:5-6). He promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on their hearts (31:33), the only answer to the deceitful heart. On the night before he died, Jesus took the cup and said, This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's promise in full to show that it has come (Heb 8:8-12). Jesus drove the traders from the temple with Jeremiah's words, a den of robbers (Matt 21:13; Jer 7:11); some thought he was Jeremiah come back (Matt 16:14); Matthew hears Jeremiah's Rachel weeping at Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18). Jesus too wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), warned that its temple would fall, and was rejected by its priests. But where Jeremiah could only announce the new covenant, Jesus made it, in his own blood.

Jeremiah is a book for anyone tempted to trust in religion instead of God, for anyone who must keep saying unpopular truth, for anyone living through the collapse of what they thought was secure, and for anyone who needs to hear that God's plans for his people run through the ruins to a future and a hope. Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth (9:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Man and His Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A priest's son from Anathoth (v. 1) receives the word of the LORD from Josiah's thirteenth year (v. 2) to the captivity of Jerusalem under Zedekiah (v. 3): about forty years, ending in the ruin of the city.
verseByVerse.theology: God's word comes to a real man, in named years, under named kings: the message of this book is anchored in history.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, to whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, and until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book begins with a name, a father and a village. Jeremiah is a priest's son from Anathoth, a small place within sight of Jerusalem, not a member of the temple establishment in the capital. He comes from the edge, and he will spend his life telling the centre what it does not want to hear.

The date matters. Josiah was the last good king of Judah, the one who did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father (2 Kgs 22:2). Jeremiah's ministry begins as a national reform is gathering pace: Josiah had begun purging the idols the year before (2 Chr 34:3), and the great reform came five years later (2 Kgs 22:3). He is called in the best years, and he will watch them end.

Forty years of preaching, and the summary of how it went is in the last phrase of verse 3: until the captivity of Jerusalem. Under Jehoiakim the empire had already closed in (2 Kgs 24:1).

Judged by results, he failed. Judged by faithfulness, he is one of the great men of the Bible. Those are not the same measure, and confusing them has wrecked more ministries and more Christians than open sin has.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, from about 627 BC to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 and beyond. Anathoth was a priests’ town about 3 miles north-east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Before I Formed You in the Womb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God knew and appointed Jeremiah before he was born (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he is only a youth (v. 6), and is told to go and speak, with the promise of God's presence (vv. 7-8). Then the LORD touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to tear down and to build (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The call rests on God's prior choice, God's presence and God's words, not on the prophet's ability.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator's voice becomes the prophet's own. What follows is Jeremiah telling you what happened to him.

Four verbs, and God is the subject of every one. He formed, he knew, he consecrated, he appointed. And all four happened before Jeremiah had done anything at all, before he had any character to commend him or any failure to disqualify him.

I knew you is more than knowing facts about him. It is the knowledge of relationship. Before there was a person to know, God knew him. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them (Ps 139:16).

The same pattern is claimed by the servant of Isaiah (Isa 49:1), and by Paul, who described God as the one who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace (Gal 1:15). John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb (Luke 1:15).

Two things follow for anyone reading. God deals with unborn children as persons he knows, names and has purposes for. And your significance is not something you are building. It was settled before you existed, by God, and no failure of yours can vote on it.

What about a child who dies before birth? Parents who have lost a pregnancy often come to this verse with an ache, and it speaks to them gently. A child carried for a few weeks and never held was known by the God who formed it, and is not forgotten. Scripture does not tell us all we would like about such little ones, but it gives ground for hope: when his infant son died, David said, I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Sam 12:23), and the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ. Such a child may be entrusted to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Gen 18:25), and whose Son took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16). A miscarriage is a sorrow, not a sin, and no mother should hear this verse as blame.

Does “before I formed you in the womb I knew you” mean souls exist before their bodies? No. It means God chose and set Jeremiah apart before his life began; the knowing is God’s, not the soul’s. It speaks first of Jeremiah’s unique call as a prophet, but it rests on a truth that holds for all God’s people: he chose us in him before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4). And it shows that God knows and forms each person in the womb (Ps 139:13–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response is not enthusiasm but dismay. Ah, Lord GOD! is a cry, not a greeting. And the objection is in two parts: I cannot do this, and I am too young to be taken seriously.

Both are probably true. That is the point. Moses said the same thing at the burning bush (Exod 4:10), and God's answer was not a compliment about his hidden potential but a question, Who has made man's mouth?, and a promise: I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak (Exod 4:11-12).

In these calls God never says, you are better than you think. He says, I will be with you. Confidence for service does not come from a higher estimate of yourself; it comes from a higher estimate of God.

And youth is not a disqualification in Scripture. Paul told a young minister, Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity (1 Tim 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to me, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not argue with the objection; he forbids it. Then he replaces the two halves of Jeremiah's excuse with two commands that put the responsibility where it belongs. Where you go is not your decision, and what you say is not your decision either.

That is a hard word and a liberating one: no freedom to choose the audience or edit the message, and no burden of inventing something worth saying.

God names the real problem. It is not inability; it is fear. Jeremiah will be beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason, so the fear is not irrational. The remedy given is not a promise that they will listen, or that he will be liked. It is a presence: I am with you.

That is the same word the risen Christ left with his church when he sent it into the world: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20), a presence he keeps by the Spirit he gives. And it is what Paul heard in Corinth when he was afraid: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you (Acts 18:9-10). Is there a conversation you are avoiding because of what the person might say back? The promise is the same for you: he goes with you into it, and he has already forgiven the times you stayed silent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. And the LORD said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection was about a mouth, so God touches his mouth. Isaiah's lips were touched with a coal from the altar to deal with his guilt (Isa 6:7). Here the touch is a commission: the words themselves are put in.

Ezekiel was made to eat a scroll (Ezek 3:1-3), and John in Revelation ate a little scroll that was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter (Rev 10:10). That is Jeremiah's life in a sentence. The word of God is sweet to receive and bitter to carry.

A village boy is set over nations and over kingdoms, not with an army but with a message. The empires of his day would have laughed. They are gone, and his words are still being read.

Six verbs: four tear down, two build. That is the proportion of this book, and it is honest about what the word of God must do in a place that has gone wrong. You cannot plant in ground that has not been cleared. Paul describes his ministry the same way: weapons with divine power to destroy strongholds (2 Cor 10:4-5).

But the two constructive verbs are not an afterthought, and later God takes them up again: so I will watch over them to build and to plant (31:28). The book that begins with demolition reaches a new covenant at its centre (31:31-34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Two Visions: the Almond and the Boiling Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two visions. An almond branch: God is watching over his word to perform it (vv. 11-12). A boiling pot tilted from the north: disaster let loose (vv. 13-14), the northern kingdoms at Jerusalem's gates (v. 15), and judgment for forsaking the LORD (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his word to do it, and the first thing it will do here is bring an army from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Jeremiah, what do you see?" And I said, "I see an almond branch." Then the LORD said to me, "You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first vision is almost domestic: a branch in blossom, the sort of thing anyone might notice on a walk. God asks him what he sees, because God is about to teach him to read ordinary things.

The answer turns on a play on words that English cannot carry: almond sounds like the Hebrew for watching. Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says, I am the watching God, and what I am watching over is my word. God is awake over what he has said.

That is the sentence to hold for the next fifty-one chapters. Not one syllable of what God says in this book will fall to the ground unattended. So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose (Isa 55:11). Has he said, and will he not do it? (Num 23:19).

It cuts both ways, which is exactly why it is here. For a prophet who will preach for forty years and see almost no response, it means his labour is not wasted. For a nation that has heard the warnings and shrugged, it means the warnings are not noise.
verseByVerse.note: Wordplay: “almond” (shaqed) sounds like “watching” (shoqed) (ESV note). The almond is among the first trees to blossom in spring.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me a second time, saying, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north." Then the LORD said to me, "Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land. For behold, I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north, declares the LORD, and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its walls all around and against all the cities of Judah. And I will declare my judgments against them, for all their evil in forsaking me. They have made offerings to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second vision is a cooking pot at the boil, tilted so that what is inside is about to pour out over Judah, from the north.

The armies came from the north because the desert lay to the east; that is the road every invader took. Within Jeremiah's lifetime Babylon would come down it.

The one doing it is God: I am calling. Babylon thought it was pursuing its own ambitions. It was being summoned. The thrones set in the gateway are the picture of a conquered city, with foreign officials sitting where Judah's elders used to give judgment.

And the reason is given plainly, so that no one can call the disaster meaningless. It is not bad luck or geopolitics. It is forsaking me, and the shape that forsaking took: worshipping the works of their own hands. They made something, then bowed to it. Every generation does, and the objects change.

Does God do evil? The word can mean “evil” or “disaster”. God brings calamity as judgment on sin (Isa 45:7), but he never does moral evil or tempts anyone to it (Jas 1:13). The disaster from the north was the just punishment of a people who had forsaken him.
verseByVerse.note: The kingdoms of the north turn out to be Babylon and its allies (25:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — An Iron Pillar and Bronze Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is told to get ready, speak, and not be dismayed (v. 17). God makes him a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls against the whole land (v. 18): they will fight, but not prevail, for God is with him (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not promise the prophet an easy audience; he promises to make him able to stand and to keep him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you. Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them. And I, behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dress yourself for work is in Hebrew "gird up your loins": gather the long robe, tie it at the waist, get ready to move. It is the posture of a man about to run or to fight.

Then a warning with a sting in it: lest I dismay you before them. Fear of the audience is not a small weakness to be indulged in a preacher; it is the thing that will break him in public. If he will not fear God more than the crowd, God will let the crowd frighten him. The cure for the fear of people is not courage summoned from inside. It is the fear of God, which crowds out every lesser fear, and it is God who gives it.

Three images follow, all defensive and immovable: a walled city, an iron pillar, walls of bronze. God does not remove the opposition, and he lists exactly who it will be: the palace, the civil service, the clergy and the public. Instead of removing them, he makes the man able to stand.

Ezekiel received the same kind of hardening (Ezek 3:8-9). God gives what the calling requires, and he gives it to the person who has just said he cannot do it. Every Christian who has kept quiet out of fear has a better word than a scolding: the one who never once flinched from the Father's word went to the cross for cowards, and his Spirit makes the fearful bold.
verseByVerse.note: The same picture of readiness is used in Job 38:3 and 1 Peter 1:13.

verseByVerse.quote: They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, declares the LORD, to deliver you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the promise it has been building toward, and it is worded with great care. Not, they will not fight you. That is stated as fact. But they shall not prevail.

Read Jeremiah's life before deciding what that promise covers. He was put in stocks, left to sink in a muddy cistern, imprisoned, accused of desertion, ignored by a king who burned his scroll, and finally carried off to Egypt. He was not protected from any of it. He was preserved through all of it, and the word he carried outlived every one of his opponents.

Jesus said of his church, the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt 16:18), and told his disciples, In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

And there is one prophet of whom this promise was not made in that form. Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem and was preserved; Christ wept over the same city (Luke 19:41) and was handed over to it. He had the words of God in his mouth in a way no prophet ever had, speaking only what his Father gave him (John 12:49), and when they fought against him, he did not call for deliverance. He was the prophet Moses promised (Acts 3:22), and he was not delivered, so that we would be.

1.title: The Call of Jeremiah: I Am Watching Over My Word
1.overview:
Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, received the word of the LORD from the thirteenth year of Josiah until Jerusalem went into captivity: about forty years of preaching that ended with his country in ruins (vv. 1-3).

God tells him that he knew, consecrated and appointed him before he was born (vv. 4-5). Jeremiah objects that he cannot speak and is only a youth; God forbids the excuse and promises, I am with you to deliver you (vv. 6-8). God touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to tear down and to build (vv. 9-10).

Two visions follow: an almond branch, because God is watching over his word (vv. 11-12), and a boiling pot tilted from the north, an invasion God himself is summoning (vv. 13-16). Finally God makes Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls: they will fight him and will not prevail (vv. 17-19).
1.theology:
God's call rests on his own prior choice, not on the one called (vv. 4-5; Ps 139:16; Gal 1:15), and he deals with the unborn as persons he knows and appoints. Fitness for service is not self-confidence but God's presence and God's words (vv. 6-9; Exod 4:11-12; Matt 28:20).

The word of God does demolishing work before it builds (v. 10; 2 Cor 10:4-5), and the building is promised (31:28). God watches over his word to perform it, so that neither warning nor promise falls to the ground (v. 12; Isa 55:11; Num 23:19).

God governs the nations that punish his people: the invader from the north is summoned by him (v. 15). Fear of man is the prophet's real danger, and the remedy is the fear of God (v. 17). God does not remove opposition but makes his servant able to stand and preserves him through it (vv. 18-19; Matt 16:18). The prophet greater than Jeremiah was not delivered from those who fought him (Acts 3:22; Luke 19:41), so that we would be.
1.examples: Jeremiah's forty years of faithful preaching, ending in national ruin, are a standing rebuke to judging a ministry by its results. And when a calling feels too large, God's answer to "I can't" is never "you are better than you think" but "I am with you".

2.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.<sup>3</sup>Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."<sup>4</sup>Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless?<sup>6</sup>They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'<sup>7</sup>And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination.<sup>8</sup>The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.<sup>9</sup>"Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend.<sup>10</sup>For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing.<sup>11</sup>Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods?
