verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Devotion of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory of Israel's early devotion (vv. 1-3), then asks what wrong their fathers found in him (vv. 4-5). They stopped asking where the LORD was (v. 6), defiled the land he gave them (v. 7), and every kind of leader failed together (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The question of verse 5 is a lover's question as well as a judge's: what did I do, that you should leave me?

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown. Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first sermon of the book does not open with an accusation. It opens with a memory, and it is God's memory.

He is thinking of the exodus and the wilderness years, and he describes them the way a husband describes the early days of a marriage. There was a time when they followed him anywhere, into a land not sown, with no crops and no guarantees, simply because he was going that way.

That is a remarkable thing for God to say about the wilderness generation, because the books of Exodus and Numbers are full of their grumbling. He remembers the love, and does not rehearse the complaints. Grace has a long memory for the good.

Firstfruits were the portion given to God and reserved for him alone; anyone else who ate them was guilty. That is what Israel was to him: set apart, his own, protected by his jealousy so that whoever touched them answered for it.

Before a word of the indictment, hear the tone. This is not a landlord evicting a tenant. It is a husband remembering a honeymoon, and it is about to become one of the saddest chapters in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless? They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The address widens. Jeremiah is standing in Jerusalem, but the summons goes to all the clans of the house of Israel, the northern tribes included, a century after Assyria scattered them. The whole family was in the wilderness, and the whole family is now called to answer.

Then the question at the heart of the chapter, and God is the one asking it. Not, what did you gain by leaving, but what fault did you find? He invites them to produce the grievance, the thing he did that justified it. There is none.

And then: went after worthlessness, and became worthless. The word is the same on both sides. You become what you worship. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8). Paul says the same of the human race: they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images, and their foolish hearts were darkened (Rom 1:21-23). Worship is never neutral. Whatever you give yourself to is shaping you into its own likeness right now.

The failure was not a decision to reject God. It was a question they stopped asking. Nobody said, where is the LORD? The rescue was still in the history books and had gone out of the conversation. That is how faith is usually lost: not in a crisis of belief, but in a slow silence.

And look at what they had stopped remembering: not a pleasant journey but deserts, pits, drought and deep darkness, a land where no man dwells. Moses had told the same people to remember the God who brought you water out of the flinty rock (Deut 8:15). The worse the road had been, the more there was to be grateful for, and the more complete the forgetting.

verseByVerse.quote: And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination. The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave them a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity (Deut 8:9), and the gift became the occasion of the forgetting. Prosperity is often harder on faith than poverty, because it removes the daily sense of need.

The possessives matter: my land, my heritage. God gave them the land and never stopped owning it. What they defiled was not their property but his inheritance. Everything a believer has is held on the same terms.

Then the leadership, four groups, and every one has failed. The priests never asked where God was. The scholars who handle the law did not know its author. The shepherds (the ESV notes the word may be rendered "rulers") broke the covenant themselves. And the prophets preached another god entirely. When a nation collapses spiritually, it is rarely the people who fall first.

And the first failures are failures of knowing. It is entirely possible to handle Scripture professionally, every day, and not know the God who wrote it. The question for anyone who teaches is not how much of the text he has mastered, but whether he still asks where the LORD is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No nation changes its gods, but God's people have exchanged their glory (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: the forsaken fountain and the broken cisterns (vv. 12-13). The lions have roared and the land is waste (vv. 14-16), a ruin they brought on themselves, and running to Egypt and Assyria for water will not mend it (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin is never only a rule broken. It is a greater good abandoned for a lesser one, and heaven itself is summoned to be appalled at the exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend. For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing. Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes them to court, and the case rests on a survey. Send west to Cyprus, send east to Kedar, and ask a simple question: does anyone do this?

And the lawsuit runs across generations: with your children's children I will contend. A God who is still contending three generations on has not given up on the defendants.

The survey is almost comic: other nations keep faith with deities that do not exist, while Israel breaks faith with the one who does. Israel traded their glory, the living God himself, their honour and their boast, for something that does not profit. It is not only wicked; it is a spectacularly bad deal.

verseByVerse.quote: Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven is called as witness, and told to be horrified. Sin has become so normal on earth that the reaction has to be imported from somewhere else.

Here is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is one of the clearest definitions of sin in Scripture. Not one evil, but two.

The first is leaving. God is the fountain of living waters: a spring, moving, fresh, free, endlessly replenished, requiring no work from anyone but a cupped hand. In a hot country that is not poetry; it is life.

The second is the substitute. A cistern is a pit cut out of rock to hold rainwater. Cutting one is brutal labour, months of it. The water it holds is still and stale at best. And these are broken cisterns, cracked, so that the digger is left with a dry hole he spent his strength on.

That is the anatomy of every sin: a real spring abandoned, and enormous effort spent on a leaking substitute. Nobody works harder than someone trying to get from a career, a relationship, a bottle or an image what only God gives. And the cistern always leaks, which is why it must be dug again next year.

Jesus stood in the temple and answered this verse directly: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37), and he meant the Spirit whom those who believed were to receive. To a woman drawing water he said, whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:14). And at the end of the Bible the offer still stands: To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (Rev 21:6). The fountain is free; only the cisterns cost.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew usage “living water” is running water from a spring, as opposed to water stored in a tank.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey? The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant. Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head. Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions and a scene of ruin. Israel was God's son, not anyone's slave, so why is he being carried off like plunder? The lions are the empires, and the roaring has already begun: towns burned, fields wasted, villages emptied.

Memphis and Tahpanhes are Egyptian cities, and the shaved crown is the mark of a slave or a mourner. The ESV notes that have shaved is in Hebrew "grazed". The allies Judah courted have treated her like pasture.

Verse 17 refuses every comfortable explanation: not the empires, not bad luck, not God's neglect. Not every sorrow is of this kind, and Scripture never says it is; but there is a kind of pain that is simply the shape of our own choices coming back to us, and this was it.

And the last clause makes it worse: when he led you in the way. They were not lost when they left. They were being led, the way a father leads a small child, and they let go of his hand. Moses had described that wilderness care: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went (Deut 1:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The water image returns, now as foreign policy. Judah's politics swung between the two superpowers, drinking first from the Nile and then from the Euphrates, buying protection with tribute and treaties. Every generation has its version of this: the fear that God is not enough, and the search for a stronger friend.

God does not need to invent a punishment; the sin administers its own. The psalm says it as a judicial act: So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels (Ps 81:12). Sometimes the severest thing God does is let a person have what he insisted on.

The verse ends at the root of it all: the fear of me is not in you. Every other failure in the chapter grows out of that absence. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Prov 1:7), and a people without it will run to Egypt and Assyria because they are more afraid of the empires than of him. What a person fears most is what he ends up obeying.
verseByVerse.note: The Nile is “Shihor” and the Euphrates “the River” in Hebrew (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Choice Vine Gone Wild
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people threw off God's yoke and bowed to idols on every high hill (v. 20). God's choice vine turned wild (v. 21), and no soap removes the stain (v. 22). They deny it, though they run like a wild animal in heat (vv. 23-25). They will be shamed like a caught thief, calling a tree their father and crying to God only in trouble (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is both a slavery that cannot be broken by willpower and a stain that cannot be scrubbed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore. Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine? Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God broke the yoke in Egypt, and the freed slave answered, I will not serve: not him, at least. And then he bowed anyway, on every hill and under every tree, to whatever local shrine was going. Nobody serves nothing. The yoke thrown off is always replaced.

The King James Version reads I will not transgress here. The Hebrew words for “serve” and “transgress” differ by one similar-looking letter, and the scribes' marginal reading gave “transgress”; most modern translations, with the Greek Old Testament, read I will not serve. Either way, the people's words were contradicted on every hill.

The gardener chose the best stock and planted it himself, and what came up was wild. The fault cannot be traced to the seed or the gardener.

Now the image changes to laundry, and it settles the question of self-improvement. Lye and soap were the strongest cleaners available. Scrub as hard as you like: the stain of your guilt is still before me. Before him: that is the problem. It is not about feeling clean.

This verse leaves only one door open, and the New Testament opens it: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The stain that no effort removes is removed by confession and by blood, and by nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there, a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her. Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The denial is answered with evidence: Look at your way in the valley. The valley is most likely the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem, where children were burned to Molech (7:31). Do not tell me what you believe; look at what you have done.

The images are deliberately undignified: a young camel bolting in every direction, a wild donkey in heat that nobody needs to chase because she comes to them. Idolatry is not sophisticated. It is compulsive.

And it is honest about addiction: Who can restrain her lust? The question expects the answer nobody, and certainly not the animal herself. Anyone who has tried to break a habit by willpower alone knows the verse from the inside. The God who broke the yoke in Egypt (v. 20) is the one who breaks this one too, by his Spirit, his word and the help of his people.

God pleads with them to stop wearing out their shoes and their throats chasing what will not feed them. The reply is the saddest line in the chapter: It is hopeless. Not defiance, but despair: I am too far gone; this is who I am now. Many people are held in something they hate by exactly that sentence, and it is a lie, because the God who is still pleading in this verse has not called it hopeless.

verseByVerse.quote: "As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets, who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!' But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shame of a thief is not remorse for stealing; it is the shame of being caught. That is the shame coming to Judah, and the list runs from the palace down, much the same list as verse 8. The failure is systemic and named.

Two sentences that between them describe most religion. In good times, a tree is my father and a stone gave me birth: whatever I have made is what I am from. In bad times, Arise and save us!, addressed to the God whose back they have been looking at.

God notices the posture: they have turned their back to me, and not their face. That is the difference between a wandering child and a settled rebellion, and it is also the whole of repentance. Turning round is all that is required, and it is the one thing they will not do.

The irony is sharp: your gods that you made for yourself. Call them, God says. See if they stand up. Isaiah put it the same way: Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? (Isa 44:10). There was a god for every town, and not one of them able to move.

The test still works. When the diagnosis comes, or the job goes, or the marriage cracks, you find out very quickly which of the things you serve can stand up and help, and that the God they had turned their back on is still the one who can.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's discipline taught them nothing, and they killed the prophets (vv. 29-30). He asks whether he has been a wilderness to them (v. 31); a bride does not forget her attire, yet his people have forgotten him (v. 32). With the blood of the poor on their skirts they still claim innocence (vv. 33-35), and Egypt will shame them as Assyria did (vv. 36-37).
verseByVerse.theology: The final defence of a guilty people is not argument but denial, and God answers it by bringing them to judgment for the denial itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD. In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion. And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'? Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are arguing with him, and he asks why. Then two sentences of terrible summary: the discipline achieved nothing, and the messengers sent to explain the discipline were killed. A nation that will neither feel a warning nor hear an explanation has closed both doors.

The question of verse 5 returns, sharper. Have I been barren ground to you, the dark place you had to escape? God asks to be shown the evidence for the way he is being treated.

And the answer his people give is the oldest lie about God there is: We are free, we will come no more to you. Freedom is defined as distance from him. It is exactly what the serpent suggested, and what every generation repeats.

A bride does not forget her dress; it is the most precious thing she owns and the day is the biggest of her life. Yet God's people have forgotten him days without number.

It is not an accusation of atheism but of forgetting, and forgetting does not feel like rebellion. It feels like being busy. God measures it in days: how many have gone by, with no thought of him at all?

Paul uses the same marriage language of the church: he had betrothed the Corinthians to one husband, Christ, and feared they would be led astray (2 Cor 11:2-3). The bride who forgot is answered by a Bridegroom who does not forget, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). His faithfulness, not hers, is what holds the marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: "How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways. Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two charges together, and their pairing is the point. They have become expert at pursuing love in all the wrong places, so accomplished that the professionals could learn from them. And there is blood on their clothes: the lifeblood of the guiltless poor, people who had done nothing.

Idolatry and injustice arrive together, always. A people who will worship anything will eventually spend anyone. The prophets never separate the two, and neither should we.

The phrase you did not find them breaking in is legal language. The law allowed a householder to strike a burglar caught at night: If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him (Exod 22:2). These poor had no such excuse attached to their deaths. They were simply in the way.

With blood on the hem, the claim is I am innocent. And God names what he will judge: not only the sin, but the denial of it.

That is a sobering line, and also a hopeful one. It means the one thing standing between this people and mercy is the sentence they keep repeating. The next chapter will show God pleading for one word of acknowledgement (3:13), and it is the same word the New Testament asks for. Self-defence is the only posture in which forgiveness cannot be received.

verseByVerse.quote: How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria. From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with restless diplomacy: first Assyria, now Egypt, always looking for a better arrangement. They will come home from Egypt with your hands on your head, the posture of prisoners and mourners.

It is the gesture Tamar made when she walked out disgraced (2 Sam 13:19). A nation that had courted every power going would end with the same gesture: used, and sent away.

The reason is given last and it is final: the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust. Every refuge that is not God is a refuge God has already rejected. Better to learn that before the crisis than during it.

Judah kept switching allies because none of them satisfied: the cistern of verse 13 again, dug in a new place each time. The only fixed point in the chapter is the one they left: the God who remembered the devotion of their youth and was still contending for them.

2.title: Two Evils: The Fountain and the Broken Cisterns
2.overview:
God sends Jeremiah to Jerusalem with a memory of the early days, Israel's devotion as a bride (vv. 1-3). Then he asks what wrong they found in him, that they went after worthlessness and became worthless; they stopped asking where he was, defiled the land he gave them, and their leaders all failed (vv. 4-8).

Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit (vv. 9-11). Heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters, and digging broken cisterns (vv. 12-13). The ruin is self-inflicted, and running to Egypt and Assyria will not mend it (vv. 14-19).

The freed slave bowed to idols anyway; the choice vine turned wild; no soap removes the stain (vv. 20-22). The people deny it and call their case hopeless (vv. 23-25), call a tree their father and cry to God only in trouble (vv. 26-28). A bride who could never forget her dress has forgotten God (vv. 29-32), and with the blood of the poor on their clothes they plead innocence (vv. 33-37).
2.theology:
Sin is defined here in two movements: forsaking God, the fountain of living waters, and constructing substitutes that cannot hold what they promise (v. 13). Christ answers the first half by offering living water freely (John 4:14; 7:37; Rev 21:6).

Worship is formative: those who go after worthlessness become worthless (v. 5; Ps 115:8; Rom 1:21-23). Prosperity and forgetfulness, not argument, are how faith is usually lost (vv. 6-7, 32). Leaders fail first (vv. 8, 26).

Sin carries its own punishment (v. 19; Ps 81:12), cannot be washed out by self-improvement (v. 22; 1 John 1:9), and is most dangerous when denied: God judges the claim I have not sinned (v. 35). Idolatry and injustice always travel together (vv. 33-34).
2.examples: The chapter's pictures stay with a reader because they are ordinary: a husband remembering a honeymoon, a man cutting a tank in rock beside a free spring, lye and soap on a stain that is before God and not before us, a bride who could never forget her dress. Each says the same thing from a different side: the fault was never in the God they left, and he is still calling them back.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom.<sup>3</sup>Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.<sup>4</sup>Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth—<sup>5</sup>will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."<sup>6</sup>The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore?<sup>7</sup>And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.<sup>8</sup>She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.<sup>9</sup>Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree.<sup>10</sup>Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.<sup>12</sup>Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever.<sup>13</sup>Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.<sup>15</sup>"'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.<sup>16</sup>And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again.<sup>17</sup>At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart.<sup>18</sup>In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.<sup>19</sup>"'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me.<sup>20</sup>Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"<sup>21</sup>A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God.<sup>22</sup>"Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God.<sup>23</sup>Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.<sup>24</sup>"But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters.<sup>25</sup>Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Would You Return to Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law forbids a divorced wife who has married another to return to her first husband, yet God asks his unfaithful people to return (v. 1). The rains have been withheld and they refuse to be ashamed (vv. 2-3), while still speaking warmly of God (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Affectionate words to God alongside unchanged behaviour are not repentance; and yet the impossible invitation to return is the one God makes.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD. Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with a point of law. Under Deuteronomy, a man who divorced his wife could not take her back once she had married someone else: her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD (Deut 24:4). The door is shut by God's own statute.

And then, in the same breath, God asks, would you return to me? That is the astonishing thing in this chapter, and everything else stands under it. What the law forbids, love offers. God is not pretending the marriage was undamaged or the adultery small (many lovers is his own phrase), and still he opens a door the law had bolted. How he can do this without ceasing to be just is the question the whole Bible answers at the cross.

The invitation does not come with amnesia: every hilltop has a shrine, and she has been at all of them. Like an Arab in the wilderness pictures a desert raider crouched beside a caravan route, watching the road for whoever comes along. Israel is not a victim ambushed by temptation but the one lying in wait for it.

The drought was a message, and it was missed. The forehead of a whore is a face that has lost the capacity to blush. Shame is painful and it is a mercy; a conscience that can still be embarrassed is still alive. The danger point in any life is not doing wrong but reaching the stage of doing it without a flicker.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words are lovely: My father, you are the friend of my youth. Warm, intimate, theologically correct, and quite compatible with having done all the evil that you could. Religious language is not repentance. It is possible to call God Father in one breath and keep every arrangement he hates in the next, and this verse exists to stop us doing it comfortably.

The theology inside their question is true: He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever (Ps 103:9). But they are using it as a licence. God will say almost those words himself, I will not be angry forever (v. 12), to people who return. The same truth is comfort to the penitent and presumption in the mouth of someone who has done all the evil that you could.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Faithless Israel and Treacherous Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets two sisters side by side, Israel already exiled and Judah who watched and learned nothing, and sends the call to return northward (vv. 6-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Watching judgment fall on someone else and learning nothing is worse than the sin that brought it; and the way back is one honest admission.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore? And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a history lesson with two sisters in it. Israel is the northern kingdom, already destroyed by Assyria a century before Jeremiah preached. Judah is the southern kingdom, still standing, listening to this sermon.

God's I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me' is the language of a patient husband waiting at the window, and it is how God describes his own long-suffering. And her treacherous sister Judah saw it: Judah had a front-row seat at her sister's funeral.

She watched the deportations, the ruined towns, the end of a nation, and drew no conclusion at all. Judah did not fear. There is no education in watching judgment fall on someone else if you have decided in advance that it cannot happen to you.

The decree of divorce is the legal image of verse 1 made concrete. Isaiah uses the same image of Zion's own exile and asks the pointed question, Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away?, before giving the answer: for your transgressions your mother was sent away (Isa 50:1). The exile of the north was not God abandoning a faithful wife. It was the consequence of a marriage she had already left.

verseByVerse.quote: Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She took her whoredom lightly: that is how nations and people fall, not by deciding sin is good but by deciding it is small. And Judah did return, but in pretense.

This is said in the days of King Josiah, during the great national reform: the idols were smashed, the temple repaired, the Passover kept. It was genuine at the top, and it never reached the heart of the people. A reformation of behaviour without a change of heart is what God calls pretence, and he can tell the difference.

Isaiah describes the same condition: this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me (Isa 29:13). And this book will later promise the cure that God himself supplies, I will give them a heart to know me, so that they shall return to me with their whole heart (24:7). What Judah could not produce under Josiah, God undertakes to give.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A shocking verdict. Israel sinned with no warning example in front of her; Judah sinned having watched the consequences, while holding the temple, the law, the priesthood and the promises. The more light, the greater the guilt.

And Jeremiah is told to face north, toward a people scattered into Assyria a hundred years ago, a lost cause by every reckoning, and preach to them. The reasons given are all about God: I am merciful, I will not be angry forever. Not, you are not as bad as you think. The ground of the invitation is his character, which is the only ground any of us has.

And the whole requirement is Only acknowledge your guilt. Not make restitution first, not clean yourself up, not produce a period of good behaviour to prove you mean it. Say what is true; that is the door. Joel says it the same way: return to me with all your heart, rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:12-13). Hosea gives the words to use: Take with you words and return to the LORD (Hos 14:2). And John says it to the church: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Shepherds After My Own Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O faithless children: God promises to gather a remnant one from a city and two from a family, and to give shepherds after his own heart (vv. 14-15). The ark will not be missed; Jerusalem will be the LORD's throne, all nations will gather to it, and Judah and Israel will come home together (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is small in its beginnings, pastoral in its care, and larger than Israel at its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion. "'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise attached to the repeated call is deliberately modest: one from a city and two from a family. God is not predicting a national landslide but a remnant, gathered person by person out of places that will not come as a whole. Revival is talked about in national terms; it usually arrives one and two at a time, and God calls that homecoming.

The ground of the call is a claim: for I am your master. The Hebrew word can also mean “husband”, as the King James Version takes it (I am married unto you), and it shares its root with the name Baal, which means “lord” or “owner”: the LORD claims the title the idol had usurped. They had left, but they had not stopped being his. Their unfaithfulness did not cancel his right to them, and it is that right, not their merit, that gives him the standing to call them back.

Chapter 2 exposed shepherds who transgressed against me (2:8). Here is the remedy: not better management but men whose hearts match God's, and whose work is feeding. The phrase echoes what God said of David, a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22). The risen Christ still gives the shepherds and teachers to his church (Eph 4:11), and behind every faithful one stands the good shepherd himself.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Faithful Christians differ here, and those who look for a future return to the land do so out of reverence for God's promises; this commentary follows the apostles, who read such promises as gathered up in Christ (2 Cor 1:20; Acts 15:14-17).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again. At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark was the most sacred object in Israel's worship, the throne of God's presence at the centre of the holy of holies, and it will not be missed. Not destroyed and mourned; simply not needed. That is not a downgrade but a promotion: a sign becomes unnecessary when the thing it signified has arrived in person.

The whole city becomes the throne room, not one gold box inside one room. All nations gather, not Israel alone. And the heart itself changes: they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart, which is exactly what chapter 31 will call the new covenant. The divided kingdoms come home together, the family reunited.

Isaiah saw the same gathering: all the nations shall flow to it, saying Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD (Isa 2:2-3). And the last pages of the Bible complete the thought about the ark. John sees the holy city and reports, I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22). The box that once marked God's throne is not missed, because God himself is present without one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God longed to be called Father, but Israel left like a treacherous wife (vv. 19-20). Weeping rises on the bare heights, God promises to heal their faithlessness, and the people come back confessing their sin (vv. 21-25).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals faithlessness rather than merely forgiving it, and the confession that follows is the evidence, not the condition.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is God speaking about his own hopes, and it is almost unbearable to read. He wanted to treat them as children, to give them the best land there was, to hear them call him Father.

Scripture is not embarrassed to show God like this. How can I give you up, O Ephraim?, he says through Hosea; My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8). Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the cold act of a God who never wanted anything else.

And the sentence lands with the marriage image again. Not a tenant breaking a lease, but a wife walking out. The offence is measured by the intimacy it violated, which is why sin against God is never merely rule-breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. "Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bare heights were the scene of the idolatry in verse 2. Now the same hills carry a different sound: weeping. The place of the sin becomes the place of the sorrow over it. And the cause is named in the right order: they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. The crooked road is the symptom; the forgetting is the disease.

I will heal your faithlessness is the gospel of this chapter. God promises not merely to forgive the faithlessness, but to heal it. He treats the disloyalty as a disease in his people rather than only a debt against himself, and he undertakes the cure.

That is the only reason anyone returns at all. If the invitation were simply "come back and do better", it would sink the very people it calls, who have already proved they cannot. The God who is wronged will himself repair the capacity to love him, and for the Christian reader that healing is the work of the Spirit he has given, who pours God's love into the heart and makes a faithless people steady (Ezek 36:26-27; Rom 5:5).

And they answer. The ESV notes that a delusion is in Hebrew "commotion": all that noise on the hilltops, and nothing in it. Repentance always includes a revised opinion of what we left God for. And they relocate their hope: Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel. Not in the hills, not in the alliances, not in a better religious programme, but in a person. It is the confession Jonah made from inside the fish, Salvation belongs to the LORD! (Jonah 2:9), and it is where every true return ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: "But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The confession is complete and it is costly. The shameful thing is a scornful name for Baal, the Hebrew word for shame put where the idol's name would go (11:13 sets the two side by side). They add up what idolatry took: the livestock, the harvests, the children given to Molech. Sin is finally accounted for not as pleasure but as loss.

Set let us lie down in our shame beside verse 3, you refuse to be ashamed. The capacity to blush has come back. In a returning people shame is not despair; it is the sign of a conscience coming back to life.

And they do not minimise: we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, the exact reverse of the people who said I am innocent in chapter 2 (2:35). This turn comes after the promise to heal, not before it; the kindness is what makes the confession possible. Nor does the returning life become flawless afterwards. The obedience Israel never gave, Christ gave in his people's place, and it is counted as theirs (Rom 5:19), so each new failure has the same way back as this one: confession and the mercy God promised.

3.title: Return, Faithless Israel: I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
3.overview:
The law says a wife who has left her husband for another cannot return, yet God asks his adulterous people, would you return to me? (v. 1). The hills show where they have been, the rains have been withheld, and they have lost the ability to blush (vv. 2-3). They still use affectionate words about God while doing all the evil they can (vv. 4-5).

In Josiah's days God contrasts two sisters: faithless Israel, whom he divorced and exiled, and treacherous Judah, who watched it happen, did the same, and returned only in pretence (vv. 6-10). So Israel is judged the more righteous of the two (v. 11), and the call goes north: Return, faithless Israel, on one condition: Only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12-13).

God promises a remnant, faithful shepherds, a city that is itself his throne, and a reunited people (vv. 14-18). He speaks of how he longed to be called Father, promises I will heal your faithlessness, and the people come back confessing their sin (vv. 19-25).
3.theology:
The invitation to return goes beyond what the law allows (v. 1; Deut 24:1-4): grace opens a door justice had shut, at a cost only the cross explains. Religious language and partial reform are not repentance (vv. 4-5, 10), and greater light brings greater accountability (v. 11).

The one condition of return is honest acknowledgement of guilt (v. 13; Joel 2:12-13; 1 John 1:9).

God gathers a remnant one by one (v. 14), gives shepherds after his own heart (v. 15; Acts 13:22; Eph 4:11), and will make the ark unnecessary because the presence it signified has come (vv. 16-17). God promises to heal faithlessness, not merely pardon it (v. 22), and the confession of vv. 24-25 follows that promise rather than earning it.
3.examples: The chapter's pictures are easy to carry away: a door the law had bolted, opened by love; a face that has forgotten how to blush; Judah in a front-row seat at her sister's funeral, learning nothing. They warn against a reform that is genuine at the top and never reaches the heart, and they steady anyone discouraged when revival comes one from a city and two from a family.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver,<sup>2</sup>and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."<sup>3</sup>For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.<sup>4</sup>Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."<sup>5</sup>Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!'<sup>6</sup>Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.<sup>7</sup>A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.<sup>8</sup>For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."<sup>9</sup>"In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded."<sup>10</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."<sup>11</sup>At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse,<sup>12</sup>a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them."<sup>13</sup>Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!<sup>14</sup>O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?<sup>15</sup>For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim.<sup>16</sup>Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.<sup>17</sup>Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."<sup>19</sup>My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.<sup>20</sup>Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment.<sup>21</sup>How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?<sup>22</sup>"For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."<sup>23</sup>I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light.<sup>24</sup>I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro.<sup>25</sup>I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled.<sup>26</sup>I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.<sup>27</sup>For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end.<sup>28</sup>"For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."<sup>29</sup>At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them.<sup>30</sup>And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. I am fainting before murderers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — If You Return, Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A true return is to God himself, with idols put away and oaths sworn in truth, and it opens blessing to the nations (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up its fallow ground and circumcise its heart, before wrath burns (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Real return is to a person, not to a programme, and it reaches the heart or it is not return at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver, and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 3 ended with the people saying Behold, we come to you (3:22). Chapter 4 tests it. The sentence turns on a single phrase: to me you should return. Not to religion, not to the temple, not to better behaviour. To me.

It is possible to reform a life without returning to God, and the two look alike for a while. The conditions given are concrete: remove the idols, and do not waver: no half-return, no shrine kept in the garden just in case.

The oath formula As the LORD lives was the ordinary way to swear in Israel, and it was being said constantly by people serving other gods. God attaches three conditions: in truth, in justice, and in righteousness. His name on the lips of someone living a lie is not devotion; it is perjury. Integrity is what makes the confession honest.

And look where it leads. If Israel returns honestly, nations shall bless themselves in him. That is the promise made to Abraham surfacing in a sermon about repentance. A people genuinely right with God becomes the means of blessing to everyone else. The world has more at stake in the church's repentance than it knows.

Paul calls that promise to Abraham the gospel beforehand, fulfilled when the nations are justified by faith in Abraham's offspring, who is Christ (Gal 3:8, 16). Israel's honest return was always meant to open onto that wider blessing, and in Christ it does.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fallow ground is land left unploughed so long it has hardened over. It is not barren; it is compacted. Seed thrown on it bounces. The command is not to sow harder but to break the ground first. Hosea said it too: Break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hos 10:12).

Many people are trying to sow good seed on hard ground: more services, more resolutions, more reading, on a heart that has not been broken up in years. And sow not among thorns: clearing what chokes the seed is part of the work, as the parable of the sower says of cares and riches.

Circumcision was the covenant sign in the flesh, and every man in Judah had it. The mark of belonging is worthless if the heart is untouched.

Here is a difficulty the whole Bible answers. The people are commanded to circumcise their own hearts. In Deuteronomy God promises, the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deut 30:6), and in this book he will promise to write his law on it (31:33). Both are true: God commands what only he can give, and the command is how people come to ask him for it. Paul completes it: a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29), and it is done in Christ, a circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11). So the Christian does not break up his own heart by willpower; the Spirit now in him does the ploughing through the word, and where his heart is still hard in places, as it will be, Christ's own wholehearted obedience is counted as his (Phil 3:9), and the way back is confession, not despair.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Alarm from the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trumpet sounds and God brings disaster from the north (vv. 5-13), yet even as the besiegers close in, Jerusalem is called to wash her heart and be saved (vv. 14-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is announced in detail, the false comfort is exposed, and in the middle of the siege the door is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone changes without warning, like an air-raid siren in the middle of a sermon. And the terrible clause in the middle of the panic: for I bring disaster from the north. The invasion is not an accident of history that God will use. He is bringing it.

This is the vision of Jeremiah's call arriving on schedule. As a young man he had been shown a boiling pot and told, Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land (1:14). What was a picture then is a trumpet now. God's warnings have dates attached.

verseByVerse.quote: A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant. For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nebuchadnezzar is never named; he is simply a destroyer of nations who has set out. This is not a threat about what might happen if things do not improve. It has started.

The right response to the news is not a strategy meeting but mourning. There is a kind of trouble that calls for grief before it calls for plans, and a church that has lost the ability to lament will meet such trouble with activity instead.

And the pronoun at the end matters: has not turned back from us. The prophet does not stand outside the verdict pointing. He counts himself among the people under it, and mourns as one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four groups again: king, officials, priests, prophets. Not one of them will have anything to say. The prophets, in particular, will be astounded: the men who had been predicting peace will be the most surprised people in the city.

Jeremiah's protest is startling, and the Bible records it without softening it. He hears the message of the official prophets, It shall be well with you, and he lays the responsibility at God's door.

How should this be read? Not as Scripture teaching that God lies. God's own answer comes later in the book: he never sent those prophets, and they have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (6:14). But there is a judicial reality here that the prophet feels: when people insist on comfortable preaching, God may let them have it, and the comfortable preaching becomes part of the judgment. The sermon you most want to hear may be the most dangerous one available.

Scripture shows that judicial reality elsewhere. When Ahab wanted only favourable prophets, Micaiah saw heaven's court decide it, and told the king, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets (1 Kgs 22:23). And Paul says of those who refuse the truth, God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false (2 Thess 2:11). God does not deceive the honest. He hands those who wanted to be deceived over to what they chose.

Jeremiah says this to God, not about him behind his back. Honest protest addressed to God is a form of faith; the psalms are full of it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them." Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!
verseByVerse.commentary:
A farmer wants a light breeze to winnow grain, separating wheat from chaff. What is coming is the desert wind that strips the field bare: not to winnow or cleanse. This is not corrective discipline any more. It is judgment.

Dust on the horizon like a storm front, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles, and then the voice of the people themselves, the first time they see it clearly: woe to us, for we are ruined!

Habakkuk describes the same army in the same terms: Their horses are swifter than leopards, and their horsemen fly like an eagle swift to devour (Hab 1:8). Two prophets watching one invasion from different vantage points, and neither sees any way to outrun it.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you? For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the siege report, an invitation. The army is on the road and God is still saying that you may be saved. Mercy runs later into the story than anyone expects.

And the diagnosis is interior again: wash your heart, and the question, how long will wicked thoughts lodge within you? The word suggests a guest who has settled in. Sins that were once visitors become residents, and the difference is how long they were allowed to stay.

The call to wash echoes Isaiah's opening sermon, Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes (Isa 1:16), and like every such command it drives the hearer to the one who can actually do it. Paul writes to converts who had been everything this chapter describes: But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Cor 6:11).

Dan is the northern border; Ephraim is the hill country just above Jerusalem. The report is a relay of dispatches as the enemy moves south, and the distance is closing between sentences.

The surrounding peoples are told too. What happens to Jerusalem is not a private family matter; the whole region is meant to learn from it what kind of God the God of Israel is.

verseByVerse.quote: Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD. Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A quiet, awful image. Besieging armies ring the city the way watchmen sit around a field at harvest: patient, settled, waiting for what is inside to be ready.

The verdict is the one already given in 2:17: they have brought this on themselves. It needs saying plainly, because people will do almost anything to avoid it. Not every disaster is deserved; Job exists to prevent that conclusion. But some are, and pretending otherwise makes repentance impossible. It has reached your very heart, the place the whole chapter has been pointing to.

Paul states the principle for the church without exception: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7). The bitterness in Judah's mouth was the taste of her own harvest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is in anguish as crash follows crash (vv. 19-21), and God names the cause: a people foolish, clever at evil, who do not know him (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who preaches the judgment is broken by it; God's word is never delivered from a safe distance.

verseByVerse.quote: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He is not reading a bulletin. He is doubled over. He announces the disaster, and the announcement tears him apart. There is no satisfaction in him at being proved right, no relish in the doom of people who have dismissed him for years.

That is the test of anyone who handles the severe parts of Scripture. Hell, judgment and wrath can be preached with a certain enjoyment, and when they are, something has gone badly wrong. The prophet who tells the truth about judgment should be the one most obviously wounded by it.

And that anguish points beyond Jeremiah. Six centuries later another man came down toward the same city under the same kind of sentence, and he wept over it, saying, Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! (Luke 19:41-42). The prophet's breaking heart was a preview of the heart of God made flesh.

He can feel his own heartbeat; he cannot sit still or stay quiet. He calls the ruined homes my tents, my curtains. These are not other people's losses to him. And then the cry every sufferer knows: How long?

verseByVerse.quote: "For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the How long with a diagnosis. The problem is not intelligence; it is that they know me not. And then the bitter irony: they are experts at evil and amateurs at good. Every culture has this shape: brilliant at what harms it, helpless at what would heal it.

Paul's hope for the Roman church is the precise reversal: I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil (Rom 16:19). Judah had it backwards, sophisticated in wrongdoing and naive about goodness, and the gospel does not simply make people cleverer. It turns their competence the right way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Looked on the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four times he looks and sees creation undone (vv. 23-26). The land will be desolate, yet God will not make a full end (vv. 27-28). The city paints her face for lovers who seek her life, and cries out like a woman in labour (vv. 29-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is creation running backwards, and even there God sets a limit: not a full end.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light. I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro. I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled. I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four times Jeremiah says I looked, and what he sees is Genesis played backwards. The first phrase is quoted from the creation account: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Then God said, let there be light. Here the light has gone out.

Day three of creation gave dry land; here the land itself is unsteady. The earth staggers like a drunken man, says Isaiah of the same day (Isa 24:20).

Days five and six are undone: the birds gone, and humanity, the crown of the creation week, simply absent. There was no man.

This passage is terrifying, and it makes a theological point that no amount of moralising could. Sin is not a private matter between a person and God with no wider consequence. It unmakes the world. Creation itself is dragged down by it, groaning, subjected to futility and waiting to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:20-21).

Which is why salvation in the Bible is never merely the rescue of souls out of a doomed world. It is new heavens and a new earth, and the same God who spoke the first light will speak again.
verseByVerse.note: The four visions run the creation week in reverse: light, land, people and birds, and last the fruitful land with its cities.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end. "For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight words that keep this book from being despair: yet I will not make a full end. They will be repeated (5:10, 18). However far the judgment goes, God draws a line beyond which it will not go, and he draws it himself. A remnant will survive, and through it the promises will run on.

Jesus says the same of the worst days: if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short (Matt 24:22).

Three verbs of settled intent: spoken, purposed, not relented. Elsewhere God does relent when people turn (18:7-8), which is exactly why this is so grave. The door in verse 14 is open, and the people are not walking through it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them. And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the army at the gates, the city is doing her make-up: scarlet, gold, painted eyes, still trying to attract the very nations whose armies are coming. The alliances she trusted have turned murderous, and she is still dressing for them. People do this. Faced with ruin, we reach for the thing that ruined us.

The chapter ends with the cry of a woman in her first labour: pain that cannot be postponed, and hands stretched out for help. In Scripture that image is not always the end: labour pains lead somewhere, and Paul uses the same picture for a creation in the pains of childbirth (Rom 8:22). But nothing of that comfort is offered here. The chapter closes on the cry, and leaves the reader inside it.

4.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
4.overview:
If Israel returns, it must be to God himself, putting away idols and swearing truly, so that the nations are blessed (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up hard ground rather than sow among thorns, and to circumcise their hearts (vv. 3-4).

Then the alarm sounds: an army is coming from the north, every leader's courage fails, and a scorching wind arrives to judge, not to winnow (vv. 5-13). Even so, God calls Jerusalem to wash her heart and be saved (vv. 14-18).

The prophet breaks down at what he must announce, and God names the cause: a people clever at evil who do not know him (vv. 19-22). In four visions creation is undone (vv. 23-26), yet God will not make a full end (v. 27), and the chapter closes on the cry of a city in labour (vv. 28-31).
4.theology:
Repentance is return to God himself, not reform of behaviour (v. 1), and it must reach the heart: the command to circumcise the heart (v. 4) is what God elsewhere promises to do (Deut 30:6; Jer 31:33) and does in Christ.

God governs the invading army: he brings the disaster (v. 6). Comfortable preaching can itself be part of judgment (v. 10; 6:14). Mercy is still offered while judgment is arriving (v. 14), and honest protest may be addressed to God (v. 10).

Sin unmakes the world: judgment is creation running backwards (vv. 23-26; Gen 1:2; Rom 8:20-22), so salvation must include a renewed creation. And God limits his own judgment: yet I will not make a full end (v. 27).
4.examples: Some hearts are like ground so hard that good seed simply bounces, and some lives carry the covenant sign with nothing beneath it in the heart. Wicked thoughts arrive as visitors and, if they are allowed to stay, become residents. And when ruin comes, people still reach for what ruined them, like a city doing her make-up while the army stands at the gate.
