verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Search the Streets for One Just Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God offers to pardon Jerusalem for one just man, and the search fails: the city swears falsely and has hardened its face (vv. 1-3). The great are no better than the poor, and the predators wait (vv. 4-6). How can I pardon you? God asks a people he fed to the full (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to spare a whole city for one just man, and the search fails.

verseByVerse.quote: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her. Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Jeremiah on an errand through the capital, and the terms are extraordinary. Find one man who does justice and seeks truth, and the whole city will be pardoned.

Abraham once bargained God down over Sodom, from fifty righteous to ten: For the sake of ten I will not destroy it (Gen 18:32). Here God does not wait to be bargained with. He starts at one, and he offers it about his own city, with the temple in it and a king of David's line on the throne.

The search fails. Ezekiel was given the same errand with the same result: I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none (Ezek 22:30). And the psalm had already said why: They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one (Ps 14:3).

Hold on to the shape of this verse, because the gospel is built on it. God is willing to spare a city for the sake of one righteous man. There was no such man in Jerusalem. So God provided one, and he did not spare him (Rom 8:32). Because the one just man was not spared, the city of God is.

Zephaniah, prophesying in the same years, pictured God searching Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph 1:12), and what the search finds is not a shortage of religion but of honesty. The name of God is still in every mouth. Religious language survives long after religion has died. Using God's name to guarantee a lie is not the opposite of the problem; it is the problem. The city was short of truth, and Jesus names what God is looking for in the same terms: the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him (John 4:23).

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three refusals, and the middle one is the most frightening: struck, and they felt no anguish. Pain is a mercy when it makes us stop. What is described here is a people who took the blows and felt nothing, whose faces have gone harder than rock. Hardness is not caused by one great sin; it is built by many small refusals.

Jeremiah frames the complaint carefully: O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? He appeals to God's own character. God is not fooled by the oath formula; the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). Amos had watched the same pattern well over a century before, with a refrain after every disaster God sent: yet you did not return to me (Amos 4:6). Discipline that is felt and not heeded does not soften a heart; it seasons it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God. I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah tries to rescue his own people with a very modern explanation. The problem is education and circumstance; these are the poor, and nobody taught them. So he goes uptown, to the educated and the powerful, and finds exactly the same thing: They all alike had broken the yoke.

That sentence dismantles a comfortable theory. Sin is not a poverty problem or an education problem, and the well-taught are not less guilty but more. The sins differ in style and are identical in substance.

The leopard is the worst image: not hunting, watching, waiting by the gate for whoever steps outside. Hosea used the same animals and put God himself behind them: So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way (Hos 13:7). The predators are not random; the verse gives the reason, because their transgressions are many, and the danger outside the walls is the shape of the rebellion inside them.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores. They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can I pardon you? is not a rhetorical shrug. It is the question of a judge who wants to acquit and cannot find grounds. God is not looking for an excuse to condemn; he is looking for a way to forgive, and the chapter has just shown that the way is not in them.

And the sequence matters: When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery. The generosity came first, and the betrayal was fuelled by it. Full stomachs and idle afternoons have ruined many who would have stood firm in hunger.

Moses had predicted exactly this in his last song: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him (Deut 32:15). And the first charge in the verse is the root of the rest: they have sworn by those who are no gods. A man who breaks faith with God will not long keep faith with his neighbour.

The image is coarse on purpose. Men with time, money and appetite, behaving like animals in a field, and the object is specifically his neighbor's wife: the woman down the street, whose husband they know. Sin here is not abstract; it has an address.

The question will be asked again word for word in verse 29. It deserves an honest answer. A God who looked at predatory men, betrayed marriages and abandoned children and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Wrath is not the opposite of love. Indifference is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vine is stripped but not ended (vv. 10-11). The people say God will do nothing and the prophets are wind (vv. 12-13), so God makes his word fire and brings a nation of unknown speech to devour everything they trust (vv. 14-17). Even then he will not make a full end, and the exile is given its reason (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Practical atheism, the belief that God will do nothing, is answered by a judgment shaped exactly like the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vineyard of chapter 2 is pruned savagely, and the invaders, who think they are looting, are being given limits they know nothing about: make not a full end. Even the destruction is on a leash.

And look at the reason given for what is cut away: for they are not the LORD's. The branches stripped off are the ones that were never his. Jesus describes his Father as the same kind of vinedresser: Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away (John 15:2). Judgment removes what does not belong; it does not uproot the vine.

verseByVerse.quote: For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD. They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine. The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the creed of Judah, and of most people who have never formally denied anything: He will do nothing. Not, there is no God. Simply that he is not going to act, so his opinion need not affect any decision. It is atheism with the religion left on. Ask what difference it would make to tomorrow if that sentence were true; for many of us the honest answer is very little.

Zephaniah heard the same creed: those who say in their hearts, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill' (Zeph 1:12). And Peter hears its modern form in scoffers who ask Where is the promise of his coming? because all things are continuing as they were (2 Pet 3:4). Delay is mistaken for absence, in every generation.

And these men call the preachers wind. Jeremiah heard this about himself for forty years. The insult contains its own answer, which comes in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They called his words wind. God calls them fire. Later Jeremiah will say the word is a burning fire shut up in my bones when he tries not to speak it (20:9), and God will ask, is not my word like fire, and like a hammer that breaks rocks in pieces (23:29).

The word of God is not inert. It does something wherever it lands. A congregation that treats preaching as background noise is not thereby safe from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say. Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors. They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The detail that would frighten an ancient city most: you will not be able to talk to them. No negotiation, no pleading, no diplomacy: soldiers in your streets whose orders you cannot understand.

It was the curse Moses had written into the covenant centuries earlier, almost word for word: The LORD will bring a nation against you from far away, a nation whose language you do not understand (Deut 28:49). Nothing in Jeremiah's warning was new. Judah had simply stopped believing the old words meant what they said.

Four times they shall eat up, and the list moves from food to children to livelihood to defences. Everything a family works for, in order. And the last phrase names the real casualty: your fortified cities in which you trust. What falls is not only the wall but the thing the heart was leaning on.

And one image sits before the list: Their quiver is like an open tomb. Every arrow in it is a grave already dug. The enemy is described by what he carries, and what he carries is death in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you. And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The limit is restated, I will not make a full end, and then God writes the answer the exiles will need. They will ask why, and the answer is to be given plainly: the punishment has the same shape as the sin. You served foreign gods at home; now you will serve foreigners abroad. Sin is allowed to become a sentence, so that its true nature is finally visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — Eyes That Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people with eyes that do not see will not fear the God whose sand holds back the sea (vv. 20-22). Their stubborn hearts never thank him for the rain (vv. 23-25); the rich trap their neighbours and refuse justice to the fatherless (vv. 26-29); and the people love the lies their prophets tell (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea obeys its limits and the people do not; and the lies they are told are the lies they want.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah: "Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not. Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The organs work; the perception does not. This is the condition Isaiah was sent to describe and Jesus applied to his own generation: people who look straight at the evidence and see nothing. It is not a failure of intelligence but of the will.

Jesus put the same question to his own disciples when they missed what he had just done in front of them: Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? (Mark 8:18). The failure can live in people who follow him.

Do you not fear me? Stand on a beach and watch the Atlantic throw itself at the shore, and then notice what stops it: sand. Not granite cliffs, but grains. The sea has more power than every army in history and it turns back at a line of sand, because God drew the line. The most violent thing in creation keeps the boundary God set, and his people will not.

God reminds Job of the same boundary, speaking of the sea: and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed' (Job 38:11). The ocean hears that sentence and stops. Judah had heard far more, and kept going.

verseByVerse.quote: But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.' Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what they fail to say, and where: in their hearts. And it is about rain: the autumn rain to soften the ground, the spring rain to swell the grain, the weeks kept for harvest, God's fingerprints on the ordinary year. Gratitude for weather is a better test of faith than most people expect.

Paul used exactly this argument with pagans who had never read a page of Scripture: God did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). If the rain testifies to the Gentiles, it testifies all the more to the people who were told who sends it.

Not every hardship is caused by sin, and this book will not let us say that. But some good things are absent from a life because sin has kept them out, and it takes honesty to consider whether that is the case.

verseByVerse.quote: For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men. Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture is clear enough. Bird-catchers crouch, wait and spring a net, and what they catch is men, among my people. Their houses are cages full of trapped birds, and that is how the wealth was made. Therefore they have become great and rich: prosperity here is evidence, not blessing.

And the two groups they refuse are always the same two: the fatherless and the needy, the people with no one to take their case. God notices who cannot get a hearing, and he counts the failure to defend them as a deed of evil in its own right, not merely an omission.

The phrase to make it prosper matters too. Justice for the fatherless was meant to be active: taking up their case until it came out well. That is the God of Israel's own way with the helpless, who took up his people's cause when they were slaves in Egypt (Deut 10:18-19). For the Christian the same Spirit who brought him from death to life now moves him to take up such cases, and where he has walked past them, as everyone has, there is forgiveness to come back to and the help of the Spirit to begin again.

The question of verse 9 returns unchanged, now with the evidence assembled.

verseByVerse.quote: An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The surprise is where the blame lands. The preachers lie. The clergy take their orders from the liars. And then: my people love to have it so.

The false prophets are not an occupying force. They are supplying a demand. A people who want to be told that everything is fine will always find someone to tell them. That is as true of a modern church choosing its teachers, or a person choosing what to read and listen to, as it was in Jerusalem.

And the last line is the question the whole book presses: what will you do when the end comes? Comfortable religion is judged by what it leaves you holding at the end, and the question is best answered before the end asks it.

5.title: Search Her Squares: Find One Just Man
5.overview:
God sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem to find one man who does justice and seeks truth, promising to pardon the whole city for his sake, and the search fails among poor and great alike (vv. 1-9).

Because the people say He will do nothing, God makes his words fire and brings a nation whose language they cannot understand, though even then he will not make a full end (vv. 10-19).

The sea keeps the boundary God set, but this people does not: they never thank him for the rain, they trap the needy, and they love the lies their prophets tell (vv. 20-31).
5.theology:
God offers to pardon a city for one righteous man and finds none (v. 1; Ezek 22:30; Ps 14:3), and the gospel answers that search with the one just man God provided. Sin is not a matter of class or education (vv. 4-5).

God's wrath is the response of love to predation and betrayal, not the opposite of love (vv. 9, 29). His word is fire, never inert (v. 14; 23:29). Judgment is limited by God himself (vv. 10, 18) and shaped to fit the sin (v. 19).

Creation obeys the boundaries God sets and his people do not (v. 22). False teaching flourishes because people want it (v. 31), and comfortable religion is tested by what it leaves a person holding at the end.
5.examples: The theory that better education would fix the human heart is tested uptown and fails. He will do nothing is atheism with the religion left on, and it is common among people who would never deny God aloud. And false teachers rarely impose themselves: they supply what a people already loves to hear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds again and enemy commanders camp round the city like shepherds round a pasture, eager to attack (vv. 1-5). God orders the siege against a city full of oppression, yet still warns her (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The siege is described in detail and the warning is still open: even here God says be warned, not farewell.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction. The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion. Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah was from Benjamin, and his own people are the first told to run. Tekoa and Beth-haccherem, on the hills south of the city, were beacon stations: the warning system is working perfectly, and it is carrying bad news. There is a pun as well: blow the trumpet is tiqʿu in Hebrew, and it sounds like Tekoa.

Tekoa had a history. It was the home town of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa (Amos 1:1), the herdsman God sent north with a warning to Israel more than a century earlier. Israel ignored him and was destroyed. Now the beacon on Tekoa's hill is lit for Judah.

The ESV notes another possible rendering, "I have likened the daughter of Zion to the loveliest pasture", which fits the shepherds in the next verse. Either way the contrast is between what she is, lovely and sheltered, and what is about to happen to her. These shepherds are enemy commanders, their flocks are armies, and each takes his own section of wall the way a shepherd takes his own patch of grass.
verseByVerse.note: Beth-haccherem means “house of the vineyard”; it is usually placed on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen! Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we hear the soldiers talking among themselves, and it is chilling because of the eagerness. Frustrated that the light is going, they decide to attack at night instead. Every war has this voice in it, and Scripture lets us hear it.

And there is a gap between what the soldiers think and what is really happening. They believe they are pursuing their own ambition; the very next verse gives the orders from above: For thus says the LORD of hosts. Men who think they are acting entirely on their own account are often carrying out a sentence they know nothing about. And their target is precise, her palaces, the grand houses of the people the next verse accuses of oppression.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her. As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me. Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The orders come from God, not from the invading general. The trees around the city are felled for the ramp, the beginning of the end. And the charge is oppression: not idolatry this time, but the treatment of people. In the prophets, worship and justice are never separated for long.

A good well keeps its water fresh; Jerusalem keeps her evil fresh, constantly replenished. And sickness and wounds are ever before me: God is not detached from what the city does to its weak. He is looking at the injuries, continuously.

After all that, a warning rather than a verdict: Be warned. The siege ramp is going up and God is still speaking as though it might be stopped. This is the pattern of the book, and it repays noticing every time, because it tells us what God is like.

And the danger named before the ruin is lest I turn from you in disgust. The first and worse thing is God withdrawing himself; the desolation comes second. Hosea put it in one line: Woe to them when I depart from them! (Hos 9:12). Losing God's presence is the judgment behind every other judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remnant will be gleaned (v. 9); their ears are closed and God's word is scorned (v. 10). The prophet is full of God's wrath (vv. 11-12). Everyone is greedy, and prophet and priest heal the wound lightly with Peace, peace, unable to blush (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: A wound treated lightly is the classic failure of false religion: comfort offered where surgery is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches." To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gleaning is the second pass over a vine, the careful hand going back along branches already picked. Applied to an army it means thoroughness: what the first sweep missed the second will take.

The prophet's despair is practical: who is left to talk to? In chapter 4 the problem was uncircumcised hearts; here it is "uncircumcised ears", sealed over. And the diagnosis ends with a phrase that should stop any reader: they take no pleasure in it.

That is the deepest measure of a spiritual condition: not whether a person can argue with the Bible, but whether it gives them any pleasure. A believer's love for the word waxes and wanes, but total distaste for it ought to be taken seriously.

The blessed man is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD (Ps 1:2), and the psalmist says How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Appetite for the word is not a personality trait. It is a sign of life, and it can be asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged. Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah, who wept in chapter 4, is here full of the wrath of the LORD and tired of containing it. Both are true of him, and neither cancels the other. A man who feels only anger at a corrupt society has stopped loving it; a man who feels no anger has stopped taking its victims seriously.

The list that follows spares nobody: children, young men, married couples, the elderly. Judgment on a nation always lands on the whole household, which is one reason it is so grievous and why God delays it so long.

I am weary of holding it in is the same exhaustion Jeremiah will confess in his darkest chapter, where the word is a fire shut up in his bones (20:9). He did not choose this message and could not keep it down. And the details of the sentence are the covenant curses coming true: You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it (Deut 28:30), a verse that also foresaw another man taking a betrothed wife. Moses had spelled out precisely what these verses announce.

How can a just God sweep up children in judgment? The whole nation fell under the judgment it had chosen, and a city’s fall strikes the young with the old. God takes no pleasure in it (Lam 3:33), and the judgment of each soul’s eternal destiny rests with him who does right (Gen 18:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two totals: from bottom to top of society, and from prophet to priest. Greed at every social level, dishonesty at every religious level. When the leadership is corrupt there is nowhere left to appeal.

This sentence has been quoted ever since, because it describes a permanent temptation. The wound is real. The treatment is a clean bandage over an infected cut and a reassuring word: Peace, peace.

Why would anyone do that? Because it is what the patient wants, because the true diagnosis is unbearable to deliver, and because the healer gets thanked for it in the short term. Micah heard the same men: yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us" (Mic 3:11).

The test for any preaching, counselling or friendship is whether it deals with the wound or only with the feeling about the wound. A gospel that never mentions sin is a bandage over an infection, and its kindness is an illusion that costs the patient everything.

Paul saw the same false peace at the end of history: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman (1 Thess 5:3). The sentence that sounds kindest is the one spoken nearest the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No: they did not know how to blush. Not that they refused; they had lost the ability. Shame is a nerve ending, and a conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does. The loss is quiet and is usually mistaken for maturity or confidence.

Paul describes the end state of the same process as consciences are seared (1 Tim 4:2). And the sentence that follows is flat: they shall fall among those who fall. There will be no special category for religious leaders; the men who assured everyone of peace go down with the people they reassured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — Ask for the Ancient Paths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls his people to ask for the ancient paths and find rest, and they refuse, ignoring the watchmen too (vv. 16-17). The nations are called to witness the fruit of their devices, and costly offerings will not turn it aside (vv. 18-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The old way is not nostalgia but the road that leads home, and refusing it is a decision, not an accident.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.' I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four imperatives, and they are the cure for everything this chapter has described. Stand: stop moving long enough to think. Look: consider the roads in front of you. Ask: for the old paths, which means asking someone who knows them. Walk: because knowing the way home and standing at the junction is not the same as going.

This is not nostalgia for an older decade. The ancient paths are the ways God gave the people he had brought out of Egypt and made his own, older than the fashion of any era. They were never a ladder up to him but the road home with him, and the promise attached is not success but rest: find rest for your souls.

Jesus takes that exact phrase and offers it in his own name: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt 11:29). The ancient path, it turns out, is a person. He walked it without one false step, in the place of people who had said We will not walk in it, and his obedience is counted to those who come to him (Rom 5:19). The walking that follows is not by willpower: those who belong to him walk by the Spirit (Gal 5:16), and when they stray the same voice still calls them back to the road.

The refusal itself is not a failure of information. It is a decision. The watchmen are the prophets, whose job was to see trouble early and shout. The refusal is of an alarm, which is a strange thing to resent until you remember what alarms interrupt.

Hebrews draws the line from this refusal to ours: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven (Heb 12:25). The watchmen of Jeremiah's day spoke for God; the voice now is the Son's.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them. Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are called as witnesses, and the sentence is described as the fruit of their devices: what grew from the seed they planted. God's judgment is often the ripening of what people have themselves sown.

And the charge is specific: as for my law, they have rejected it. Not forgotten, not misunderstood, but rejected. Judah was not a people who lacked the law but a people who had it and put it down.

verseByVerse.quote: What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expensive imported incense, the best available, and God says it is no use to him. The prophets say this repeatedly (I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams, Isa 1:11; I hate, I despise your feasts, Amos 5:21; I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, Hos 6:6), and it is never an attack on worship as such. It is the refusal to accept worship as a substitute for obedience. Generous giving and faithful attendance can both be ways of trying to buy God off.

The road they refused to walk becomes a road they cannot walk. Refused grace hardens into obstacles, and whole families go down together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A cruel nation comes from the north with a sound like the sea, and terror is on every side (vv. 22-26). Jeremiah is made a tester of metals, and the refining fails: Rejected silver they are called (vv. 27-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The assay is run honestly and the metal fails; only a better refining, and a better price, can save such people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sound before sight: an army heard before it is seen, like surf. Cruel and have no mercy is not propaganda; it is the plain character of ancient warfare, and God is telling his people the truth about what is coming rather than letting them imagine a manageable version.

Hold this description in mind, because the book will use it again. Near the end, the same words are turned on Babylon herself: a people from the north, they are cruel and have no mercy, riding against you, O daughter of Babylon! (50:42). The God who sends an army from the north against Zion will, in time, send one against Zion's destroyer. No instrument of judgment is exempt from judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor. Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side. O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the first time the people are not arguing. Our hands fall helpless. The bravado of chapter 5 is gone. It took the sound of the sea to produce it.

Terror is on every side becomes a refrain in this book, and later a nickname thrown at Jeremiah himself (20:10). Here it is simply life under siege: going to the field, walking the road, become impossible.

Among the deepest griefs the ancient world could name was the loss of an only son: the end of a family line and every hope with it. Zechariah saw where that mourning would finally be directed: when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zech 12:10). The grief God prescribes for Jerusalem's ruin becomes the grief of Jerusalem's repentance, when it recognises the Son it rejected. John saw that verse fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways. They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new picture for the prophet's work. He is an assayer: the man who takes a sample, heats it, and reports what the metal actually is. Preaching tests people. The same word that softens one heart hardens another, and the reaction is the assay.

The sample comes back as base metal. Bronze and iron are useful and they are not silver, which is what this refining was meant to produce.

And one phrase names what the assayer found among the people: going about with slanders. The corruption is not only in the temple and the courts. It is in ordinary conversation, the steady traffic of reputations damaged in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed. Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refiners used lead to draw impurities out of silver. Here the process is run to the limit: the bellows roar, the lead burns away, and nothing pure emerges. The fire is the long series of disasters God has already sent. Suffering refines some people and hardens others, and the difference is not in the furnace.

Malachi promised a different refiner, who does not fail: He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and refine them like gold and silver (Mal 3:3). Where the fire of disaster could only expose the metal, he will actually purify it.

The chapter ends with the assayer's certificate: metal that failed the test, put aside. It is exactly why the New Testament's language about redemption lands with such force. Peter tells Christians they were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Rejected silver cannot buy anything. But rejected people can be bought back, by a price that does not come from the furnace at all.

6.title: Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
6.overview:
The alarm sounds again and enemy commanders camp around Jerusalem, yet God, who orders the siege against a city full of oppression, still says Be warned (vv. 1-8).

No one will listen. Everyone is greedy, and prophets and priests heal the wound lightly with Peace, peace where there is none (vv. 9-15).

God calls them to ask for the ancient paths and find rest for their souls, and they answer We will not walk in it (vv. 16-21). A cruel nation approaches with a sound like the sea, and Jeremiah, made a tester of metals, finds only rejected silver (vv. 22-30).
6.theology:
God directs the armies that punish his people (v. 6), and warns even while the siege ramp rises (v. 8). Spiritual deadness shows itself as an inability to hear and a distaste for God's word (v. 10).

False ministry treats a deep wound lightly and calls it peace (v. 14); true ministry names the wound. The remedy is the old way God gave, and the rest it promises is fulfilled in Christ's invitation (v. 16). Worship offered as a substitute for obedience is rejected (v. 20).

Judgment is often the ripening of what people themselves sowed (v. 19). Suffering refines some and hardens others (vv. 27-29), and those who fail the assay are redeemed, if at all, by a price from outside the furnace (1 Pet 1:18-19).
6.examples: A clean bandage over an infected wound, with a reassuring word, is still the most tempting kind of ministry, because everyone thanks the healer for a while. A conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does, and the loss is usually mistaken for confidence. And it is possible to stand at the junction knowing the way home, and still not walk it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the temple gate Jeremiah calls the worshippers to amend their ways and stop trusting the chant the temple of the LORD (vv. 1-4). God names what amendment means: justice, protection for the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, no innocent blood and no other gods (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A building, however holy, guarantees nothing; God attaches his promise to repentance and to the treatment of the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The place is chosen deliberately: the temple gate, on a day when crowds are streaming in to worship. Jeremiah is to preach to religious people on their way to a service. That is a harder assignment than preaching to pagans. Everyone coming through those gates believes they are doing the right thing, and the worship is commanded. The problem is not that they are absent from church.

This sermon is told again in chapter 26, where we learn what it cost: priests and prophets seized him and said, You shall die! And the parallel account adds the instruction that made it so dangerous: speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the LORD all the words that I command you to speak to them; do not hold back a word (26:2). The easiest way to survive a sermon like this is to leave out the paragraph that will cost you. Jeremiah was told in advance not to.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 26 dates the sermon to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign (26:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place. Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offer is unchanged from chapter 4: change, and stay. God is naming a condition, not an unavoidable fate, and the condition is your ways and your deeds: conduct, not ceremony.

Then the chant, three times, like a slogan at a rally. It was their confidence: God lives here, and he will never let this city fall, because his own house is in it. God calls it deceptive words, though every word of the chant was true. What made it deceptive was what they were doing with the truth: using it as a reason to feel safe while living as they pleased.

It is the easiest error in the world to repeat. A denomination, a confession, a conversion experience, a baptism, a family heritage: all good, all capable of becoming a chant that shields a person from the question of how he actually lives. Jesus finished the Sermon on the Mount on this note: the man who hears and does not do is building on sand, and great was the fall of it (Matt 7:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm, then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of what amendment would look like repays a slow reading. It begins with justice one with another: ordinary dealings between neighbours. Then three groups: the sojourner, the immigrant with no family network; the fatherless; the widow. In that society these three had no one to take their case. God names them every time, and makes his continued presence with the nation turn on how they are treated.

Then innocent blood, and only last the matter of other gods. A modern reader expects a religious checklist; God gives a mostly social one, without making devotion to him any less important. He refuses to let the two be separated. A church that is orthodox on Sunday and indifferent to the vulnerable on Monday has failed the half of the test that God put first. And the word truly comes twice: there is a way of doing justice for the appearance of it.

Idolatry is to your own harm: the false gods damage the people who serve them. And the promise at the end reaches back to the beginning: the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever. The land was a gift before it was ever a condition. The gift had not been withdrawn; it was still on offer to a generation that had done nothing to keep it. That is the order for the Christian reader too. We take up the cause of the stranger and the widow because God first took up ours, and the Spirit he has given is the one who turns that mercy outward (Gal 5:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — As I Did to Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They break the commandments and then claim deliverance in God's house, as if it were a robbers' den (vv. 8-11). So they are sent to look at Shiloh, where God's name first dwelt: the same will be done to this house (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The place God chose can be destroyed by God: Shiloh is the precedent, and the temple is not exempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail. Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known, and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read that list against the Ten Commandments: stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, other gods. God lists them as a bill of particulars. Then from the sin straight to the service, saying We are delivered! and going out to do it all again. The language of rescue is being used as an insurance policy.

Only to go on doing all these abominations is the sting. Worship had become the thing that made the sin sustainable. Confession without any intention to stop is not repentance; it is maintenance.

Paul met the same logic in the church and answered it the same way: Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? (Rom 6:1-2). Grace that is used as permission to keep sinning has been misunderstood at the root. The cross that forgives sin is also the death of the old life that loved it.

verseByVerse.quote: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A den is not where robbers rob. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe and divide the takings. That is what the temple had become: they did their damage in the city and came here to be secure.

Six centuries later Jesus walked into the same courts, overturned the tables and quoted this verse: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers (Matt 21:13). He was charging that generation with Jeremiah's indictment, and, like Jeremiah, he went on to predict that the building would come down (Mark 13:2).

Mark gives the fuller form: Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers (Mark 11:17). Jesus joined Isaiah's promise of what the temple was for (Isa 56:7) to Jeremiah's verdict on what it had become. And he did more than repeat Jeremiah: he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21). The meeting place of God and the nations would no longer be a building but himself.

And the last clause removes every hiding place: Behold, I myself have seen it. He who formed the eye, does he not see? (Ps 94:9). The worshippers imagined that what happened in the city stayed in the city. God saw both, and how they were connected.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records the same saying (Luke 19:46).

verseByVerse.quote: Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends them on a field trip. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations before the temple was built. In Eli's day the ark was carried out of Shiloh into battle as a talisman, and the ark of God was captured (1 Sam 4:11). The psalm records the end of it: He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind (Ps 78:60).

The ruins were about twenty miles north, close enough to walk to. That is what God does to a holy place that has become a charm.
verseByVerse.note: Shiloh had been destroyed, probably by the Philistines after the battle of 1 Samuel 4.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer, therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house in which you trust will go the way of Shiloh. Misplaced trust is not protected by being religious trust. If anything it is treated more severely, because it uses God's own gifts as insulation against him.

And the history that led here is a conversation that only went one way: when I called you, you did not answer. Isaiah gives the same reason for the same sentence: because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen (Isa 65:12). Judgment in Scripture is rarely sudden. It is the end of a long, unanswered call.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim is the northern kingdom, gone a century before. Judah had watched it happen (3:8) and concluded that it could not happen to them, because they had the temple. God says the precedent stands.

The phrase cast you out of my sight has an old shape. The first human beings were sent out of God's garden, and He drove out the man (Gen 3:24). Exile in the Bible is always a small repetition of Eden lost: removal from the place where God had made himself present. And that is why the promise of return, when it comes, is always more than a promise of real estate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Do Not Pray for This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for the people, while whole families bake cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 16-18). They harm themselves more than they provoke God, and his wrath will fall on land and people (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The forbidding of intercession is deeply solemn, and even it is framed by the fact that sin destroys the sinner first.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is aimed at the intercessor rather than at the guilty. Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for his own nation. The prohibition comes three times in this book (11:14; 14:11), which suggests he kept doing it anyway; in chapter 14 he is still pleading (14:7-9, 19-22).

What does it mean? Not that God has stopped being merciful; the same book will promise a new covenant. It means that a point can be reached where judgment is settled and further pleading will not turn it aside; and it means God is telling his prophet in advance, so that when the city falls Jeremiah will not think his prayers failed.

John writes something in the same territory: There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that (1 John 5:16). These are not verses to wield against people we have given up on. Nobody can read another person's file. They are warnings about how serious sustained refusal is, and they are rare precisely because the normal command is to pray for everyone.

Should I stop praying for someone who seems hardened? No. Jeremiah received a direct word from God about a nation whose sentence was already fixed; no one today receives such a word about a son, a friend or a country. Our standing command is to pray for all people (1 Tim 2:1), even for those who persecute us (Matt 5:44), and many parents have prayed for years over a child who seemed beyond reach and seen that child come home. And the prophet who was told to stop interceding points to an Intercessor who was never told to stop. Christ prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and he always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? It is a family scene, and that is what makes it terrible: children collecting kindling, fathers at the fire, mothers making the dough. Everyone has a job, and the whole household is at work on idolatry. It is cosy. It is also a very effective way to hand a religion to the next generation.

And the queen of heaven does not go away. Decades later, after the city has burned, the survivors in Egypt will defend this exact practice to Jeremiah's face: we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven, because then we had plenty of food, and prospered (44:17). A religion taught around the family fire outlasts even the ruin it caused.
verseByVerse.note: The “queen of heaven” was probably the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar (Astarte).

verseByVerse.quote: Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame? Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A question that changes the temperature. God is not a deity whose dignity has been dented. The damage of sin falls first on the sinner: Is it not themselves? His anger is not wounded pride; it is the response of love to people destroying themselves and their children.

And the land itself suffers with the people, as it did in the un-creation vision of chapter 4. Human sin is never contained within the human sphere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sacrifice was never the first word: at the exodus God called his people to obey his voice, and they went backward (vv. 21-24). He sent prophets day after day, each generation did worse, and Jeremiah too will go unheard, for truth has perished (vv. 25-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Sacrifice was never meant to replace obedience, and centuries of persistent preaching have met a stiffened neck.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone is sardonic. In the burnt offering the whole animal was burned to God; in other sacrifices the worshippers ate part of the meat. God says: put them all together and eat the lot yourselves. If the sacrifices mean nothing, they may as well be dinner.

Read carelessly, this sounds like a denial that God gave the sacrificial law, which would contradict Leviticus. Read in its own terms, it is about what came first and what it was for. The founding word came in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt: rescue first, and then not a manual of offerings but a relationship, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. The sacrifices were given inside that covenant to serve it, never to replace it.

The prophets say this in one voice. To obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hos 6:6). Bring no more vain offerings, and instead learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause (Isa 1:13, 17). Let justice roll down like waters (Amos 5:24).

The modern equivalents are attendance, giving, service and the right doctrinal words: all good, and all able to be offered instead of obedience. And none of us obeys that voice perfectly either. The one who did was the Son, who could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and his obedience is counted to those who trust him (Rom 5:19). That does not make obedience optional; it makes it the glad answer of people already claimed, with a way back when they fail.

verseByVerse.quote: But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Backward and not forward: the whole history in four words. There is no standing still in this book. A people either walks in the way it is shown or drifts back from it.

And the alternative to God's voice is named exactly: walked in their own counsels. Not a rival god this time, but their own judgment. Proverbs puts the choice the same way: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (Prov 3:5). Every drift backward starts with a person deciding he can find the way without being told.

verseByVerse.quote: From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day. Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers. "So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persistently, and day after day, for centuries: that is God's patience measured in messengers, not one warning ignored but a stream of them across generations, each one a mercy. A stiffened neck is the animal that will not turn its head to the rein. And They did worse than their fathers: each generation had the added evidence of what the previous one had suffered, and went further anyway.

Here is a commission almost no one would accept: preach, and they will not listen. God tells his servant the outcome in advance, and still sends him. Jeremiah is not sent to be effective; he is sent to be faithful. Results are God's business. Anyone serving in a hard place, a stagnant church, an indifferent family, is standing where Jeremiah stood, and the standard by which the work will be judged is the one given here.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips. "'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truth has perished: not merely that people tell lies, but that truth itself has died as a public commodity, so that no one expects it in a courtroom, a market or a temple. A society can survive a great deal of wickedness; it cannot survive the death of truth, because nothing can then be repaired.

Cutting the hair was a public sign of grief, and the bare heights were the hills of the idolatry: hold the funeral at the scene of the sin.

And one charge explains the rest: did not accept discipline. Discipline, Hebrews says, seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it (Heb 12:11). The pain was never the problem. The refusal to be trained by it was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have defiled the temple and burned their children at Topheth, which God never commanded (vv. 30-31). The valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will fall silent (vv. 32-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned gives its name to the place of judgment, and the sound that ends is the sound of weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idols are inside the temple now. The building they chanted about had been furnished with the very things that made it uninhabitable for God.

This is the floor of the book. In a ravine outside Jerusalem, parents were burning their children alive as offerings. The law had forbidden it plainly: You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech (Lev 18:21).

And then a phrase that is almost unbearable: God says the thought never entered his mind. Whatever these people told themselves about pleasing a god, it had no connection whatever to the God who was speaking. Religion untethered from revelation does not drift toward kindness.

Two things follow. First, every generation should ask what it does to its own children and calls necessary. Second, see where this valley leads. The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom in Hebrew, Gehenna in Greek) became the New Testament word for hell itself; the name of a real ravine where children burned became the name for final judgment, the place Jesus described as one where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9:48).

Does “nor did it come into my mind” mean God did not foresee child sacrifice? No; he knows all things (Ps 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.
verseByVerse.note: The name Topheth is probably linked to a word for a hearth or fireplace.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere. And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The punishment takes the shape of the crime, as in 5:19. The valley where they killed their children becomes the valley where their own dead are buried, so many that the graveyards overflow into it. The renaming is God's verdict written on the map.

Jeremiah will stand in this valley again, holding a clay flask, and repeat the renaming there: this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter (19:6). God said it twice, in two places, so that nobody could claim to have missed it.

To be left unburied was a terrible disgrace in that world, and there will not even be anyone left to wave off the birds.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends not with an image of violence but with silence. No laughter in the streets, and no weddings. Of all the sounds God could name as the mark of a living community, he chooses the voices of a bride and bridegroom: the sound of people betting on a future.

That is what judgment takes away, and it is how John describes the fall of Babylon at the end of the Bible: the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more (Rev 18:23).

But this is the God who later says to these same exiles that he will bring back into this ruined land the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (33:11), because his purpose was never the silence. Jeremiah preached in the temple gate that the house would fall. It did. And the one who quoted this sermon in the same courts went out and was himself destroyed, so that the wedding could be held after all.

7.title: The Temple Sermon: Do Not Trust in Deceptive Words
7.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the temple gate to preach to worshippers on their way in: amend your ways, and do not trust the chant the temple of the LORD (vv. 1-7). They break the commandments and then claim deliverance in God's house, so they are sent to look at the ruins of Shiloh: the temple will go the same way (vv. 8-15).

Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them while whole families bake cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 16-20). Obedience, not sacrifice, was God's first word, and centuries of prophets went unheard (vv. 21-29). Because they burned their children at Topheth, the valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will fall silent (vv. 30-34).
7.theology:
Religious privilege guarantees nothing: true words about God's house became deceptive words when used as a shield for unrepentance (vv. 4, 8; Matt 7:26-27). God ties his presence to repentance and to justice for the weakest (vv. 5-7), and refuses to let worship and ethics be separated (vv. 9-11).

Shiloh proves that God will destroy a place he chose when it becomes a charm (vv. 12-15). Sacrifice was given inside the covenant to serve obedience, never to replace it (vv. 21-23). Sin's damage falls first on the sinner (v. 19), and God's wrath is love's response to people destroying themselves and their children.

Prayer for a people can be forbidden when refusal has hardened (v. 16; 1 John 5:16), and faithfulness, not results, is the standard for the messenger (v. 27). Jesus took this sermon up in the same courts and went to his death outside its walls, so that the silenced wedding might be restored (33:11).
7.examples: The hardest congregation is the one already on its way into church, and the most dangerous words are true ones used as a shield. A den is not where the robbery happens but where robbers feel safe afterwards, and any place of worship can become one. And a family with a job each, working together at the fire, can hand on idolatry as warmly as faith.
