Send them out of my sight, and let them go!<sup>2</sup>And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.'<sup>3</sup>I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.<sup>4</sup>And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>"Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare?<sup>6</sup>You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting.<sup>7</sup>I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways.<sup>8</sup>I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly.<sup>9</sup>She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."<sup>10</sup>Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me.<sup>11</sup>The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?<sup>12</sup>Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze?<sup>13</sup>"Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory.<sup>14</sup>I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."<sup>15</sup>O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach.<sup>16</sup>Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.<sup>17</sup>I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation.<sup>18</sup>Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?<sup>19</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them.<sup>20</sup>And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD.<sup>21</sup>I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Though Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God refuses the prayer even if Moses and Samuel made it, and allots the people their destinations because of Manasseh (vv. 1-4). No one will pity Jerusalem, and God is weary of relenting (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history could not turn this, and the sins of a king two generations back are still working themselves out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go! And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.' I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy. And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the answer to the faultless prayer at the end of chapter 14, and it is devastating.

Moses and Samuel are named because they are the two men in Israel's story whose prayers most famously turned judgment aside. Moses stood in the breach at Sinai when the nation deserved destruction, and the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people (Exod 32:14). Samuel said it would be a sin against God for him to stop praying for Israel (1 Sam 12:23). The psalm remembers both: They called to the LORD, and he answered them (Ps 99:6).

God says that if those two were standing here making that case, his heart would not turn. It is the strongest way of saying that the moment for this generation has passed, and it explains why Jeremiah has three times been forbidden to pray.

They will ask the practical question people always ask in a crisis: where do we go? The answer is a grim allocation list. Not a refuge, but a destination each.

Sword, dogs, birds, beasts: the sequence of a battlefield after the fighting stops. It is deliberately without dignity, because that is what the end of a siege looks like.

Manasseh had been dead for decades. He reigned fifty-five years, filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, and, Chronicles records, repented late in his own life (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). Kings does not mention the repentance; it is not denying it but explaining why judgment still came (2 Kings 23:26), while Chronicles shows that even Manasseh could be forgiven. His personal forgiveness did not undo what he had built into the nation.

Sin can be forgiven and still leave consequences running through families and institutions for generations. A father restored to God may still watch his children live with what his years of neglect made normal. Grace does not undo the past, but it does not leave him alone in it either: he can pray for them, own what he did, and show them the mercy he has found.

Are there people Christians should stop praying for? God forbade Jeremiah to pray for a nation whose judgment was fixed. Christians are commanded to pray for all people (1 Tim 2:1) and for enemies (Matt 5:44). John speaks of sin that leads to death and does not command prayer for it (1 John 5:16), but we cannot see who is beyond hope, so we keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting. I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways. I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly. She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions, and they are about loneliness rather than punishment. Who will feel sorry? Who will mourn? Who will even stop to ask how you are? A city that made itself a byword will find the neighbours passing on the other side.

You keep going backward is the same charge as 7:24. And then a phrase to stop at: I am weary of relenting.

Relenting is what God has been doing for centuries. Every warning not carried out, every disaster postponed, every prophet sent instead of an army was God relenting. He is not saying that mercy has run out in principle; three chapters later he will say that if a nation turns he will relent of the disaster he intended (18:8). He is saying that this generation has used his patience as a policy.

Three first-person verbs, and the third is I have destroyed my people. God does not distance himself from what is happening, and he does not stop calling them his.

The reason is stated last, plainly: they did not turn from their ways. Everything in this book comes back to that sentence.

The promise to Abraham was descendants like the sand of the sea; now the widows are counted that way. Seven sons was the picture of a blessed mother, and this one has lost them all: her sun went down while it was yet day.

That phrase has comforted and haunted the bereaved ever since, because it names the particular cruelty of losing a child: the light going at noon. Scripture does not hurry past that grief or explain it away; it gives it words, so that those who carry it can bring it to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — A Man of Strife and Contention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah wishes he had never been born (v. 10); God answers with his care for him, and with the unbreakable iron from the north (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet wishes he had never been born, and God answers him without apology and without contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me. The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prophet breaks, and this is the third of his confessions. He turns to the woman who gave him birth and wishes she had not. Job said it in his ashes: Let the day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3).

What he cannot bear is what he has become: a man of strife and contention to the whole land. He never wanted to be a controversialist. He is a village priest's son who would have been content to be ignored, and he is the most argued-about man in the country.

The detail about lending is the saddest touch. Debt was the usual reason for a man to be hated in a small society. I have not lent, nor have I borrowed: he has given nobody any of the ordinary grounds for a grudge, and they curse him anyway. He is hated purely for the message.

Anyone who has been disliked for their faith rather than for their faults will understand the particular loneliness of this verse.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, and translations differ. What comes through is that God answers, and that his answer is about his own care: he has been at work for Jeremiah's good and has pleaded for him when enemies pressed.

God does not rebuke the outburst, and he does not pretend the pain is unreasonable. He replies. Anyone who has wished they had never been born should notice that: the wish is written down in Scripture, and God answers the man who made it with his care, not his contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze? "Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory. I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A question about metallurgy that is really about politics. The iron from the north is Babylon, and nobody breaks it, certainly not Judah's foreign policy. It is the answer to every plan for escape that the palace has been making.

Without price: no ransom, no tribute paid to buy it back, no compensation. The treasures simply change hands. A nation that trusted its reserves discovers they were never security.

The sentence of 5:19 again, and the point of it is precision: you served foreign gods at home, so you will serve foreigners abroad. Exile is not random misfortune; it is the sin made visible and lived in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Your Words Were Found, and I Ate Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet's prayer: God's words were his delight (vv. 15-16), and they have left him alone, asking whether God is like a deceitful brook (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The same words that were his joy have cost him every friendship, and he tells God that he feels like a dry streambed.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach. Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He prays, and the first words are the ones every sufferer needs: O LORD, you know. Not, explain it; you know.

Then a request that shows how well he understands his own situation. God is being patient with his persecutors, and that patience is the very thing endangering the prophet. In your forbearance take me not away: do not let me be killed while you are being slow to judge them. It is a real prayer from inside a real danger.

And the ground of the appeal: for your sake I bear reproach. A psalm uses the same words (Psalm 69:7), and Paul hears Christ praying that psalm: The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (Romans 15:3). Jeremiah bore reproach for God's sake; Christ bore it in full, and those who suffer for him share it (Hebrews 13:13). That is what makes the suffering bearable.

This lovely sentence about Scripture comes from a man in the middle of a breakdown. Your words were found may be a memory of the scroll discovered in the temple in Josiah's reign, perhaps simply the moment God's word came to him. And I ate them: not admired, studied or filed. Eaten, taken in as food, made part of himself. Ezekiel was given a scroll to eat and found it as sweet as honey (Ezek 3:3). The psalmist said, How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Jesus answered the tempter, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4).

And the result: a joy and the delight of my heart. This is the man who has just wished he had never been born. Both are true at once, and anyone who has walked with God through a hard season knows that they can be.

May a believer pray for vengeance on persecutors? Jeremiah hands his cause to God instead of taking revenge (Rom 12:19). Christians may pray for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, while praying for their persecutors to repent (Matt 5:44), as Jesus did (Luke 23:34).

verseByVerse.quote: I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation. Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the cost of the previous verse. The word that was his joy has taken away his company. He did not join the parties, partly because he could not bring himself to, partly because a man who says what he says is not invited twice.

I sat alone, because your hand was upon me. The hand of God is usually spoken of as protection or power. Here it is what keeps a man out of the room. Faithfulness is often isolating, and Jeremiah does not pretend it is noble or that he enjoys it. He is lonely, and he tells God so, knowing that God's hand is in it.

This is among the sharpest things Jeremiah ever says. In a dry country a wadi runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in the summer. Travellers died going to one on the strength of a memory.

He is saying to God: I think you might be a stream that dries up. And the accusation lands exactly where this book began: God had called himself the fountain of living waters and the people's idols the broken cisterns (2:13). Now the prophet who preached that sermon asks whether the fountain is seasonal.

Scripture writes it down and keeps it. The Bible is not embarrassed by a servant of God accusing God of unreliability, because the God of the Bible is not fragile, and because believers need to know that somebody in the book has felt what they are feeling.

If you are where Jeremiah was, with pain that will not lift and a God who seems to have run dry, this verse is for you. Feeling abandoned is not proof that you are, and saying so to God is prayer, not unbelief. Depression is often an illness as well as a spiritual trial, so tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor. And remember who hears you: a High Priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), who was himself a man of sorrows, and who does not dry up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — If You Return, I Will Restore You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls his prophet to return, and renews the promise of the bronze wall (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: God calls his own prophet to repent, and then gives him back his commission with the original promise attached.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD. I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's answer is not what a modern reader expects, and it is exactly right. He does not comfort first. He calls his prophet to repent.

If you return, I will restore you: the word Jeremiah has been preaching to the nation is now addressed to him. His complaint went past lament into accusation. God does not call him to repent of his pain or his tears, which he never rebukes, but of the bitter words that had begun to call God false. He treats him as an adult: turn, and you will be restored to your place, standing before me as a servant stands before a king.

If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. He is to sort his speech. Self-pity and bitterness are worthless; God's word is precious; and the promise attached is staggering: you shall be as my mouth.

Then the rule for every minister since: They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. The pressure of an audience is constant, and the temptation is to be shaped by the people you are speaking to until you are saying what they would have said anyway. That is how the false prophets of chapter 14 were made. The direction of influence must run one way. No servant of God keeps this rule perfectly; the one who did, who always did what pleased the Father (John 8:29), is the one whose faithfulness covers those who fail at it, and the way back for them is the one offered here: return, and be restored.

And God gives him back his call, in the words of the first chapter (1:18-19). A bronze wall; opposition that does not prevail; I am with you.

Two things stand out. The promise is repeated rather than improved, because it was always sufficient and the man had simply lost sight of it. And it is given after the rebuke, not instead of it. God's way with his exhausted servants is neither to ignore their sin nor to withdraw his promise, but to call them back and then hand them the same commission again.

Jeremiah went back to work, and kept at it until the city fell and after.

15.title: A Deceitful Brook, and the Bronze Wall
15.overview:
God answers the faultless prayer of chapter 14: even Moses and Samuel could not turn his heart toward this generation (vv. 1-9).

Then the prophet breaks. He wishes he had never been born (vv. 10-14), and he asks whether God, whose words were his delight, has become a brook that fails (vv. 15-18). God calls him back, restores him, and renews the promise of the bronze wall (vv. 19-21).
15.theology:
There is a point at which even the greatest intercessors would not turn God's heart (v. 1), and forgiven sin can still leave consequences running for generations (v. 4). God's long patience is real and can be presumed upon (v. 6; compare 18:8).

God's word is food and delight to those who receive it (v. 16), and it can isolate the one who carries it (v. 17). Scripture keeps a prophet's accusation that God may be a brook that fails (v. 18), because faith may speak honestly to God. And God calls his weary servant back from accusation, then restores him with the same promise he was first given (vv. 19-21; 1:18-19).
15.examples: Two of the chapter's pictures stay with a reader: the light going at noon for a mother who has lost her children, and a wadi that runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in summer. Between them stands a man who ate God's word with joy and lost every invitation because of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three prohibitions make Jeremiah's life a sign: no marriage (vv. 1-4), no funerals (vv. 5-7), no feasts (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's private life is confiscated and made into the sermon: no marriage, no funerals, no parties.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place. For thus says the LORD concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning the mothers who bore them and the fathers who fathered them in this land: They shall die of deadly diseases. They shall not be lamented, nor shall they be buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. They shall perish by the sword and by famine, and their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a society where marriage and children were the whole of a man's future, his security in old age and his name after death, God forbids his prophet both. Jeremiah is to be single and childless, not by preference but by command, and the whole town will see it.

This is the cost of the calling at its sharpest. He has already lost his village (11:21) and his family (12:6); now he is denied the family he might have made. Ezekiel would face something similar when God took his wife and forbade him to mourn: Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead (Ezek 24:17).

And here is the reason, which turns the command from cruelty into mercy. Children born in Jerusalem now will die in the siege. God is sparing his servant the sight of his own family starving.

Paul reasoned in the same direction for a different crisis: the appointed time has grown very short, so let those who have wives live as though they had none (1 Cor 7:29). And Jesus spoke of those who renounce marriage for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:12). Singleness is never second-class in Scripture, and here it is a prophetic office.

The command was Jeremiah's alone; it tells no one else to stay unmarried. But for those who are single or childless without having chosen it, he is company: a man with no wife and no children whom God called, kept and used, and whose greater Son also lived unmarried.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah’s unmarried life was itself a sign of coming judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Do not enter the house of mourning, or go to lament or grieve for them, for I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy, declares the LORD. Both great and small shall die in this land. They shall not be buried, and no one shall lament for them or cut himself or make himself bald for them. No one shall break bread for the mourner, to comfort him for the dead, nor shall anyone give him the cup of consolation to drink for his father or his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second prohibition takes away the ordinary duties of a neighbour. He may not go to funerals. In a village culture that is not a minor absence; it is a public insult, and it is meant to be noticed and asked about.

And the reason is the most frightening sentence in the chapter: I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy. These are the covenant words, peace, steadfast love and mercy, the things God had bound himself to show, and now he withdraws them.

Remember where the same words go later, in Lamentations, when the city has actually fallen: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end (Lam 3:22). What is withdrawn from a generation is not lost from the world.

Every custom of comfort is listed and cancelled: the burial, the lament, the mourning rites, the meal brought to the bereaved, the cup of consolation pressed into the hand of a man who has lost his mother.

The horror here is not only death but the collapse of the community that normally carries people through it. There will be too many dead and too few living to sit with them.

Gashing the body and shaving the head were mourning rites for the dead that the law forbade (Lev 19:28; Deut 14:1); the people had adopted them.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and drink. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will silence in this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the third prohibition takes the other half of social life. No funerals, and now no weddings or celebrations either. He may not sit down and enjoy an evening with his neighbours.

Jeremiah has already said that he sat alone (15:17). This is the command behind it. A man who tells the truth in such a time will find himself outside both the grief and the gladness of his people.

The same sentence closed the temple sermon (7:34), and it is the sound of a civilisation ending: no laughter, and no weddings. Jeremiah's enforced absence from the feasts is a preview. He is not invited to them because soon there will be none.

And there is mercy hidden in the timing: before your eyes and in your days. God tells him plainly that he will live to see it, so that when it comes he will not think God has lost control.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people will ask what their iniquity is; the answer covers two generations, and the sentence is shaped like the sin (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A people can be so far gone that they cannot name a single sin, and the sentence simply gives them what they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when you tell this people all these words, and they say to you, 'Why has the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?' then you shall say to them: 'Because your fathers have forsaken me, declares the LORD, and have gone after other gods and have served and worshiped them, and have forsaken me and have not kept my law, and because you have done worse than your fathers, for behold, every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen to me. Therefore I will hurl you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God predicts the reaction, and it is not defiance but blank incomprehension. What is our iniquity? They genuinely cannot think what they have done.

This is the condition the whole book has been describing from a different angle. A conscience that has lost feeling (6:15), a people who never ask What have I done? (8:6), religion carried on as a trade (14:18). The end of that process is not a guilty nation pleading for mercy but a puzzled one asking what the fuss is about.

The answer is given in two generations. The fathers forsook God; and you have done worse than your fathers (compare 7:26). Inheritance explains a great deal and excuses nothing, because each generation had the evidence of the last.

And the mechanism is named exactly: every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen. Not one national decision, but thousands of private ones.

The sentence is shaped like the sin, as in 5:19. You wanted other gods; you shall have them day and night, in a country where they are the only ones on offer. God's severest judgment is often to give people what they insisted on, in quantities they never wanted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — A New Exodus, and Fishers and Hunters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A promised homecoming greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), but first the fishers and hunters (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Even while announcing the hunt, God promises a rescue that will make the exodus a second-best story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it shall no longer be said, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' For I will bring them back to their own land that I gave to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, without warning, hope, and on a scale that is easy to miss. The exodus was the foundation of Israel's whole identity. Every oath, every feast, every creed began there: the God who brought us out of Egypt. It was the story that defined them.

God says that the rescue he is planning will be so much greater that people will stop swearing by the exodus and start swearing by this. The Red Sea will become the second-best story about him.

Isaiah said the same in his own way: Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing (Isa 43:18-19). And the saying is repeated later in this book (23:7-8), attached there to the coming of a righteous Branch.

Christians can hardly read it without looking further. There is a rescue that makes even the return from Babylon a rehearsal: a greater exodus, out of a deeper slavery, led by one who kept a passover the night before he accomplished it.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Faithful Christians differ on whether a future return to the land is also promised, and those who expect one share the same hope in the same Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am sending for many fishers, declares the LORD, and they shall catch them. And afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks. For my eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from me, nor is their iniquity concealed from my eyes. But first I will doubly repay their iniquity and their sin, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the homecoming, the round-up. Fishermen drag a net through the water and take everything in it; hunters go after what escaped the net, into the hills and the rock crevices where refugees hide. Between them, nobody gets away.

Many think Jesus had this image in mind and turned it inside out: Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matt 4:19). The same picture of men caught in a net serves judgment here and salvation there, and the difference is who is doing the sending and what he does with the catch.

The reason no one escapes the hunters is not the skill of the hunters. My eyes are on all their ways. There is no cleft of the rock out of God's sight, which is terrible here and is the same fact that makes him a refuge two verses later.

Doubly repay means full payment, the complete penalty their sin deserved; many think double here means a full equivalent, as when Isaiah says Jerusalem has received double for all her sins (Isaiah 40:2).

The idols are called carcasses, dead things whose presence defiles a place like an unburied body. It is the language of contamination, and the land God calls my inheritance has been filled with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — To You Shall the Nations Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet worships, and sees the nations coming to renounce the lies they inherited (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of judgment the prophet sees Gentiles arriving from the ends of the earth to renounce the lies they inherited.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth and say: "Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit. Can man make for himself gods? Such are not gods!" "Therefore, behold, I will make them know, this once I will make them know my power and my might, and they shall know that my name is the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet answers the announcement of judgment with worship, and the titles he uses are a soldier's: strength, stronghold, refuge in the day of trouble. David piled up the same words: The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer (Ps 18:2). The man forbidden to marry, bury or feast has this.

And then his eyes lift to the horizon and he sees something no one else in the chapter is looking at: to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth. Not Judah restored, but the nations arriving.

Listen to what they say when they come. Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit. That is a whole conversion in one sentence: a verdict on the religion they were raised in, named as inherited, named as a lie, named as worthless. Paul says of the same moment that people exchanged the truth about God for a lie (Rom 1:25) and must turn from these vain things to a living God (Acts 14:15).

They arrive having worked out chapter 10 for themselves: Can man make for himself gods? answers itself once it is asked out loud.

Isaiah saw the same procession: all the nations shall flow to it (Isa 2:2). It is one of the great surprises of the prophets that the books most full of judgment on Israel are also the books that see the world coming in.

God answers the prayer, and three times he says know. The judgment that is falling on Judah is itself part of how the nations will come to know him. The disaster is not only an ending; it is an announcement, and people who never heard of the LORD will learn his name from what he does with his own people.

16.title: A Life Made into a Sign
16.overview:
Jeremiah's own life becomes the sermon: God forbids him to marry, to mourn at funerals or to sit at feasts, because death and silence are coming on the city (vv. 1-9). The people cannot even name their sin, and they will be given the other gods they wanted (vv. 10-13).

Then, without warning, a promise of a homecoming greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), but first the fishers and hunters (vv. 16-18). The prophet answers with worship, and sees the nations coming from the ends of the earth to know the LORD's name (vv. 19-21).
16.theology:
A servant's life may itself be made into the message, at great personal cost (vv. 1-9; Ezek 24:16-18), and singleness can be a calling rather than a deprivation (1 Cor 7:29-31; Matt 19:12). God can withdraw his peace and steadfast love from a generation (v. 5), though his mercies do not fail in themselves (Lam 3:22).

Hardened people lose the ability to name their own sin (v. 10), and judgment often consists of being given what was insisted on (v. 13). Yet God promises a rescue greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), and he will be known by the nations, who come renouncing their inherited lies (vv. 19-21; Isa 2:2-3).
16.examples: The chapter is full of absences: a man the whole town watches not marrying, a cup of consolation with no one left to hand it over, a guilty people who cannot think of a single thing they have done. Against them stands one great arrival, the nations coming from the ends of the earth and calling the religion they inherited a lie.

Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory.<sup>4</sup>You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."<sup>5</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD.<sup>6</sup>He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come.
