Disease in a besieged city, with the water fouled and the dead unburied, needs no explanation. It killed more than the swords did.

The king is named, and his fate is spelled out to his own messengers. The three verbs of withheld mercy, no pity, no sparing, no compassion, were used of God in 13:14; here they describe the man he is handing them to. Babylon will not be gentle, and God says so in advance rather than letting them imagine a negotiated peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Life and Death Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the people, the way of life and the way of death: staying in the city means death, and surrender means life (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The way of life runs out through the gate of surrender, which is why the offer sounds like treason.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war. For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words are Moses' words. At the end of Deuteronomy he set the same choice before the nation: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life (Deut 30:19). Jesus put it as two gates and two roads, one wide and easy, one narrow and hard (Matt 7:13-14).

What is startling here is the content of the two ways. The way of life is surrender. Walk out of the gate, hands empty, and give yourself up to the enemy, and you will keep your life, though nothing else, as a prize of war, the way a soldier keeps his skin when everything else is lost.

No wonder they called Jeremiah a traitor. This is the sermon that later gets him thrown into a cistern for demoralising the troops (38:4). He is telling a besieged city to give in, and he is telling them so because the siege is God's judgment and resisting it is resisting God.

There is a hard and useful lesson in it. Sometimes the godly response to a disaster we have brought on ourselves is not to fight for the position we held but to surrender it and accept the loss, because the discipline is from God, a Father's discipline and not a sentence of rejection (Heb 12:6), and the life on the other side of it is real. Surrender looks like defeat and is the only way out.

Jesus put the same paradox at the heart of following him: whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it (Mark 8:35). The way of life still runs through surrender, now to a King who has gone through death himself and come out the other side.

The city itself is not being saved. Individuals within it still can be, one at a time, by walking out. Judgment on a community and mercy to persons inside it are not contradictory, and this verse holds them together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Execute Justice in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the royal house, a call to do justice first thing in the morning (vv. 11-12); and to a city confident in its rock and its walls, I am against you (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Even at this hour the word to the palace is not military but moral: do justice before breakfast.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'" "Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?' I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With an army at the gates, the word to the royal household is about the courts. Execute justice in the morning means make this the first business of the day, before anything else.

And the concrete duty is named: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Not issue a statement about justice; get the stolen thing back to the person it was taken from.

This is the measure by which the house of David is judged all through the prophets. Not the size of the army or the splendour of the temple, but whether a poor man who has been cheated can get a hearing before lunch. Two chapters on, God promises a son of David who will at last execute justice and righteousness in the land (23:5): the King this house never produced.

Jerusalem sits on rock above its valleys, and the confidence in that geography has become a slogan: Who shall come down against us? Good walls in a good position, and the question is asked as if it had no answer.

God's reply is the opening words: I am against you. That is the answer to the question. It is not the Babylonians coming down; it is God.

According to the fruit of your deeds is the harvest language of 17:10, where God searches the heart and gives each according to his ways. The fire kindled in the forest is probably the cedar palaces of the royal quarter, which the next chapter addresses directly.

The chapter that began with a king asking for a miracle ends with God pointing at the palace and telling him where the fire will start.

21.title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
21.overview:
With Nebuchadnezzar's army at the walls, King Zedekiah asks for a miracle like the old days, and is told that God himself will fight against the city (vv. 1-7).

To the people God sets the way of life and the way of death, and the way of life is surrender (vv. 8-10). To the house of David the word is still to do justice first thing in the morning, and to a city confident in its walls, I am against you (vv. 11-14).
21.theology:
Prayer used as a last-resort lever by people unwilling to repent is refused (vv. 1-2; compare 14:11-12), and God may turn the language of redemption against his own people: the outstretched arm that freed Israel now fights them (v. 5).

The choice of Deuteronomy is set again, but the way of life now runs through surrender (vv. 8-9; Deut 30:15-19), and judgment on a community and mercy to individuals within it stand together. The first duty of God's appointed king is justice for the robbed and oppressed (v. 12), the duty fulfilled at last by the righteous Branch (23:5).
21.examples: After twenty years of ignoring the prophet, the palace sends an official delegation when the siege lines go up, wanting Hezekiah's outcome without Hezekiah's posture. The answer turns their slogan, Who shall come down against us?, into God's own reply: I am against you.

22.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word,<sup>2</sup>and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.<sup>4</sup>For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people.<sup>5</sup>But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city.<sup>7</sup>I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.<sup>8</sup>"'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?"<sup>9</sup>And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"<sup>10</sup>Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.<sup>11</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more,<sup>12</sup>but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."<sup>13</sup>"Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages,<sup>14</sup>who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.<sup>15</sup>Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him.<sup>16</sup>He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."<sup>18</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!'<sup>19</sup>With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."<sup>20</sup>"Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.<sup>22</sup>The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil.<sup>23</sup>O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"<sup>24</sup>"As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off<sup>25</sup>and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die.<sup>27</sup>But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."<sup>28</sup>Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know?<sup>29</sup>O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Do Justice, or This House Becomes a Desolation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The royal charter preached at the palace gate (vv. 1-3), with two futures for the dynasty (vv. 4-5), and the cedar palace burned for a forsaken covenant (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne is held on terms, and the terms are the treatment of people who cannot defend themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet is sent to the palace, and told to preach at the gate again, the same method as the temple sermon (7:2) and the Sabbath sermon (17:19). He addresses the king, the civil service and the public together, because all three are implicated in how a country is run.

The title matters: who sits on the throne of David. Everything that follows is measured against what that throne was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the royal job description, and it is strikingly concrete. Not defend the borders, not maintain the temple, not manage the economy: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Get the stolen thing back. And protect the same three groups God names every time, the immigrant, the orphan and the widow, the people with no family power to protect them.

This is not a political programme read back into Scripture; it is the charter of Israel's monarchy, and the prophets judge every king by it.

The psalm of the ideal king says the same, and the church has long heard Christ in it: May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor! (Ps 72:4), because he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper, and precious is their blood in his sight (Ps 72:12, 14). The job description Jehoiakim ignored is the one the true Son of David fulfils.

Does this apply to immigrants today? It commands God’s people to do justice to the vulnerable: the resident alien, the fatherless, the widow. Christians must treat foreigners with love and justice (Matt 25:35); how a nation sets its laws of entry is for governments to decide justly.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same two futures as chapter 17, and the same door: obedience keeps the dynasty riding through these gates; refusal empties the palace.

And God binds himself to it: I swear by myself. There is nothing higher to swear by. The promise to David was never a licence for his descendants to behave as they liked.

Hebrews notes the same form of oath when God promised Abraham: since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself (Heb 6:13). The oath that guarantees God's promises is the same oath that guarantees his threats. Both rest on the one foundation there is.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city. I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The palace is compared to the grandest landscapes the region knew: the wooded highlands of Gilead, the cedar summits of Lebanon. Partly this is about the building itself, which was panelled with imported cedar, and partly about how the dynasty looked to everyone: solid, green, permanent.

The ESV notes that an uninhabited city is in Hebrew "cities". Either way, what looked like a forest becomes desert.

The image turns from forest to logging camp. God will prepare destroyers, the way a builder lines up his woodcutters, and the cedars the king was so proud of will be firewood.

Anything built to display our own permanence is, in the end, timber. And the image fits the building exactly. Solomon's great hall in Jerusalem was called by a forest's name: He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon, built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars (1 Kgs 7:2). When God says like the summit of Lebanon and your choicest cedars, he is describing the royal complex itself, a manufactured forest cut down for fuel.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?" And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruins will preach. Travellers will ask the question, and the answer will be public and accurate: not bad luck, not the superior power of Babylon's gods, but a broken covenant.

Israel was called to make God known among the nations. She does it here, from the rubble, and the sermon is true.

And the conversation between the travellers was scripted long before. Moses had told Israel exactly what the nations would say over its ruins: Why has the LORD done thus to this land?, and the reply, It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers (Deut 29:24-25). Jeremiah's hearers were watching Deuteronomy come true in their own streets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Woe to Him Who Builds by Unrighteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shallum will not return (vv. 10-12). Woe to Jehoiakim, who builds with unpaid labour, set beside his father Josiah, who judged the cause of the poor (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Knowing God is defined, in God's own words, as judging the cause of the poor and needy.

verseByVerse.quote: Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A funeral instruction that reverses the usual grief. The dead man is Josiah, killed at Megiddo, and the whole country mourned him. God says: stop weeping for the king who died in his own land and start weeping for the one being marched away alive.

There are worse things than dying at home. Josiah was spared what is coming (2 Kgs 22:20); his son was not.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more, but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shallum is Jehoahaz, who reigned three months before Pharaoh deposed him and took him to Egypt. Of the kings named in this chapter, he and Coniah both end their lives in a foreign country.

The history confirms the sentence exactly: Pharaoh Neco took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there (2 Kgs 23:34).

Twice in one sentence: He shall return here no more, and he shall never see this land again. Exile is not only punishment; it is the specific loss of home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages, who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jehoiakim, and the charge is unpaid labour. He is building a palace during a national crisis, and he is doing it with forced work: makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages.

The law was emphatic about this: The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning (Lev 19:13), and You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD (Deut 24:15). James says the cry is heard: the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you (Jas 5:4). God notices payroll.

Habakkuk pronounced the same woe on the same kind of builder: Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm! (Hab 2:9). A house built on unpaid labour is built on sand, however many cedar beams it has.

Listen to the king's own voice: I will build myself a great house. The details are the details of a brochure: spacious rooms, large windows, cedar panelling, expensive red paint.
verseByVerse.note: Jehoiakim built a lavish palace with forced labor.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? The question cuts through everything: kingship is not a building project or a standard of living. Then Josiah is held up, and the description is ordinary. Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? He enjoyed his life; there is no asceticism here. And twice comes the refrain: it was well with him, and then it was well.

And then the sentence that should stop every religious reader: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me?

God defines the knowledge of himself by the treatment of the poor. Not instead of worship, prayer or doctrine (this book has spent twenty chapters on idolatry), but as inseparable from them. A man who defends the cause of people who cannot pay him knows God; a man who does not, whatever else he knows, does not know him.

And the Lord makes the connection personal at the last judgment. The King says to those who fed the hungry and visited the prisoner, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt 25:40). To judge the cause of the poor is not merely to know about God. It is to meet the King who has chosen to stand with them. And it is that King, not Josiah and not us, who has kept this charter perfectly. Those whose neglect of the poor is forgiven for his sake are given his Spirit, who turns eyes and heart from the take toward the neighbour (Gal 5:22).

verseByVerse.quote: But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."
verseByVerse.commentary: Eyes and heart only: attention and affection both fixed on the take. That is a portrait of a man whose inner life has narrowed to one thing, and the consequences run outward into blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Burial of a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiakim's unmourned burial (vv. 18-19), and Judah's cry from the mountains, because she would not listen in her prosperity (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The king who built himself a cedar palace is dragged out of the city gate like a dead animal.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!' With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The funeral cries of that world are quoted and cancelled. Nobody will say the family words, and nobody will say the court words. The man who spent his reign building a monument will get no ceremony at all.

A dead donkey is hauled out of the city and left. That is the burial of the king of Judah: dragged and dumped.

Set it beside the cedar and the vermilion: he built a house to be remembered by, and has no grave anyone would visit.

The sentence is repeated after he burned Jeremiah's scroll, in even starker terms: his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night (36:30).

Jehoiakim was to have the burial of a donkey, yet Kings says he slept with his fathers (2 Kgs 24:6). That phrase means simply that he died; it says nothing of honourable burial. Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chr 36:6), but not that he arrived. Scripture does not say how Jeremiah's word was carried out; many think he died around the start of the siege in 598 BC and that his body was thrown out unburied.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is told to climb the high places in every direction and shout, north to Lebanon, north-east to Bashan, south-east to Abarim, and everywhere the news is the same. All your lovers are destroyed: the allies courted since chapter 2 are gone.

God spoke in your prosperity, while things were going well, when listening would have cost nothing and prevented everything. Good times are when warnings are cheapest to heed and hardest to hear.

Proverbs names the mechanism: the complacency of fools destroys them (Prov 1:32). And Jesus told of a rich man in exactly this condition, talking to his own soul in his prosperity, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry, until God said, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil. O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bitter joke: the shepherds who were supposed to lead the flock will themselves be herded, and by the wind. And the city nested among the cedars, comfortable, elevated and expensively furnished, will cry out like a woman in labour.

Height and cedar were supposed to keep trouble out. They only made the fall longer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Signet Ring Torn Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Coniah, the signet ring torn off and hurled into exile (vv. 24-28), is written down as childless (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The signet ring of the house of David is pulled off and thrown away, and the line looks finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coniah is Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, three months on the throne, deported to Babylon in 597 BC. Kings gives his age as eighteen (2 Kgs 24:8); most Hebrew copies of Chronicles read eight (2 Chr 36:9), very likely a copying slip, since some ancient copies there read eighteen.

A signet ring was a king's identity: it carried his seal, it went everywhere with him, it was never taken off. To call the Davidic king the signet on God's right hand is to say he is God's own authority displayed in the world.

And God says he would tear you off. The verb is violent. Even so intimate a symbol of the covenant with David is not immune when the man wearing it is faithless.
verseByVerse.note: Coniah is Jehoiachin (Jeconiah).

verseByVerse.quote: and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four times into the hand, and the last phrase is the ache of every exile: the land to which they will long to return. The longing is granted and the return is not.

His mother goes with him, as 13:18 said she would. His release to eat at the king's table is the note on which the book of Kings closes (2 Kgs 25:27-30), a flicker of light at the end of that history, and the appendix to this very book records it too: in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin, Evil-merodach graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison (52:31). The ring was torn off; the man was not forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question echoes the broken flask of chapter 19. A pot that has been smashed is swept up and thrown out without a thought, and that is what happened to the king: a vessel no one cares for.

Hear the tone of the question, too. It is almost pity: Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? Even under judgment, God does not describe the ruin of a young king without feeling. Many Christians have heard in despised an echo of the King who later came through this very line: He was despised and rejected by men (Isa 53:3).

O land, land, land: three times, like a herald in the street. The land itself is summoned to hear what is about to be said about the house of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enter it in the record: childless. He had sons, but for the purposes of the throne the line stops here. No descendant of Jehoiachin will reign in Jerusalem, and none ever did.

That looks like the end of the promise to David, and for centuries it hung there.

Two things happen afterwards, and they must be held together. First, Haggai takes this very image and gives it back: to Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin's grandson, God says, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you (Hag 2:23). The ring torn off is put back on.

Second, Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy that runs straight through this cursed name: Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon, and then Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel (Matt 1:11-12), and on to Joseph, the husband of Mary.

The line that carried the throne also carried the curse, and the King who finally sat on David's throne came into that family without coming from that seed. What God said stands, and what God promised stands, and the gospel is how both are true at once.

God said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (22:30), yet Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matt 1:11–12). Jesus was Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father, but not his physical descendant; Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31). The throne passed to a Son of David by another branch.
verseByVerse.note: No son of Jehoiachin reigned; on Jesus' descent, see the question above.

22.title: The House of David on Trial
22.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the palace with the royal charter: do justice, rescue the robbed, protect the immigrant, the orphan and the widow (vv. 1-3). Refuse, and God swears the house will be a desolation (vv. 4-9).

Shallum is deported, never to return (vv. 10-12). Woe to Jehoiakim, who built a cedar palace with unpaid labour, while his father judged the cause of the poor: Is not this to know me? He will have the burial of a donkey (vv. 13-23). Finally Coniah, the signet ring torn off, is written down as childless (vv. 24-30).
22.theology:
The Davidic throne is held on covenant terms, and the test is justice for those who cannot defend themselves (vv. 3-5). God defines the knowledge of himself by the judging of the cause of the poor and needy (v. 16), not as a substitute for true worship but inseparable from it.

God speaks to people in their prosperity, when heeding him is cheapest (v. 21), and grandeur built on injustice ends as firewood and an unmourned burial (vv. 7, 19). Not even the signet ring of David's house is immune (v. 24), yet God gives the signet back to Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23), and the throne passes to Christ: the curse stands and the promise is kept.
22.examples: The chapter judges a king by whether a robbed man can get his property back, and sets cedar panelling and vermilion paint, paid for with wages never handed over, beside a dead donkey dragged out of the gate as the state funeral. It ends with a signet ring torn off a king's hand and, in Haggai, put back on his grandson's.

23.text: <sup>1</sup>"Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply.<sup>4</sup>I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>6</sup>In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>7</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'<sup>8</sup>but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."<sup>9</sup>Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words.<sup>10</sup>For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.<sup>11</sup>"Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.<sup>14</sup>But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah."<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"<sup>18</sup>For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened?<sup>19</sup>Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked.<sup>20</sup>The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.<sup>21</sup>"I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.<sup>22</sup>But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.<sup>23</sup>"Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?<sup>24</sup>Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.<sup>25</sup>I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!'<sup>26</sup>How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart,<sup>27</sup>who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?<sup>28</sup>Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD.<sup>29</sup>Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?<sup>30</sup>Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another.<sup>31</sup>Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.'<sup>34</sup>And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household.<sup>35</sup>Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>36</sup>But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.<sup>37</sup>Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>38</sup>But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'"<sup>39</sup>therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.<sup>40</sup>And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to the shepherds, and God's promise to gather the flock himself (vv. 1-4); the righteous Branch and his name (vv. 5-6); and the new-exodus oath (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against every failed shepherd God sets one King who will do what the house of David was given the throne to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD. Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD. Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply. I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds are the kings and leaders of chapter 22, and the charge is precise. They did not merely fail to gather; they destroy and scatter. Bad leadership is not neutral.

And they are the sheep of my pasture. The flock was never theirs. That is the reason the woe is so heavy: they mishandled someone else's property, and the owner was watching.

There is a grim play on words here. They did not attend to the flock, so God will attend to them. The visitation they neglected to make will be made on them.

Anyone with pastoral responsibility should feel the weight of it: the opposite of caring for people is not cruelty but inattention, and God treats inattention as an evil deed. The one safe place for a shepherd who has failed is under the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for sheep and shepherds alike.

And now God takes the job himself: I will gather. Ezekiel puts it even more strongly: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out (Ezek 34:11). When human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock; he comes for them personally.

Then he gives them shepherds again, a promise fulfilled in the pastors and teachers Christ gives his church, and finally in the chief Shepherd himself (1 Pet 5:4). And the measure of the new arrangement is a shepherd's measure: neither shall any be missing. Every sheep is accounted for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 22 ended with the royal line written down as childless. Here is the answer, and the timing is deliberate.

The righteous Branch is a shoot growing from a stump: a tree cut down to the ground, and one living green shoot coming up out of it. Isaiah had used it: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit (Isa 11:1). The dynasty is a felled tree; God will grow a king out of the stump.

And what he will do is exactly what chapter 22 demanded and no king delivered: execute justice and righteousness in the land. The job description is unchanged; at last there is someone to fill it.

The name is the summit of the book so far. The king reigning as Jeremiah spoke was Zedekiah, a weak, faithless man whose reign ended in fire. The coming King will be everything he was not, and his name is not about himself at all: our righteousness.

Think about what that means. The King's name is a statement about his people's standing. He is called what they receive. His righteousness is reckoned as theirs, credited to them as if they had lived his life, which is why they are saved and dwell securely in his days rather than in their own.

The New Testament does not quote these verses, but it says in plain prose what they promise. The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe (Rom 3:21-22). Christ became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21).

Everything Jeremiah has exposed, the deceitful heart, the leopard's spots, the sin engraved with an iron pen, requires a righteousness from outside. Here is his name.

Later in this book the same name is given to Jerusalem (33:16): the people are called by their King's name, because what he is, they are counted to be in him. Hebrew names often made a statement about God, as Zedekiah's did, so the name need not by itself call the Branch the LORD; yet many Christians have seen here a hint of what the New Testament makes plain, that the King who is our righteousness is himself God come in the flesh.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers have always taken the righteous Branch as the Messiah, the King of David's line still to come: the Targum renders Branch here as Messiah, and the Talmud (Bava Batra 75b) counts the Messiah among those called by the name of God, citing this verse. Most Jewish interpreters take the name as a sentence praising God, not a claim that the King is divine. On the King himself the two readings agree. This commentary sees him in Jesus, descended from David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), in whom God's righteousness is given to his people (1 Corinthians 1:30).
verseByVerse.note: The “righteous Branch” is the Messiah; his name, “The LORD is our righteousness,” plays on King Zedekiah’s name (“the LORD is righteous”).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new-exodus oath of 16:14-15 is repeated, and its position here is the point: it comes immediately after the righteous Branch. The greater rescue and the greater King belong together.

The ESV notes a small textual difference in verse 8. The substance is unaffected: the God who is bringing them home will be known by that, as he was once known by the Red Sea.

Christians read this with the knowledge that the return from Babylon, when it came, was modest: some fifty thousand people (Ezra 2:64-65), a small temple, no king. The oath still waits for its full weight, and it finds it in a rescue out of a deeper exile than Babylon.

How is this return fulfilled? Its first fulfilment was the return from Babylon. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel; faithful Christians differ here. In this chapter the promise is tied to the Branch, and its scope is his: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. It is fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered sheep from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26), and it will be complete in the new creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Both Prophet and Priest Are Ungodly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Concerning the prophets: Jeremiah shaken by God's words (vv. 9-10), prophet and priest ungodly even in God's house (vv. 11-12), and Jerusalem's prophets worse than Samaria's (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Preaching that comforts people in their sin is not a minor failure; it is the source from which a nation's ungodliness spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words. For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading Concerning the prophets opens a collection that runs to the end of the chapter. Having dealt with the kings, God now turns to the preachers.

Before he says a word against the false prophets, Jeremiah describes what God's word does to him: heart broken, bones shaking, unsteady on his feet like a drunk. Not because of the opposition, but because of the LORD and because of his holy words.

That is the contrast the whole section turns on. Here is a man wrecked by handling the word of God, about to describe men who handle it lightly and sleep well. Anyone who teaches Scripture might ask which of the two he more resembles.

The land is full of adulterers. It is literal (verse 14 will say the prophets themselves commit adultery), and it is covenantal, a nation unfaithful to the God it was married to. The two are rarely separate for long.

And the drought is read for what it is. Because of the curse the land mourns: this is the curse written into the covenant long before, the heavens over your head shall be bronze and The LORD will make the rain of your land powder (Deut 28:23-24). The pastures are dying because the people broke faith, and the ground itself is pictured grieving.

Sin is never as private as it feels. A nation's unfaithfulness reaches its fields.

Then the verdict on the powerful: Their course is evil, and their might is not right. They hold the influence in the land and they use it wrongly, and strength that has lost its moral right is simply force.

verseByVerse.quote: "Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD. Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both prophet and priest. These were the two offices that should have checked each other: the priest teaching the law that had been given, the prophet bringing the word God was speaking now. Each could have called the other back. Instead they agreed, and when the institutions meant to correct one another collude, nobody is left to raise the alarm.

Even in my house. Not only in the streets and the high places, but inside the temple, among the men conducting the worship. Corruption at the centre of religion is worse than corruption outside it, because there is nowhere left for a seeker to go.

Men who gave others no light will walk in the dark on wet stone, and the punishment fits. A psalmist once envied men like these, secure and prosperous, until he went into the sanctuary and saw their end: Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin (Ps 73:18). The false prophets looked as though they were standing on the firmest ground in Jerusalem: the pulpit, the temple, the favour of the court. They were on a wet slope in the dark, and they were being driven.

And the date is already set: the year of their punishment. Judgment is not improvised when patience runs out. It is on the calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray. But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah." Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samaria is the northern kingdom, destroyed a century before, and its prophets were openly pagan. God calls that an unsavory thing: repellent, but at least undisguised.

And the men in Jerusalem, who preach in the name of the LORD, are worse: a horrible thing. Their private lives are corrupt and their public message is false, and the two are connected.

The phrase to weigh is they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil. That is the effect of their preaching, and it is the exact opposite of a prophet's job. A man goes to church intending to break with something, hears that God is fine with it, and goes home reinforced.

Judged by outcome rather than intention, that is more destructive than Baal worship, because it uses God's own name to do it.

Then the comparison no Jerusalemite could hear calmly: like Sodom to me. Isaiah had already addressed the city's leaders that way, Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! (Isa 1:10), and Ezekiel names what Sodom's guilt actually was: pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy (Ezek 16:49). The likeness is not only in the sexual sin. It is a comfortable city that has lost the capacity to be shocked. Sodom had no prophets; Jerusalem had prophets, and they made it Sodom.

The bitter food and poisoned water of 9:15 are now served to the preachers, and the reason names them as the source: ungodliness did not seep up from the people to the pulpit; it flowed out from the pulpit into the country.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Visions of Their Own Minds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not listen to prophets who never stood in God's council (vv. 16-20); the test of their fruit (vv. 21-22); and the God who fills heaven and earth (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The test of preaching is not sincerity or eloquence but whether it comes from God and turns people from evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A direct instruction to the congregation: Do not listen. Hearers are responsible for what they sit under.

What the false prophets supply is vain hopes. Hope is a gift; false hope is a cruelty, because it spends the time a person had for turning. A doctor who tells a man with a treatable illness that nothing is wrong has not been kind to him.

The mechanism is named again (14:14): visions of their own minds. This is not fabrication in the crude sense; these men very likely believed their own material. Sincerity is not the test; origin is: not from the mouth of the LORD.

Look at the audiences: people who despise the word of the LORD and people who stubbornly follow their own hearts. To exactly those people they say, all will be well, and they say it continually, reassurance on a loop.

Paul saw the same market forming: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim 4:3). False prophets are not only a supply problem. There is always demand.

verseByVerse.quote: For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened? Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The test is put as a question about the council chamber. A true prophet has stood where God's decisions are made and has listened. These men never went in, which is why they can only report their own minds.

Scripture lets us glimpse that room. When four hundred court prophets told King Ahab to go up to battle and triumph, one man stood apart and said, I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left (1 Kgs 22:19). Micaiah had been in the council; the four hundred had only been in the palace. And Amos states the principle: the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7).

Count the verbs of receiving in the question: stood, to see, to hear, paid attention, listened. Five of them before a single verb of speaking. A preacher is first a listener, and a man who speaks more than he listens has reversed the order God requires.

While they promise fair weather, the storm is already moving. These two verses return almost word for word at the end of the Book of Consolation (30:23-24). There they guard the promise, reminding the restored that God's anger against evil has not been cancelled; here they are aimed at the men who said no disaster would come. It is the same storm. What differs is whether a person is sheltered from it.

And the anger is not a mood. It will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart: it is a settled purpose, which is terrifying for those who oppose it and steadying for those who trust the same heart's other intentions.

The last line is honest about timing: In the latter days you will understand it clearly. Some things only make sense afterwards, and the people telling you otherwise now will not be there to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two flat denials with two energetic verbs. They ran; they prophesied. Zeal and output are not evidence of a call. It is possible to be extremely busy in ministry that God never commissioned.

And here is the practical test, and it is a wonderfully usable one. Preaching that comes from God turns people from evil. That is its fruit.

Not that everyone repents; Jeremiah's own ministry is proof that faithful preaching can be widely rejected. But the aim and the tendency of the word is to turn people, and a message whose effect is to leave everyone exactly as they were, comfortable and unchallenged, has already told you where it came from. Deuteronomy gave a test by fulfilment (Deut 18:21-22); Jeremiah adds a test by fruit.

The turning is concrete: from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds. The direction of a life and the particular things done in it. God's word does not stop at general improvement; it names the road and the acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets have been behaving as though God were at hand in the smallest sense: a local deity, the resident of the temple precinct, near enough to be managed and too small to see what went on in their houses. A god like that can be quoted freely, because he will not object.

God insists he is also a God far away: above, beyond, not contained by the building or by anyone's theology of it. They wanted a God close enough to use and not great enough to fear.

Scripture holds both truths together, and in a particular order. I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit (Isa 57:15). God is near because he chooses to come near, not because he is small, and the ones he comes near to are the humble, not the men using his name.

Think of what was being done in secret places in this chapter: adultery behind closed doors (v. 14), dreams rehearsed in private and passed off in public (v. 25). Can a man hide himself in secret places? The question answers itself. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13).

And Do I not fill heaven and earth? is not a picture of a very large being in a very large room. It means there is no location without him: no study, no bedroom, no pulpit, no private thought.

The psalm turns the same truth into comfort: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7). Paul told pagans in Athens that he is actually not far from each one of us (Acts 17:27). To a liar it is terror; to a child it is home. The God who sees the unconfessed sin is the same God who sees the faithfulness nobody else noticed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dreams and God's word: straw and wheat (vv. 25-29), and three frauds God is against (vv. 30-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Dreams and God's word are not two grades of the same thing; they are straw and wheat.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!' How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart, who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard. The God who fills heaven and earth has been listening to the sermons.

The repetition mimics them: I have dreamed, I have dreamed! It is the excited claim of a private revelation that cannot be checked. And God traces it to its source, which is the heart of chapter 17: the deceit is in the prophets' own hearts, and they are its first victims.

How long is the voice of patience nearing its end. God has let this go on, and he asks how much longer it will be allowed to.

Their dreams have the same effect as Baal did: they make people forget God's name. Ministry that draws attention to the minister's experiences is not neutral; it crowds out the name it claims to serve.

And the comparison across the generations is sobering. The grandfathers forgot God by bowing to an idol; the grandsons forget him by listening to dreams told in his name. The method differs and the result is the same: idolatry does not require a statue.

Does God give dreams and visions today? He spoke by dreams and visions when Scripture was being given; now he has spoken finally in his Son (Heb 1:1–2), and his word is complete. A dream may stir the conscience, but no believer should treat one as a word from God. Let him who has my word speak my word faithfully (v. 28). Many continuationist Christians believe God still guides by dreams, always to be tested by Scripture; this commentary is cessationist, holding that nothing received today adds to the finished word, and it honours brothers who see it differently.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD. Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruling is not that dreams must be suppressed. Tell the dream, and call it a dream. What is forbidden is passing it off as the word of God.

And the requirement laid on the one who has God's word is a single adverb: faithfully. Not originally, not impressively, not with fresh angles. A messenger's whole excellence is delivering the message as it was given.

The comparison settles it: What has straw in common with wheat? Both come off the same field; one feeds people and one does not. Preaching that is mostly the preacher's own material may be pleasant, but nobody lives on straw.

Here is what the real thing does. It burns, as it burned in Jeremiah's bones when he tried to keep silent (20:9); and it breaks rock, which is the only hope for a people whose faces are harder than rock (5:3).

If preaching never burns or breaks anything, the problem may not be the congregation. The power is not the preacher's to produce: the word does its work in the hands of the Spirit, which is why a preacher's first task is to deliver it faithfully and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another. Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.' Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times God says I am against the prophets, and each names a different fraud.

The first is plagiarism: they steal my words from one another. Having nothing from God themselves, they recycle each other's material. A prophetic culture can run for years on borrowed phrases with no fresh dealing with God behind any of it.

The second is the formula. They have learned the phrase that makes speech sound authoritative and they attach it to their own opinions. The verse is almost comic in its precision: they use their tongues and say, declares the LORD.

Every generation has its version, a tone of voice, a way of quoting, a confident "God told me", by which personal judgment is given divine weight.

The third is recklessness: not only malice but carelessness with other people's souls. And the verdict is quietly devastating: they do not profit this people at all. All that ministry, and nobody was helped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–40 — The Burden of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A joke about the burden of the LORD is banned and turned back on those who make it (vv. 33-40).
verseByVerse.theology: A reverent-sounding phrase had become a joke about God's word, and God takes the joke away.

verseByVerse.quote: "When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.' And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household. Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This last section turns on a word. The burden of the LORD was a way of speaking about a prophet's message, and a burden is also a load. People had started asking Jeremiah, with a smirk, what today's burden was, treating God's word as a heavy, tiresome thing and the prophet as the man who carries it round.

God takes the joke and returns it: You are the burden, and I will cast you off. The ESV notes a textual variation in the question, but the wordplay is plain enough. You think my word is a weight? You are the weight, and I am putting it down.

The phrase is banned, and the ban reaches everyone, prophet, priest, ordinary citizen and his household, because an attitude to God's word is taught at home before it is voiced in public. It is a striking example of God legislating against a piece of religious slang because of the contempt packed into it.

And he gives them the replacement wording, which is humble and expectant: What has the LORD answered? Not, what is today's burden, but what has God said. The change of phrase is a change of posture.

The correction happens between neighbours: every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother. Not in the temple, but in ordinary conversation. The way believers talk to each other about God's word, flippant or expectant, weary or hungry, shapes how they receive it.

Here is the heart of it: the burden is every man's own word. Everyone had made his own opinion the oracle. And the charge is the gravest in the chapter, you pervert the words of the living God: twisting them until they say something else.

Weigh the three titles stacked at the end: the living God, not a dead text to be joked about; the LORD of hosts, the commander of heaven's armies; our God, the one who belongs to these very people. They were bending the words of someone alive, powerful, and theirs.
verseByVerse.note: A pun: “burden” and “oracle” are the same Hebrew word (massa).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'" therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instruction is repeated, now addressed to how people speak to the prophet himself, and then the case against them is built with the precision of a legal charge. They were told plainly not to say it. They said it anyway.

That moves the offence from attitude to defiance. The first use of the phrase was contempt; its use after an explicit command was rebellion, and verse 38 records the command in God's own voice so that no one can plead ignorance.

The sentence uses their own word against them one last time: they called God's message a burden, so he will lift you up like a load and put it down outside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "surely forget you", and both readings land. They could not stop saying the word; God will stop remembering them.

And what is cast away with them is a gift: the city that I gave to you and your fathers. Everything they had came from the God they were mocking.

Put the last two verses side by side. God will "surely forget" them, and their shame shall not be forgotten.

Now set that beside the promise eight chapters later: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (31:34). Those are the only two outcomes Scripture offers. In the new covenant God forgets the sin and keeps the person. Outside it, he lets go of the person and the shame is never forgotten.

The chapter that gave us the most beautiful name in the book, The LORD is our righteousness, ends with everlasting reproach for those who made his word a joke. The two belong together: the King who is our righteousness is the Word made flesh, and how people handle the word is finally how they handle him.

23.title: The Righteous Branch: The LORD Is Our Righteousness
23.overview:
Against the shepherds who scattered God's flock stands the promise of a righteous Branch for David, whose name is The LORD is our righteousness (vv. 1-8).

Then the prophets: men who never stood in God's council, who strengthened the hands of evildoers, and who passed off their own dreams as his word, which is wheat to their straw, a fire and a hammer (vv. 9-32). The chapter ends by banning the phrase the burden of the LORD, by which they had made his word a joke (vv. 33-40).
23.theology:
Leaders are accountable for a flock that belongs to God, and when shepherds fail, God gathers his people himself and gives them true shepherds under the chief Shepherd (vv. 1-4; John 10:11). The righteous Branch is the King who does what David's house failed to do, and his name declares what his people receive: his righteousness counted as theirs (vv. 5-6).

False prophecy is sincere, energetic and self-derived (vv. 16, 21), and is tested by its origin and its fruit: God's word turns people from evil (v. 22; Deut 18:20-22). God is near because he chooses to come near to the humble, not because he is small enough to be managed (vv. 23-24). And there are only two ways to be forgotten by God: in the new covenant he remembers the sin no more and keeps the person (31:34); for those who make his word a joke he lets go of the person, and the shame is never forgotten (vv. 39-40).
23.examples: The chapter's images are memorable: a shoot growing out of a stump that everyone had written off, preachers recycling each other's material with nothing fresh from God, and straw and wheat off the same field, of which only one feeds people. Its sharpest warning is the churchgoer who comes intending to break with something and goes home reinforced.

24.text: <sup>1</sup>After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>6</sup>I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up.<sup>7</sup>I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.<sup>8</sup>"But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them.<sup>10</sup>And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Two Baskets Before the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the first deportation, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple, one very good and one rotten, and asks what he sees (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: Two baskets at the temple door, and the sorting is not the one anybody in Jerusalem would have made.

verseByVerse.quote: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD. One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten. And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date fixes everything. This is after 597 BC, when Babylon took the young king Jeconiah — the Coniah of chapter 22 — along with the court, the skilled workers and the metalworkers. The first deportation has happened, and Jerusalem is still standing with Zedekiah on the throne.

That situation produced a very natural theology in the city: God has judged those people and spared us. The deportees must have been the sinners. We are the survivors, we still have the temple, and that proves whose side God is on.

So the vision is set before the temple, in the very place where that theology was preached, and it is a picture of the harvest offering: two baskets of figs brought to God's house.

First-ripe figs, picked in June, were a delicacy — the best of the crop. The other basket is not mediocre fruit but rotten: so bad that they could not be eaten. There is no middle category anywhere in this chapter.

The question is the one from the almond branch and the boiling pot (1:11, 13). God's method with this prophet is to make him look at something ordinary and say what is there, and then to tell him what it means. Jeremiah's answer is simply accurate, and it commits him to nothing — which is why what follows lands so hard.
verseByVerse.note: The good figs are the exiles taken in 597 BC with Jehoiachin; the bad, Zedekiah and those left behind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — The Good Figs: the Exiles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good figs are the exiles God sent to Babylon. He will bring them back, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The people who lost everything are the good figs, and God promises to give them the one thing they cannot give themselves: a heart to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans. I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up. I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good figs are the people in Babylon, which reverses everything Jerusalem believed. The men in chains, who lost their homes, their positions and their temple, are the first-ripe fruit. And note the phrase whom I have sent away: God, not Nebuchadnezzar, sent them. Their deportation was not abandonment but transplanting.

Were the exiles better people? Not by nature: Ezekiel, who lived among them, called them a rebellious house (Ezekiel 2:5). They are good figs because God says I will regard them so and sets his eyes on them for good. The difference lies in his choosing and his gift, not in their merit.

It is a hard lesson for comfortable believers. Circumstances are not a scoreboard. The people whose lives look broken may be the ones God has his eye on, and the ones still holding the property may be the rotten basket.

Listen to the verbs: build, plant, and the refusal of tear down and pluck up. They are four of the six verbs of Jeremiah's call (1:10), and here the two constructive ones stand on their own, with the destructive pair expressly set aside. Ruin is not the last word of this ministry, and the exiles are where the building starts.

Here is the promise the whole book has been driving toward. Chapter 13 asked whether a leopard could change its spots; chapter 17 said the heart is deceitful and unsearchable. The answer is not better instruction: I will give them a heart to know me.

God gives what he requires. Ezekiel says the same: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh (Ezek 11:19). And the covenant formula follows, as it always does: they shall be my people and I will be their God.

Because he gives the heart, they shall return to me with their whole heart. Their wholehearted return is real, and it is the fruit of his gift rather than the price of it. That is the shape of the new covenant in 31:31-34, and of every conversion since.
