And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."<sup>12</sup>Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard.<sup>13</sup>Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you.<sup>14</sup>But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you.<sup>15</sup>Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."<sup>16</sup>Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God."<sup>17</sup>And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.'<sup>19</sup>Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."<sup>20</sup>There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah.<sup>21</sup>And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt.<sup>22</sup>Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him,<sup>23</sup>and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.<sup>24</sup>But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Do Not Hold Back a Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign God sends Jeremiah to preach in the temple court without holding back a word (vv. 1-2). The aim is mercy, that they may turn and God relent (v. 3); if they will not listen, this house will become like Shiloh (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon that could save them is the sermon that will cost the preacher his life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD: Stand in the court of the LORD's house, and speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the LORD all the words that I command you to speak to them; do not hold back a word. It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date, about 609 BC, tells you the temperature of the room. Josiah is dead, killed at Megiddo, and his son Jehoiakim is on the throne. The reform that had cleaned out the shrines is unravelling, and the men who ran it are still in post. Jeremiah is sent into the middle of that — into the temple courtyard, at the season when the worshippers of every town in Judah are streaming in.

Then comes the clause that makes the whole chapter dangerous: do not hold back a word. God knows exactly which sentences his preacher will want to leave out. There is always a way to give a congregation ninety percent of a message and keep the ten percent that would cost something, and the edit is never announced. It is simply that the hard line does not get said.

And here is why the words must not be trimmed. The sermon is not a formality before a verdict already filed; it is God's own attempt to avoid the verdict. It may be they will listen — the offer is real, on the terms the potter laid down: the moment a nation turns, God relents of the disaster (18:7-8). The trimmed sermon is the cruel one, because it withholds the very warning that could have saved them.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.
verseByVerse.note: The reaction to the temple sermon of chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law that I have set before you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets whom I send to you urgently, though you have not listened, then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse for all the nations of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One word does all the damage in this sermon, and it is a place name.

Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations — Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first (7:12). It was not a rival sanctuary or a pagan site. It was the address God himself had chosen. Then Israel carried the ark into battle as a lucky charm, and the day ended with thirty thousand dead and the news that the ark of God was captured (1 Sam 4:11). A dying woman named her baby Ichabod and said The glory has departed from Israel (1 Sam 4:22). By Jeremiah's day Shiloh was a ruin people could walk to and look at.

So the claim is not that God is weak but that God is free. He is not a tenant of any building, and he has already once let his own house be levelled rather than let his name be used as a charm by people who would not obey him.

The promise to Abraham is reversed as well. Jerusalem was to be the place through which the nations were blessed; now it becomes a curse for all the nations of the earth. Privilege abused does not go neutral. It inverts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — You Shall Die: The Prophet on Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests, prophets and people seize him with a death sentence, and the officials convene a court in the New Gate (vv. 7-11). Jeremiah retracts nothing, renews the offer of mercy, puts himself in their hands, and warns them of innocent blood (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers a death sentence by offering his judges the mercy they are refusing.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the LORD had commanded him to speak to all the people, then the priests and the prophets and all the people laid hold of him, saying, "You shall die! Why have you prophesied in the name of the LORD, saying, 'This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate, without inhabitant'?" And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He held nothing back, and the sentence came before he was off the step.

Consider who seizes him. Not the idolaters, not the foreign party, not the street — the priests and the prophets. The clergy. Men whose professional existence was bound up with the building he had just said could fall, standing inside that building, laying hands on the man God had sent to them. Nothing in this scene is irreligious. It is a religious riot.

They quote him correctly. That detail matters, because it removes the usual excuse. This was not a misunderstanding to be cleared up with a better explanation; they had heard him exactly and they wanted him dead for what he had actually said. Offence at the message is not always a failure of communication.

Six centuries later two witnesses would stand in another trial and repeat another temple saying: I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days (Matt 26:61). A word against the house is the charge that gets a prophet killed in this city.

verseByVerse.quote: When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD. Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lynching becomes a trial. The civil officials walk up from the palace, take their seats in the gateway where legal cases were heard, and the mob has to turn into a prosecution. That is a mercy in itself, and it arrives in an ordinary way: God protects his servant here through ordinary civic procedure — men doing their jobs properly.

The charge is capital and the evidence is the sermon. As you have heard with your own ears — there is no need for witnesses, because everyone present heard it. The prosecution's whole case is that the defendant said what God told him to say.

Set that beside the other trial. There they were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, and could not find it (Matt 26:59). Jeremiah's judges needed no lies to convict him; Jesus' judges could not convict him without them. The innocence in the second case had to be manufactured away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard. Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you. But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you. Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His defence opens by repeating the offence. No softening, no clarification that he had been quoted out of context — he says it again, in front of the court, with his life on the table.

And then, astonishingly, he preaches to them. The men conducting his capital trial are offered the way out. He is not fighting for an acquittal; he is still doing the job he was arrested for. A man with nothing left to protect can afford to love his judges.

There is no bargaining here and no bravado either. He does not threaten them with God, and he does not plead. He simply puts himself down in front of them. That kind of composure is not temperament; it comes from being certain who actually sent him. Christ promised the same help to his witnesses on trial: the Spirit of their Father would speak through them (Matt 10:19-20).

Even the warning is for their sake, not his. And it is the exact sentence that another court would one day hear and wave away. A governor washed his hands and said I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves, and the answer came back, His blood be on us and on our children! (Matt 27:24-25). Jeremiah's judges took the warning and lived. The others took the blood — and the mercy of God is that the blood they called down on themselves is the only blood in the world that could wash them, which is precisely what was preached to that city seven weeks later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The officials and people acquit him, because he has spoken in the LORD's name (v. 16). The elders recall Micah, who said the same of Zion a century earlier, and Hezekiah, who sought the LORD instead of killing him (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone in the room had read the prophets and could remember how a king ought to answer one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God." And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying, "Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.' Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict turns on one test, and it is the right one: has he spoken in the name of the LORD? Not is he popular, not is the message good for morale, not will the city's confidence survive it.

The elders save his life with a quotation. A hundred years earlier a country prophet from Moresheth had said this same unthinkable thing about this same city, and the words were still on record — we can still read them at Micah 3:12. Someone in that assembly knew his Bible well enough to recognise that the intolerable sermon had a precedent.

What they may not have quoted is the verse just before it, where Micah names the confidence he was demolishing: Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us (Mic 3:11). That was the theology in the room in Jeremiah's day too. It had not learned a thing in a century.

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Three questions and a conclusion, and the conclusion turns the precedent on the hearers. Hezekiah heard his city sentenced to rubble and responded by seeking God's face, and the city stood. Kill this preacher, the elders say, and the disaster we are trying to avoid is one we will have fetched ourselves.
verseByVerse.note: The elders cite Micah’s prophecy from about a century earlier.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–24 — Uriah, and the Hand of Ahikam
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second precedent cuts the other way. Uriah son of Shemaiah preached the same message, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim (vv. 20-23). The chapter ends on one man, Ahikam son of Shaphan, whose hand was with Jeremiah (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Two faithful prophets, one buried in a pauper's grave and one spared — and God was not absent from either.

verseByVerse.quote: There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah. And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt. Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him, and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the narrator adds a second case, and it does not comfort anybody.

Uriah preached the same message and ran for his life. It is hard not to feel the sympathy in the telling — he was afraid is not written as an accusation. Jeremiah himself had begged God to let him stop (20:9), and the man who never bolted had no room to despise the man who did.

An extradition party, a royal execution, and a body thrown into the public pit. Jehoiakim would not spend an hour listening to a prophet, but he would fund an expedition to Egypt to silence one.

Why is this paragraph in the chapter at all? Because the Bible refuses to sell faithfulness as a survival strategy. Two men preached the same word from the same God in the same decade. One was acquitted and one was murdered, and the difference was not the quality of their obedience. Some escaped the edge of the sword and some were killed by it, and Hebrews 11 puts both in the same chapter of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, one name, and the prophet lives.

Ahikam was a son of Shaphan the scribe — the man who had read the rediscovered book of the law aloud to Josiah and watched the king tear his clothes (2 Kgs 22). This family keeps appearing at the hinges of the story, on the right side each time, and Ahikam's own son Gedaliah will one day be the governor who shelters Jeremiah after the city falls. Generations of quiet faithfulness turn out to be load-bearing.

The verse does not say that God protected Jeremiah, though he did. It says the hand of Ahikam was with him. Providence in this chapter has fingerprints: officials who convened a proper court, elders who remembered a text, and one man with standing who used it. God's care for his servants is very often somebody's decision to stand next to them when it is expensive.

And there the chapter leaves a shadow across the page. Jeremiah was not given over to the people to be put to death. Another prophet stood in that same temple, said that same kind of word about that same house, and was tried by that same court — and when the moment came there was no Ahikam. The officials did not acquit him, no elder rose with a precedent, and his own people asked for a murderer instead. He was given over. The high priest had already explained the arithmetic: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (John 11:50) — truer than he knew. Jeremiah was spared by a friendly hand; Jesus was handed over by his Father's (Acts 2:23; Rom 8:32), and that is why anyone reading this has a hope beyond a fair trial.
verseByVerse.note: Ahikam was the father of Gedaliah, later governor.

26.title: The Trial of Jeremiah
26.overview:
At the start of Jehoiakim's reign God sends Jeremiah into the temple court to preach to every worshipper in Judah, with one condition: he must not hold back a word. If they will not listen, God will make this house like Shiloh and this city a curse among the nations (vv. 1-6).

He preaches it, and the priests and prophets seize him with a death sentence on their lips. The officials come up from the palace and convene a court in the New Gate, where the clergy press a capital charge: he prophesied against this city, and everyone heard him do it (vv. 7-11).

Jeremiah repeats the message rather than retracting it, urges his judges to mend their ways so that God may relent, hands himself over to their judgment, and warns them that killing him will bring innocent blood on the city (vv. 12-15). The officials and the people acquit him, and the elders back the verdict with a precedent: Micah of Moresheth said the same of Zion, and Hezekiah sought God instead of killing him (vv. 16-19).

A darker precedent follows. Uriah son of Shemaiah preached the same word, fled to Egypt, was extradited by Jehoiakim, executed and thrown into a common grave (vv. 20-23). Jeremiah survives because the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with him (v. 24).
26.theology:
The warning is the mercy. God sends the sermon precisely so that he may relent, on the terms of 18:7-8, which is why no word may be held back (vv. 2-3).

God is not the tenant of his own house. Shiloh proves he will let a sanctuary fall rather than be used as a charm by people who will not obey him (v. 6; 7:12-15).

Opposition to the word is often religious, professional and sincere, and it can quote the sermon back accurately (vv. 8-9).

Faithfulness is not a survival strategy. Uriah and Jeremiah preached the same word; one was murdered and one spared, and the difference lay in God's purpose, not their obedience (vv. 20-24).

The trial is a rehearsal. A charge about the temple, a court in this city, and a warning about innocent blood all return at the trial of Jesus — where the verdict goes the other way, and the blood called down becomes the only blood that can cleanse (v. 15; Matt 26:59-61; 27:24-25).
26.examples:
Preaching the ninety percent that costs nothing.

A ruin you can walk to, where God's own house once stood.

Clergy seizing a man inside the building he warned about.

Offering mercy to the court that is trying you.

An elder who had read his Bible well enough to remember Micah.

A royal extradition party sent to silence one preacher.

One man with standing, deciding to stand next to you.

27.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Thus the LORD said to me: "Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck.<sup>3</sup>Send word to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.<sup>4</sup>Give them this charge for their masters: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters:<sup>5</sup>"It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whomever it seems right to me.<sup>6</sup>Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, my servant, and I have given him also the beasts of the field to serve him.<sup>7</sup>All the nations shall serve him and his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.<sup>8</sup>"'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand.<sup>9</sup>So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.'<sup>10</sup>For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish.<sup>11</sup>But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"<sup>12</sup>To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live.<sup>13</sup>Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?<sup>14</sup>Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>15</sup>I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."<sup>16</sup>Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>17</sup>Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation?<sup>18</sup>If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon.<sup>19</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,<sup>20</sup>which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem—<sup>21</sup>thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem:<sup>22</sup>They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Straps, Yoke-Bars, and the Owner of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Early in Zedekiah's reign Jeremiah puts a yoke on his neck and sends a message home with the envoys of five neighbouring kings (vv. 1-3). The God who made the earth gives it to whom he pleases, and he has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, my servant, until Babylon's own time comes (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire everyone was plotting against is on a lease, and the landlord is the one who made the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD. Thus the LORD said to me: "Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck. Send word to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah is Babylon's appointee, put on the throne after Jeconiah was carried off, and the small nations around Judah are already testing whether a coalition could throw the empire off. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “Jehoiakim” here, probably a copyist’s slip carried over from 26:1; a few Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read “Zedekiah”, as the ESV does, and the Greek omits the verse. The scene itself is unmistakably Zedekiah's: his envoys, his court, his crisis (vv. 3, 12; 28:1), in about 594 BC.

And God's instruction is to get dressed. Not to write a letter — to build a wooden yoke, the double bar that goes over an ox's neck with leather straps to hold it, and to wear it. Jeremiah walks the streets of Jerusalem as a draft animal.

He has done this kind of thing before: the ruined loincloth, the smashed flask, the two baskets. A message you can see is harder to forget and harder to argue with, and this one puts the humiliation on the messenger first. Before he asks five kings to accept a yoke, he carries one himself.

The postal arrangements are ironic. The ambassadors have gathered in Jerusalem to organise a revolt, and God uses the conspirators' own delegation to carry his instruction home to their masters. The summit called to plan resistance leaves with a word from the God of Israel in its diplomatic bag.
verseByVerse.note: Yoke bars were wooden beams tied to an animal’s neck — a sign of submission to Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: Give them this charge for their masters: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters: "It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whomever it seems right to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word about politics, a word about creation. These are pagan courts with their own gods, and the God of Israel does not open by arguing his case or asking for a hearing. He states who made the ground they are standing on.

The logic is simple enough that it cannot be evaded. Ownership follows from making. The one who made the earth, and everything walking about on it, is the one entitled to say who holds which part of it — I give it to whomever it seems right to me. Nothing in that sentence submits itself to a vote.

The phrase my great power and my outstretched arm is exodus language, the vocabulary of the night Israel came out of Egypt. It is being used here about the God of a small defeated country, addressed to the superpowers of the region. And Nebuchadnezzar himself would eventually be brought to confess it, after hearing that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Dan 4:25, 34-35).

Paul draws the line that reaches to every government since: there is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1). No regime, however it came to power and however it behaves, is holding anything it was not handed.

Must Christians submit to any government? Judah was told to submit to Babylon because God had given Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom. Christians are to honour and obey rulers (Rom 13:1–7), but never to obey a command to sin: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), as Daniel and his friends showed under the same Babylon (Dan 3; 6).

verseByVerse.quote: Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, my servant, and I have given him also the beasts of the field to serve him. All the nations shall serve him and his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words in that sentence would have stopped the room: my servant.

The title belongs to Moses, to David, to the prophets. It is now given to an idolatrous Babylonian king who worships Marduk, has no interest in the God of Israel, and will burn his temple. He is not called righteous and he is not called godly; he is called useful. God employs men who do not know they are employed, and the wages are settled later. This is the second time the book has said it (25:9), and the shock has not worn off.

And now the lease is read out. Three generations, and then Babylon's own turn on the block — many nations and great kings shall make him their slave. The empire that looks permanent has an expiry date already written into the message announcing its power.

That is the double comfort of this chapter for anyone living under something they cannot change. The power over you is real, and it is temporary, and both of those facts are God's doing. Submission to it is not the confession that it is ultimate; it is the confession that God is.

Who are the son and grandson? Nebuchadnezzar’s son Evil-merodach succeeded him (52:31), and after a few short reigns Babylon fell in 539 BC under Nabonidus and his son Belshazzar, who reigned alongside him (Dan 5). They were probably not Nebuchadnezzar’s descendants by blood, though Daniel 5 calls him Belshazzar’s “father” in the ancient sense of predecessor. The phrase most likely means a span of about three generations, and Babylon’s empire did not outlast it: it fell some sixty-five years after Nebuchadnezzar came to the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The terms are stark: refuse the yoke and face sword, famine and pestilence; bear it and stay on your land, and do not listen to the diviners who say otherwise (vv. 8-11). Zedekiah hears the same terms, and the prophets promising independence are disowned (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Submission is the way to live, and the comforting sermon is the one that kills.

verseByVerse.quote: "'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand. So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.' For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish. But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three-fold sentence of this book — sword, famine, pestilence — now falls on the nations for a political decision, because the political decision is a religious one. Refusing the yoke means refusing the hand that placed it.

Five kinds of religious professional, and every one of them predicting what the king wanted to hear. Independence sells. It always has, in every court and every pulpit, and the market for it does not care whether it is true.

Trace the chain in that last clause, because it is the anatomy of a comfortable lie: they prophesy, you believe, you resist, you are driven out, you perish. The falsehood does not stay in the sermon. It ends up costing the land and the lives of the people who found it encouraging.

And there is the mercy inside the sentence. Accept the yoke and you keep your fields, your house and your ordinary life. Judgment is being offered with a survivable form, which is more than justice required.

verseByVerse.quote: To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live. Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same word to Judah as to Moab, with no discount for the covenant. Judah has the temple, the promises and the line of David, and the instruction is identical: bend your neck and live.

Why will you and your people die is not rhetorical cruelty; it is the question of a God who does not want this. He asks the king outright why he would choose it, which is the tone of a man reasoning with someone about to walk off a cliff.

The disowning is total: I have not sent them. They were using the name, the formulas and probably the same solemn voice, and the God they invoked had no part in any of it.

And they go down with their congregation — you and the prophets who are prophesying to you. A preacher who tells people what they want does not escape the wreck he talked them into. Within a chapter one of them, Hananiah, will walk up and snap the yoke off Jeremiah's neck (28:10-11), promising the vessels back inside two years (28:3). He will be dead before the year is out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Test of a Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests and people are being told, Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon (v. 16). It is a lie, and Jeremiah answers it with a test rather than an argument: If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts that the vessels still in Jerusalem may not be taken too (v. 18). Then he names the furniture — the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city (v. 19) — the great bronze fittings of Solomon's temple, still standing where everyone could see them.
verseByVerse.theology: A true prophet prays; a false one predicts, and the test is whether he will get on his knees.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation? If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon. For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The popular sermon has found its subject, and it is a good one. Nebuchadnezzar had already taken temple treasure away, first under Jehoiakim — with some of the vessels of the house of God, as Daniel puts it (Dan 1:2) — and again with Jeconiah (2 Kgs 24:13) — and the promise going round Jerusalem was that the gold would be back shortly. Restoration without repentance, and soon.

Again the plea, and again the offer of life. God is arguing for the city's survival while the popular prophets are the ones marching it toward ruin.

Here is the test, and it is a beautiful one. If these men really have God's ear, let them use it. Stop forecasting and start praying. Intercession is the work of a true prophet — Abraham for Sodom, Moses on the mountain, Samuel for Israel — and a man who only ever announces good outcomes has never once had to plead for one.

The inventory is deliberate. The pillars Jachin and Boaz, the great bronze sea, the wheeled stands — the immovable landmarks of Solomon's temple, the things a Jerusalemite would have pointed to as proof that some things never change. Those are the items on the removal list.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — Until the Day When I Visit Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vessels Nebuchadnezzar left behind when he deported Jeconiah and the nobles (v. 20) are the subject of the last word, and the sentence on them is loss followed by recovery: They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is not that nothing will be lost, but that God knows the day he will come for what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem— thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What survived the first deportation will not survive the second. The comfort people had drawn from the leftovers was misplaced; the fact that the pillars were still standing proved only that God had not finished speaking.

And the chapter ends by refusing both of the easy positions. The optimists said the vessels would be home within two years; they were wrong. But the despairing, watching the bronze loaded onto carts, would have said they were gone for good, and they were wrong too.

God keeps the date himself: until the day when I visit them. Not two years, not never — his day. And it came. Decades later a Persian king who had never read this page gave the order, and Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem (Ezra 1:7), counted out piece by piece to a prince of Judah. God had told them the bowls were coming back, and the bowls came back.

Yet the last word of the chapter is still a yoke on a prophet's shoulders, and that image does not rest until another Prophet takes it up. He told the truth about a temple's fall and was killed for it; he stood before a governor and said what Jeremiah said to the nations — You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above (John 19:11). And having borne the weight that breaks men, he says: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt 11:29). Babylon's yoke bought survival in a ruined land. His yoke is easy, his burden is light, and it carries you home.

27.title: The Yoke of Babylon
27.overview:
Early in Zedekiah's reign, with the envoys of five neighbouring kings gathered in Jerusalem to plan a revolt, God tells Jeremiah to make straps and yoke-bars, wear them on his neck, and send a message to their masters by the hand of those same envoys (vv. 1-3).

The message argues from creation: the God who made the earth gives it to whomever he pleases, and he has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, whom he calls his servant. The nations will serve him, his son and his grandson, and then Babylon's own time will come (vv. 4-7). Any nation refusing the yoke faces sword, famine and pestilence; any nation accepting it stays on its own land. So they must not listen to their prophets, diviners and sorcerers, who are lying (vv. 8-11).

Zedekiah hears the same terms — serve and live — and the prophets promising independence are disowned outright: God did not send them, and they will perish alongside the people who believed them (vv. 12-15).

To the priests and people Jeremiah answers the popular claim that the temple vessels will shortly return. Let these prophets intercede, if the word of the LORD is really with them, that the pillars, the sea and the stands are not taken too (vv. 16-19). They will be taken, and they will stay in Babylon until the day God visits them; then he will bring them back (vv. 20-22).
27.theology:
God's right over the nations rests on creation, not on covenant privilege: he made the earth and gives it to whomever it seems right to him (v. 5; Dan 4:25; Rom 13:1).

A pagan idolater can be called God's servant without being called godly (v. 6; 25:9). God uses men who do not know they are being used, and Babylon's own lease has an end written into the same message that announces its power (v. 7).

Judgment comes with a survivable form. Bearing the yoke means keeping house and field; the mercy is inside the sentence (v. 11).

The mark of a false prophet is that he flatters and forecasts; the mark of a true one is that he intercedes (v. 18). And a lie told from God's name costs the hearers their land and the preacher his life (vv. 15, 22; 28:10-11).

God times his own restoration. Not two years and not never, but the day when he visits — kept to the letter under Cyrus (v. 22; Ezra 1:7-8). The yoke itself finds its rest only in Christ, who submitted to an authority given from above and offers a yoke that is easy (John 19:11; Matt 11:28-30).
27.examples:
A prophet walking through the city wearing an ox's harness.

A conspiracy's own ambassadors carrying God's message home.

An idolatrous emperor with the title that belonged to Moses and David.

Five kinds of religious expert, all predicting independence.

Stop forecasting and start praying: the test nobody volunteered for.

Bronze pillars everyone assumed would always be there.

Temple bowls counted out, one by one, decades later.

28.text: <sup>1</sup>In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.<sup>3</sup>Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon.<sup>4</sup>I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."<sup>5</sup>Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles.<sup>7</sup>Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.<sup>8</sup>The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms.<sup>9</sup>As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."<sup>10</sup>Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them.<sup>11</sup>And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.<sup>12</sup>Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron.<sup>14</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"<sup>15</sup>And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie.<sup>16</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'"<sup>17</sup>In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Have Broken the Yoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the temple, before priests and people, Hananiah son of Azzur announces in the LORD's name that Babylon's yoke is broken, and that within two years the vessels, the exiles and King Jeconiah will be back (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the packaging is correct, and the contents are a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon. I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year is about 594 BC. At the beginning of the reign and the fourth year sound contradictory, but the first phrase probably means the earlier part of Zedekiah's eleven-year reign, as in 27:1; the Greek simply reads “in the fourth year”.

Everything about this scene is credentialled. A named man from a known priestly town, standing in the temple, with the clergy and the congregation as his audience, using the full formula — Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel. If you were grading the delivery you would give him full marks.

And the content is the exact reverse of what God had just said through the man wearing the yoke. Not a shading of it, not a softer version: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon, spoken in the first person as God's own speech. Two men in one city, both saying thus says the LORD, saying opposite things.

The lie is generous. The gold comes home, the deportees come home, the rightful king comes home, and it all happens inside two years — soon enough to plan for, not so soon as to be tested next week. Nothing is asked of anybody. No repentance, no change, no turning; simply a reversal handed over by God to people who had earned nothing.

That is the shape false comfort always takes. It offers everything the true word offers, minus the repentance, and on a shorter timetable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Amen, and Yet Hear This Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah's first answer is a prayer that Hananiah were right (vv. 5-6). Then the turn: the prophets of old mostly announced war, so a prophet of peace is proved sent only when his word comes to pass (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who wants the comfortable message to be true, and will not say it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD, and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles. Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of all the things a man in his position might have said, he says amen.

That one word settles the question of what kind of man Jeremiah was. He had been called a traitor for decades, mocked, beaten, put in the stocks, tried for his life — and when a rival announces that the whole burden is lifted, his first instinct is to wish it were so. May the LORD do so. No relish in the bad news. No investment in being proved right.

That is one of the surest marks of a true messenger. A man who enjoys announcing judgment has stopped loving the people he is announcing it to, and the tone of his message has already begun to falsify it. Jeremiah's tears run through this whole book for exactly this reason: he never wanted a word of it to be true.

And then the yet. Love for the promise does not license him to endorse it. He will say what he wishes were true and then say what is, in public, in front of the same crowd, without pretending the two are the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms. As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument is historical, and it is disarmingly modest — Jeremiah does not claim a superior experience or a better vision. He points at the record. Look at the men God has actually sent across the centuries, he says, and see what they mostly had to say to comfortable nations. It was not congratulation.

That does not make gloom a credential. Scripture is full of promise, and Jeremiah himself will write chapters 30 to 33. The point is narrower: a message which asks nothing of its hearers and confirms what they already want has very little precedent among the men God commissioned.

So the burden of proof is placed on the preacher of peace, and the test is the plain one from the law: when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken (Deut 18:22). Wait and see is not scepticism here; it is obedience to an explicit instruction.

And the law adds a second filter that keeps the first from being crude. A sign can come true and the man still be false, if what he teaches leads you away from God — you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams (Deut 13:3). Fulfilment alone never settles it. A prophet is judged by outcome and by fidelity together, which is why the Lord's own summary is You will recognize them by their fruits (Matt 7:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hananiah answers with theatre, breaking the yoke-bars off Jeremiah's neck, and Jeremiah, with nothing to say, goes his way (vv. 10-11). Later the word comes: the wooden bars have been replaced with iron (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Breaking the sign does not cancel the sentence; it only exchanges wood for iron.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them. And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He does not answer the argument. He performs.

It is a superb piece of staging: walk up to the old man in the harness, snap the bars off his neck in front of the crowd, and let the sound of splitting wood be the sermon. Prop-prophecy was a known technique — another court prophet once made for himself horns of iron to promise a king his victory (1 Kgs 22:11) — and it works on a crowd the way a gesture always beats a paragraph.

And he has stolen Jeremiah's own method. The yoke, the loincloth, the smashed flask were all visual sermons; now the visual sermon is turned against the man who wore it, and the audience goes home having watched Babylon's power break in the temple courtyard.

Then Jeremiah simply went his way. He does not shout, produce a second yoke, or defend his reputation. He has no word from God about this, so he says nothing about it, and walks out of the temple publicly humiliated.

Silence like that is not weakness; it is the discipline of a man who will not manufacture a message to win an argument. He would rather lose the room than invent a sentence God had not given him — and he is willing to look beaten for as long as God leaves him without an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sometime after. Not that hour, and not while the crowd was still there to see him vindicated. God's servant had to carry the defeat for a while before he was given anything to say, and the delay was not neglect. Vindication on Hananiah's schedule would have been a smaller thing than vindication on God's.

Here is the answer, and it is devastating in its economy. The gesture worked — the wood really did break. It simply had no authority over the thing the wood stood for. All Hananiah achieved by snapping the sign was to exchange it for a harder one.

That principle reaches a long way past this courtyard. A word from God is not disarmed by being defied; resistance does not remove the yoke, it changes its metal. Sin's consequences are not avoided by breaking the warning; they harden.

The terms of chapter 27 are restated with the metal upgraded, and the closing phrase gives away the scale of the claim. Even the wild animals are assigned. A God who allocates the beasts of the field is not negotiating about the borders of Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — You Have Made This People Trust in a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah tells Hananiah to his face that the LORD has not sent him and pronounces the law's sentence on a presumptuous prophet (vv. 15-16). Two months later Hananiah is dead (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: He had two years to be proved right and was given two months.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'" In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two charges, and the second is the graver one. The LORD has not sent you — the man had no commission, whatever he sincerely believed. This is the book's standing verdict on the professionals: I did not send the prophets, yet they ran (23:21).

Then: you have made this people trust in a lie. The damage is not to Jeremiah, and it is not chiefly Hananiah's private guilt. A whole congregation has been persuaded to rest its weight on something that will not hold it, and they will still be resting on it when the Babylonians come. False comfort is not a harmless over-optimism; it is a floor built over a hole. The same book says it of the same trade: they healed the wound lightly, saying Peace, peace, when there was no peace (6:14).

The sentence is the law's own, written centuries earlier for precisely this case: the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak... that same prophet shall die (Deut 18:20). And the charge is named exactly — not error, not enthusiasm, but rebellion against the LORD. Speaking for God without being sent is treated as an act of war against him.

Does this mean false teachers should be put to death today? No. Here God himself carries out the sentence; Jeremiah lays no hand on Hananiah. The church bears no sword: it answers false teaching by refuting it from Scripture, warning, and finally refusing fellowship to those who will not turn (Titus 1:9–11; 3:10; 2 John 10), while praying that God may grant them repentance (2 Tim 2:25).

One flat line, two months after the promise. He had asked for two years and was given the seventh month. The verification Jeremiah had told the crowd to wait for arrived quickly, and it fell on the prophet instead of the prophecy.

The warning has never expired — there will be false teachers among you (2 Pet 2:1) — and the shape has not changed either: full assurance, no repentance, a short timetable. But between the two men in the temple stands a third. One prophet died because he spoke a word God had not given him. The other was the Prophet who spoke nothing except what the Father gave him (John 12:49), who went his way in silence when he was contradicted, and who was put to death all the same. Hananiah died for his own lie; Jesus died for ours — and the iron yoke that our lies keep forging was laid on his shoulders, so that the yoke now offered to us is the one he calls easy.
verseByVerse.note: Hananiah died two months later, as Jeremiah said.

28.title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
28.overview:
In Zedekiah's fourth year, in the temple and before the priests and people, Hananiah son of Azzur announces in God's name that the yoke of Babylon is broken, and that within two years the temple vessels, the exiles and King Jeconiah will all be back (vv. 1-4).

Jeremiah answers first with a prayer that it were true — amen, may the LORD do so — and then with a warning. The prophets God has sent through the centuries have mostly announced war, famine and pestilence to comfortable nations; so a prophet of peace is proved genuine only when his word comes to pass (vv. 5-9).

Hananiah replies with a gesture instead of an argument, breaking the yoke-bars off Jeremiah's neck in front of the crowd and promising Babylon's yoke broken within two years. Jeremiah, with no word from God to give, says nothing and walks away. Later the word comes: the broken wooden bars have been replaced with iron, and an iron yoke is on the neck of all these nations (vv. 10-14).

Jeremiah then tells Hananiah to his face that the LORD did not send him and that he has made the people trust in a lie, and pronounces the law's sentence on a presumptuous prophet: this year you shall die. Two months later Hananiah was dead (vv. 15-17).
28.theology:
Orthodox form is no guarantee of a true word. Hananiah has the formula, the venue, the audience and the confidence, and none of it makes him sent (vv. 1-2, 15; 23:21).

False comfort offers everything the true word offers, minus repentance and on a shorter timetable, and its real victims are the hearers who rest their weight on it (vv. 3-4, 15; 6:14).

A true messenger takes no pleasure in judgment. Jeremiah's amen shows a man who would rather be wrong than see his people ruined (v. 6).

Scripture supplies the tests and expects them to be used: fulfilment (Deut 18:21-22) together with fidelity (Deut 13:1-3), which is the Lord's own rule of fruit (Matt 7:16).

Defiance does not cancel a decree; it hardens it. Wooden bars broken become bars of iron (v. 13).

Faithfulness sometimes means public silence while God withholds an answer, and waiting for vindication on his timetable rather than manufacturing one (vv. 11-12).
28.examples:
Full marks for delivery, and the opposite of the truth.

A promise of everything restored, with nothing asked of anybody.

Saying amen to the message you are about to contradict.

Snapping the old man's harness in front of the congregation.

Walking out of the temple beaten, with nothing from God to say.

Wood exchanged for iron.

Two years asked for; the seventh month granted.
