verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Loved with an Everlasting Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God grounds the whole chapter in an everlasting love older than Israel's failure (vv. 1-3). So the ruined nation will be built again, with dancing and vineyards, and gathered from the ends of the earth, the weakest among them, by a father and shepherd, until their mourning turns to joy (vv. 4-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything promised here rests on a love that started before the ruin and did not depend on it ending.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people." Thus says the LORD: "The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; when Israel sought for rest, the LORD appeared to him from far away. I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with the sentence the whole Bible is driving at, and it opens with all the clans — the ten tribes lost to Assyria more than a century before, written off by everyone as gone, included by name.

The picture reaches back to the exodus — survivors of the sword, out in the desert, finding grace there. That was the pattern once and it will be the pattern again: God meets his people in the wilderness, not after they have got themselves home.

The ESV notes that where the main text reads that the LORD appeared to him from far away, following the Septuagint, the Hebrew reads "me". Either way the striking thing stands: God appears, and the distance is crossed from his side.

I have loved you with an everlasting love is the ground of everything that follows in this chapter, and it is not anything in them.

Weigh the word everlasting. A love with no beginning cannot have been started by anything Israel did, and a love with no end cannot be stopped by anything Israel did either. It was not switched on by her obedience in the wilderness and it was not switched off by her adultery in Canaan.

And then therefore. God's faithfulness is not the cause of his love but its consequence. He keeps on with this people because he loved them first — which is the only explanation the Bible ever gives for why any of us are still here.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! Again you shall adorn yourself with tambourines and shall go forth in the dance of the merrymakers. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit. For there shall be a day when watchmen will call in the hill country of Ephraim: 'Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times in two verses: Again. Again built, again dancing, again planting. The word is doing pastoral work, because the fear of a ruined people is not that God is unable but that the good days are simply over.

And consider what he calls her. O virgin Israel — spoken to the nation this book has called a prostitute, a faithless wife, a camel in heat. The name is not a polite fiction; it is what God intends to make her, and he uses the future name now.

The restoration is not solemn. It is tambourines and dancing, the noise of a village wedding.

Samaria is the old northern capital, the heartland of the tribes everyone had given up on, and the promise is of vineyards there — a crop that takes years to bear, planted by people who expect to be around to drink the wine. The curse of sowing what others eat is lifted.

And the most unlikely sentence yet. Watchmen in Ephraim — northern territory, where the rival shrines had stood for two centuries specifically so nobody would go up to Zion — now shouting at their own people to go and worship in Jerusalem. The schism that split the kingdom is healed from the northern side.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob, and raise shouts for the chief of the nations; proclaim, give praise, and say, 'O LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel.' Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, together; a great company, they shall return here. With weeping they shall come, and with pleas for mercy I will lead them back, I will make them walk by brooks of water, in a straight path in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are told to sing the rescue before it happens, and to pray for it in the same breath. Praise and petition are not two stages here; the certainty of the promise is exactly what makes the asking confident.

Consider who is on this march. Not the fit and the useful, but the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor — the four categories any commander would leave behind, because a column moves at the pace of its slowest member.

God lists them deliberately. A rescue that quietly loses the weak on the road is not the rescue he is describing; nobody here is expendable, and the party travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

They come home crying. The tears are not a failure of faith but the sound of repentance, and God leads a weeping people gently — brooks of water, level ground, a road chosen so the lame will not stumble on it.

And the reason is family: I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. Ephraim, of all names — the tribe that led the rebellion, the shorthand for everything that went wrong in the north, called the firstborn son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, 'He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.' For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him from hands too strong for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are called as witnesses. They had watched the scattering and drawn the obvious conclusion — that Israel's God was weak, or finished — and now they are told to publish the correction as far as the coastlands reach.

The sentence they must carry holds the two halves together without flinching: He who scattered Israel will gather him. Not a rival power scattered them. The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the hand that drove the flock apart is the hand that keeps it.

Two words from the slave market and the family law court — ransomed, redeemed — and a phrase that explains why any of this had to be God's work: from hands too strong for him.

That is the honest assessment. Jacob was not held by something he could have shaken off with more effort. Babylon was stronger than him, and so was the sin that put him there. Self-rescue was never on the table, which is why the verb throughout this chapter is always in the first person: I will build, I will gather, I will lead, I have ransomed.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall come and sing aloud on the height of Zion, and they shall be radiant over the goodness of the LORD, over the grain, the wine, and the oil, and over the young of the flock and the herd; their life shall be like a watered garden, and they shall languish no more. Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy; I will comfort them, and give them gladness for sorrow. I will feast the soul of the priests with abundance, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Radiant over the goodness of the LORD. Their faces shine, and the thing they are shining about is named — grain, wine, oil, lambs, calves. Ordinary provision, received as goodness from a person.

The image of the watered garden would land hard on people who knew what a dry season did to a field. Everything in this book about drought, cracked cisterns and withered pasture is reversed in four words.

Three generations dancing in the same sentence — girls, young men, the old. The community that lost its future is given one with children in it.

And the verb is turn: I will turn their mourning into joy. Not replace the mourning with joy once it has run its course, but turn the thing itself. The grief is not deleted from their history; it is converted, which is a harder and better promise.

The word to end on is satisfied. This book opened with people digging broken cisterns that could hold no water, forsaking the fountain; it promises here that the thirst will finally be met, and met with God's own goodness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Rachel's Tears and Ephraim's Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rachel weeps for her children, and God answers her tears with the promise that they will come back (vv. 15-17). He has overheard Ephraim praying to be brought back, and answers with a father's yearning and mercy (vv. 18-20); Israel is to mark the road home (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: God overhears a prayer for the very turning he commands, and answers it with yearning.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more." Thus says the LORD: "Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, declares the LORD, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back to their own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the singing, someone is crying, and God stops the chapter to listen.

Rachel is Jacob's beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and tradition placed her tomb in Benjamin's territory near Ramah (1 Sam 10:2). Ramah is where the deportees were mustered in chains before the walk to Babylon. So the poem pictures the long-dead mother of the northern tribes waking to watch her descendants marched past her grave, and weeping — and she refuses to be comforted, which is not rebuked here. Some griefs should not be talked out of themselves too quickly. Parents who have buried a child may take that as permission: God does not hurry their tears, and he answers them, as he does here, with a promise rather than a lecture.

Matthew heard this verse again on a night in Bethlehem when soldiers came for the children: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more (Matt 2:18). The mothers of Bethlehem wept while the child who would end all such weeping was carried to safety in Egypt.

God does not answer the tears with an explanation. He answers them with a fact: they shall come back.

And he calls her grief your work, with a reward attached — the years of weeping over lost children counted as labour that will be paid. There is hope for your future is said to a woman in a graveyard, which is the only place that sentence ever needs saying.

How does Herod’s slaughter “fulfil” this? Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping at Ramah for her children going into exile, with God’s promise that they will return (vv. 16–17). Matthew sees the same grief at Bethlehem, near Rachel’s tomb, and the same hope: the Child who escaped would bring the true return from exile (Matt 2:17–18). Scripture links Rachel’s tomb both with the road to Bethlehem (Gen 35:19) and with Benjamin’s territory (1 Sam 10:2); Ramah and Bethlehem both lie a few miles from Jerusalem, and Matthew’s point is the pattern, not the map. “Fulfil” here means that the exile’s grief, and its promised end, reach their full meaning in Jesus’ story.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay north of Jerusalem, on the road into exile. Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps for her “children.” Matthew applies it to Herod’s killing of Bethlehem’s infants.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard Ephraim grieving, 'You have disciplined me, and I was disciplined, like an untrained calf; bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God. For after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth.' Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has been listening to his son talk to himself.

The image Ephraim reaches for is honest: like an untrained calf, a young animal that fights the yoke, bucks, and has to be broken to be any use. He does not dispute the discipline or ask for it to stop.

And then the prayer that lies at the heart of all true conversion: bring me back that I may be restored. He asks God to do the turning. He knows he cannot return under his own steam, and this is the answer to the question the book has pressed since the leopard and its spots — the return God commands is the return God must give.

Striking the thigh is a gesture of grief at oneself. The order in the sentence matters: the turning came first, then the instruction, then the shame. Real repentance is usually the last thing to arrive, not the first — shame here is the fruit of being brought back, not the fee for it.

Two questions, and God answers them by the way he asks them. Even while pronouncing judgment — as often as I speak against him — he never stopped remembering him.

Where the ESV has my heart yearns for him, the note records that the Hebrew word is "bowels": the physical seat of feeling, the churn you feel in your stomach over someone you love. This is not benign divine goodwill. It is a father who cannot get his son out of his mind.
verseByVerse.note: “My heart yearns” is literally “my bowels” (ESV note) — the seat of deep feeling.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up road markers for yourself; make yourself guideposts; consider well the highway, the road by which you went. Return, O virgin Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman encircles a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A practical instruction for people about to be marched away: mark the route. Pile the stones, note the landmarks, pay attention to the road you are being taken along, because you are coming back down it.

It is a strange kind of comfort — plan your return journey while you are still going out — and it treats the promise as solid enough to survey.

The rebuke is gentle and impatient at once: How long will you waver? The wavering is the old habit of hedging between God and the alternatives.

Then a line that has puzzled readers for as long as there have been readers, and it is better to say so than to pretend otherwise. The words are plain — a woman encircles a man — and the sense is not. What the verse does make clear is its frame: this is a new thing that the LORD has created, and created is the verb Genesis uses when God makes the heavens and the earth.

Something is coming that reverses the expected order, and it will be God's own creation rather than Israel's achievement. That is as far as the text takes us, and it is the same direction the rest of the chapter runs: the faithless daughter will be made new by an act of creation, not by finally pulling herself together.

“A woman encircles a man” is one of the hardest lines in Jeremiah. The likeliest sense is a reversal of the natural order, a new thing God will do: Israel, the faithless daughter (v. 22), will embrace and cling to her LORD. Some early Christians saw the virgin conceiving a son, but that reads more into the words than they say.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — Watching to Build and to Plant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's towns will bless Jerusalem again, the weary will be satisfied, and the prophet wakes from a sweet sleep (vv. 23-26). The God who watched over the tearing down will watch over the building and planting, and the sour-grapes proverb is retired (vv. 27-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The same watchfulness that pulled the nation down is now set to building it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Once more they shall use these words in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their fortunes: "'The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill!' And Judah and all its cities shall dwell there together, and the farmers and those who wander with their flocks. For I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish." At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An old blessing comes back into everyday use — the sort of thing neighbours say to each other in the street. And the name it uses for Jerusalem is habitation of righteousness, which is precisely what the city had stopped being.

The picture in the next line is of ordinary society knitted back together: settled farmers and wandering herdsmen living in the same land without preying on each other.

Two words for exhaustion — weary and languishing — and two promises, to satisfy and to replenish. This is the pastoral centre of the chapter for anyone reading it tired.

And here the prophet himself appears, waking up.

Think of what this man's nights had been like: the boiling pot, the drought, the broken flask, the trial for his life, the stocks, the day he cursed his own birth. Now, after being shown all this, he wakes and records that his sleep had been sweet. It is the only moment of personal comfort he is given in the entire book, and it comes from having seen what God intends to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast. And it shall come to pass that as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land that was emptied gets resown, and the metaphor is agricultural: God scatters people across it as a farmer scatters grain. Both houses again, and livestock with them — a country coming back to life at the level of herds.

These are the verbs of Jeremiah's commission (1:10), forty years on, with one more added to the demolition. For four decades he has been fulfilling the first four, and here the last two finally get their turn with the same divine attentiveness behind them.

The repeated word is watched over. God was not careless in the demolition and he will not be casual in the rebuilding. The same vigilance that saw every stage of the tearing down is now fixed on the building and planting — which means the ruin was never a loss of control, and the restoration will not be left to chance.

For a man who had spent his life announcing the first four verbs, it must have been something to be told that he had always been serving the last two.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days they shall no longer say: "'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But everyone shall die for his own iniquity. Each man who eats sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proverb was the popular theology of a defeated generation, and it was a complaint: our grandfathers sinned and we are the ones with our teeth on edge. There was something true in it — consequences do run downhill through families and nations — but as they used it, it was a way of saying that nothing they did mattered either way.

Ezekiel was told to stop the same saying among the exiles: this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel (Ezek 18:3).

The answer is not that inherited consequence is a myth. It is that no one will be able to hide behind it. Everyone shall die for his own iniquity — each person dealt with by God directly, for what he himself has done.

That sounds severe until you see where it sits. It comes immediately before the new covenant, where God deals with each person individually in mercy — writing on this heart, knowing this man, forgetting these sins. The end of hiding behind your ancestors is also the end of being trapped by them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a new covenant, unlike the one Israel broke after the exodus (vv. 31-32): the law written on their hearts, every member knowing him, and their sin forgiven and remembered no more (vv. 33-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The law moves from tablets to hearts, and the sins move out of God's memory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the sentence the rest of the Bible is built on, and the phrase new covenant is a rare one in the Old Testament — this is where it is given.

Consider who says it and when. A prophet standing in a doomed city, watching the old arrangement collapse around him, announces that God's answer is not a repair. It is a new covenant — and the promise is made to the same two houses that had just finished breaking the old one.

The tenderness of the memory is startling: the day when I took them by the hand, like a father teaching a child to walk out of Egypt. That is how God remembers the exodus.

And then the failure, stated without excuse — my covenant that they broke — followed by five words that carry the ache of the whole book: though I was their husband. The problem with the old covenant was never its terms, which were holy, or its giver. It was that one party to a marriage kept the vows and the other did not.

Hebrews quotes this passage at length and draws the conclusion: God finds fault with them (Heb 8:8), not with the covenant. A law written on stone can tell you what to do and cannot make you want to do it.

Is the new covenant with Israel or with the church? It is promised to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Dispensationalists hold that it awaits fulfilment with national Israel. But Jesus established it in his blood at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes this passage of the church (Heb 8:6–13). It is made with the true Israel, Jews and Gentiles who believe in Christ (Gal 6:16; Rom 11:17). Many dispensationalists today agree that the church already shares in its blessings through Christ, while still expecting a future fulfilment for national Israel; faithful Christians differ on that second part. This commentary’s reason for its reading is that the New Testament applies the whole promise, forgiveness and the law on the heart, to every believer now (Heb 10:15–18).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers hear this as God's promise to renew, not replace, the covenant of Sinai: the same Torah, written no longer only on stone but on Israel's heart, so that the people at last keep it. Many place its fulfilment in the days of the Messiah, and note that it is made with Israel and Judah. This commentary agrees that the law is not changed but written within, and that the promise belongs to Israel. It reads it as begun in Jesus, who called the cup the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), and as opened to Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17).
verseByVerse.note: The only place in the Old Testament that speaks of a “new covenant.” Jesus inaugurated it at the Last Supper.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law does not change. Its address does.

The old covenant put God's commands on tablets outside the man, where they instructed him and condemned him and could not help him. The new one puts the same law within them and writes it on their hearts — which answers precisely the diagnosis this book has been making for thirty chapters: sin engraved on the tablet of the heart (17:1), a heart deceitful above all things (17:9), a people who could no more change than a leopard could change its spots (13:23). If the problem is the heart, only a new heart is a solution.

Paul saw it happen in his converts: a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3).

Under the old arrangement the covenant community was a mixed body — circumcised men who did not know God at all, which is why they had to be told to know him. In the new one, membership and knowing God are the same thing. Not that teaching ends, but that nobody inside this covenant needs to be introduced to its God. They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest — the child and the scholar on the same footing.

And then the foundation, introduced with For, because it is the reason the rest is possible: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Not overlook, not suspend. God puts his people's sin out of his own memory.

It cost him everything to be able to say it. On the last night, holding a cup, the Lord told his friends what would make this covenant new in fact and not only in promise: This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). Hebrews, having quoted these verses twice, rests the whole assurance of a Christian on the final clause — I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more (Heb 10:17).

If all in the new covenant shall know the LORD, what of a church with unbelievers in it? Paedobaptists hold that the covenant community, like Israel, includes the children of believers, and some who do not truly know God. Baptists answer that this verse marks the difference between the covenants: in the new, every member knows the Lord, so the church should receive by baptism those who profess faith. The second reading fits the verse best, though no church can see hearts perfectly. That is the view of the 1689 London Baptist Confession, which this commentary follows; Presbyterian and other paedobaptist brothers, with the Westminster Confession, read the covenants as more continuous, and they hold their view from Scripture with equal seriousness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–40 — As Fixed as the Sunrise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes Israel's future on the fixed order of sun, moon and stars (vv. 35-37). The city is surveyed for rebuilding, and even the valley of the dead bodies and the ashes is declared sacred to the LORD forever (vv. 38-40).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where they burned their children is the last plot of land God claims as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name: "If this fixed order departs from before me, declares the LORD, then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation before me forever." Thus says the LORD: "If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the guarantee, the credentials. The God about to make a promise is the one who runs the solar system and the tides.

The logic is a chain with a hinge: Israel's continuance is as secure as sunrise. Anyone doubting the promise is invited to test it against the evidence available every morning.

And this is said about a nation that was, at that moment, being dismantled. Its survival was not a projection from its circumstances. It was staked on the constancy of the God who keeps the moon in its course.

The second guarantee is built on immensity rather than regularity: measure the sky, survey the foundations of the earth, and then we can discuss rejection.

The last clause is honest: for all that they have done. God does not minimise the record. The guilt is real and it is not the deciding factor, because the question was never whether they deserved to be cast off. Paul was still resting on this when he wrote that God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1-2).

Does this guarantee ethnic Israel’s future as a nation? It promises that God will never cast off the offspring of Israel. Paul says the same: God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1–2), and, on the most natural reading, he looks for a great turning of Jews to Christ (Rom 11:26). That is a promise of salvation, not of a modern state or territory. Faithful Christians differ on whether the modern State of Israel has a place in prophecy; this commentary holds that the promise here is God’s faithfulness to save, while gladly affirming that Jewish people remain beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Rom 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther, straight to the hill Gareb, and shall then turn to Goah. The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes, and all the fields as far as the brook Kidron, to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a survey. Named towers, named gates, a measuring line pulled across specific hills — the promise given as a plan an engineer could work from.

And the line goes farther. Gareb and Goah can no longer be located, but the picture seems to be of a city larger than the one about to be destroyed.

Of every acre God could have chosen for the last word of this chapter, he takes the worst one.

The valley of the dead bodies and the ashes is most likely the ravine below the city, the Valley of Hinnom — the place Jeremiah had stood with a clay flask and called the Valley of Slaughter, where they had burned their own children to Baal (19:5-6). It was the most defiled ground in Israel, and its name became the New Testament's word for hell.

That valley, God says, shall be sacred to the LORD.

The book that began by measuring a nation's guilt ends this chapter by measuring a city that includes its own worst place inside the holy ground. This is what the new covenant does. It does not quarantine the shameful part of the record and build around it; it takes the ash heap into the city and calls it holy, and it fixes the boundary with a promise that has no expiry — It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever. The verbs of the demolition are used one last time, in the negative, and put beyond recall.

31.title: The New Covenant
31.overview:
God promises to be the God of all the clans of Israel, and grounds it in an everlasting love that explains his continued faithfulness. The ruined nation will be built again, dancing with tambourines and planting vineyards in Samaria, with watchmen in Ephraim calling people up to Zion. He will gather them from the ends of the earth — the blind, the lame and women in labour among them — leading them by brooks of water as a father, so that their life is like a watered garden and their mourning is turned into joy (vv. 1-14).

Rachel is heard weeping for her lost children and refusing comfort, and God answers her with a promise that they will come back. He repeats Ephraim's own prayer — bring me back that I may be restored — and responds with yearning and mercy. Israel is told to mark the road home, and a new thing is announced that God himself has created (vv. 15-22).

Judah's towns will bless Jerusalem again, the weary soul will be satisfied, and Jeremiah wakes from a sweet sleep. God will sow the land with people and beasts, and will watch over the building and planting as attentively as he watched over the tearing down; the proverb about sour grapes is retired, and each person will answer for himself (vv. 23-30).

Then the new covenant: not like the broken one made at the exodus, but with the law written on hearts, God as their God and they as his people, all of them knowing him from the least to the greatest, because he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (vv. 31-34). Israel's future is staked on the fixed order of sun and moon and the unmeasurable heavens, and the city is surveyed for rebuilding — with even the valley of dead bodies and ashes declared sacred to the LORD, never to be overthrown again (vv. 35-40).
31.theology:
God's faithfulness is the consequence of his love, not its cause: an everlasting love has no beginning that Israel's obedience could supply and no end her sin could force (v. 3).

The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the rescue was necessary because Jacob was held by hands too strong for him (vv. 10-11). The weakest travellers set the pace of the return (v. 8).

Repentance is asked for as a gift — bring me back that I may be restored — and shame follows the turning rather than purchasing it (vv. 18-19). God's compassion is visceral, not merely benign (v. 20).

The same divine watchfulness governs the demolition and the rebuilding, so the ruin was never loss of control (v. 28; 1:10).

The new covenant differs from the old not in its law but in where the law is written. If the heart is the problem (17:1, 9; 13:23), only a new heart is a solution; and because all its members know God, its membership and its reality are the same thing (vv. 33-34; 2 Cor 3:3; Heb 8:8-12).

Forgiveness is the foundation, not the reward: God puts his people's sin out of his own memory, sealed in the blood of Christ (v. 34; Luke 22:20; Heb 10:17).

Grace claims the worst ground. The valley where they burned their children is taken inside the holy city and put beyond overthrow forever (v. 40).
31.examples:
Again, again, again — the word spoken to people who thought the good days were over.

A nation called virgin Israel by the God who had called her faithless.

Watchmen in Ephraim shouting: let us go up to Zion.

A column that travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

A mother in a graveyard told there is hope for her future.

Asking God for the turning he has commanded.

A father who cannot get his son out of his mind.

Piling up road markers for a journey home you have not yet left on.

The one night in the book when Jeremiah slept well.

A law that moves from stone to the inside of a person.

Sins put out of God's memory.

The valley of corpses and ashes declared holy ground.
