verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — A Field Bought in a Besieged City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Zedekiah's tenth year the Babylonian army is around Jerusalem and Jeremiah is shut up in the court of the guard for saying the city will fall (vv. 2-3). There God tells him his cousin will come with an offer, and Hanamel duly arrives: Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours (v. 8). Jeremiah buys it — seventeen shekels of silver, and he signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales (vv. 9-10) — then hands both copies to Baruch to be sealed in a jar, that they may last for a long time (v. 14). The reason is given last: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A prisoner buys real estate in a country that is about to be confiscated, and has the paperwork witnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it; Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fix the situation before reading the story, because everything in this chapter depends on it. It is 588 or 587 BC. The Babylonian army is camped around the walls. Food is running out. And the prophet is under arrest in the palace compound.

It is an unpromising moment for a property transaction.

The king's question is almost plaintive. Not is it true, but why do you keep saying it. Zedekiah spends this whole book half-believing Jeremiah and never acting on it, and here he jails the man rather than answer him.

The detail about seeing Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye would be fulfilled with terrible precision: Zedekiah was brought before him at Riblah, watched his sons killed, and was then blinded. He saw the king of Babylon eye to eye, and the last thing those eyes saw was his own sons dying.

And even here the wording is open: until I visit him. In this book God's visiting can mean coming in judgment or in mercy; it is the same verb that carried the promise to the exiles (29:10). Scripture does not tell us which Zedekiah met; it records only that he died a prisoner in Babylon (52:11).
verseByVerse.note: The tenth year of Zedekiah was 588 or 587 BC, during the final siege.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.' Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells him what is about to happen before it happens, and it is nothing spectacular: a relative is going to turn up with a business proposition.

The legal background is the law of redemption. When an Israelite fell into poverty and had to sell family land, the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy it, keeping the inheritance inside the family — his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold (Lev 25:25). It is the transaction Boaz performed at the gate, calling the town to witness that he had bought the inheritance of a dead man to keep his name alive (Ruth 4:9-10).

Christians have long heard in this law a picture of Christ, though Jeremiah does not draw it. The redeemer had to be a near kinsman, and the Son of God became our brother, sharing our flesh and blood that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb 2:14), and buying back an inheritance we had lost and could not recover.

Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD. The confirmation did not come by a vision or a voice. It came when a cousin walked into the guardhouse and said what God had said he would say.

Hanamel's motive is easy to guess and not held against him. Anathoth was three miles north of Jerusalem, in territory the Babylonians already controlled. The field was worthless and he wanted out. What he was selling was, commercially, a liability — and God had told his prophet to be the buyer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver. I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales. Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He paid. That is the whole force of the sign, and it cost him real silver — seventeen shekels, recorded exactly, as a man records a sum he has genuinely parted with.

Faith here is not a feeling about the future. It is money leaving a purse for land the buyer will never walk on, in a district already under enemy control, paid by a man who had just been told the country was finished.

Four verbs, and every one of them is ordinary conveyancing: signed, sealed, witnessed, weighed. God's prophet does not make a gesture; he completes a legally binding sale with the correct number of formalities in front of observers.

There is something bracing in that. An extravagant act of hope is carried out with paperwork. Faith that expects God to keep his word will generally look like something concrete and slightly inconvenient rather than like an inspiring mood.

Two documents, which was the standard practice: a sealed copy that could not be tampered with, and an open copy for consultation. Both are kept, because the sale is meant to be verifiable generations later by people who will need to know exactly where the boundary ran.
verseByVerse.note: Seventeen shekels was about 7 ounces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard. I charged Baruch in their presence, saying, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baruch appears, the scribe who will carry this book into existence. And note the audience: the cousin, the official witnesses, and all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard — a yard full of prisoners and hangers-on, watching a man buy a field he could not reach.

The sign was performed publicly on purpose. In a city where everyone was calculating how long the food would last, here was a man behaving as though there would be a Judah in which to own land.

An earthenware jar, that they may last for a long time. The instruction quietly concedes the whole tragedy: this will take decades. Jeremiah will not be redeeming anything himself; the jar is for somebody's grandchildren.

Storing documents in sealed pottery is how the ancient world preserved what mattered, and how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived two thousand years in the same region. Hope with a long timescale needs a container.

And here is the interpretation, given after the act rather than before it. The point of the purchase was never the field. It was the sentence: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land — normal life, markets functioning, families buying property, in the country whose destruction had just been guaranteed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — Nothing Is Too Hard for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the deed filed, Jeremiah prays. He begins with the Creator for whom Nothing is too hard, rehearses the exodus and the gift of the land, agrees that the disaster is deserved, and lays his bewilderment down: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16-25).
verseByVerse.theology: He obeyed first and asked his question afterwards, which is the right order.

verseByVerse.quote: "After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying: 'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sequence matters. He obeyed, completed the transaction, filed the deeds — and then prayed about it. The obedience was not waiting on the explanation.

The prayer opens with a sigh — Ah, Lord GOD! — the sound of a man who has done something he does not understand and has come to talk about it.

And then, before any question, he states what he knows: God made the heavens and the earth, and Nothing is too hard for you. That is the right foundation for a confused prayer. He does not begin with the problem; he begins with the Creator, and the problem gets measured against him rather than the other way round.

The words are borrowed. When Sarah laughed behind a tent flap at the idea of a baby, the LORD said to Abraham, Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14). The same question would be put to a girl in Nazareth in the plainest form: For nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). A barren womb, a doomed city, a virgin — the question turns up at every point where God's promise looks physically ridiculous.

verseByVerse.quote: You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts, great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah holds two things together that we find easier to separate. Steadfast love to thousands, and guilt repaid into the next generation. He is quoting the words God used of himself at Sinai, and he does not edit them to make the prayer more comfortable.

Praying honestly means praying to the God who is actually there, including the parts of him that are currently battering your city.

The words come from the moment God proclaimed his own name to Moses: keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children (Exod 34:7). And the proportion inside that sentence is telling. Love reaches thousands; the visiting of guilt reaches three or four generations. Even in the verse that warns, mercy is the larger number.

Two pairs, and they are the qualities a man in a besieged city most needs to believe. Great in counsel and mighty in deed — God both knows what he is doing and is able to do it; wisdom without power would be tragic, and power without wisdom would be terrifying.

Then whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man. Nothing in the siege, or in the guardhouse, or in the conduct of the men who put him there, is unobserved.

And the last clause is one God had already spoken about himself in this book: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds (17:10). Jeremiah prays God's own words back to him. That is often the safest way to pray when a situation makes no sense — not with a theory, but with what God has said.

Does God punish children for their fathers’ guilt, when 31:30 says each dies for his own sin? Each is judged for his own guilt; but sin’s consequences fall on families, and children who continue in their fathers’ sin share their judgment (Exod 20:5, of those who hate me).

verseByVerse.quote: You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror. And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer turns to history, which is where Israel always went for confidence. He does not reason from his circumstances to God's character; he reasons from what God has already done.

The exodus, recited by a prisoner during a siege. And the phrase outstretched arm is the one he had already used in verse 17 of creation — the arm that made the world is the arm that emptied Egypt, and it has not shortened.

Praying through the record like this is not nostalgia. It is how a believer talks himself into hope: God has done the impossible before, with witnesses, and the account is public.

The land was a gift and an oath — which you swore to their fathers. That is precisely what makes the present moment so painful to pray about. The property Jeremiah has just bought is part of a gift God swore to give, and it is about to be taken away. He lays that contradiction in front of God rather than resolving it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them. Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it. Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet's prayer contains no defence of his people. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do, and the disaster is traced to its author without complaint: you have made all this disaster come upon them.

He is not asking God to be fair. He agrees with the verdict, which is the only honest place to pray from.

He describes what is out of the window. Earth ramps rising against the wall, the three-fold judgment of the whole book arriving on schedule, and a flat acknowledgement: What you spoke has come to pass.

Forty years of being called a traitor for saying this, and there is no vindication in his tone at all.

And there is the question, finally, and it is left unfinished. Everything you said would happen is happening — Yet you told me to buy a field.

He does not accuse God of anything and he does not pretend to understand. He simply sets the command beside the circumstances and leaves them both in God's hands. That is what faithful bewilderment sounds like, and it is available to anyone who has obeyed something they could not explain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Is Anything Too Hard for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hands the confession back as a question, Is anything too hard for me? (vv. 26-27). Then he confirms the city's burning, with an indictment running from the day Jerusalem was built through every class of its people to the valley where they offered their children (vv. 28-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The question that carries the promise is the same question that carries the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the prayer by quoting it.

Jeremiah had said Nothing is too hard for you; God replies Is anything too hard for me? It is the gentlest possible correction, and it is a real one. The prophet had stated the doctrine and then laid a difficulty beside it as though the two might not fit. God takes the man's own confession and turns it into the answer to his problem.

There is a great deal of pastoral help in that. What we mostly need in bewilderment is not new information but the application of what we already say we believe.

And the title God chooses is exact for the occasion: the God of all flesh. Not the God of Judah only, whose reach ends at a besieged wall, but of every living thing — including the Babylonian army, the cousin selling a field, and the generations who will one day open a clay jar.

Zechariah heard the same question asked after the exile, when the returned remnant thought the promised restoration too great to believe: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight? (Zech 8:6). What looks impossible to people standing in rubble does not look impossible from where God stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it. The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger. For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the comfort, God confirms the catastrophe. He does not answer the hard question by softening the facts, and the first thing he says after Is anything too hard for me? is that the city will fall.

The detail about the roofs is precise and damning. Flat roofs were where families sat in the evening, and they had been using them as private altars. Those same houses are named as fuel.

The assessment is unrelieved, and it matters that it comes here rather than in a chapter of pure judgment. The restoration promised in a few verses is not going to rest on a reassessment of the nation's record. That record is being read out at full severity first.

verseByVerse.quote: This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the day it was built. Not since Manasseh, not since the monarchy went bad — from the beginning. God's review of Jerusalem's history finds no golden age to appeal to.

That is a sobering word about institutions and cities we are tempted to idealise, and it clears away any idea that the coming restoration is a return to an earlier, purer Jerusalem. There was never one.

Ezekiel said the same thing even more bluntly about the city's origins: Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite (Ezek 16:3). Jerusalem had been a pagan city before David took it, and it never fully stopped being one. Whatever God does with it will be grace from the ground up, not a restoration of past merit.

Six groups, and the list runs from the palace to the street. Kings, officials, priests, prophets, the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem — leadership and laity together, with no class exempted and nobody left to blame the others.

verseByVerse.quote: They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction. They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image is domestic and wounding: a person who will not turn round. Not argument, not rival theology — the posture of someone who has decided not to look at you.

And though I have taught them persistently, which is the adverb of this whole book. God as the long-suffering teacher, sending prophet after prophet into a classroom whose pupils face the wall.

Idols inside the temple. The building existed to display his name and was used to insult it.

The indictment ends at the bottom: the valley below the city where they burned their children.

And God adds a clause about himself that is almost unbearable to read — nor did it enter into my mind. The thing had never so much as occurred to him. Whatever the worshippers told themselves about devotion and cost, God disowns the whole idea as something that had never crossed his mind to want.

This valley is very likely the same ground God promised in 31:40 would be sacred to the LORD. The place named here as the floor of Judah's guilt is the place named there as holy, and between the two statements stands everything the gospel has to do.

Does “nor did it come into my mind” mean God did not foresee child sacrifice? No; he knows all things (Ps 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — One Heart and One Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now therefore (v. 36) turns the whole chapter. God will gather them from every country he drove them to, bring them back and make them dwell in safety (v. 37), and the covenant formula follows: And they shall be my people, and I will be their God (v. 38). He will give one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever (v. 39), make an everlasting covenant and put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (v. 40). And then a sentence about God's own disposition: I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul (v. 41).
verseByVerse.theology: God secures the perseverance he requires, and says he will enjoy doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence': Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words carry the weight of the chapter: Now therefore.

Read what precedes them — evil from the beginning, every class guilty, children burned in the valley, the city to be removed from God's sight. A therefore after that should introduce the sentence. Instead it introduces the promise. There is no logic in the world by which verse 37 follows verse 35, except the logic of grace.

The same hand appears on both ends of the action: he drove them, and he will gather them. The anger was real — God does not now describe the exile as a misunderstanding — and it is the same God who ends it.

The covenant sentence again, and in this setting it is the answer to everything in the indictment. Not a people who deserve him. A people who are his.

Hosea gave the same promise to a people who had been named for their rejection: I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God' (Hos 2:23). And Peter applies it to Gentile believers who had never belonged to Israel at all: Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy (1 Pet 2:10). The covenant sentence spoken to exiles in a doomed city is the sentence spoken over every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me. I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gift is a heart, as it has been throughout this book — the heart to know him (24:7), the law written inside (31:33), and here one heart and one way. Ezekiel was given the same promise in almost the same words: I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them (Ezek 11:19).

One is doing real work. A divided heart was Judah's disease, wavering between the LORD and Baal, the temple and the roof altar. The cure is not more willpower but an undivided heart, given.

Two guarantees, one on each side of the relationship. God will not turn away from doing them good, and — this is the astonishing half — he will see to it that they do not turn away from him either. The covenant is secured at both ends by the same person. Hebrews calls it the eternal covenant and names the price: the blood of the great shepherd of the sheep (Heb 13:20).

And then God says something about his own feelings. He will rejoice in doing them good, and he will do it with all my heart and all my soul — the phrase Israel was commanded to use about loving him, turned round and spoken by God about blessing them.

This is not a God who forgives reluctantly and blesses on sufferance. Zephaniah saw the same thing: he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (Zeph 3:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–44 — Deeds Signed and Sealed Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The argument closes with a symmetry: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them (v. 42). Fields will be bought in the land everyone is calling a desolation, without man or beast (v. 43), and the detail is deliberately clerical — Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in Benjamin, around Jerusalem, in the hill country, the Shephelah and the Negeb (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: The land registry will reopen, district by district, and that is the shape the hope takes.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them. Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.' Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument is an equation, and it is a practical sentence for anyone who has watched God keep a hard word.

They had just seen every threat land — siege mounds, famine, the city given over. Fine, says God: that same reliability is now working for you. The accuracy of the judgment is the evidence for the promise. A God whose warnings come true is a God whose assurances can be banked, and the logic runs the way Paul's does when he argues from the greater gift to the lesser (Rom 8:32).

God quotes the pessimism of the moment accurately — a desolation, without man or beast — and does not dispute it. That is exactly what the land is about to become. And in that land, fields will be bought.

The chapter ends in a solicitor's office, and the vocabulary is the vocabulary of verse 10: bought for money, signed, sealed, witnessed. Jeremiah's private transaction in a prison yard turns out to be the first entry in a register that will reopen across six named districts — Benjamin, the area round Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, the hill country, the Shephelah, the Negeb.

That is how this hope is described: not as a vision or a feeling, but as ordinary people doing ordinary business in a country God had promised to empty and then promised to fill. And the man who bought the first field never saw it. He paid seventeen shekels, filed the deeds in a jar, and died elsewhere — which is the pattern for every believer who has ever acted on a promise whose fulfilment lay past his own lifetime.

32.title: The Field at Anathoth
32.overview:
In Zedekiah's tenth year, with Babylon besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah imprisoned in the court of the guard for prophesying the city's fall, God tells him his cousin Hanamel will offer him the family field at Anathoth. Hanamel comes exactly as predicted, and Jeremiah buys it for seventeen shekels — signing, sealing, weighing the silver before witnesses — then has Baruch store both copies of the deed in an earthenware jar to last a long time, because houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (vv. 1-15).

Jeremiah then prays. He begins with the Creator and confesses that nothing is too hard for God, rehearses the exodus and the gift of the land, agrees that the present disaster is deserved and God-sent, describes the siege ramps outside, and lays down his bewilderment: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16-25).

God answers by returning the confession as a question — is anything too hard for me? — and then confirms the city's burning, with an indictment running from the day Jerusalem was built through every class of its people to the high places where they burned their children, a thing that never entered his mind (vv. 26-35).

Now therefore: God will gather them from every country he drove them to, bring them home in safety, be their God, and give them one heart and one way. He will make an everlasting covenant, put his fear in their hearts so they do not turn away, and rejoice in doing them good with all his heart and soul (vv. 36-41). Just as he brought the disaster, so he will bring the good: fields will be bought and deeds signed, sealed and witnessed across six named districts (vv. 42-44).
32.theology:
Faith acts before it understands. Jeremiah completed a binding purchase and prayed his question afterwards, and the obedience did not wait on the explanation (vv. 9-10, 16, 25).

Hope takes concrete and slightly inconvenient forms — silver weighed, deeds witnessed, documents sealed in a jar for a generation the buyer would never meet (vv. 10-14).

Jeremiah acts as kinsman-redeemer, buying back the family inheritance at the moment it is worthless (vv. 7-8; Lev 25:25; Ruth 4:9-10).

God answers bewilderment by applying what the believer already confesses, not by supplying new information (vv. 17, 27; Gen 18:14; Luke 1:37).

Grace does not rest on a reassessment of the record. The indictment is read at full severity — evil from the day the city was built, every class guilty — and then comes the therefore that introduces the promise (vv. 30-37).

The covenant is secured at both ends by God: he will not turn from doing them good, and he will put his fear in their hearts so that they do not turn from him (vv. 39-40; 24:7; Ezek 11:19; Heb 13:20).

God delights in blessing. He rejoices to do them good with all his heart and all his soul (v. 41; Zeph 3:17), and the threats that came true are the guarantee that the promises will (v. 42).
32.examples:
A prisoner buying farmland in a country under sentence.

A cousin arriving with a worthless field and a legal right.

Seventeen shekels, weighed on scales, in front of witnesses.

Deeds sealed in a clay jar for somebody's grandchildren.

Praying the doctrine first and the problem second.

Reciting the exodus from inside a besieged city.

Evening roofs used as private altars, named as fuel.

A therefore that should have introduced a sentence, introducing a promise.

God blessing with all his heart and all his soul.

A land registry reopening, district by district.

33.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name:<sup>3</sup>Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.<sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword:<sup>5</sup>They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security.<sup>7</sup>I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first.<sup>8</sup>I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.<sup>9</sup>And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it.<sup>10</sup>"Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again<sup>11</sup>the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks.<sup>13</sup>In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.<sup>15</sup>In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>16</sup>In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>17</sup>"For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,<sup>18</sup>and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever."<sup>19</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>20</sup>"Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time,<sup>21</sup>then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers.<sup>22</sup>As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."<sup>23</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>24</sup>"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth,<sup>26</sup>then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word to the imprisoned prophet, with an invitation to call and be told hidden things (vv. 1–3). The city is tearing down its houses for a defence that cannot hold, because God has hidden his face (vv. 4–5). Then the turn to healing, resting on the forgiveness of all their guilt (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers a man in prison by offering to tell him things he could not have worked out.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard: "Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details, and both matter. A second time: God had not finished speaking after the field was bought. And still shut up in the court of the guard, with the siege tightening outside and the prophet no closer to release.

The circumstances have not improved by one degree between chapter 32 and chapter 33. What arrives instead is more revelation. God's answer to a faithful man in a bad situation is often not a change of situation but a further word about himself.

Before the promise, the credentials again: the God who made the earth and formed it to establish it. He built it to stand. The ESV notes that its wording here follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew simply has "it"; but the sense of a Creator who makes things in order to make them last is what the verse is for, and it is the ground of everything promised in the chapter.

Here is the invitation, and consider its recipient. A prisoner. A man whose preaching has failed by every visible measure, who has just spent silver on a field he will never see, and who prayed a bewildered prayer in the previous chapter.

God's reply to that prayer is to invite more of them. Call to me and I will answer you: not a rebuke for asking, but an offer of more. And what is promised is not a change of policy but disclosure: great and hidden things that you have not known. There are things about God's purposes that will not be worked out by looking at the siege ramps. They have to be told, and they are told to people who ask.

Is this a promise of private revelation? It was God’s word to Jeremiah, then promising the restoration that follows. Believers today are given God’s great and hidden things in the gospel, revealed in Scripture (1 Cor 2:9–10; Col 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword: They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A picture of a city in its last weeks. They are pulling down their own homes, royal buildings included, for stone and timber to block the breaches where the Babylonian ramps are coming over the wall.

That is what the end looks like in practice: dismantling your own house to slow the enemy down for another day. Every resource turned to a defence that cannot hold.

The ESV's note explains what gets filled with the dead: "That is, the torn-down houses". The improvised barricades become the morgue. The stones pulled from bedrooms end up packed with the bodies of the men who stacked them.

And underneath the military facts is the theological one: I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil. That is the real cause of the collapse. Not siege engineering, not the balance of power, but the averted face of God. The worst thing that can happen to a people is not that their walls fail but that God looks away, and this verse names it as the reason the walls fail at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security. I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first. I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same Behold that introduced the barricades full of corpses now introduces healing, in the same breath and about the same city. This is the wound of chapter 30, the hurt God called incurable, with no medicine and no healing, and here is the physician arriving. Nothing has changed in the patient. What changes is that God announces he will do it himself.

Both houses again, the northern kingdom included well over a century after it vanished, and as they were at first, with the damage of the centuries undone.

Under the health, the prosperity and the security lies this foundation: the guilt has to go, and the sentence says it twice, with all both times.

Cleansing and forgiveness are not quite the same thing, and both are needed. Forgiveness deals with the record; cleansing deals with the stain. A pardoned man who still feels filthy has only half of what God is promising here.

And the offence is named for what it is: sin against me, twice. Judah's problem was never merely social collapse or bad policy. It was personal, and so is the remedy: God himself takes the guilt away, which is why a believer who has failed can come back by confession rather than by first making himself clean (Ps 32:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Voice of the Bridegroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The place everyone calls a waste will hear weddings and thanksgiving again (vv. 10–11), and shepherds will count their flocks in every district (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Weddings, singing and a shepherd counting sheep: the restoration measured in ordinary noise.

verseByVerse.quote: And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it. "Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city that had become a curse and a byword among the nations becomes a name of joy, a praise and a glory, and the reversal is not in her reputation for strength but in what God does for her.

The odd phrase is the last one. The nations shall fear and tremble, not at judgment but because of all the good. God's generosity is itself awe-inducing. Grace on that scale is not a comfortable thing to watch.

God quotes the pessimism verbatim, as he did in the previous chapter, and grants every word of it. The place is a waste. Then: there shall be heard again.

Earlier in this book God had silenced exactly these sounds, promising to take away the voice of mirth and the voice of the bridegroom and bride (7:34; 16:9). Now he gives them back, item by item, in the same words: weddings in the streets, singing, people walking up to the temple with thank offerings.

And the song they sing is the one Israel had always sung, the refrain of Psalm 136: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever (Ps 136:1). It is sung by people who have watched the worst happen. They are not singing that nothing bad occurred; they are singing that his steadfast love outlasted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the weddings, the sheep. The promise keeps getting more ordinary, which is how you can tell it is meant literally: shepherds with somewhere to settle, flocks lying down in country that had been emptied.

The same six districts as the land-registry promise at the end of chapter 32, listed again. God maps his promises.

And the closing image is a man counting sheep as they file past him under his hand. It is the smallest detail in the chapter and one of the most reassuring: flocks numerous enough to need counting, a shepherd unhurried enough to count them, and peace enough in the countryside for both. Nothing dramatic. Just a working farm in a land God had promised to empty and then promised to fill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — A Righteous Branch, and a Name for the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous Branch of chapter 23 returns (vv. 14–15), but the name has moved: where chapter 23 gave it to the king, here the city wears it (v. 16). Throne and priesthood are guaranteed in perpetuity (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's own name is handed to the people who live under him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is fulfill, and the object is a promise already made. God is not improvising a new plan to cope with the disaster; he is keeping an old word, and the disaster has not altered it. Ten chapters earlier, amid an indictment of worthless shepherds, God had said Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (23:5). Now the same promise is repeated to a man in prison in a city about to fall.

The image is agricultural and deliberately humble. A branch is what sprouts from a stump, which is what the house of David was about to become, with Zedekiah blinded and his sons dead. Out of that stump, a shoot. And spring up is the language of something growing quietly rather than being installed by force. What he does when he comes is named in the plainest terms: justice and righteousness in the land. Not ceremony, not conquest. The two things chapter 22 said a king was for, and that the actual kings never delivered.

A note on the text: verses 14 to 26 are absent from the ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah, which is shorter than the Hebrew in many places. They are part of the Hebrew text our Bibles follow, and they echo 23:5–6 closely.

The righteous Branch is Jesus, the Son of David (23:5–6); he is The LORD is our righteousness, for Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.' "For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read this beside chapter 23 and you find one word changed, and it is a glorious change. There, the name belonged to the king: this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness' (23:6). Here it is given to the city.

The king's name has passed to his people, a picture of justification in a single change of pronoun. His righteousness is not admired from a distance; it is worn by the community as its own address. Jerusalem is not renamed The City That Finally Got Its Act Together. It is called by his name, because the righteousness it lives on is his. That is the gospel for every reader who has not kept God's law: Christ's obedience is counted as ours (2 Cor 5:21).

This is the promise of 2 Samuel 7, restated at the moment of its apparent collapse: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam 7:16).

Within months there would be no king in Jerusalem at all, and no son of David would sit on that throne again. The promise held anyway, and an angel told a girl in Nazareth how: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

Will the Levitical priests and sacrifices be restored literally? Some dispensationalists expect them in a millennial temple. But the promise is kept in Christ, who is both King of David’s line and the high priest who offered one sacrifice for ever (Heb 7:24–27; 10:12), and in his people, a royal priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Pet 2:5, 9). Faithful Christians differ on this; this commentary reads it through Hebrews, which says Christ’s one offering has made the old sacrifices obsolete (Heb 8:13; 10:18), so that a return to animal sacrifice would look backward rather than forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Covenant with the Day and the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes the throne and the altar on the sunrise (vv. 20–21), and promises not mere survival but increase, in the terms sworn to Abraham (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Anyone who wants the promise cancelled must first stop the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever." The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alongside the endless throne, an endless altar. The temple was not much more than a year from being burned and its priesthood scattered, and God promises that there will never be a moment without a priest in my presence making offerings.

Taken literally that promise failed twice over: the sacrifices stopped in 586, resumed, and stopped again in AD 70, this time for good. So either the word was broken, or it was pointing at a priesthood that does not depend on mortal men.

Hebrews takes the second view and explains what was always wrong with the Levitical arrangement: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb 7:23-24). The reason Israel needed a succession of priests was that each one kept dying. A priest who does not die needs no successor, and there has not been an hour since the cross when God has lacked a man in his presence offering, because he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25).

A new word begins, and the formula itself says something in a chapter about permanence. God keeps speaking to this prisoner, paragraph after paragraph, while the city burns down around him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time, then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers. As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offers a test anybody can attempt. Stop tomorrow morning from arriving.

Calling the sunrise a covenant is a striking way to describe creation's regularity. Day and night are not mere physics; they are God keeping an appointment he made, every evening and every morning, without fail, in front of everyone.

The logic is a chain with one hinge. Break the sunrise and you may argue about the throne; until then, the argument is closed.

And the man hearing this could see the Babylonian army from the courtyard. His own eyes told him the Davidic line was finished. God does not dispute the evidence of his eyes; he gives him a better one, available every morning.

Not merely preserved but multiplied, and in the exact terms of the oath to Abraham: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen 22:17).

That is a promise of a royal family and a priesthood beyond counting, spoken over a dynasty about to lose its last king. It is hard to read it, on this side of the cross, without thinking of a kingdom of priests too many to number from every tribe and tongue (Rev 5:9–10; 7:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Two Clans He Chose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the rumour that he has rejected the two clans he chose (v. 24) with the same covenant of day and night (v. 25), and the Book of Consolation ends in mercy (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The rumour was that God had finished with them; the reply ends in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight. Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has been listening to the talk, and he repeats it back. The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose: Israel and Judah, both apparently finished, and the conclusion drawn everywhere that God had changed his mind about his own election.

The consequence is public: his people are despised and no longer a nation in their sight. When God's people are visibly defeated, the watching world does not usually conclude that God is disciplining them. It concludes that he has dropped them, or was never there.

The same argument as before, now aimed at the rumour rather than at the prophet's doubt. God answers gossip about his faithfulness the way he answered his servant's confusion, by pointing at the sky.

And the name-stacking at the end is deliberate: Jacob, David, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob again. Every layer of the promise is named, so that rejecting this people would mean breaking all of it at once.

And so the Book of Consolation ends, not with an argument won but with mercy.

Weigh where these four chapters have come from. They were written by a man in custody, in a city eating itself, under a king who would be blinded, about a temple that would be ash within months. And they contain the new covenant, the everlasting love, the sins remembered no more, the healed wound, the field bought in faith, the Branch, and this last word of mercy. The circumstances never improved while he wrote. The revelation simply got better.

That is the answer to the invitation at the head of the chapter. He called, and God told him great and hidden things he had not known, and the greatest of them was a name he would not live to hear anyone use, given first to a king and then handed to his people: The LORD is our righteousness.

33.title: Call to Me and I Will Answer You
33.overview: Jeremiah is still a prisoner in the court of the guard, and the siege is closing in, when a second word comes with an invitation: call to me, and I will tell you great and hidden things (vv. 1-3). The chapter then sets the city's last weeks, with houses torn down for barricades that will fill with the dead, beside the healing, forgiveness and joy God promises afterwards (vv. 4-13). It returns to the righteous Branch of chapter 23, now giving his name to the city, and stakes the throne of David and the priesthood on the sunrise, God's covenant with day and night (vv. 14-22). It answers the rumour that God has rejected his people, and the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33) closes in mercy (vv. 23-26).
33.theology: The chapter turns on two things God gives a prisoner in place of release: a further word about himself, and an invitation to ask for more. Its promises rest on forgiveness that deals with both the record and the stain of sin (v. 8), and they reach their height when the name of the king, The LORD is our righteousness, is given to his people (v. 16; 23:6). That is justification pictured in a change of pronoun, and it is fulfilled in the Son of David whose kingdom has no end and the priest who always lives to intercede (Luke 1:32-33; Heb 7:23-25). God answers both private doubt and public rumour the same way, by pointing at the sunrise he keeps as a covenant (vv. 20, 25).
33.examples: A family dismantling its own bedroom to plug a breach in the wall for one more day is what verse 4 describes, and it is a picture of every defence that cannot hold once God has hidden his face. Against it stand the smallest images of hope in the chapter: wedding songs back in streets God had silenced, and a shepherd unhurried enough to count his sheep. And when doubt says God has finished with his people, the chapter's own answer is still available to anyone: stop tomorrow morning from arriving, and then we will talk.

Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.<sup>21</sup>And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the empire's armies at the walls, Jeremiah brings Zedekiah a message that gives and takes in the same breath: capture, and yet a death in peace (vv. 1–5), delivered while Lachish and Azekah still hold (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise of an honourable funeral, offered to a king who will be blinded first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire. You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scale is spelled out to make the odds plain: not merely Babylon but every vassal nation in the empire, conscripted into the siege lines. Jerusalem is facing the known world.

And the prophet is sent to the palace with it. Not a written note: Go and speak to Zedekiah, face to face, the man who had already imprisoned him for saying this.

The phrase eye to eye had been used of this king before (32:4), and its fulfilment was exact in a way nobody would have wanted. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, made to watch his sons executed, and then blinded. He did meet him eye to eye, and it was the last thing he ever saw.

God's words come true in their detail, and the detail is not always the comfort we imagined when we heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword. You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet. After the sentence, a concession, and it is addressed to him personally, by name and title, with an urgency that reads almost like pleading.

What is offered is a decent death and a proper funeral: the royal spices, the formal lament, the cry Alas, lord! that had been denied to Jehoiakim, who was promised the burial of a donkey (22:18-19).

It is a strange mercy. Zedekiah will lose his city, his sons and his sight, and be told he will die in his bed with mourners at the door. But weigh it against the alternative he was courting, and against the treatment his brother received, and it is real. God keeps a kindness back even for a weak and faithless king.

And the guarantee is the same one attached to every threat in this book: For I have spoken the word. The promise of the funeral rests on exactly the same authority as the promise of the fire.

Did this promise fail? Zedekiah was promised to die “in peace”, yet he was blinded and died in prison (52:11). Some take the promise as conditional on his obeying (vv. 2–5; 38:17–18): he refused, and so lost it. Others read “in peace” as meaning not by the sword, with mourning rites, which he may have received in Babylon. This commentary prefers the second reading, since verse 5 contrasts his death with the sword and speaks of the mourning itself; but the appeal in Yet hear the word of the LORD also shows how much more he could have had if he had listened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem, when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these words. He delivered the funeral and the fire, the concession and the sentence, without editing either half to suit the audience. It is the same obedience as chapter 26: do not hold back a word.

Two names, and they date the scene precisely. Lachish and Azekah were the last strongpoints in the Judean lowlands, and archaeologists digging at Lachish found in a guardroom a group of ostraca, letters written on pottery by officers in these final months. One of them reports that the writer could no longer see the signals of Azekah, which many take to mean that Azekah had already fallen.

The kingdom has been reduced to a capital and two garrisons, the beacons are going out one by one, and in that atmosphere the king of Judah decides to do something religious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Proclamation and the Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah covenants to free every Hebrew slave, the people obey, and then they take them back (vv. 8–11). God answers from the exodus and the law of release (vv. 12–14): they had repented, and then profaned his name (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform lasted exactly as long as the siege did.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them, that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free. But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For one moment, Judah does the right thing. This is a genuine reform, formally covenanted, and its wording is beautiful: no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. The word brother is the argument. A fellow Israelite is not labour to be owned; he is family.

The motive was very probably the siege. With the enemy at the wall, freeing slaves put more men on the ramparts and fewer mouths in private households, and a public act of obedience might move God to relent. Repentance under pressure is still repentance, and God takes it at face value in verse 15.

They obeyed, says the narrator, twice, in a book where nobody obeys anything. For a short while in the last months of Judah, the law of Moses was actually kept in Jerusalem. Then they took them back. Men and women who had walked out of their owners' houses, perhaps found family and started to plan a life, were rounded up and put back. Somebody had to go and fetch them. It is one thing never to free a slave; it is another to free him, watch him taste it, and then take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying, 'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's answer begins with the exodus, and the phrase he chooses is the knife: out of the house of slavery. He is talking to slave-owners who have just re-enslaved their brothers, and he identifies himself as the God who empties houses of slavery.

Everything Israel possessed came out of that rescue; the law of release was the shape of life for people God had already freed. To hold a fellow Hebrew in bondage was to contradict the event that made them a people at all.

The law being quoted is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12: six years of service, release in the seventh, he shall go out free, for nothing (Exod 21:2). It was not an obscure statute. It was one of the first ordinances given after Sinai, designed precisely so that poverty could never become a permanent status in Israel. So At the end of seven years means in the seventh year, after six of service; the two counts agree.

Why did God’s law allow Hebrews to be held as slaves at all? What it regulated was mostly debt-service: a man too poor to pay what he owed sold his labour for a limited term, and the law hedged it round with protections (release in the seventh year, gifts to start again (Deut 15:13–14), no ruling with harshness (Lev 25:43), and death for kidnapping a man to sell him (Exod 21:16)). That is far from the race-based slavery of later centuries. The law did allow foreigners to be held longer (Lev 25:44–46), a concession to a hard world which the gospel undoes by making slave and free one family in Christ (Gal 3:28; Philem 16).

And it had been ignored for centuries: your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me. Zedekiah's proclamation was not an innovation but the overdue obedience of generations, which makes its reversal worse. They restored a law their ancestors had let lapse, and then let it lapse again almost at once.

verseByVerse.quote: You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name, but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives them full credit for it. You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes. He does not dismiss the reform as insincere theatre, even though the timing was self-interested. It was right, and he says so.

And the setting is noted: the covenant was made in the house that is called by my name, in the temple, with God as witness to a promise about other people's freedom.

The charge is profaned my name. Not merely broke a promise, not merely wronged the poor, but dragged God's reputation through it, because his name had been invoked over the transaction.

That is what makes a broken religious commitment different in kind from a broken private one. When a vow is made before God and then reversed, the watching world learns something false about God.

The small phrase according to their desire says much. The freed slaves wanted their freedom. The masters knew it, and took it away anyway.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence is built from their own word, liberty (v. 17), and from the ceremony they used to ratify the covenant (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: They walked between the halves of a dead animal to seal their promise, and became the animal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts— the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes their own word and turns it round, and the result is one of the grimmest lines in Scripture. You would not proclaim liberty, so I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine.

The sword, plague and famine are given their freedom. The three judgments that have stalked this book are released into the city like slaves let out of a house: the only emancipation Jerusalem will get, because it refused the one it had promised.

Sin is answered in its own coin here. Refuse to release, and something else gets released.

Now we learn how the ceremony had been conducted. They had cut a calf in half, laid the two halves apart, and walked between them, in the oldest and most graphic form of covenant-making, whose meaning is unmistakable: may this be done to me if I break my word. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is more compressed than the English here, lacking "them like", which leaves the identification even starker.

It is the ceremony of Genesis 15. Abram cut the animals and laid the halves against each other (Gen 15:10), and then, in the dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces (Gen 15:17). God walked the path alone, as many read it, taking the curse of the covenant on himself while Abram slept.

The list names everyone who took that walk, and the sentence is simply that the oath be honoured.

And this is where the chapter turns toward the gospel, because there are only two ways the curse of a broken covenant can fall. It can fall on the one who broke it, as here. Or it can fall on someone who walks the bloody path alone in the dark on his behalf, which is what God did for Abram, and what he did at the cross for covenant-breakers who have taken back every freedom they ever promised: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: The rite lies behind the Hebrew idiom for making a covenant, which is literally to “cut” one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Army That Withdrew Will Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unburied bodies (v. 20), and a king handed to the army which has withdrawn (v. 21), the detail that explains the whole chapter. God will command it back (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The relief that made them confident enough to re-enslave their brothers was temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you. Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No burial. The men who had denied their brothers a life will be denied a grave, left in the open for scavengers, the ancient world's picture of total disgrace.

Set it beside verse 5, where the king is promised spices and mourners. God distinguishes between people, and the difference here is not rank.

The siege had lifted. Egypt had marched north, and Nebuchadnezzar pulled back to deal with it (37:5), and suddenly the pressure was off. That is when the slaves were taken back. The covenant had been made when the ramps were rising; it was revoked when the dust cleared and the fields were safe to work again.

It is a devastating diagnosis of a certain kind of religion: sincere while frightened, and no longer required once the danger passes. The vow made in the hospital corridor, forgotten in the car park. Peter described the pattern bluntly: the last state has become worse for them than the first (2 Pet 2:20).

God recalls the army. I will command: Nebuchadnezzar will think he is choosing his moment, and he will be answering an order he never heard.

And the chapter ends by leaving the word liberty ringing. Judah proclaimed it, took it back, and lost everything. The Hebrew word for liberty here is the word for the release of the Jubilee year (Lev 25:10), and Isaiah used it of the anointed one’s mission (Isa 61:1). Centuries later a man stood up in a synagogue in Nazareth, read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim liberty to the captives, and told the room it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18). He proclaimed it and did not take it back. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery (Gal 5:1), which is the one warning this chapter exists to give. Christ gives the freedom, and his Spirit, not our nerve under pressure, is what keeps us in it (Gal 5:16).

34.title: Liberty Proclaimed and Taken Back
34.overview: The armies of the whole empire are at the walls, and Jeremiah brings King Zedekiah a word that gives and takes at once: capture, and yet a death in peace (vv. 1-7). Then comes the story the chapter is really about. Under pressure of the siege, king and people covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew slaves, they obey, and as soon as the Babylonian army withdraws they take them back (vv. 8-11). God answers from the exodus and the law of release, and turns their own word, liberty, and their own covenant ceremony against them (vv. 12-22).
34.theology: God credits repentance honestly, even when it comes under pressure (v. 15), but a vow made in his name and then reversed profanes that name (v. 16), and a religion that lasts only while the danger lasts is exposed the moment the siege lifts (v. 21). Sin is answered in its own coin: refuse to release, and God releases sword, famine and pestilence instead. Above all, the chapter shows that the curse of a broken covenant falls either on the breaker or on a substitute. They became the calf they walked between; God walked that path alone for Abram in the dark, and Christ bore the curse at the cross (Gal 3:13). Liberty proclaimed and withdrawn by Judah is proclaimed and never withdrawn by him (Luke 4:18; Gal 5:1).
34.examples: Somebody had to go and fetch the freed slaves back, and that small detail is the measure of the chapter: freedom given, tasted, and taken from people who plainly wanted it. The same pattern shows in the promise made to God in a hospital corridor and forgotten in the car park, and in any kindness that lasts only as long as we feel we need God's help.

35.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."<sup>3</sup>So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites.<sup>4</sup>I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold.<sup>5</sup>Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."<sup>6</sup>But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever.<sup>7</sup>You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'<sup>8</sup>We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters,<sup>9</sup>and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed,<sup>10</sup>but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us.<sup>11</sup>But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."<sup>12</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command.
