I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.<sup>15</sup>I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."<sup>18</sup>But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you,<sup>19</sup>therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Wine Set Before the Rechabites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's reign God tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabite clan into a temple chamber and set wine before them (vv. 1–5).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet sets out drinks in the temple and presses them on men he knows will refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date takes us back. Jehoiakim died in about 598 BC, and the raiders named in verse 11 (compare 2 Kgs 24:2) probably place this episode in his last years, so it belongs some ten years before the siege chapters on either side of it. The book is arranged by theme here rather than by calendar, and this chapter has been placed next to the broken covenant of chapter 34 for a reason: there, men who promised obedience to God reneged almost at once; here, men who never promised God anything have kept their word for generations.

It is one of the strangest commands given to any prophet. Fetch a particular family, take them into the temple, and put wine in front of them.

God knows exactly what will happen. This is not a test of the Rechabites, who are in no danger of failing it; it is a piece of theatre with an audience in mind, and the audience is Judah. Jeremiah has smashed a flask and worn a yoke; now the visual aid is a group of teetotal nomads and a tray of drinks.
verseByVerse.note: Jonadab appears in 2 Kings 10:15-16; the clan's tents and abstinence are explained in verses 6 to 10 below.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites. I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold. Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Names, and a whole household: brothers, sons, the entire clan. Their head's father happens to share the prophet's name, which is a coincidence the narrator lets stand.

Who were they? Descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab, and that man appears once elsewhere in Scripture, riding in Jehu's chariot during the purge of Baal worship. Jehu asked him, Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?, and then said Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD (2 Kgs 10:15-16). So the family's founder was a man known for his allegiance, two and a half centuries before this scene.

The address is given with a surveyor's precision: whose room, next to which, above which. The point of the detail is that this happened somewhere real, with officials in the adjoining rooms who could look in.

Not a token glass. Pitchers full of wine, and cups, laid out properly, with a prophet of the LORD in the temple of the LORD telling them to help themselves.

Every pressure in the scene runs one way. The setting is sacred, the host is a man of God, the invitation is direct, and refusing would look rude and possibly impious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — We Will Drink No Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They decline, citing their father Jonadab's rule: no wine, no houses, no fields, tents only (vv. 6–10), with one honest exception, the flight into Jerusalem from the Chaldean army (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Two and a half centuries of obedience to a man none of them had ever met.

verseByVerse.quote: But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever. You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do not hesitate and they do not argue. They simply cite their father.

What they do not say matters. They do not claim wine is evil, or that God forbade it, or that they are holier for abstaining. Their whole reason is that Jonadab told them not to. Their obedience does not need a justification beyond the person who gave the command.

The rule is wider than drink. No houses, no crops, no vineyards, tents only. It is a deliberate refusal of settled life, and the likeliest reason is spiritual: Canaanite religion was bound up with agriculture, with Baal as the god of rain and harvest, and a family that owned no fields had less to be tempted by. The tents kept them strangers.

And a purpose is attached: that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn. Even the word sojourn concedes that the land was not theirs. The Rechabites were resident aliens who had made peace with never settling down.

It must be said plainly that God nowhere commanded this. It is a family rule, not a law of Moses. Scripture does record a God-given abstinence, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, in which a man shall separate himself from wine and strong drink (Num 6:2-3), but that was voluntary, usually temporary, and instituted by God. Nothing here is being held up as a standard for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters, and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed, but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us. But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report is in the plural and covers everybody: wives, sons, daughters. This was not one impressive individual but a culture, handed down until it was simply how the family lived.

And it cost them. We have no vineyard or field or seed is a statement of poverty. Generation after generation watched their neighbours plant, harvest, build and inherit, and stayed in tents.

The verb obeyed appears again, and it is the word the whole chapter turns on. In a book where Judah has not obeyed anything, here is a family whose summary of two and a half centuries is: we did what we were told.

And here they volunteer the exception, which is the most attractive thing about them. They are not in a tent as they speak; they are inside city walls, in a room in the temple, because an army was in the countryside.

They do not pretend otherwise and God does not reproach them for it. Their obedience was intelligent rather than wooden: the rule existed to keep them separate from Canaan's settled religion, not to get them killed by Babylonian cavalry. That distinction, between the purpose of a command and its letter, is one the people next door in the temple had never learned to make in either direction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Will You Not Receive Instruction?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the sermon the scene was arranged for (v. 13): Jonadab's command has been kept, but God has spoken persistently and Judah has not listened (vv. 14–15), so the disaster comes (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A dead man's house rule was kept for centuries; the living God's word was not kept for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD. The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sermon begins, and the Rechabites were never the subject; they were the exhibit. The question is put to Judah with the tray of untouched wine still in the room.

On one side: a command from a man long dead, about a matter of no moral weight, with no sanction attached, kept for eight or nine generations. On the other: the word of the living God, on matters of life and death, backed by every warning and every mercy, delivered persistently by prophet after prophet, and ignored.

The argument is not that the Rechabites were righteous. It is that Judah cannot plead difficulty. Obedience across centuries is evidently possible, because a family of nomads managed it over wine. What Judah lacked was not capacity but willingness, and the untouched pitchers proved it in front of witnesses.

The scene leaves a question over the whole Old Testament: will anyone ever answer God's voice with a whole heart? The New Testament's answer is the Son. Jesus could say, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), and he learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8), all the way to the cross. The Rechabites kept a father's rule about wine; Christ kept his Father's whole will, and by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19).

verseByVerse.quote: I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me. The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me. Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message had been reasonable. Not a demand for tents or abstinence, but Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, with the promise of keeping the land attached. God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more for compliance.

And the word persistently appears a second time in three verses. This is the pathos of the whole book: God as the sender who will not stop sending.

The charge is not that they failed to keep a code, but that this people has not obeyed me. Disobedience in this book is always personal. God does not list idols or injustices here, though the book has catalogued both. The charge is simply that he kept speaking and calling, and they never replied: two attempts, two silences. Behind it stands a God who, after centuries of being ignored, is still the one doing the talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–19 — Never Lack a Man to Stand Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last word is a blessing on the visual aid. Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you (v. 18), God promises: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The same promise given to David's throne and Levi's altar, handed to a clan from outside the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you, therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the chapter closes God speaks to the men used as an illustration for their own sake, beginning with a full recital of what they did right.

Weigh that promise against the one given two chapters earlier. David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne, and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence (33:17-18). The formula is identical, and here it is given to a clan that was not one of the twelve tribes at all, most likely a family of Kenite outsiders (1 Chr 2:55), attached to Israel but not descended from Jacob.

And to stand before me is priestly language, the posture of a servant in the sanctuary. Outsiders are promised a permanent place in God's presence in the same breath that insiders are told their city will burn. The book has been moving this way for a while, and it is where the gospel goes: a household with no tribal claim, blessed for faithfulness, given standing before God. In Christ, people who were once strangers to the covenants of promise become fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph 2:12, 19).

Their tents turn out to have been preaching all along. Abraham had lived the same way, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, because he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb 11:9-10). Men who refused to build houses were saying, for two hundred and fifty years, that they were not home yet.

And a last word so nobody mistakes the lesson. This chapter is not a call to abstinence or to canvas. God never issued the Rechabite rule, and the Lord himself warned about the trick of treating human tradition as divine command: So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God (Matt 15:6). He came eating and drinking and was slandered for it, while John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and was called demon-possessed (Luke 7:33-34): the same crowd finding fault either way. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). The pitchers were only ever a mirror, and the question they asked was never about wine: he has spoken to you persistently. Have you answered? The same God who kept calling Judah still calls the one who has not answered, not to be scolded but to come home, and the Spirit he gives is what turns a deaf ear into a listening one (Ezek 36:27).

35.title: The Rechabites
35.overview: This chapter steps back about ten years, to the reign of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah sets wine before the Rechabites, a clan who for generations have kept their ancestor's rule of no wine, no houses and no fields (vv. 1-11). Their refusal becomes a living sermon to Judah: a dead man's house rule has been kept for centuries, while the living God's word has been ignored (vv. 12-17). The chapter ends with a blessing on the Rechabites themselves (vv. 18-19).
35.theology: The chapter is comparative, not prescriptive. God never gave the Rechabite rule, and it is held up as an example of constancy, not as a standard of holiness (Matt 15:6; Rom 14:17). Its point is that Judah cannot plead difficulty: God asked less of them than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more. Disobedience is personal; God spoke and called, and they neither listened nor answered. And the outsiders are given the promise of David's throne and Levi's altar, a standing in God's presence, while the insiders are told their city will burn, which is where the gospel goes (Eph 2:12, 19).
35.examples: The scene is a mirror held up to anyone who keeps a family custom, a sports routine or a work habit with perfect discipline while leaving God's plain word unanswered. The Rechabites' tents also have something to say: like Abraham's, they told the neighbours for two hundred and fifty years that this family was not home yet (Heb 11:9-10).

36.text: <sup>1</sup>In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD:<sup>2</sup>"Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today.<sup>3</sup>It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."<sup>4</sup>Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him.<sup>5</sup>And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities.<sup>7</sup>It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people."<sup>8</sup>And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.<sup>9</sup>In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD.<sup>10</sup>Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house.<sup>11</sup>When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,<sup>12</sup>he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials.<sup>13</sup>And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people.<sup>14</sup>Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.<sup>15</sup>And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them.<sup>16</sup>When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king."<sup>17</sup>Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"<sup>18</sup>Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll."<sup>19</sup>Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."<sup>20</sup>So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king.<sup>21</sup>Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king.<sup>22</sup>It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.<sup>23</sup>As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot.<sup>24</sup>Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.<sup>25</sup>Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.<sup>26</sup>And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.<sup>27</sup>Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>28</sup>"Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.<sup>29</sup>And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"<sup>30</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.<sup>31</sup>And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'"<sup>32</sup>Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Write It on a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jehoiakim's fourth year God tells Jeremiah to write twenty-three years of preaching on a scroll (v. 2), in the hope that Judah may turn and be forgiven (v. 3). Baruch writes it, and since the prophet is banned from the temple, Baruch must read it there (vv. 4–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of sermons copied out, on the chance that somebody might still repent.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth year of Jehoiakim is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the fact everyone had to live with. And Jeremiah is told to make a book.

Count the span: from the days of Josiah until today. He had begun in Josiah's thirteenth year, so this is twenty-three years of preaching to be collected into one document: the sermons nobody acted on, gathered up and written down.

And here is why God wanted it written, in words that should govern how the whole book is read: It may be.

The scroll is not an archive for the record, or evidence for the prosecution. It is an attempt. The aim is that they might turn, and the goal beyond that is forgiveness: that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin. Every threat in the collection exists to make the pardon possible.

“It may be that they will turn” (v. 3): God knows the end, but he speaks to people as responsible beings, and his call to repent is real. His foreknowledge never makes the offer insincere.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah's call had come in Josiah's thirteenth year, 627 BC (1:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him. And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah spoke, Baruch wrote, and the prophetic word is moving from air into text, where it can be carried, copied, read in rooms the prophet cannot enter, and survive him. This chapter is the Bible describing its own production.

The reason for the arrangement is a restraining order. The prophet is barred from the temple, presumably since the trial of chapter 26, or the confrontation of chapter 20.

So the man with the message cannot reach the place where the crowds are. And God's response to that obstacle is not to remove it but to route around it: if the preacher is banned, send the book.
verseByVerse.note: Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and friend.

verseByVerse.quote: so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities. It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people." And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instructions are strategic. A fast day, when the temple is full and the mood is already serious, and an audience including country people up from the towns. Maximum hearing for one reading.

Consider what is asked of Baruch. He is to stand in the temple and read aloud a document predicting national ruin, in the name of a man the king has banned, to a crowd that has beaten and imprisoned that man before. The scribe is taking the prophet's risk with none of the prophet's calling.

It may be, a second time, now on Jeremiah's own lips. He had no illusions left about his audience and he still would not close the door.

That hope and the sentence in the same breath, great is the anger and wrath, is the whole posture of faithful preaching. The severity is exactly what makes the appeal urgent.

He did all of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — Read It to the Officials
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On a fast day Baruch reads the scroll in the temple (vv. 9–10); word reaches the officials, who hear it read, turn to one another in fear and resolve to tell the king (vv. 11–18). First they tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The civil servants were frightened by the book, and warned the men who wrote it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD. Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house. When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A year has passed between the command and the reading: the scroll took time to write, and the right day had to come. The fast in the ninth month was probably called because of Babylon; fear makes people religious, as chapter 34 showed.

The location is given exactly, and two details in it carry weight. The chamber belongs to a son of Shaphan, that family again, whose members keep turning up on the right side of this story, as Ahikam did when he saved Jeremiah's life (26:24). Somebody sympathetic lent Baruch a room.

A clay seal impression reading “Gemaryahu son of Shaphan” was found in excavations in the City of David in the 1980s. Many think it belonged to this very man, though that cannot be proved.

And it stands at the entry of the New Gate, which is where the officials had convened the court that acquitted Jeremiah (26:10). The book is being read at the spot where its author was once tried.

Three generations of the same family are named across these verses (Shaphan, Gemariah, Micaiah), and the young man who hears the reading does not shrug it off. He goes to tell the government.

verseByVerse.quote: he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials. And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people. Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cabinet meeting, with the members listed by name. These lists are not padding; they are the marks of eyewitness testimony.

One name should stop us: Elnathan the son of Achbor. He is the man Jehoiakim sent to Egypt to extradite the prophet Uriah, who was brought back and executed (26:22-23). In a few verses he will be one of three men urging the king not to burn this scroll. People are not always consistent, and God uses them at the point where they are willing.

A summons from the government, and Baruch goes, carrying the evidence against himself in his own hand. He could have hidden it or left it behind. He takes it to the palace because he was asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them. When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king." Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sit down and read it. They want to hear the whole thing, not a summary, and they give the scribe a chair. It is the second public reading of the day.

And this is the reaction the book has been waiting twenty-three years to record. They turned one to another in fear. Not agreement necessarily, not repentance yet, but men visibly shaken by what they have heard, looking at each other because it is too much to absorb alone.

Their instinct is that the king must hear it. They are not trying to suppress the document; they are ordinary officials doing their job well, and God's word is making its way up through a bureaucracy.

The question is the mark of serious men. How did you write all these words? They want to know where it came from: is this really Jeremiah's, and how did it get onto the page?

verseByVerse.quote: Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll." Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer is unglamorous and precise: he spoke, I wrote, with ink.

There is a doctrine sitting in that sentence. The words are God's, given to a prophet, spoken to a scribe, and fixed in ink by an ordinary man doing careful work, and the humanity of the process takes nothing away from the divinity of the words. All Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Tim 3:16), and this chapter shows what that looked like from the inside: a voice, a pen, a bottle of ink, a long labour.

They know their king. Before they walk into his presence with this, they tell the two men to disappear, and they tell them properly: hide, and let no one know where you are, so that no official, under pressure, can give them away.

It is a small act of courage from men with careers to protect. God's care for his servants keeps arriving in this book through people who decide to act decently at some cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Knife and a Fire Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiakim has the scroll read to him by the winter fire and cuts it up column by column into the flames, unafraid (vv. 20–24). Three men urge him not to; he orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hid them (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: He listened to three or four columns at a time, and only long enough to know what to cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king. Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king. It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They leave the scroll behind in a side room, perhaps hoping a verbal report would be enough, and the document itself might survive.

Jehoiakim will not have it second-hand. He sends for the scroll and has it read aloud, and the detail that the officials stood beside the king while he sat is the small print of a court: everyone else on their feet, the king in his chair by the fire.

The scene is set with a novelist's economy. The ninth month, around December, the winter palace, a brazier of coals at the king's feet, and a man standing in front of him unrolling the word of God. The narrator lets us see the fire before the king uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot. Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the tense carefully: would cut them off. This was not one hot-blooded gesture. It was a rhythm, repeated the length of a long document: listen to three or four columns, slice them off with a knife, feed them to the coals, listen again.

He heard every word. He simply destroyed each section as soon as he had heard it. There is a kind of attention paid here that is worse than not listening at all: the deliberate, unhurried, methodical disposal of God's word by a man warm and comfortable in his winter room.

Now set this against the officials in Elishama's chamber, who turned one to another in fear. Same words, opposite response.

And set it against his father. Some eighteen years earlier a scroll had been found in this same temple and read to King Josiah, and When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes (2 Kgs 22:11). That tearing began the last reformation Judah ever had.

Josiah tore his robe at the word of God. His son took a knife to the word of God and kept his robe intact. The two men are father and son, the two scrolls were read in the same city, and everything that follows in the history of Judah runs out of that difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them. And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men speak up, and they are named so that we know somebody in that room tried. Elnathan, who had once been the instrument of a prophet's death; Delaiah; Gemariah, in whose son's hearing the scroll had first been read.

He would not listen to them. It is the verdict of the whole book, applied here to a man refusing not a prophet but his own advisers. By this point Jehoiakim will not hear God, will not hear Jeremiah, and will not hear the officials he appointed.

Burning the book is not enough; he wants the men. A royal prince and two officers are detailed to find them, with the same energy that once sent an extradition party to Egypt after Uriah.

And then five words end the paragraph: but the LORD hid them. No angel, no miracle described, no method given. The officials had said go and hide; the narrator says God hid them. Both are true, and that is usually how providence looks: sensible advice taken, a friend's back room, and behind it all a hand the searchers never see.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's answer is immediate: write it again (v. 28). The king is sentenced for the burning (vv. 29–31), and the scroll is rewritten with many words added (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The book came back longer than the one he burned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned. And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king destroys the words, and the word comes again. That sequence is the point of the chapter, and the narrator does not even pause over it.

The instruction is almost dismissive in its simplicity. Write it again.

A book can be burned; the word it carries cannot. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8), and the Lord said the same of his own: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matt 24:35). Peter quotes Isaiah's line and then says what that enduring word is: And this word is the good news that was preached to you (1 Pet 1:25). Every regime that has since burned Bibles has been doing what Jehoiakim did in a warm room in winter, with the same result.

The pattern reached its end in Jesus. The God who spoke at many times and in many ways by the prophets has in these last days spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1-2), and Jesus told the parable of the vineyard owner who sent servant after servant and at last his beloved son, whom the tenants killed (Mark 12:1-8). The rulers of his day dealt with God's final word as Jehoiakim dealt with the scroll: they heard him out, and then got rid of him. And as the scroll came back, so he came back from the grave, and the message they tried to silence went out to the nations.

God quotes the king's objection back at him, and the offence, it turns out, was specific. Not the moral demands, not the accusations of injustice, but the prediction about Babylon. He burned the scroll because of its politics.

Burning a forecast does not alter the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night. And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'" Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence answers the crime in kind. He fed the scroll to the fire in his warm room; his own body will lie out in the open, in the heat by day and the frost by night.

Both halves had been announced before. Jeremiah had already said of this king that With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem (22:19), and of his son Coniah that none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David (22:30). His son Jehoiachin reigned three months and was deported, and that was the end of it.

Readers ask how Jesus can then be David's heir, when Matthew's genealogy runs through Jeconiah, that is Jehoiachin (Matt 1:11-12). The sentence meant that no son of this line would reign on David's throne in Jerusalem, and none ever did. But God had not abandoned David: he had already promised a righteous Branch who would reign (23:5-6; 33:15), and Jesus, David's son through Joseph as his legal father, reigns not from Jehoiakim's palace but from the right hand of God (Acts 2:30-36).

The last clause is the epitaph of the whole reign: but they would not hear. Everything else in the verse is consequence; this is the cause.

So they sat down and did it all over again: the same long labour, voice and pen and ink, with a price now on both their heads.

And the final clause is the quiet triumph of the chapter: And many similar words were added to them. The second edition was longer. Everything Jehoiakim had cut off came back, and more with it, including the paragraph about his own corpse that only exists because he burned the first one. He could not even succeed in making the book shorter.

What he held in his hands that December was the book we are reading. It survived him, outlasted his dynasty, outlasted Babylon, and is still being read aloud in rooms full of people, which is what it was written for in the first place: It may be that someone will hear, and turn, and be forgiven.

Jehoiakim was to have the burial of a donkey, yet Kings says he slept with his fathers (2 Kgs 24:6). That phrase means simply that he died; it says nothing of honourable burial. He probably died in late 598 BC, as the Babylonian army closed in. Chronicles adds that Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chr 36:6), which may never have been carried out. Scripture does not describe what was done with his body, but this commentary takes Jeremiah's word as fulfilled.

36.title: The Scroll Burned and Rewritten
36.overview: In 605 BC, the year Babylon became master of the region, God has Jeremiah dictate twenty-three years of preaching to Baruch, in the hope that Judah may yet turn and be forgiven (vv. 1-8). Baruch reads the scroll in the temple and then to the shaken royal officials, who send him and Jeremiah into hiding (vv. 9-19). King Jehoiakim hears it by his winter fire and burns it column by column, but the LORD hides his servants (vv. 20-26), and the scroll is written again, with more added (vv. 27-32).
36.theology: God's purpose in writing down the threats is repentance and pardon, not record-keeping: it may be that they will turn. When the preacher is barred, God sends the book, and the word moves from air into ink so that it can enter rooms the prophet cannot and outlive the men who carry it (2 Tim 3:16). Attention is not obedience: Jehoiakim heard every column and destroyed each one, while his father Josiah had torn his clothes at a scroll. And a book can be burned, but the word cannot; it came back longer, as God's final Word came back from the grave (Matt 24:35; Mark 12:1-8).
36.examples: The officials who warned Baruch and Jeremiah to hide had careers to protect, and still did what was decent; much of God's care for his servants in this book arrives that way. Jehoiakim's knife is the opposite: the reader who hears the Bible out, column by column, only to know which parts to cut away.

37.text: <sup>1</sup>Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim.<sup>2</sup>But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.<sup>3</sup>King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God."<sup>4</sup>Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison.<sup>5</sup>The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet:<sup>7</sup>"Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land.<sup>8</sup>And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.<sup>9</sup>Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away.<sup>10</sup>For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"<sup>11</sup>Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army,<sup>12</sup>Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people.<sup>13</sup>When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans."<sup>14</sup>And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.<sup>15</sup>And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison.<sup>16</sup>When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,<sup>17</sup>King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon."<sup>18</sup>Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison?<sup>19</sup>Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?<sup>20</sup>Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there."<sup>21</sup>So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah, Babylon's appointee, does not listen (vv. 1–2), yet he asks the still-free prophet to pray for them (vv. 3–4), just as an Egyptian army draws the Chaldeans away from Jerusalem (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They will not hear a word he says, and they would like him to pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence tells you everything about his position. He is Josiah's son, so the blood is right, but he sits on the throne because a foreign emperor put him there, in place of a nephew who was deported. Every day of his reign he is somebody else's arrangement.

That is the man the rest of this chapter shows us: a king with a title and no authority, frightened of his own officials, frightened of Babylon, and half-persuaded that Jeremiah is right.

Before a single event is narrated, the narrator gives the verdict, and it covers the whole society: the king, the civil service, and the ordinary population. Nobody listened.

Put that verdict beside what happens next and the chapter's real subject appears. This is a study of what religion looks like in people who have settled the question of obedience in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God." Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison. The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A polite request for intercession, one verse after we are told this king listens to nothing the prophet says. Weigh the phrase the LORD our God. They claim him as theirs while ignoring his word, and they want his power without his instruction, as if prayer were a service the prophet provides, detached from the message the prophet brings.

Both messengers have histories. Zephaniah son of Maaseiah had come on this same errand once before, when Zedekiah sent to say Inquire of the LORD for us (21:2), and he was the priest who read Shemaiah's hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah rather than acting on it (29:29). Jehucal will shortly stand in front of the king demanding this prophet's death, on the ground that he is weakening the hands of the soldiers (38:4). The man who carries the prayer request is the man who will call for the execution.

Not yet is a quiet note of foreboding. And here is why the palace suddenly wants prayer, and why it is about to stop wanting it. Pharaoh Hophra (almost certainly the king of 44:30) has marched north, Nebuchadnezzar has broken off the siege to deal with him, and the pressure is off.

This is the same withdrawal named three chapters earlier, the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you (34:21): the breathing space in which the slave-owners of Jerusalem went and fetched back the people they had just freed. The same lifted siege that produced the broken covenant produced this request for prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Hophra reigned in Egypt from 589 to 570 BC; his name appears in Scripture only at 44:30.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer is unwelcome: Egypt will go home and the Chaldeans will come back and burn the city (vv. 7–8). Do not deceive yourselves (v. 9): even wounded Babylonians would rise and burn it (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The outcome was never a military calculation, so a lifted siege proves nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: "Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land. And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked for prayer; they get a word. God answers the request, and the answer is not what was ordered. It begins by dismantling the very thing that had raised their spirits: the relieving army is going home. Not defeated in a great battle, just about to return: the help everyone was counting on will simply turn around and leave.

Judah's reliance on Egypt was an old sickness. Isaiah had named it a century before: men who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt (Isa 30:2), and who would find that the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame (Isa 30:3).

Come back, capture, burn: the empty siege lines are a pause, not a deliverance, and God says so before anyone builds a theology out of the good news.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away. For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The command is about the inside of their heads: Do not deceive yourselves.

Nobody was lying to them here. They were doing it themselves, and they were doing it with evidence: the army really had gone, the fields really were passable again, the relief was real. Self-deception rarely needs false facts; it only needs true facts read the way we want them read. God even supplies the sentence they were saying to each other, in quotation marks, and answers it directly: for they will not go away. The cure is not sharper willpower but letting God's word, which knows the exact form our wish has taken, tell us the truth; he says hard things to people he means to save.

The picture is deliberately extreme. Suppose you won. Suppose the entire Babylonian army lay wounded in their tents. Those men would get up and burn Jerusalem anyway.

That is not a comment on Babylonian toughness. It is a statement that the fall of this city is God's decision, and therefore not available to be overturned by force of arms. The question in this war was never military.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving for Benjamin during the lull, Jeremiah is arrested at the gate as a deserter (vv. 11–14), beaten, and held many days in the dungeon cells (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty years of being called a traitor, and when the charge is finally laid it is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people. When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans." And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the roads briefly open, the prophet goes home to Anathoth on family business, to receive his portion there among the people: some matter of inherited land. Scripture does not say what, though it may have been the same family property his cousin Hanamel would later offer him (32:6-9).

It is an ordinary errand, and that is what makes what follows so bitter.

A sentry with a name and a grandfather, doing what sentries do in a war. And the charge was not absurd on its face: Jeremiah had publicly advised the city to surrender, telling them that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live (21:9). A man with those views, walking out of the north gate during a lull, looked exactly like a defector.

The denial is blunt and it is true. It is a lie. For nearly forty years he had been called a traitor for telling Judah what God said, and when an actual charge of treason was finally laid against him it was false. He had urged surrender because God had spoken, and he was not slipping away himself.

And then the phrase that has echoed through the whole book, now from a soldier at a gate: Irijah would not listen to him. Nobody in this chapter listens to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison. When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are not the officials of chapter 26 who convened a fair court, nor those of chapter 36 who trembled at the scroll and told Baruch to hide. A different generation is in office now, and they are enraged.

He is beaten and locked in a private house converted into a jail. There is no trial mentioned, no hearing, no examination of the sentry's claim. The man who had just been asked to pray for the king is flogged by the king's officials.

Two details, and they are the whole cost of his obedience in this chapter: dungeon cells, and many days.

The narrator does not dwell on it and gives us no lament from the prophet. But this is the same man who had written that God's word was a fire in his bones he could not hold in, and this is what speaking it out cost him: a cellar, for weeks, with no prospect of release and a fair expectation of dying there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Is There Any Word from the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king questions him secretly and gets the same word (v. 17). Only then does Jeremiah plead his own case (vv. 18–20), and he is moved to the court of the guard with a daily loaf until all the bread of the city was gone (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers honestly first and asks for mercy second, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything about this interview is furtive. The king has the prophet brought up from the cells and questions him secretly in his house, because he dare not be seen consulting the man his officials have just beaten.

His question is one of the saddest in Scripture: Is there any word from the LORD? He has heard the word for years, refused it, imprisoned the man who brought it, and now asks in a private room whether there is any more of it. He wants a different answer, and he asks the one person guaranteed not to give him one.

And consider Jeremiah's position as he replies. He is standing in front of the only man who can release him, bruised from a beating, expecting to die in a cellar. One softened sentence would have helped his case enormously.

What he says is There is, and then the same sentence that put him where he is: You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. No hedging, no trading. The message did not change because the prophet's circumstances had.

Six hundred years later another prisoner stood in front of another frightened ruler who kept asking questions in private, and there the answer was different: he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed (Matt 27:14). Jeremiah spoke the word and was spared; the Word himself was silent before his judge, and was not spared, and it was for us.

Only after delivering the word does he speak for himself, and both questions are fair.

The first is the protest of an innocent man: What wrong have I done? The second is unanswerable: Where are your prophets, the ones who promised Babylon would never come? They had been believed and he had been beaten, and now the Babylonians were camped in the fields and the optimists had nothing to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there." So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And here the iron prophet asks for something, courteously and without pretence. Let my humble plea come before you.

He does not ask for vindication, or for his accusers to be punished, or even for freedom. He asks not to be sent back to that particular cellar, and he says plainly why: lest I die there. There is no false bravery in this. He was afraid of dying in a hole, he said so, and asking a weak king for a small mercy was not beneath him.

The king does the one decent thing within his power. Not release, for he has not the courage for that, but a transfer to the court of the guard, and a daily loaf.

Compare the rations another prophet was promised for telling a king the truth: Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water (1 Kgs 22:27). Jeremiah gets a loaf a day from the bakers' street, and it comes through the frightened man who had him beaten.

Then the clause that quietly measures the whole siege: until all the bread of the city was gone. His provision lasted exactly as long as there was any bread in Jerusalem to be had. God kept him alive on the last supplies of a starving city, one loaf at a time, in a courtyard. And it was in that courtyard, on that daily bread, that he bought the field at Anathoth and was given the promises of chapters 32 and 33.

Which is the answer to Zedekiah's question, though he never grasped it. Is there any word from the LORD? There was, and the chapters we have just read are it, given to a beaten man on a bread ration, about fields bought again and a righteous Branch for David.

37.title: Arrested at the Benjamin Gate
37.overview: The Babylonian siege has lifted for a time, because an Egyptian army has marched north, and King Zedekiah, who will not listen to Jeremiah, asks him to pray (vv. 1-5). The answer is that Babylon will return and burn the city (vv. 6-10). During the lull Jeremiah is arrested at the city gate as a deserter, beaten and thrown into a cellar (vv. 11-16), until the king secretly sends for him, hears the same word again, and moves him to the court of the guard with a daily loaf of bread (vv. 17-21).
37.theology: People who have settled the question of obedience in advance still want the benefits of prayer, claiming the LORD as our God while ignoring his word. Self-deception rarely needs false facts, only true facts read as we wish: the siege really had lifted, and the conclusion drawn from it was still a lie. Against this stands a prophet who will not trade the message for better treatment, yet is honest enough to ask for mercy and admit his fear. And God's provision can come through the hand of a frightened man who wronged you, and be exactly enough: a loaf a day, as long as the city had bread.
37.examples: Most of us know the pull of Zedekiah's position: asking God for help in a crisis while having decided in advance not to do what he says. And most of us know the relief that makes us read a lull as a deliverance. Jeremiah's plea not to be sent back to the cellar is a gift to anyone who has been ashamed of being afraid: the bravest prophet in the book asked a weak king for a small mercy, and God gave it through him.
