verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Is in Your Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four officials hear Jeremiah urging surrender (vv. 1–3) and demand his death (v. 4). Zedekiah's reply gives away his whole reign (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who cannot say no, and hands over a man he believes to be a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people: "Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live. Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men, each named with his father, and one of them we have met. Jucal son of Shelemiah is the Jehucal who carried the king's request for prayer to this same prophet one chapter ago (37:3). The man sent to ask for intercession now appears at the head of the party demanding an execution.

See also where Jeremiah is and what he is doing. He is confined to the court of the guard, and he is still preaching to all the people. A prison in the middle of a palace compound turned out to be a pulpit.

This is the word that made him hated, and it pays to be clear about what it actually offered. It was not propaganda for Babylon. It was an escape route: stay and die, go out and live, and live, repeated as if to make sure nobody missed the offer inside the threat.

And the ground of the offer is the certainty of the outcome. Because the city will fall, leaving is life. Everything depends on whether the announced future is true, which is precisely what his hearers would not grant.

The phrase his life as a prize of war means that he will come out of the disaster alive, and that his life is all he will carry off.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm." King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge is morale, and on its own terms it is not stupid. A man telling the garrison that the city will fall and they should surrender is, militarily, a liability. Any war cabinet in history would have said the same.

But listen to the last clause, because it is the exact inversion of the truth: this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm. This is the prophet who had written to the exiles telling them to seek the welfare of the city and pray for it (29:7), who had pleaded with Judah for forty years to turn and live, and who was at that moment offering the only survivable course available. The men who were marching the city into a furnace accused him of wanting its harm.

That accusation has a long life. The person who tells an uncomfortable truth is charged with wishing the harm his warning is trying to prevent.

The king's plea of powerlessness is one of the most pitiful sentences in the book, and it is not true: he will overrule these same men almost at once when someone asks him to. What he lacks is not authority but nerve. He hands over a man he believes to be a prophet, to men he is afraid of, and consoles himself with the fiction that he had no choice. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25).

Another ruler would one day say the same thing with water and a basin, knowing the prisoner was innocent, and give him up because the crowd was louder than his conscience (Matt 27:24; John 19:12-16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Cast Into the Mud, and Lifted Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is lowered into a muddy cistern (v. 6). Ebed-melech the Ethiopian goes to the king, wins permission (vv. 7–10), and draws Jeremiah up with ropes padded with old rags (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A foreigner and a eunuch, thinking about how the ropes would cut.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud. When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate— Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cistern is a bottle-shaped pit cut into rock, narrow at the neck and wide below, designed to hold rainwater. This one held no water, only mud.

So they lowered him into a stone jar in the ground, in the dark, and he sank in the mud. There is no way out of such a hole without help from above: the walls curve inward and the floor gives way beneath you. They did not need to kill him; they only needed to leave him.

Hold the image, because a psalm turns it into the picture of salvation itself: He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure (Ps 40:2). That is exactly what is about to happen to Jeremiah, and it is what God does for sinners: not advice shouted down the shaft, but someone coming to haul us out.

And the rescuer is introduced with three details that in that society were all disqualifications: a foreigner, from Ethiopia, and a eunuch.

Every Judean official in this chapter behaves badly. The one man who moves is an African court servant who, under the law of Deuteronomy 23:1, could not enter the assembly of the LORD, and he moves immediately: he heard, and then he went. No committee, no delay.
verseByVerse.note: Ebed-melech means “servant of the king”; he was a Cushite, from south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: "My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city." Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He says it to the king's face, in public at the Benjamin Gate, with the officials' faction in power and his own position entirely dependent on royal favour: these men have done evil.

He calls Jeremiah what the officials would not, the prophet, and his argument is practical and humane: the man will starve down there, because there is no bread left in the city. The daily loaf of the previous chapter has run out, which probably places this scene in the last weeks of the siege.

And Zedekiah, who so recently can do nothing, immediately orders thirty men to the rescue. The king could act all along; the difference between a prophet dying in mud and a prophet drawn out of it was one man willing to speak up.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes. Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so. Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had his authorisation and thirty men, and before he pulled, he went looking for rags.

Think about what that means. He detoured to a palace storeroom, found old rags and worn-out clothes, and lowered them down the shaft first, because a man hauled out of a pit on bare ropes, by thirty men pulling hard, would have the rope cut into his armpits.

He even explains the padding to the exhausted man below, telling him exactly where to place it.

Scripture spends three verses on this. It could have said they pulled him out. Instead it records the wardrobe, the old clothes, the instruction about the armpits, because God takes notice of kindness that troubles itself over details. Anyone can want a man rescued. This is what it looks like to actually care whether the rescue hurts.

Out of the mud and back to the courtyard: still a prisoner, but alive and above ground.

Ebed-melech is not finished in this book. When the city falls, God sends a private word to him: I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). The same phrase offered to anyone who would leave the city is given personally to the man who pulled the prophet out, and the reason given is not his courage but his trust.

And there is a promise made for men in exactly his position. Isaiah had said: let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree", for God would give such men a monument and a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isa 56:3-5). A childless foreign servant has his name written in Scripture, remembered for one day's decency, long after the officials who outranked him are recalled only as the men who did evil.

The New Testament shows that promise coming true. On a desert road an Ethiopian eunuch, another court official from the same far country, was reading Isaiah's servant song, heard that it spoke of Jesus, and was baptised (Acts 8:26-39). The outsider who pulled a prophet from a pit was a forerunner of a great company of outsiders welcomed into God's household by Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a secret meeting (vv. 14–16) the offer is set out twice: surrender and live with the city spared, or refuse and see it burn (vv. 17–18). The king fears the deserters (v. 19), and a vision answers him (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience was offered to the end, and refused for fear of the wrong people.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me." Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me." Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another secret meeting, in a discreet corner of the temple. The king who let him be thrown in a pit wants a private consultation, and he opens with a demand for total honesty from a man he has failed to protect.

The prophet's reply is two accusations, and both are accurate.

The first is about his own safety; he had just been left to die and had every reason to expect it again. The second is sadder and sharper: if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me. He has read the man. There is no point in advising someone who has already decided that advice will not move him, and Jeremiah says so before he speaks.

The oath is solemn and beautifully phrased, As the LORD lives, who made our souls, and it is sworn secretly. A king who dares not be seen keeping faith with a prophet swears by the God who made them both, in a side entrance, where nobody will hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live. But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand." King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And here, in the final weeks, with the walls about to break, God is still making an offer.

Read what is on the table: the king's life, his household, and this city shall not be burned with fire. Jerusalem could still have been spared. The temple need not have burned. Everything depended on one man walking out of a gate.

Two roads, stated plainly, with nothing hidden: exactly what the king had asked for. This is the same structure as the whole book: repent and live, refuse and perish, and the choice genuinely open until the last hour.

And this is his answer to the offer of his city's survival: he is worried about being mocked.

The men who had already defected, following Jeremiah's advice, would jeer at the king who arrived last. That is the calculation. Weigh it: Jerusalem burned, the temple destroyed, his sons killed, his own eyes put out, thousands dead of famine, because a frightened man could not bear the humiliation of walking out to people who had gone before him.

Fear of man does this. It will accept enormous real disaster to avoid a small loss of face, and it always presents itself as prudence. Its cure is not a stronger nerve but a greater fear, of the LORD, who made our souls and still holds out life; and the Spirit given to believers is a Spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Tim 1:7).

The city would certainly fall (v. 3), yet Zedekiah is told it need not burn if he surrenders. The fall was certain, but its manner depended on him: surrender, and the city and his household would be spared the fire. God’s warnings are real, and they call for a response.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared. But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me: Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.' All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet answers the actual fear directly, You shall not be given to them, and then presses the one thing needed: Obey now the voice of the LORD.

Note the pastoral patience of it. He does not lecture the king on cowardice. He removes the objection, promises that it shall be well with you, and asks for obedience today.

The vision is of the royal harem marched out of the palace, and the words God gives them are a taunt in verse, the sort of thing that would be sung about him afterwards. Now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you. The king who left a prophet to sink in mud will himself be stuck in it, abandoned by the officials he was too frightened to cross. Jeremiah was pulled out by a foreigner with rags; nobody will come down for Zedekiah.

His trusted friends, the men whose approval cost him his city, will be the ones who prevailed against you and then walked away. That is the standing testimony of every idol: it demands everything, and abandons you when you need it.

The last word of the appeal is the list of what refusal will cost: wives, sons, his own capture, the city burned. Every item arrived exactly as stated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah's last concern is secrecy (vv. 24–26); Jeremiah answers the officials as instructed, and stays in the court of the guard until the city falls (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The king protected the secret of the conversation and not the city it was about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die. If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,' then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'" Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offer of life for his city has just been laid before him, along with the vision of his wives led away. His response is to worry about who might find out that they had spoken.

He scripts the answer, and the line he supplies is a real one, the same plea Jeremiah had made to him at their last meeting: do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there (37:20). The king is telling him to give a true statement about an earlier conversation instead of the subject of this one.

The officials, too, will offer Jeremiah the same bargain the king just did: tell us everything and we will not kill you. Everyone in this palace negotiates with a man's life as the currency.

They came, exactly as the king predicted, and Jeremiah answered as instructed. The interrogation stopped because nobody could contradict him.

He stayed in the courtyard while the food ran out, and the city fell around a man nobody would listen to.

Set the two figures of this chapter side by side. A king of David's line, with armies, officials and the word of God delivered privately into his hand, who could do nothing; and an African eunuch with no rights at all, who heard about an injustice, walked to the gate, said so, fetched rags, and saved a prophet's life. God's verdict on them is already recorded: one lost his sons, his sight and his city; the other was told, because you have put your trust in me (39:18).

And the mud is the picture to keep: a man who could not climb out, and the ropes, padding and hands that came down for him (Ps 40:2). That is the gospel in a cistern, and the one who came down for us was not embarrassed to be seen doing it.

Was Jeremiah lying? He told the officials only what the king instructed, a true part of the conversation (cf. 37:20), and withheld the rest. Withholding the truth from those who have no right to it, to protect life, is not the same as bearing false witness.

38.title: The Cistern and the Ethiopian
38.overview: In the last weeks of the siege, officials who hate Jeremiah's call to surrender have him lowered into a muddy cistern to die, with the king's weak consent (vv. 1-6). An Ethiopian palace servant, Ebed-melech, pleads for him and draws him out with ropes padded with old rags (vv. 7-13). In a final secret meeting Zedekiah is offered his life and the city's survival if he will surrender, and refuses for fear of mockery (vv. 14-23); Jeremiah stays in the court of the guard until Jerusalem is taken (vv. 24-28).
38.theology: The message that made Jeremiah hated was an escape route, and it stayed open until the final weeks. Fear of man is a snare that disguises itself as helplessness: the king who said he could do nothing ordered thirty men the moment somebody asked him (Prov 29:25; John 19:12-16). God notices kindness that troubles itself over details, and he commends the outsider with no standing: a foreign eunuch is given a name in Scripture for his trust (Isa 56:3-5). And the mud is a picture of salvation, a pit with no way out but hands from above.
38.examples: A rescuer who stops to fetch rags so that the ropes will not cut is a model for every kind of practical care: the hospital visit, the meal left on a doorstep, the hard conversation with someone in power. And Zedekiah's choice, a city lost rather than face being laughed at, is a warning to anyone who knows what is right and fears the opinion of friends more than God.

And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.<sup>6</sup>The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.<sup>7</sup>He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>8</sup>The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained.<sup>10</sup>Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.<sup>11</sup>Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you."<sup>13</sup>So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon<sup>14</sup>sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.<sup>15</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>16</sup>"Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day.<sup>17</sup>But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.<sup>18</sup>For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Breach Was Made in the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A long siege ends in one line, a breach was made in the city (vv. 1–3). Zedekiah flees by night, is caught near Jericho and judged at Riblah (vv. 4–5), where he sees his sons killed and is then blinded (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing he ever saw was what his refusal cost his own children.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city. Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two dates, roughly January 588 BC and July 586 BC (some reckon a year earlier), and about a year and a half of siege between them.

The narrator gives the siege no adjectives. Everything that happened inside those walls, the bread running out, the cistern, the last loaf from the bakers' street, the horrors Lamentations records of starving families, sits compressed into the gap between one month and another. Then seven words: a breach was made in the city.

This is the sentence the whole book has been walking toward. Forty years of warning, and when it arrives it is reported like a line in a chronicle.

Foreign officers sit down in the gate, and the detail is precise: these are Babylonian names and Babylonian titles, one of which, Rab-saris (chief officer), has turned up on a clay tablet from Nebuchadnezzar's court bearing a name very like Nebu-sar-sekim's.

And the gate is the point. The gate was where Israel's elders sat to judge, where Boaz called witnesses, where the officials had once acquitted Jeremiah. Now other men sit there, and their language is not Hebrew. The seat of justice in Jerusalem has changed occupants.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 52 and 2 Kings 25 give fuller accounts of the same events.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had been told, twice and plainly, that if he walked out to the Babylonians his life would be spared and the city would not burn (38:17). He would not do it in daylight as an act of obedience.

So here he goes out anyway: at night, by a garden gate, through a gap in the walls, running for the Jordan valley. The same feet that would not carry him out in surrender carry him out in flight. What obedience would have cost him was his dignity; what disobedience cost him is in the next three verses.

They catch him on the flat ground near Jericho, where Israel had first entered the land. The story of the possession of Canaan ends where it began, with the last king of Judah taken prisoner.

And he is brought to Riblah, some two hundred miles north, to have sentence passed on him. He is tried as a rebel vassal, because that is what he was: Nebuchadnezzar had put him on the throne and he had broken his oath.

verseByVerse.quote: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order of events is deliberate: his line is ended while he watches, as the parallel accounts record identically (52:10; 2 Kgs 25:7), and then they blind him.

God had told him, through the man he left in a cistern, that he would see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face (32:4), and that he would go to Babylon. Every clause came true, and not one the way he would have imagined. The last image his eyes ever held was his own children dying. They had done nothing; his fear of being laughed at had cost them everything, and the narrator records it without a word of comment, as if it were too heavy for one.

God's words are not riddles, but they are not tame either. Zedekiah had heard this sentence for years and treated it as a bargaining position. It was a description.

Is anything left of the promise of chapter 34, that he would not die by the sword but in peace, with mourners and spices (34:4-5)? It is a thin mercy beside what he lost, but as far as we are told he died in prison in Babylon, not by the sword (52:11), and this commentary reads that as the promise kept, even to a king who had earned nothing.

Ezekiel said Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon yet he shall not see it (Ezek 12:13). Here is the answer: he was blinded at Riblah, then taken to Babylon, where he died.

Why would God allow children to be killed for their father's sin? It is a terrible question, and the text does not soften the scene; Jeremiah himself would weep over the children of this city (Lam 2:11). The cruelty was Nebuchadnezzar's, and Scripture never calls it good. God foretold it and used it as judgment on a king who had broken a sworn oath (Ezek 17:15-19), and Babylon's own cruelties would in turn be judged (25:12; 51:24).

And what became of the promise that David would never lack a man on the throne (33:17)? On this day the throne is empty and the king's sons lie dead at Riblah. But David's line survived in the exiled Jehoiachin (52:31-34), and the promise waited for the Branch. Six centuries later a son of David was crowned with thorns outside this same city, hailed in mockery as King of the Jews, and raised to the throne of his father David that has no end (Luke 1:32-33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The city is burned and its people deported (vv. 8–9), and then the poor who owned nothing are given vineyards and fields (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The people with nothing to lose ended the day owning land.

verseByVerse.quote: The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The palace, the houses, the walls. Everything Judah had trusted in, dynasty, city and defences, dismantled in one verse, exactly as had been said of the scroll Jehoiakim burned: the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land (36:29).

The temple is not mentioned here. Chapter 52 will supply that detail, and perhaps this account cannot bring itself to say it yet.

Three groups, all deported: those who held out, those who defected, and the remainder. Even the deserters go, which shows that surrendering was never a trick to avoid exile; it was how to stay alive. Jeremiah had promised life as a prize of war, not a comfortable outcome.

And then this, in a chapter about catastrophe.

The people left in the land are the poor people who owned nothing, and a pagan general hands them vineyards and fields. The landless get land on the day the landowners lose everything. Men who had been at the bottom of every list in Judah, cheated by the officials of chapter 34, sold and re-enslaved, denied their wages by the house-builders of chapter 22, wake up as freeholders.

Nobody planned this as justice. Nebuzaradan was solving an administrative problem: keep the countryside producing, deport anyone who could organise a revolt. But the effect is a reversal so exact that it reads like a verdict, and the New Testament says out loud what this verse only does: has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (Jas 2:5). Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Deal With Him As He Tells You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar orders that the prophet be treated well (vv. 11–12), and the Babylonian officers entrust him to Gedaliah (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The emperor's standing order for one prisoner: do whatever he asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying, "Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you." So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The emperor of the world has one named prisoner on his mind, with the extraordinary instruction deal with him as he tells you. Weigh the irony without missing the providence. For forty years the rulers and priests of Judah imprisoned this man, beat him, banned him from the temple, burned his book and dropped him in a pit. The pagan king who destroyed the city gave orders that he was to be treated well and have his own way.

Presumably the Babylonians knew he had urged surrender and counted him useful. God's protection of his servants routinely arrives through people acting for their own reasons.

The whole senior staff of the occupying army is involved in fetching one old man out of a courtyard, and the name at the end of the chain is a gift. Ahikam protected him at a trial decades earlier (26:24); Ahikam's son takes him home after the city falls. Shaphan's family has turned up at every hinge of this book: reading the law to Josiah, lending Baruch a room, carrying the letter to Babylon, and now this. Faithfulness across generations does not make headlines, and it keeps quietly holding things up.

So he lived among the people. After the stocks, the cistern, the dungeon cells and the court of the guard, the prophet ends the chapter a free man living among ordinary Judeans.

Jeremiah was released into Gedaliah’s care here, but 40:1 finds him in chains at Ramah. He was most likely rounded up with the captives by mistake, then released again at Ramah when the commander recognised him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Because You Have Put Your Trust in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter reaches back into the siege for a word to Ebed-melech: he will see the city fall (vv. 15–16), but God will deliver him, because you have put your trust in me (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who fetched the rags is told why he will live, and it is not because of the rags.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard: "Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day. But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid. For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This word, given before the walls broke, is placed out of sequence so that it lands after the catastrophe it was spoken into. It begins with the truth: Ebed-melech will see the palace he worked in burn. There is no promise that he will be spared the sight; only that he will come through it.

The men of whom you are afraid. God names the fear without rebuking it. Ebed-melech had walked up to the king at a public gate and accused four powerful officials of evil, and he had been frightened of them ever since, as well he might be.

Courage, in this book, is not the absence of fear. It is what Ebed-melech did while afraid, and God's answer is not that his fear was foolish but that those men will never have him.

The phrase your life as a prize of war is the one Jeremiah had shouted to the whole city: go out to the Chaldeans and you shall have his life as a prize of war, and live (38:2). What was offered publicly to everyone is now guaranteed personally to one man.

And mark the reason God gives. Not because you rescued my prophet. Not because you were brave, or kind, or fetched padding for the ropes, but because you have put your trust in me.

That is the verdict of the chapter, and it sorts everyone in it. A king of David's line, who had the promises, the temple and the prophet's private counsel, lost his sons and his sight because he trusted the opinion of men he was afraid of. A foreign eunuch with no tribe, no children and no rights was saved because he trusted God, and his trusting showed itself, as it always does, in what he did about a man sinking in mud. It is the same ground on which any sinner is rescued: by grace you have been saved through faith (Eph 2:8), trusting the God who keeps his word, a faith that then shows itself in love.

The city fell, and the promise held: God knew the name of the one servant in Jerusalem who believed him, and had a word addressed to him by name before the first stone came down.

39.title: The City Falls
39.overview: After a siege of a year and a half, the wall of Jerusalem is breached. Zedekiah flees by night, is caught near Jericho, sees his sons killed at Riblah and is blinded (vv. 1-7). The city is burned and its people deported, while the poorest are given vineyards and fields (vv. 8-10). Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be treated well, and he is entrusted to Gedaliah (vv. 11-14). The chapter closes by reaching back into the siege for God's promise to Ebed-melech, the man who pulled Jeremiah from the cistern (vv. 15-18).
39.theology: God's words are descriptions, not bargaining positions: Zedekiah treated the sentence as an opening offer, and every clause of it came true. Yet even here God's care shows. The landless are given land on the day the landowners lose everything, and the prophet whom Judah's rulers imprisoned is protected by a pagan emperor and taken home by a faithful family (Jas 2:5; Matt 5:5). And in the ruins, the one man promised his life is saved not for his bravery but for his trust, as every sinner is (Eph 2:8).
39.examples: Zedekiah walked out of the city in the end, by night and in flight, having refused to walk out by day in obedience. It is a picture worth keeping for anyone putting off a costly step God has made plain: delay does not usually spare us the step, only the blessing that went with it. Ebed-melech, frightened and faithful, is the other picture, and the more hopeful one.

Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.<sup>4</sup>Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands.
