Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.<sup>10</sup>As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."<sup>11</sup>Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them,<sup>12</sup>then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.<sup>13</sup>Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah<sup>14</sup>and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.<sup>15</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?"<sup>16</sup>But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Whole Land Is Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Found in chains among the captives at Ramah, Jeremiah hears the Babylonian captain preach Judah's own theology to him (vv. 1–3). Freed and given the choice, he goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and stays among the people left in the land (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A pagan officer with better theology than Judah's kings, handing a prophet his freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon. The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place. The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something has gone wrong between chapters, and the narrator does not hide it. The emperor had ordered that this man be looked after and given his own way (39:12), and here he is bound in chains in a column of deportees at Ramah, the staging camp where the prisoners were mustered.

Ramah is where Rachel was heard weeping for her children (31:15). The prophet who wrote that verse is now standing in the very place, chained, among the people it was about. Matthew would hear that weeping again when Herod killed the children of Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18), on the night the child in whom Rachel's comfort would come was carried to safety.

Orders get lost, and God's promises to his servants are not always administered smoothly by the people carrying them.

A Babylonian general, an idolater, summarises Jeremiah's entire ministry in three sentences and gets it right. He names the agent: The LORD has brought it about. He names the reliability: has done as he said. He names the cause: Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice.

Forty years of preaching that to Judah had produced a beating, a cistern and a burned scroll. The occupying officer worked it out from the outside, and said it to the one man in the country who had been saying it all along.

It is a strange, bleak vindication. The nations understood what Judah would not, and there is a warning in that for anyone who has grown deaf inside the church while outsiders can see plainly what God is doing. The God who says so still speaks, and the deaf who turn to him are heard.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay about five miles north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go. If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go. Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chains come off, and the old man is handed something he has not had in decades: a choice.

Babylon means comfort, safety and status: the deportees included the skilled and the well-connected, and a prophet with a record of urging surrender would have been honoured there. Judah means rubble, poverty and a wrecked community.

See, the whole land is before you. The phrase would echo for any Israelite; it is the language of Abraham and Lot looking over Canaan. Except that the land before him now is ash.

The ESV notes that the opening of verse 5 follows the Syriac, the Hebrew being uncertain; what is clear is the kindness: rations and a gift, from the man who burned the temple, to the prophet who said it would burn.

He stays. Offered Babylon, with a pension and a hearing, he chooses the ruined country and the poor people in it.

It is one of the last great acts of his ministry. He had wept for this people for forty years while they hated him; now that they are broken and leaderless he will not leave them. A man who had every reason to shake the dust off his feet went and lived among them instead.

It is a small picture of a far greater choice. The Son of God, who had every right to the glory of heaven, emptied himself and came to live among a ruined people (Phil 2:7), and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11). Jeremiah stayed with the poor of Judah; Christ became poor himself, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Gather Wine and Summer Fruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The captains still at large come in to Gedaliah (vv. 7–8), who swears that serving Babylon will be well with them and sends them to the harvest (vv. 9–10). The scattered Judeans come home and gather in abundance (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: A harvest in the year the city burned.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon, they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is now a province run by a Judean governor, and its population is described without flattery: the poorest of the land. The people Nebuzaradan gave vineyards to (39:10) are the nation now.

Out in the countryside are armed bands, officers whose units survived by staying out of the city. They come in when they hear there is a government again.

Five commanders, named. The first of them, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, will murder the governor within months; the second, Johanan the son of Kareah, will try to prevent it and then lead the survivors into the mistake of chapter 42.

The narrator lists them flatly, the assassin first, as it looked at the time.
verseByVerse.note: Gedaliah ruled from Mizpah, north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you. As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gedaliah's inaugural policy is Jeremiah's sermon turned into government.

Compare what the prophet had been saying for years: bring your neck under the yoke of Babylon and serve him and his people and live (27:12), and it shall be well with you. Gedaliah says the same three things (do not be afraid, serve Babylon, dwell in the land) and adds an oath to guarantee it.

This is what it looks like when someone finally believes the prophet. And it is no accident that the man doing it is Ahikam's son. He grew up in a house where Jeremiah was taken seriously.

He takes the unpleasant job himself, to represent you before the Chaldeans, standing between his people and the occupiers, and gives everyone else the ordinary work: pick the grapes, gather the summer fruit, press the oil, fill the jars, live in your towns.

It is the same instruction God had sent to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, live (29:5). After catastrophe, the path back is not a grand project but harvest, storage and settled homes. Leaders who take the hard conversations on themselves and leave their people free to get on with ordinary faithful life are doing something very close to pastoral work.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them, then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refugees hear. Judeans had scattered into Moab, Ammon, Edom and further during the invasion, and news reaches them that there is a remnant and a governor.

They come home, and the year produces a harvest in great abundance.

It is a real mercy, and the book does not oversell it. In the year Jerusalem burned, with the temple gone and the king blinded, the vines and the fruit trees of Judah bore heavily, and scattered people came back from Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands to pick them. God had said he would gather them from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you (29:14), and here is a first small instalment, small enough to miss and real enough to eat.

Mercies after judgment often look like this: not a restored temple, but a good grape harvest and somewhere to put it. The God who had every right to leave the land empty sent fruit on the vines for people who had nothing, in the very year they had least reason to expect it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — He Would Not Believe Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Johanan and the commanders warn Gedaliah of an Ammonite plot, and he will not believe them (vv. 13–14). Johanan offers privately to kill Ishmael, and Gedaliah calls the warning false (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: A good man's refusal to think ill of anyone, and the remnant paid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The intelligence is specific: a named foreign king, a named agent, a named target. Baalis of Ammon wants the Babylonian settlement destabilised, and Ishmael, who (chapter 41 tells us) was of the royal family, has a claim of his own to resent a commoner governing Judah.

It is brought by several commanders together, not by one grudge-bearer, and it was true.

One sentence, and the remnant of Judah turns on it.

Why would he not believe it? Everything we know of him suggests a generous man: he had sheltered Jeremiah, he had sworn oaths of safety to these very officers, his policy was trust and ordinary life. A man like that finds it hard to credit that someone who eats at his table is planning to kill him.

And that is the uncomfortable point of the paragraph. This is not the failure of a fool or a cynic. It is a good man's charity applied where discernment was needed, and Scripture does not praise it; it simply records what it cost. Refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and leaders who will not hear a warning about a colleague can be as destructive as leaders who trust nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Johanan tries again in private, and his proposal is ugly: let me kill him quietly, and no one will know it. A secret assassination to prevent an assassination.

Gedaliah was right to refuse that. There is no warrant for murdering a man on intelligence, however good, and the governor who had just sworn oaths of safety could hardly begin with a private killing.

But look at the reasoning Johanan attaches, because he had seen further than anyone: Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish? He understood that everything now rested on one man's survival. Kill Gedaliah and the harvest, the returning refugees, the whole fragile settlement come apart.

He was exactly right, and he was proposing the wrong remedy. Sound analysis and a sinful solution frequently arrive together.

And there is the sentence that ends the chapter, and very nearly ends the remnant. He does not merely decline the murder; he calls the warning a lie. You are speaking falsely of Ishmael.

He could have refused the assassination and still taken precautions: kept Ishmael at a distance, declined to dine with him, posted a guard. Instead he accused the men telling him the truth of slander, and took no measures at all. Soon afterwards, in the seventh month and probably the same year, Ishmael came to Mizpah with ten men, and as they ate bread together there they rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword (41:1-2).

So the last good governor of Judah, from the family that had protected the prophet for three generations, was murdered at his own table by a man he refused to suspect, and the remnant scattered exactly as Johanan had said. The book gives him no rebuke and no eulogy. It simply records that he would not believe them, and lets the next chapter say what it cost.

Judah's story does not end with a Babylonian army but with a dinner party and a knife, which is a sober word about how communities that have survived catastrophe are usually lost. Not to the great enemy outside, but to one of their own, welcomed at the table, while a warning went unheeded.

40.title: Released at Ramah
40.overview: The fall of Jerusalem is over, and this chapter begins the story of those left behind. Jeremiah, found in chains among the deportees at Ramah, is freed by the Babylonian commander and chooses to stay with the poor of the land under the new governor, Gedaliah (vv. 1-6). Gedaliah gathers the scattered soldiers and refugees, and the year yields an abundant harvest (vv. 7-12). But he refuses to believe a warning that Ishmael has been sent to murder him (vv. 13-16).
40.theology: An outsider can state plainly what those inside the covenant refuse to hear: a Babylonian officer summarised Jeremiah's whole message and got it right. Offered comfort in Babylon or ruin in Judah, the prophet chose his broken people, a small picture of the Son of God who became poor for us (2 Cor 8:9). After catastrophe, God's mercy often looks like a harvest and settled homes rather than a grand restoration. And the chapter ends with two warnings for leaders: refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and sound analysis can arrive with a sinful remedy.
40.examples: Communities that survive a catastrophe are often lost not to the enemy outside but to trouble within, welcomed at the table while a warning goes unheeded. A church, a family or a business can learn from Gedaliah to take a sober warning seriously without slandering anyone, and from Johanan that seeing the danger clearly does not justify doing wrong to stop it.

41.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah,<sup>2</sup>Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.<sup>3</sup>Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.<sup>4</sup>On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it,<sup>5</sup>eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam."<sup>7</sup>When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.<sup>8</sup>But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions.<sup>9</sup>Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.<sup>10</sup>Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,<sup>12</sup>they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.<sup>14</sup>So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.<sup>15</sup>But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.<sup>16</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt<sup>18</sup>because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — As They Ate Bread Together
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael, a prince of the royal family, comes to Mizpah with ten men and kills Gedaliah at his own table (vv. 1–2), and the Judeans and Chaldean soldiers with him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A guest at the governor's table, with a sword under the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land. Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Probably barely two months after the city fell (the year is not given), the assassin arrives, and now we learn who he was. Of the royal family, and one of the chief officers of the king. A prince of David's line, and Gedaliah was a commoner appointed by Babylon.

That is motive enough without Ammonite money. What makes it more than politics is As they ate bread together: received as a guest, he drew his sword across the table.

In the ancient world a shared meal was a bond. To eat a man's bread was to place yourself under obligation to him, which is why a psalm reaches for exactly this image to describe the deepest wound available: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps 41:9).

The Lord took that verse onto his own lips in an upper room, of a man sitting at his table with the money already counted: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). And there is a difference between the two tables that is the whole gospel. Gedaliah did not know, and had refused to be told. Jesus knew exactly who was reaching for the dish, and passed him the bread anyway.

The full genealogy is given as an epitaph: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. Shaphan read the law to Josiah; Ahikam's hand saved Jeremiah's life at his trial; Gedaliah took the prophet home when the city fell. Three generations of quiet faithfulness, and the line ends at a dinner table.

The Chaldean garrison dies too, and with them any hope that Babylon will treat this as an internal matter. Ishmael has not merely killed a governor; he has guaranteed a reprisal, which is what drives the rest of the book.

The fast of the seventh month that the Jews later kept (Zech 7:5; 8:19) is usually taken to remember the murder of Gedaliah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Eighty Pilgrims and a Cistern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day eighty mourning pilgrims from the north arrive with offerings (vv. 4–5). Ishmael weeps his way into their confidence and slaughters them (vv. 6–7), sparing ten who know where food is hidden, and fills Asa's great cistern with the dead (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief counterfeited at the gate, and a reservoir built to save life packed with the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it, eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For one day Mizpah looks like a functioning capital with a governor in it. These eighty men are among the saddest details in the book. They come from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, the old northern kingdom, whose people had been deported by Assyria well over a century before. These are the descendants of those left behind, and they are still walking south with offerings for the God of Israel.

They are in mourning for Jerusalem: beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies cut. And two of those three were expressly forbidden. You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead (Lev 19:28); You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). Their grief was genuine and their practice borrowed what the law forbade, learned from neighbours over generations without the law to correct it.

And they are carrying grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD, to a temple that had been ash for perhaps two months. Either they had not heard, or they were going to the site anyway to lay offerings in the ruins.

It would be easy to be superior about them, and it would be wrong. Eighty men walked thirty miles or more through occupied country, disfigured with grief, to bring flour and incense to a God whose house was rubble. Their theology was muddled and their hearts were not. God's people are often more sincere than they are well-taught, and the answer to that is teaching, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weeping as he came, the day after the murder. The tears were the trap: the one sure way into mourners' confidence was shared grief, and then the name of a dead man as an invitation.

This is what hypocrisy is for. Not self-deception, but a tool: the borrowing of the forms of godliness and sorrow in order to get close enough to do harm. Wolves come in sheep's clothing because the clothing works.

Eleven men killed seventy of the eighty pilgrims inside the walls, and the bodies went into a water pit. Each of them had a name and a home in the north, and had come to mourn; Scripture does not let them become a statistic, and neither should we.

Hold the cistern beside the one three chapters ago. Jeremiah had been lowered into a cistern with no water in the cistern, but only mud (38:6), and a foreigner came with ropes and old rags and drew him out. Here the same kind of pit is used to hide a massacre. The identical feature of the identical landscape: in one, a man is hauled up to live; in the other, seventy worshippers are thrown down. What differs is not the hole but the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions. Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten men live because they knew where food was buried, hidden in the open country because anything kept in a house was taken. And it shows what Ishmael valued: seventy murders were nothing to him, and a cache of grain was enough to stay his hand.

There is no comment on the ten. They bought their lives with the location of their food, which is the kind of bargain famine forces on people, and Scripture records it without either praise or blame.

The narrator stops to tell us who dug the hole, and the ESV notes that where the English reads that these men were struck down along with Gedaliah, the Hebrew has "by the hand of": the bodies of the men killed by Gedaliah's side, in his company.

Three hundred years earlier King Asa had fortified Mizpah against the northern kingdom, carrying away the stones of Ramah to build it (1 Kgs 15:22). The cistern was part of that work: a reservoir to keep a garrison alive through a siege. It was engineering in the service of survival.

And a prince of Asa's own line filled it with the slain. Things built by good men to preserve life get used by later men for atrocity, with the institution intact and the purpose inverted. Judah's story is full of it: a temple built for God's name used to house idols, a covenant ceremony used to seal a lie, and now a waterworks made into a grave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — Recovered at the Pool of Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael drives the remnant toward Ammon (v. 10); Johanan pursues and overtakes him at Gibeon, and the captives rejoice and come over to him (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The one glad moment in the chapter: prisoners seeing who has come for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole remnant of Judah walks east in ropes, and it is a small shock to find the king's daughters here. Zedekiah's sons were killed at Riblah; his daughters survived the fall of the city, were left behind as no threat to anybody, and are now being driven toward Ammon as spoil by a man of their own royal house.

They had been formally entrusted to Gedaliah, and the man who murdered him is now stealing them.

And the destination is the point. Ishmael is taking them to the Ammonites, to the king who had sent him to do the killing (40:14). This may never have been a bid for the throne of Judah. It looks like a foreign operation, and the remnant were the payment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon. And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced. So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But. The first good word in the chapter.

And it is Johanan, the man who brought the warning Gedaliah would not believe, who had asked permission to deal with Ishmael quietly and been told he was a liar (40:14-16). He had every excuse to say he had told them so. Instead he raised his men and went after the column.

Being disbelieved is a real injury, and the test of a man is what he does for people who dismissed him once they are in trouble. Johanan passes it.

The place is named because everyone knew it: the great pool at Gibeon, where Joab's and Abner's men had once fought a murderous tournament in David's day.

They rejoiced. It is the only gladness in the chapter, and it is the gladness of prisoners who look up and see who has come over the hill.

The captives had been with Ishmael only for the few miles from Mizpah, and their loyalty was never his. The moment there was an alternative, it was obvious where they stood, which is usually true of people held by force, and it is easy to forget when strength looks like consent.

No battle is described. The hostages simply turned around and walked to the rescue party, and Ishmael's operation collapsed, because the captives were people and not cargo, and they walked away from him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Intending to Go to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael escapes to Ammon (v. 15). Johanan leads the recovered remnant to camp near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Frightened people walking back toward the country God had brought them out of.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites. Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon. And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gets away to Ammon, where his paymaster is. He murdered a governor, seventy pilgrims and a garrison, and the chapter simply records that he escaped. There is no execution, no capture, no word of judgment pronounced over him in this book at all.

Scripture is honest about this. Wickedness frequently walks away from the scene, and the person who wants the ledger balanced on the page will not always find it there. What we are given instead is the assurance that the accounts are kept elsewhere by someone who said I am the one who knows, and I am witness (29:23).

Read the list slowly: soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs. This is what was left of the people of God in the land of promise. Not a nation, but a column of survivors on a road, with their governor dead behind them.

Their reasoning is not stupid: Babylon's governor and soldiers have been murdered, and a reprisal is coming. So: Egypt.

Every word of that is sound risk assessment, and it points them at the one direction God had forbidden. Egypt is where the story of this people began, and the whole shape of their existence is that God brought them out of it. To walk back in is to unpick the exodus.

And fear is what does it. Not appetite, not idolatry in any obvious form, but fear, with a plausible case attached. Gedaliah would not believe a warning and died of it; these men believe the evidence of their eyes and are about to make a worse mistake. Between credulity and calculation there is a third thing, and the next chapter is them asking for it: that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do (42:3).

It is the right question, asked by men who have already decided the answer. And the last picture the chapter leaves is a company of refugees encamped beside Bethlehem, facing south, afraid. And that is where, six centuries later, the answer to all of it would be born (Mic 5:2; Matt 2:6): the true Shepherd of Israel, who would not run from danger but go to meet it for his sheep.

41.title: Murder at Mizpah
41.overview: A few weeks after the fall of Jerusalem, Ishmael, a prince of the royal house, murders Gedaliah at his own table, with the Judeans and Babylonian soldiers at Mizpah (vv. 1-3). The next day he lures in eighty mourning pilgrims from the north and massacres seventy of them, throwing the bodies into King Asa's great cistern (vv. 4-9). He drives the rest of the people toward Ammon, until Johanan overtakes him at Gibeon and the captives walk free (vv. 10-14). Ishmael escapes, and the frightened survivors camp near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt (vv. 15-18).
41.theology: This is the darkest chapter of the aftermath, and Scripture tells it without softening. Betrayal at the table is one of the deepest wounds there is, and the Lord himself bore it knowingly (John 13:18). Hypocrisy appears here not as self-deception but as a tool, tears used to get near enough to kill. Wickedness escapes on the page, and the accounting is left to the God who is witness (29:23). And fear with a plausible case attached is what turns God's people back toward Egypt, beside the town where the true Shepherd would one day be born (Matt 2:6).
41.examples: The eighty pilgrims carrying flour and incense to a temple of ashes are a reminder that God's people are often more sincere than well taught, and deserve teaching rather than contempt. And Johanan, who raised his men for the very people who had called him a liar, shows what to do with the injury of being disbelieved.

42.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near<sup>2</sup>and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant— because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us—<sup>3</sup>that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."<sup>4</sup>Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you."<sup>5</sup>Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us.<sup>6</sup>Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."<sup>7</sup>At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah.<sup>8</sup>Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest,<sup>9</sup>and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:<sup>10</sup>If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you.<sup>11</sup>Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.<sup>12</sup>I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.<sup>13</sup>But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God<sup>14</sup>and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,'<sup>15</sup>then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,<sup>16</sup>then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die.<sup>17</sup>All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.<sup>18</sup>"For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more.<sup>19</sup>The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day<sup>20</sup>that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.'<sup>21</sup>And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you.<sup>22</sup>Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Whether It Is Good or Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole remnant asks Jeremiah to pray for guidance (vv. 1–3). He promises to keep nothing back (v. 4), and they swear to obey, whether it is good or bad (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A perfect prayer and a total oath, from people who have already decided where they are going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant— because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us— that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone comes. Not a delegation this time, but the commanders, the officers, and all the people from the least to the greatest. After Mizpah there is nobody left who can afford to be indifferent.

The request is beautifully put, and every part of it is right. They ask for prayer, they plead for mercy, they name their condition honestly, we are left with but a few, and they appeal to what the prophet can see with his own eyes.

One phrase is a small warning light: the LORD your God. Not ours. Zedekiah's messengers had at least said the LORD our God (37:3); men who keep God at one remove in their grammar are often keeping him at one remove elsewhere.

And there is the question, and it is the right question. Which way, and what to do. You could not improve on it as a prayer for guidance, and the tragedy of the chapter is that it was asked by men with their bags already packed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you." Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us. Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He agrees at once, and then makes one promise about himself: I will keep nothing back from you.

Forty years of ministry stand behind that sentence. He had been beaten, put in stocks, dropped in a cistern and had his book burned for keeping nothing back, and he was too old and too tested to start editing now. A preacher who tells his people in advance that he will not trim the answer has given them the most useful thing he has.

Inviting God to witness against them is the most solemn commitment available. Whether it is good or bad: they anticipate the possibility of an unwelcome answer and pledge obedience anyway. And the grammar has improved: twice now it is the LORD our God.

Every word is correct and the whole thing is hollow, as chapter 43 will show within a day. There is a way of praying for guidance that is really a search for endorsement, and it can produce sincere-sounding oaths. The test of whether we meant whether it is good or bad only comes when the answer is bad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — If You Will Remain in This Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After ten days the answer comes (vv. 7–9): stay, and God will build and plant them (v. 10). Their fear of Babylon is named and answered with his presence and mercy (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stay, and God will build and plant — and handle Nebuchadnezzar himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten days of nothing.

The prophet prayed and God did not answer for a week and a half, with a frightened camp waiting outside and a Babylonian reprisal expected any day. Jeremiah had to go out each morning with nothing to report.

God is not on call. He answers according to his own timetable even when the request is urgent and the people are genuinely afraid, and the delay is not indifference. Ten days also gave the remnant ten days to examine what they actually wanted, and gave the oath time to be more than a mood.

He calls the same crowd back, all the people from the least to the greatest, because the answer belongs to everyone who asked, not to the leadership alone. There will be no private briefing and no managed release.

He begins by reminding them that this was their idea. To whom you sent me. Whatever follows, they asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand. I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen to the verbs, because they are the verbs of Jeremiah's ordination. He was appointed to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10), and for forty years the first four had done the work. Here only the last two are used, with the destructive pair explicitly refused: built up and not pulled down, planted and not plucked up.

And the reason given is staggering: for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. God speaks of turning from the harm with something like grief, not that he was wrong to send it, but that he takes no pleasure in it and is ready to reverse his posture the moment they will stay put.

The whole offer turns on one condition, and it is not a religious programme. It is geography: If you will remain in this land. Stay where God has put you.

God names the fear precisely and says do not fear twice, because a frightened man needs the sentence repeated. The ground offered is not a change in Nebuchadnezzar's plans but a presence: for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.

That promise of presence runs through the whole Bible, and it reaches its height in the child named Immanuel (which means, God with us) (Matt 1:23), who sent his frightened disciples out with the words I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). The remedy for fear has always been a person, and in Christ that person has come.

Follow the chain. God will show them mercy, and the effect will be that the emperor shows them mercy. The disposition of the most powerful man alive is treated as something God adjusts in order to keep a promise to a small band of refugees.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alternative is quoted in their own voice, Egypt for peace and bread (vv. 13–14), and the answer turns it inside out: the sword and famine they fear will follow them there (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The two things they were running from were waiting at the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,' then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God quotes the sentence before they say it, and labels it: saying We will not remain in this land is disobeying the voice of the LORD your God. There will be no room afterwards to present the move as prudence rather than rebellion.

Their case is a good one: after a long siege, a murdered governor and a country of ashes, who would not want peace and bread? That is what makes this passage searching. The sin is not a craving for something wicked. It is a craving for peace and bread in a place God had forbidden. Their instincts were humane and their destination was disobedient.

And Egypt was forbidden by name. The law had said of the king that he must not cause the people to return to Egypt, because You shall never return that way again (Deut 17:16), and Isaiah had pronounced Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). Egypt is the house of slavery they were brought out of. Walking back is not a change of address; it is a reversal of the exodus.

The phrase set your faces carries the whole problem. This is not drifting; it is a deliberate turning of the head in a chosen direction.

verseByVerse.quote: then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die. All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer takes their two reasons and hands them back.

They were going to Egypt to escape war and hunger. God says the sword they fear will overtake them there, and the famine they dread will follow close after them: a picture of two pursuers outrunning a column on the road.

There is no safe country. What a man flees from is not escaped by distance if the thing he is fleeing was sent, and the only refuge available was obedience in a ruined land. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (Prov 14:12).

The three-fold sentence of the whole book falls one last time, now on the survivors of it. And the closing phrase is the bitterest thing in the chapter: no remnant or survivor.

These people are the remnant. The word had been their identity and their comfort for two chapters. If they go down to Egypt, the remnant will have no remnant.

Even this is not quite the last word. Two chapters later God allows that a few fugitives will get home (44:14, 28), and Scripture never closes the door on anyone who turns back from a wrong road: let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him (Isa 55:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Shall See This Place No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem's wrath will follow them to Egypt (v. 18). The warning is made formal (v. 19), their oath is read back to them, and the verdict falls on the place where you desire to go to live (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The last words of the oracle are the place where you desire to go.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more. The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day
verseByVerse.commentary:
The comparison is exact and it should have ended the discussion. They had just watched what that looked like; the smoke was barely gone.

Then four words for their reputation, an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt, the same list pronounced over Jerusalem, now transferred to the refugees.

And a short sentence that would fall hardest on anyone who loved the country: You shall see this place no more. Go, and you will never come back.

The instruction is reduced to five words so that nobody can claim it was ambiguous: Do not go to Egypt.

And Jeremiah puts his own testimony on record: Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day. He is establishing that the warning was given, plainly, on a particular day, in front of everyone. A faithful minister makes sure that if his people go wrong they cannot say they were not told.

verseByVerse.quote: that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.' And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you. Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their oath is read back to them, and the tense is the sting. You have gone astray, already, before a single step south. God treats the decision as taken, because it was taken before they ever asked.

And he quotes their promise with the possessive they had used: whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it. They had called him theirs and pledged obedience in advance. The words are now evidence.

Jeremiah has kept his side exactly, nothing held back, and the charge against them is total: not obedient in anything. They received a specific, urgent, gracious answer to the exact question they had asked, sworn in advance to obey, and obeyed none of it.

And the oracle ends on a phrase that diagnoses the whole human problem: the place where you desire to go to live.

That is where they will die. Not in the place they feared, but in the place they wanted. The destination chosen for safety, bread and quiet turns out to be the grave, and it is chosen freely, with a warning ringing in their ears and an oath still warm on their lips.

Which is why this chapter is more than a piece of sixth-century politics. God gave them a plain word, named their fear, promised his presence, offered to build and plant them, and undertook to manage the emperor himself, and they preferred a country of their own choosing. The offer was If you will remain in this land, and remaining is generally harder than moving, because it requires trusting a person rather than changing a circumstance.

Every reader has asked for guidance with the bags already packed. The way back is not a better oath but the mercy this chapter itself offers, I relent of the disaster: Christ kept his Father's word perfectly where we have not, and his obedience is counted as ours (Rom 5:19). And the Spirit he gives is what makes a frightened heart able to stay where God has put it and trust the One who says I am with you.

42.title: Whether It Is Good or Bad
42.overview: The frightened survivors of Mizpah ask Jeremiah to seek God's guidance and swear to obey it, whether it is good or bad (vv. 1-6). After ten days the answer comes: stay in the land, and God will build and plant them and protect them from Babylon (vv. 7-12). But if they go to Egypt for peace and bread, the sword and famine they fear will follow them there (vv. 13-17), and Jeremiah warns them plainly that they have already chosen the place where they will die (vv. 18-22).
42.theology: There is a way of asking for guidance that is really a search for endorsement, and it can produce faultless prayers and sincere oaths; the test of whether it is good or bad comes only when the answer is bad. Against that stands a God who answers in his own time, who relents of disaster and takes no pleasure in it, and whose answer to fear is not a change in the enemy's plans but his own presence, fulfilled in Immanuel (Matt 1:23). The sin here is not appetite for evil but a craving for peace and bread in a place God forbade, and its end is death in the very place they wanted.
42.examples: Most of us have asked God for guidance with the bags already packed: praying over a move, a job or a relationship we have in fact already chosen. The chapter does not answer that with scorn but with an offer. God still says to the frightened, Do not fear, twice, because frightened people need it twice, and he promises to be with those who stay where he has put them.

43.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them,<sup>2</sup>Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,'<sup>3</sup>but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."<sup>4</sup>So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah.<sup>5</sup>But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—<sup>6</sup>the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah.<sup>7</sup>And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:<sup>9</sup>"Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,<sup>10</sup>and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.<sup>11</sup>He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword.<sup>12</sup>I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace.<sup>13</sup>He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Are Telling a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The moment Jeremiah finishes, the leaders call him a liar and blame Baruch for the oracle (vv. 2–3). So they do not obey the voice of the LORD, and they gather the whole remnant, even those who had just come home from the nations (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: An oath to obey "whether it is good or bad" lasted exactly as long as the answer was welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them, Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,' but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator sets the record straight before anyone speaks: these were all these words of the LORD their God, and God had sent him with them.

Azariah son of Hoshaiah is probably the Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah of 42:1; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads Azariah in both places.

Ten days they waited for this answer. They swore an oath to obey it whether it is good or bad. Within a day of hearing it they call the prophet a liar.

They do not say the message is hard, or ask for time, or admit they are afraid. They say God did not send it. When obedience becomes unbearable, the tempting move is not open rebellion but reclassification: decide the word was never really God's, and the problem dissolves.

And Johanan is among them. The man who brought the true warning to Gedaliah and was called a liar for it (40:16) is now doing to Jeremiah exactly what was done to him.

Then the conspiracy theory, aimed at the scribe: the old prophet has been captured by his secretary, and the oracle is really policy. It need not deny that Jeremiah is godly, only that he is being handled. A word you cannot refute can still be neutralised by explaining where it came from, and forty years of proven ministry were set aside with one accusation about the man holding the pen.

verseByVerse.quote: So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah. But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had called it a lie; the narrator calls it what it is, did not obey the voice of the LORD, and names the command they broke: to remain in the land of Judah. Nothing was required of them but to stay where God had put them and let him build and plant them there (42:10). The command came with the promise already attached.

And these were the people who had returned, home from Moab, Ammon and Edom when they heard there was a governor and a harvest (40:11-12). God had begun gathering them, in a small and real way, as he promised. Now they are taken out again by their own leaders. The gathering is undone by the people it had gathered.
verseByVerse.note: From here to the end of chapter 44, Jeremiah's ministry takes place in Egypt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everyone left in Judah goes down to Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and they arrive at Tahpanhes (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The two men who had told them not to go were carried along with them.

verseByVerse.quote: the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inventory is complete and it is heartbreaking: men, women, children, the royal daughters, and every single person the Babylonians had entrusted to Gedaliah. Whatever was left of Judah in Judah is on this road.

And then, at the end of the list, as if incidental: also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. The two men who had just been called a liar and a manipulator are taken along.

He had been offered Babylon with a pension and had chosen his ruined country to stay with these people (40:4-6). This is what that choice cost him. He is an old man, and the last journey of his life is a forced march into the one country his whole message had warned against, in the company of men who had just disowned his ministry.

There is no lament recorded. He does not protest, and the text gives him no speech. He simply goes with them, which is the shape of his entire life: tied to a people who would not hear him and would not let him go.

The reason is stated a second time in four verses: for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. The narrator is making sure no future reader mistakes this for migration.

Tahpanhes was a frontier garrison town in the eastern delta, the first substantial place on the road in. And the geography is the theology: the people God took out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm walked back in of their own accord.

What became of Jeremiah? Scripture does not say. He was last seen in Egypt, still preaching (ch. 44); later tradition, outside Scripture, says he died there, some accounts say at the hands of his own people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Tahpanhes Jeremiah buries stones in the pavement at Pharaoh's palace, where God will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God lays a foundation in Pharaoh's forecourt for a throne that is coming whether Egypt likes it or not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes: "Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks to him in Egypt.

That is not a small thing. Jeremiah had been dragged into a country of forbidden refuge by men who denied his commission, and the word of the LORD arrives there as it always had. He was disobedient in nothing, and God does not treat him as though he were. He remains a prophet on the wrong side of a border he never wanted to cross.

One more acted sign, and after the yoke, the flask and the field, this one is characteristically odd: bury large stones in the wet mortar of the pavement outside Pharaoh's palace, and do it in the sight of the men of Judah.

He is an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pushing stones into mortar while his countrymen watch. The stones will be invisible within a day, which is the point — they are hidden, and they are still there.

And the meaning lands hard. They came to Egypt to get away from Nebuchadnezzar, and God says he will set the man's throne on this very pavement, with his canopy spread over the spot. The buried stones are a foundation stone for a Babylonian dais in Pharaoh's own doorway.

Once more the title appears that has run through this book: my servant (25:9; 27:6). The emperor is still an instrument, and the God who moves him is the God these refugees were running from — I will send and take him.

There is no hiding place from providence. You may cross a border to escape a man, and find that the one who commands him was waiting at the destination.

Did Nebuchadnezzar invade Egypt? A fragmentary Babylonian tablet records a campaign against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568/567 BC, against Pharaoh Amasis. How far into Egypt he went is not known, but the record fits Jeremiah’s word (and Ezek 29:17-20), which this commentary takes as fulfilled.
verseByVerse.note: Tahpanhes is usually identified with Tell Defenneh, where nineteenth-century excavators found a large brick platform in front of a fort; some linked it with this pavement, though that cannot be proved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — As a Shepherd Cleans His Cloak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Egypt itself is sentenced: its land struck, its temples burned, its obelisks broken (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge they chose receives the same sentence as the city they left.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword. I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace. He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt gets the sentence of Judah. The three-fold judgment follows them across the frontier, sorted with the same grim precision, and the refuge turns out to be under the same verdict as the place they left.

Note who lights the fire: I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt. God says he will do it, and Nebuchadnezzar will carry it out. The gods that Judah had gone down to live among will be burned and carted off as loot by an army God sends.

And then an image of startling contempt: he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin. A shepherd sitting in the sun picking lice out of his coat and flicking them away. That is the sack of one of the great old civilisations, described as delousing a garment — and the shepherd walks off afterwards in peace, unhurried, having lost nothing.

The last thing named is the obelisks of Heliopolis — the sun-god's city, whose pillars were the most permanent objects in the world these people had fled into. Stone that had stood for a thousand years, broken.

So the chapter ends where it began, with buried stones and standing ones. The obelisks that looked eternal come down; the stones an old prophet pushed into mortar mark where an emperor's throne will stand. What is visible is temporary, and what God has hidden is the thing that holds.

And this is not the last word on Egypt in Scripture. Six centuries later an angel would tell a carpenter to take a child down into Egypt to keep him alive from a king who wanted him dead, and then to bring him home again, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: Out of Egypt I called my son (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1). Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and did not come back. The true Son went down in obedience, and came out — and made the road home for everyone who had taken the wrong one.

43.title: Down Into Egypt
43.overview:
Jeremiah has barely finished giving God's answer when the leaders call it a lie and blame Baruch for it. Against the plain command to stay, they march the whole remnant down to Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and arrive at the frontier town of Tahpanhes (vv. 1-7).

There God speaks to his prophet again. Jeremiah buries stones in the pavement at Pharaoh's palace and announces that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on that very spot, burn the temples of Egypt's gods and break the obelisks of Heliopolis (vv. 8-13). The people fled from Babylon into the arms of the next country Babylon would strike.
43.theology:
The chapter shows how people refuse a word they cannot answer. They do not argue with it; they reclassify it as human and explain where it came from (vv. 2-3). The sin itself is a failure to stay where God had put them, under a command that came with the promise already attached (42:10).

It also shows that there is no running from God's providence. The word reaches Jeremiah in a country he never chose, and the king the refugees fled is called God's servant and sent to the very door of their refuge (v. 10). Over it all stands the contrast the Gospels draw: Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and never came back, but the true Son went down in obedience and was called out (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15).
43.examples:
Think of someone who waits for counsel, promises in advance to take it, and then, once it is given, decides the adviser must have been got at by someone else. That is Johanan here: it is easier to blame the secretary than to obey the sermon.

Or think of an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pressing stones into wet mortar while his countrymen watch. Within a day nothing can be seen. The thousand-year obelisks across the country look far more permanent, yet they are the things that fall, and the hidden stones are the things that hold.

44.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them,<sup>3</sup>because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.<sup>4</sup>Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!'<sup>5</sup>But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.<sup>7</sup>And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant?<sup>8</sup>Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth?<sup>9</sup>Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>10</sup>They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah.<sup>12</sup>I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed.
