verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Seen All the Disaster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes to the Judeans scattered across Egypt and begins with evidence they cannot dispute: the ruin of Jerusalem, caused by offerings to unknown gods, after God had persistently sent his prophets to plead with them (vv. 1–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument opens with a ruin they had walked through themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them, because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four place names, and they tell a story on their own. The company that arrived together at Tahpanhes has spread — north to Migdol on the frontier, south to Memphis, and up the Nile into Pathros, which is upper Egypt. They are settling in, scattering through the country, making lives.

God begins with what is not in dispute. You have seen — not heard, not been told. These people had walked out through the rubble. Whatever else is arguable, the ruin is a fact they carry in their own memories.

And he claims it: the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem. Babylon was only the instrument; the ruin was his doing.

The cause is stated in one word — idolatry — and there is a small devastating clause attached: gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.

These were not ancestral deities with a long claim on the family. They were novelties, picked up from neighbours, unknown to the generations that had actually seen God act. A nation abandoned the God who brought it out of Egypt for gods it had only recently met.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!' But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods. Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is the adverb of the whole book again — persistently — and this time it carries an interjection that sounds like nothing else in Jeremiah.

Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! That is not the language of a statute. It is the cry of someone trying to stop a person he loves from doing something that will destroy them, and God puts it in his own mouth as the summary of four centuries of prophetic preaching. Generation after generation of warning, distilled to a single Oh.

Two verbs of refusal, and they are the epitaph of the kingdom: did not listen, did not incline their ear. The second is worse than the first. To incline the ear is to lean in; they would not even turn their heads toward it.

And as at this day is the hinge of the argument. The evidence is present tense. God is not asking them to accept a theory about judgment; he is pointing at a country they can still see from where they stand, and asking them to read it correctly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Why Do You Commit This Great Evil Against Yourselves?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their idolatry is put as self-harm, resumed in Egypt (vv. 7–8); five kinds of evil are listed as one inheritance, and none of them has humbled himself even to this day (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: From God's side, sin is a wound the sinner opens in his own household.

verseByVerse.quote: And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant? Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth? Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God describes their sin as committed against yourselves.

It is the truest thing said about idolatry anywhere in the chapter. He has already told them it provokes him to anger, and here he frames it as self-mutilation — a knife taken to man and woman, infant and child, cutting away their own future. Sin is treason against God and self-destruction in the family, and the second is often what finally gets a person's attention.

The works of your hands. They made the thing they are worshipping. Paul's summary of the same exchange runs the same way: men who exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals (Rom 1:23).

And note where you have come to live. They had gone to Egypt for safety and immediately resumed the practice that had cost them their own country. A change of address does nothing to the heart that made the move.

Five generations and classes of evil in one sentence, and the ESV notes that where the English has the plural, the Hebrew reads "his" — the kings' wives spoken of in the singular. Either way the list is comprehensive: fathers, kings, royal wives, the hearers themselves, their own wives. Nobody in the assembly is outside it, and the wives are named twice, which prepares for verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, three failures, and a phrase that should stop any reader: even to this day.

Consider what this day contains. The city burned. The temple gone. The king blinded after watching his sons die. A long famine, a governor murdered at his table, seventy pilgrims in a cistern, and a forced march into Egypt. If catastrophe by itself produced humility, these would be the humblest people alive.

They are not. They have not humbled themselves, nor have they feared. Suffering does not soften a heart on its own; it only reveals what the heart already was. The same fire hardens clay and melts wax, and Judah in Egypt is the proof.

And the third failure is the plainest: they have not walked in my law and my statutes, the law given to a people he had already brought out of Egypt. The charge is simply that nobody did them. No one ever has, fully (Eccl 7:20). That is why this book's hope rests on a new covenant with the law written on the heart (31:33), and on the one who walked in that law perfectly in our place, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him (Rom 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — They Shall All Be Consumed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets his face against those who set their faces toward Egypt: they will be punished there as Jerusalem was, and none will return, except some fugitives (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: They wanted Egypt for a while and Judah in the end, and are told they will have neither.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah. I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will set my face against you. Earlier in this book God had hidden his face from the city (33:5); here he turns it toward these people, and it is worse. An averted face means abandonment; a set face means deliberate opposition.

The phrase is answered exactly. They set their faces toward Egypt (42:15), and God set my face against them. Two settings of the face in opposite directions, and only one of them can hold.

And From the least to the greatest is the phrase used of the crowd that came asking for guidance and swore to obey (42:1, 8). The whole company that took the oath is the whole company under the sentence.

The comparison is the argument: as I have punished Jerusalem. They had seen what that looked like. Egypt will not be an exception clause.

Here is the hidden assumption of the whole migration, exposed in one clause: to which they desire to return to dwell there. They never meant to stay in Egypt. The plan was to sit out the danger and go home afterwards — the reasoning of everyone who intends a short detour away from obedience and fully expects to come back.

They will not come back. And then, at the very end, three words that refuse to close the door completely: except some fugitives. A handful will straggle home. Even in this sentence God keeps a remnant of a remnant, and it matters that he says so, because the chapter is about to record the most direct refusal in the book and this clause is spoken before it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — We Will Not Listen to You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great assembly, men and women together, refuses outright and vows to keep serving the queen of heaven, because in her days they prospered (vv. 15–18); the women add that their husbands approved (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: They read the ruin of Jerusalem as evidence that they had not sinned enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah: "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you. But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The description is careful. The men knew what their wives were doing; the women are standing there; it is a great assembly. This is not a faction muttering. It is a congregation, organised, with the households aligned.

For forty years this people had not listened, but they had always said something else — that Jeremiah was a traitor, or mad, or Baruch's puppet, or that the LORD had not sent him. Here the pretence is dropped. They grant the premise — the word was spoken in the name of the LORD — and refuse it anyway: we will not listen to you.

It is one of the plainest sentences of unbelief in the Old Testament, and it is not the speech of ignorant people. It is informed, deliberate and corporate.

The queen of heaven was a pagan goddess of fertility and provision, probably Ishtar or Astarte, and this cult is not new. Jeremiah had described it decades earlier in Jerusalem: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven (7:18). A whole family working together at it, which is exactly what is happening again here.

And the argument they give is economic. When we served her, we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. It is the reasoning of a woman in Hosea: I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink (Hos 2:5) — and God's answer there is the answer here: she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil (Hos 2:8).

She was worshipped with cakes and drink offerings. Some Christians later gave the title to Mary; Scripture gives her no such title, and offerings and prayers to anyone but God are forbidden.
verseByVerse.note: This is the last time in the book that Jeremiah's hearers answer him, and their answer is the refusal itself.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine." And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sentence is a reading of history, and it is exactly upside down.

What they are describing is most likely Josiah's reformation. The idols were cleared out, the high places pulled down, the queen of heaven's cakes went off the family table — and then came Megiddo, Egypt, Babylon, the siege, the famine and the fall. They have drawn the obvious conclusion from the sequence: the trouble started when the reform did.

The facts are not in dispute; the causation is inverted. And they are so nearly right that it is frightening. There is a way of reading providence that is careful, empirical, and completely wrong, because it leaves out the four centuries of patience that preceded the reform and the fact that the reform was too late and never reached the heart.

People still argue this way. Things went badly after I began to take God seriously, therefore taking God seriously was the mistake. The timeline is accurate and the verdict is a lie.

The women speak for themselves, and the ESV notes that the introduction here follows the Syriac — "Compare Syriac; Hebrew lacks And the women said" — so in the Hebrew the voice simply continues.

Their point is legal. Under the law a husband who heard his wife's vow and said nothing had confirmed it, and only by opposing it on the day he heard could he annul it (Num 30:6-8). So: our husbands knew, and never once forbade us. That is unanswerable as far as it goes, and it is an indictment of the men standing beside them, who had known all along (v. 15).

But look at what they are actually doing with the argument. They are not asking forgiveness or pleading pressure; they are establishing that the guilt is shared, as a reason to carry on. Spreading the blame feels like a defence and functions as a confession — and Jeremiah's reply goes, deliberately, to all the people, men and women (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah answers that God remembered those offerings and could bear them no longer (vv. 20–23). Their vow is handed back as a sentence, God's name will no more be spoken by them in Egypt, and the few survivors will know whose word stands; the sign is Pharaoh Hophra (vv. 24–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Two words were on offer in this book, and the end of it is finding out which one holds.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer: "As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind? The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day. It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He accepts their own framing. They had argued that everybody was in it together, so he addresses everybody together.

Two questions, and they go straight at the hole in the argument. They had said that in the days of the cakes there was plenty of food and no disaster — as though God had not noticed. Did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind?

God's patience had been mistaken for God's approval. The years of prosperity were not evidence that he was pleased; they were the long stretch in which he sent prophet after prophet saying Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! Delay is not indifference, and every unpunished season is being remembered.

Could no longer bear. The phrase implies that he had borne it for a very long time, and that there was a limit, and that the limit was reached. The desolation they keep pointing at is not the result of the reformation; it is the end of God's forbearance with the very practice they have resumed.

The causation is stated without a gap: It is because. Their reading of history had one word wrong, and Jeremiah corrects that single word. The disaster came because of the offerings, not because they stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. The address is almost a definition of what they have become: not Judah in Judah, but Judah in Egypt — a people identified by the place they should not be.

God quotes their oath back to them, and then says: do it.

Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! There is no sarcasm in it and no bluff. It is one of the most terrible things God says in the book, because it is the withdrawal of resistance. They have insisted on their vows for long enough; he stops arguing and lets them keep them.

Scripture knows this judgment elsewhere — God giving people up to what they have chosen. It is not that he has grown indifferent, but that pleading has an end, and being left alone with what you insisted on is the worst answer prayer can receive.

A tender conscience may fear that this has happened to it. The fear itself is a good sign: those whom God has given up do not grieve over their sin or long for him. The door stays open for anyone who comes, for Christ has said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

And here is the sentence. God swears by my great name that his name will never again be spoken by a Judean in Egypt.

Weigh what is being removed. Not their lives first, but their liturgy — the oath formula As the Lord GOD lives, the ordinary speech of a covenant people. They had gone on using his name while serving the queen of heaven, invoking him as a matter of habit, and he will not have his name in their mouths on those terms. It is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it constantly.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them. And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm: Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is the one from Jeremiah's first vision. God had shown him an almond branch and said he was watching over his word to perform it (1:12), and the same attentiveness that promised to build and plant in chapter 31 is here watching over them for disaster and not for good.

It is the same eye, the same care, the same refusal to be distracted. That is a sobering thought about the character of God: his watchfulness is not automatically comfort. What it means for you depends on which side of his word you have placed yourself.

A few will get home — few in number, the fugitives of verse 14 — and the reason given for their survival is not comfort but demonstration: so that everyone shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.

That is the question the whole book has been asking since the almond branch. Two words had been on offer in Jerusalem for forty years: Jeremiah's and everybody else's. Hananiah said two years; the queen of heaven's devotees said prosperity; the prophets of peace said no disaster would come. Every one of those words had a date on it, and every date passed.

The sign is aimed at the precise thing they trusted. They had come to Egypt because Pharaoh's army had once marched north and lifted a siege, and Hophra is the man they were relying on. He will go the way Zedekiah went, and the comparison is spelled out so nobody can miss it: as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

And history records it. Hophra (the Greeks called him Apries) lost his throne to his general Amasis after an army revolt in about 570 BC, and within a few years he was dead, most likely killed trying to win it back, which is exactly into the hand of those who seek his life.

So the last recorded words of Jeremiah to his own people end on a question rather than a curse: whose word will stand, mine or theirs. It is a question with an answer, and the answer is the reason this book exists. Every word spoken against Jerusalem stood; and that means the other words stand too — the everlasting love, the law written on the heart, the sins remembered no more, the shepherd who gathers, the Branch called The LORD is our righteousness. The God who kept the hard half of his word to the letter is the God who has promised the rest of it, and every one of those promises is kept in Christ: For all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Cor 1:20).

44.title: We Will Not Listen to You
44.overview:
This is Jeremiah's last recorded sermon, preached to Judeans now settled all over Egypt. God points to the ruin of Jerusalem they have seen with their own eyes and to its cause: the gods they served though he had pleaded with them persistently to stop. They have taken up the same worship in Egypt, and he warns that the refuge will share Jerusalem's sentence, with only a few fugitives returning (vv. 1-14).

A great assembly of men and women answers plainly: we will not listen to you. They will keep serving the queen of heaven, because in her days they prospered (vv. 15-19). Jeremiah replies that the disaster came because of those offerings, not because they stopped. God hands their vows back to them, swears that his name will no longer be on their lips, and gives the fall of Pharaoh Hophra as the sign of whose word will stand (vv. 20-30).
44.theology:
The chapter is a study of how a people can see God's judgment with their own eyes and still read it upside down. Suffering did not humble them (v. 10); God's long patience was mistaken for approval (vv. 21-22); and an accurate timeline was turned into a false verdict, as though the trouble began when the idols were removed (v. 18; Hos 2:5, 8).

Against that stands the faithfulness of God's word. His watchfulness is not automatically comfort: the eye that watched to build and plant can watch for disaster (v. 27; 1:12; 31:28). Yet because every hard word against Jerusalem stood, the promises of the same book stand too.
44.examples:
Some people say that things went badly from the time they began to take God seriously, so taking God seriously must have been the mistake. The women of Judah argued exactly that, and the timeline they gave was accurate. What they left out was four centuries of God's patience, and the fact that the reform never reached their hearts.

Others keep using God's name as a habit while their real trust lies elsewhere, the way the refugees went on saying As the Lord GOD lives while baking cakes for the queen of heaven. The chapter warns that it is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it every day.

45.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch:<sup>3</sup>You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'<sup>4</sup>Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land.<sup>5</sup>And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dated to the year of the scroll Jehoiakim burned, this is God's word to the scribe by name, and it opens by quoting his own complaint back to him (vv. 1–3).
verseByVerse.theology: God repeats a tired man's private complaint to him, word for word, and it is not a rebuke.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch: You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses, addressed to one man, and they are placed here on purpose.

The date takes us back nearly twenty years, to the year Baruch wrote twenty-three years of sermons onto a scroll at Jeremiah's dictation (36:4) and watched the king cut it up and feed it to a brazier. But the book keeps this word until now, so that Jeremiah's words to his own people end not with a nation's refusal but with God bending down to one exhausted assistant.

The full prophetic formula, which introduced oracles to kings, Babylon, Egypt and the nations, is used here to speak to a secretary, and it is to you, O Baruch. The God who commands the empires has a private message for the man holding the pen, and he uses his name. That is a word for anyone who has served in a supporting role and wondered whether the work registered.

God quotes him, and there is no reproach in the quotation. The LORD has added sorrow to my pain: he is not blaming circumstances but God, openly. I am weary with my groaning: worn out by his own complaining, which is a particular kind of exhaustion.

He had reason. He came from a prominent family (his brother Seraiah, it seems, was a royal official, 51:59), and by attaching himself to Jeremiah he had chosen the losing side of every argument in Jerusalem. He saw his book burned, had to go into hiding, and was blamed as the sinister influence behind the prophet (43:3).

And his master had said the same kind of thing: I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot (20:9). Serving God faithfully does not exempt a man from being worn out by it, and Scripture records the complaints of both of them without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets Baruch's grief inside his own demolition of the whole land, tells him not to seek great things for himself, and promises him his life as a prize of war wherever he goes (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: Baruch is promised no career, no safety and no acclaim, only his life, wherever he ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land. And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first move is not consolation but perspective.

Baruch's own scroll had recorded Jeremiah's commission, to pluck up and break down, to build and to plant (1:10). Now God takes those verbs and applies them to himself, and the object is the whole land. God is not losing; he is demolishing, deliberately, his own work.

That reframes Baruch's grief. His pain was real, and it was a small part of something God was doing rather than something happening to God. The scribe was not watching a disaster; he was watching a purpose.

The question goes straight to what was wrong, and it is asked without contempt: do you seek great things for yourself? A man of his background, on the right side of the argument, might reasonably have looked for vindication and a future, and God names it and closes it. Not because ambition is always wicked, but because of the timing: this is not the hour for building a career. And the command comes wrapped in a gift: the God who tells him to want less is about to give him his life.

God's way with his weary servants is often this: not a rebuke, but a clear-eyed account of what he is doing. Jeremiah himself had been answered the same way (12:5).

The New Testament says it to everyone. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt 6:33). The appointed time has grown very short (1 Cor 7:29-31). And a man who had thrown away far better prospects than Baruch's put it plainly: whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ (Phil 3:7). None of us lets go of great things for ourselves by resolve; it is the Spirit who shows us Christ as worth more than they are, and the one who never sought his own glory has already done that perfectly in our place.

The promise is one Jeremiah had shouted across Jerusalem: go out to the Chaldeans and you will have your life as a prize of war (38:2). It was given personally to Ebed-melech, because you have put your trust in me (39:18). Now the scribe receives it.

It is a soldier's phrase: the one thing you carry off the field. And it is exactly calibrated to a man about to be marched into Egypt against his will: in all places to which you may go. God does not promise him a destination he would choose. He promises to keep him in whatever place he ends up.

So the last word to Baruch is: the great things are not for you, and you will live. And we can see what he was given instead of a career. Much of what we possess of Jeremiah probably came through his hand. He wrote the burned scroll again, longer (36:32), and the book in which the new covenant stands came to us through his pen. That book has outlasted Jehoiakim, Babylon and Egypt, and is being read still.

For a Christian the promise reaches further. Baruch was given his life in every place he might go; those who belong to Christ are given a life no place and no power can take. The one who said I do not seek my own glory (John 8:50) laid down his life and took it up again, and of his sheep he says, I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

45.title: A Word for Baruch
45.overview: This short word to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, dates from the year he first wrote the prophet's sermons on the scroll Jehoiakim burned (ch. 36), but the book places it here, after the last sermon to the people. God quotes Baruch's private complaint back to him without reproach (vv. 1-3), sets his grief inside God's own demolition of the land, tells him not to seek great things for himself, and promises him his life in every place he may go (vv. 4-5).
45.theology:
God has private words for those who serve in supporting roles, and he uses their names (v. 2). Faithful service does not exempt anyone from exhaustion, and Scripture records Baruch's weariness, like his master's, without embarrassment (v. 3; 20:9).

God's comfort here comes by perspective rather than sympathy, and his answer to ambition comes by timing rather than shame: this is not the hour for great things (vv. 4-5; Matt 6:33; 1 Cor 7:29-31; Phil 3:7). What he promises is not the destination his servant would choose but his keeping in every place the servant is taken (38:2; 39:18).
45.examples:
Picture a secretary who has spent twenty years writing down another man's unpopular words, watched the work cut up and burned, written it all out again, and been blamed for it by people who would not blame the prophet himself. Baruch's "woe is me" is the voice of every faithful assistant who has wondered whether anyone noticed.

God's reply is not a speech about his feelings. It tells him what God is doing, asks him to want less, and gives him one promise he can carry anywhere. Many weary Christians have found that the way through: not a better career, but the Lord's own company in the places they did not choose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Rising Like the Nile, and Fallen at Carchemish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracles concerning the nations open at Carchemish (vv. 1-2), where Nebuchadnezzar broke Pharaoh Neco in 605 BC. The poem begins as a mustering order and breaks off as the line collapses (vv. 3-6); Egypt's boast of rising like the Nile becomes the LORD's day of vengeance by the Euphrates, and there is no healing for her (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: An army dresses for victory on the very field where God is holding a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations. About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle! Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor! Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back— terror on every side! declares the LORD. "The swift cannot flee away, nor the warrior escape; in the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen. "Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge? Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.' Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! Let the warriors go out: men of Cush and Put who handle the shield, men of Lud, skilled in handling the bow. That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new section begins here, and it widens the horizon of the whole book. For forty-five chapters God has dealt chiefly with Judah; now come six chapters concerning the nations. (In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, these oracles stand after 25:13 and in a different order; the Hebrew text, which our English Bibles follow, places them here.) The God who judged his own people is not a local deity with jurisdiction over one hill country.

And the date matters: the fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605 BC. That is the year of the scroll (36:1), and Carchemish is the battle that made Babylon the master of the world.

The poem opens inside the Egyptian camp, and the voice is a drill sergeant's. Shields up, horses harnessed, helmets on, spears polished. It is all noise and confidence, and verse 5 will show that the voice is the LORD's, which should warn the reader that something ironic is coming.

The poem breaks mid-parade. Why have I seen it? The armour was polished and the line has already collapsed.

And the phrase at the end is one Jeremiah had worn as a nickname. Terror on every side was what he cried and what his enemies called him (6:25; 20:3, 10). The thing he had suffered under is now pronounced over the army Judah was trusting in.

The image is Egypt's own. The Nile flood was the source of everything she had, and the boast borrows its language: I will rise, I will cover the earth.

The battle is renamed. Egypt thought it was a campaign; God calls it a sacrifice, with himself as the one holding it. Isaiah had used the same terrible picture of a sword sated with blood at a sacrifice in Edom (Isa 34:6).

Is God bloodthirsty? The picture is meant to shock, but it is not delight in slaughter; God says he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11). It is the language of justice. Egypt had killed Josiah at Megiddo and ruled Judah by force (2 Kgs 23:29-35).

Gilead was where the balm came from, and Jeremiah had once asked over his own people, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (8:22). Judah's wound was called incurable too — and then God said I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal (30:17).

Here the sentence stops at the diagnosis: there is no healing for you. The difference between Judah and Egypt is not the severity of the wound. It is that one of them had a covenant, and a God who heals wounds he inflicted.
verseByVerse.note: Carchemish stood at a crossing of the upper Euphrates, on today's border between Turkey and Syria.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — Noisy One Who Lets the Hour Go By
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second word concerns Nebuchadnezzar's coming against Egypt itself (v. 13), proclaimed in the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled (v. 14). The LORD thrusts the mighty down, the mercenaries break for home, Pharaoh is renamed, and Egypt is told to pack for exile (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The great power everyone trusted is renamed as all noise and no timing.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: "Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.' Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down. He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.' Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.' "As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come. Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the place names and remember who is living in them. Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes — the exact towns where the Judean refugees had settled (44:1). They fled to these cities to escape the sword, and the sword is being proclaimed over the streets they chose.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "He does not stand", a single champion falling rather than many. Either way the cause is the same, and it is stated without decoration: the LORD thrust them down.

Egypt's army was full of foreign mercenaries, and here they break for home. Hired soldiers fight for pay and leave when the pay is not worth the risk, which is the standing weakness of any strength you have purchased.

A nickname, and it is devastating. All sound, no timing — a man who blusters while the moment passes him. The refugees in Egypt had staked their lives on Pharaoh (44:30), and God gives him a name that says he will not turn up.

In a chapter full of pharaohs and emperors, only one is called King, and he swears by his own life: As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. Pharaoh is a noise that misses its moment; the King of all the armies of heaven and earth has never missed one.

And the invader will come like Tabor and Carmel — not as a raid but as a landmark, permanent and immovable. So: Prepare yourselves baggage for exile. The country the refugees chose as a refuge is told to pack.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Beautiful Heifer and a Biting Fly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The pictures turn rural and dismissive: Egypt is a sleek heifer driven frantic by a fly from the north, her troops fattened calves, her forest felled by countless woodcutters. Judgment reaches Pharaoh, Egypt's gods and all who trust in him, and then, unexpectedly, Egypt is promised an afterward (vv. 20-26).
verseByVerse.theology: A superpower is reduced to livestock troubled by an insect, and is still given an afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: "A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her. Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment. "She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees. They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number. The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north." The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him. I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The imagery turns to the farmyard, and it is deliberately belittling. Egypt is a beautiful heifer — sleek, well fed, worth looking at — tormented by a biting fly. Anyone who has watched cattle in summer knows the picture: a huge animal made frantic by an insect it cannot reach.

Her professional soldiers are fattened calves, which is what you call an animal being prepared for slaughter rather than for work.

Then three more pictures in quick succession: a snake sliding off through the grass, woodcutters swinging axes, and locusts beyond counting. Egypt's forest is called impenetrable and it comes down anyway.

The list reaches past the politics to the religion — her gods — and then ends on a phrase that is aimed straight at the Judeans reading it: those who trust in him. They had trusted him. They are on the list.

And then one word that changes the temperature: Afterward.

Egypt will be inhabited again, as in the days of old. This is not an oracle of annihilation. The God who judges the nations has a future for them beyond the judgment, which is a remarkable thing to say about the house of slavery.

Egypt’s restoration after judgment came in history as it recovered under later rulers; Isaiah looks further, to Egypt worshipping the LORD (Isa 19:21–25), a hope that began to be fulfilled when Egyptians heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — But Fear Not, O Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by turning from Egypt to Israel, in words lifted from the Book of Consolation (30:10-11): God's servant need not fear, for he will save, discipline in just measure, and never make a full end of his people (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Egypt closes with the exact comfort once spoken to Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: "But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns, and anyone who has read chapter 30 will recognise every word. This is 30:10-11, repeated almost exactly, dropped here at the end of an oracle against Egypt.

Think about who first needed to hear it. Judeans living in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes, who had just been told that the sword would come to those streets. They are also told: fear not, O Jacob my servant. The same word that announces Egypt's ruin turns to the exiles trapped inside it and calls them God's servant.

And the ground of the comfort is a presence: for I am with you.

Then the distinction the whole section rests on. The nations get a full end; Israel does not — but of you I will not make a full end. And the reason is not that Israel behaved better, which this book has spent forty-five chapters disproving. It is covenant, and nothing else.

Nor is the comfort soft. The same sentence promises discipline in just measure and adds I will by no means leave you unpunished. This is a father's measured hand, not an enemy's, and the difference between being disciplined and being ended is the difference between belonging to him and not.

For those in Christ the line runs deeper still. The full end that their sin deserved was not simply cancelled; it was borne by the one who was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people (Isa 53:8). What remains for God's children is a Father's discipline, never an enemy's wrath (Heb 12:6-11; Rom 8:1).

So the first oracle against the nations closes on an unexpected note. Egypt is given an afterward; Israel is given a promise; and both come from the same God on the same page. Judgment on the nations is never the last word in this book — not even for the house of slavery, and never for the people he keeps.

46.title: Against Egypt
46.overview:
Here the oracles concerning the nations begin (chs. 46-51), and Egypt comes first. The opening poem stands at Carchemish in 605 BC, the battle that made Babylon master of the world: an army polishing its spears for a victory, collapsing in terror, and told there is no healing for its wound (vv. 1-12). A second poem carries the sword into Egypt itself, into the very towns where the Judean refugees had settled (vv. 13-26).

Yet the chapter does not end in ruin. Egypt, of all countries, is promised an afterward (v. 26), and the exiles living inside her are told not to fear, for God is with them and will not make a full end of them (vv. 27-28).
46.theology:
The God who judged Judah is not a local deity, and the nations that talk in the first person (I will rise, I will cover the earth) find their campaigns renamed as his sacrifice (vv. 8, 10). Yet his judgment of the nations is not annihilation; Egypt is given an afterward (v. 26).

The chapter also marks the difference between Judah and Egypt. Both are wounded, but only one has a covenant and a God who heals what he has struck (v. 11; 30:17). Israel is spared a full end by that covenant, not by better behaviour, and its discipline is a father's, measured and purposeful (vv. 27-28).
46.examples:
Any power can look like the Nile in flood, rising to cover the earth. Jeremiah shows the same army polishing its spears and then fleeing, and the Pharaoh everyone was relying on renamed "Noisy one who lets the hour go by." It is a sobering picture for anyone tempted to trust a government, an employer or a market more than God.

It is also a comfort for those who live inside a world under judgment. The Judeans in Migdol and Memphis heard the sword proclaimed over their own streets, and in the same breath heard God call them his servant and say, I am with you.

47.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail.<sup>3</sup>At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands,<sup>4</sup>because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.<sup>5</sup>Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves?<sup>6</sup>Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still!<sup>7</sup>How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Waters Rising Out of the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word comes concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza (v. 1). The invader is a flood out of the north, heard before it is seen, so terrible that fathers do not look back for their children, and every helper is cut off (vv. 2–4).
verseByVerse.theology: The flood comes out of the north, and fathers are too weak to turn round for their own children.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. "Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail. At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands, because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven verses for a people who had been Israel's tormentors since the judges. Samson, Goliath, the ark carried into Ashdod, Saul's body hung on the wall at Beth-shan: the Philistines are woven through the whole earlier history, and here they are dealt with in a single short poem. This oracle names no crime, but other prophets do: Amos charged Gaza with carrying whole communities into exile to be sold (Amos 1:6), and Ezekiel spoke of their never-ending enmity (Ezek 25:15).

The dating is by an Egyptian raid on Gaza, which most likely belongs to the years around Carchemish (perhaps 609 or about 601 BC; the date is debated). The great powers are moving, and the small nations on the coast road are in the way.

The invader is described as a flood, and the direction is the one this book has used from the beginning: out of the north. The boiling pot tilted from the north in chapter 1; the enemy from the north hung over Judah for twenty-five chapters. The same water that drowned Jerusalem now comes down the coast.

A flood does not defeat a city so much as cover it, and there is nothing to fight, only something to be submerged by. You hear the army before you see it.

Then one image that does more than any casualty figure: men running who do not turn round for their own sons and daughters, and the reason given is not cowardice but collapse, so feeble are their hands. Scripture is not sneering here. It is telling the truth about what overwhelming force does to ordinary people.

Their allies to the north are cut off too: no help will come from Tyre or Sidon, because they will have their own problem.

And the Philistines are called the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor, Caphtor being their old homeland, the place Genesis names in the table of nations (Gen 10:14; compare Amos 9:7). They were sea people who had arrived from somewhere else centuries before. God knows where every nation came from, and the word remnant quietly says that they are already the leftovers of something larger.
verseByVerse.note: Caphtor is probably Crete, the Philistines’ ancestral home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Sword of the LORD, How Long?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gaza and Ashkelon mourn (v. 5). The poem pleads with the sword of the LORD to rest, and is answered that it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone begs the sword to stop, and is told who is holding it.

verseByVerse.quote: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves? Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still! How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of the five Philistine cities are named, and the mourning takes the forms these people used: heads shaved, bodies cut. The gashing is the same practice the eighty pilgrims from Shechem and Shiloh had been wearing when Ishmael met them on the road (41:5), and the same that Israel was expressly forbidden: You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). What God prohibited in his own people was the ordinary grammar of grief among their neighbours, and the question how long will you gash yourselves? is not mockery but a comment on futility. Cutting yourself changes nothing.

Then the poet turns from the victims and speaks to the weapon. The tone is not triumph. It is the cry of a man who has watched too much of this. Jeremiah had wept over his own people's ruin, and he does not gloat over the ruin of Israel's old enemies either. Even the enemies of God's people are pitied by the man who has to announce their fall.

That is a standing rebuke to a certain way of holding the doctrine of judgment. Anyone who can contemplate it without grief has not understood it.

The answer is not comfort: the sword cannot rest because it is under orders. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "you" where the English has "it", the poet still addressing the weapon directly. God has given it a charge and appointed it: this is commission, not chaos, with a named target.

So one of the shortest oracles in this section makes the point the whole section exists to make. History is not a series of accidents in which the strong happen to eat the weak. There is a sword, and it is the LORD's, and it moves when he gives it a charge and stops when he does not.

And there is one more thing to say, standing where we do. A day came when the sword of the LORD was given a charge and did not fall on Ashkelon or on Judah. Zechariah had heard God say Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and Jesus took that verse to himself on the night he was betrayed (Zech 13:7; Matt 26:31). The sword fell on a man who had asked in a garden that his cup might pass from him, and who then put himself in its way, so that the question How long till you are quiet? finally has an answer for everyone who is his.

47.title: Against the Philistines
47.overview: A short oracle against the Philistines, Israel's old enemies since the days of the judges. The invader from the north comes down the coast like a flood, and the terror is so great that fathers flee without looking back for their children (vv. 1-4). Gaza and Ashkelon mourn, and the poet pleads with the sword of the LORD to rest, only to be told it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge (vv. 5-7).
47.theology:
The flood from the north that covered Judah now covers the coastal plain: God's instruments are not reserved for one nation, and he knows where every nation came from (vv. 2, 4; 1:13-15; Gen 10:14). History is commission, not chaos. The sword moves when he gives it a charge and rests when he says so (v. 7; Isa 34:5-6).

Yet the prophet does not gloat. He tells the truth about what terror does to ordinary people and pities even Israel's old tormentors (vv. 3, 6). Anyone who can think about God's judgment without grief has not understood it.
47.examples:
When news comes of a war far away, it is easy to read it either as random chaos or as the deserved fall of people we never liked. Jeremiah refuses both. The sword is the LORD's and is under orders, and the man who announces it still cries out, "How long?"

The father fleeing without turning back for his children is not mocked. Scripture lets us see what overwhelming force does to people, so that we feel it before we analyse it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Town after town falls until the renown of Moab is no more (vv. 1–5). Moab trusted in its works and treasures, and Chemosh goes into exile with his priests (vv. 6–9); the section ends with a hard word on doing the LORD's work with slackness (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Moab's national god is carried off into exile alongside the clergy who served him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down; the renown of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!' You also, O Madmen, shall be brought to silence; the sword shall pursue you. "A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!' Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction. Flee! Save yourselves! You will be like a juniper in the desert! For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The destroyer shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape; the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken. "Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away; her cities shall become a desolation, with no inhabitant in them. "Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab was the nation across the Dead Sea, close kin and old enemy. Genesis records the ugly beginning, when Lot's daughter bore a son and called his name Moab (Gen 19:37), and from then on they are neighbours, sometimes allies, mostly trouble.

The poem moves through their towns like a casualty list, and it is full of proper names for a reason. These were real places with markets and families in them. Judgment in Scripture is rarely abstract.

The sound that carries is a child's. Her little ones have made a cry: the detail a prophet includes when he is not enjoying his subject.

The ESV notes two things in verse 5: the Hebrew reads "weeping goes up with weeping", and the Septuagint has "heard the cry", comparing Isaiah 15:5. Isaiah had written the same scene a century before, with fugitives climbing the same road: at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping (Isa 15:5). Two prophets, the same hill, the same people stumbling up it.

The indictment: you trusted in your works and your treasures. What you have made and what you have saved. It is the most respectable idolatry there is, and it needs no shrine.

And then the picture that exposes it: Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The national god of Moab is deported. A god who has to be carried into captivity by the men who served him is not a god; he is luggage.

The curse on slackness is a hard word, spoken to the invading army, the Babylonians God had sent to judge Moab: to do his work half-heartedly would be to defy him. Why would God command bloodshed? Because here he acts as the judge of a nation whose guilt was full, and the army is only the officer who carries out his sentence; the verdict was his, not Babylon's. It is no warrant for violence today, for the church does God’s work with other weapons (2 Cor 10:4). But the principle beneath it reaches us: work God assigns is not to be done with slackness, whatever the task. For us the curse has already fallen elsewhere: Christ, who did his Father's work perfectly, became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), and the Spirit he gives is the one who makes us diligent in it now.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab's problem is comfort: settled on his dregs, never poured from vessel to vessel (v. 11). God will send pourers, Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was of Bethel, and the neighbours are told to mourn the broken scepter (vv. 12–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Wine left undisturbed keeps its taste; a nation never poured out keeps its sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces. Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. "How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'? The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. The calamity of Moab is near at hand, and his affliction hastens swiftly. Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.' "Come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground, O inhabitant of Dibon! For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has destroyed your strongholds. Stand by the way and watch, O inhabitant of Aroer! Ask him who flees and her who escapes; say, 'What has happened?' Moab is put to shame, for it is broken; wail and cry! Tell it beside the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture comes out of a winery.

New wine was left to stand so the sediment — the dregs — would settle, and then it was poured off into another jar, and another, leaving the lees behind. Wine that was never decanted kept its strength but also kept everything that should have been removed. It stayed exactly as it was.

That is Moab. At ease from his youth, never carried into exile, never poured out — and therefore never changed. His taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.

Judah had been poured from vessel to vessel until she hardly knew herself. Moab had been left alone on the shelf, and the text treats that as the worse condition. Undisturbed comfort is not the same as God's favour; it can be the reason a nation or a life never becomes anything different.

So God sends pourers. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads "their" where the English has "his". The decanting Moab never had is coming as an invasion, and this time the jars are broken as well as emptied.

An even-handed line. Israel's golden calf at Bethel is named in the same breath as Moab's Chemosh, and both are called their confidence. God does not flatter his own people by contrast.

The boast is answered by events, and the oracle is signed by the one who answers it: declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. In a section full of nations and their kings, one King keeps signing the oracles, and every throne in them stands or falls at his word.

The neighbours are told to mourn, and the words given them are not gloating: How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff. Moab's greatness is acknowledged in the act of lamenting its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–33 — He Magnified Himself Against the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment runs through a roll-call of towns (vv. 21-24). Moab is made drunk because he magnified himself against the LORD and mocked Israel (vv. 25-27), and his pride is catalogued (vv. 28-30). Then the voice changes: Therefore I wail for Moab (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the sentence and then weeps over the country he is sentencing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath, and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, declares the LORD. "Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision. Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head? "Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge. We have heard of the pride of Moab— he is very proud— of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false. Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn. More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah! Your branches passed over the sea, reached to the Sea of Jazer; on your summer fruits and your grapes the destroyer has fallen. Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven towns in four verses, and then the sweep: all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The roll-call is slow on purpose. Somebody knew these places.

The charge is stated at last, and it is not the towns or the treasure: he magnified himself against the LORD. And the punishment fits the image of the chapter — the nation that was never poured out is now made to drink, and ends up in its own vomit. There is nothing dignified in the picture, which is the point about pride.

Here is the specific offence, and it is startling: Moab is being judged for mockery. Whenever Israel was humbled, Moab laughed and wagged your head. Zephaniah records the same charge — I have heard the taunts of Moab... how they have taunted my people, and the sentence comes in return for their pride (Zeph 2:8, 10).

God had sent the disaster on Judah himself, and he still holds the onlookers accountable for enjoying it. How we speak of another's downfall is noticed. The answer is not a stricter tongue alone but a new heart: those who have been shown mercy at their own lowest point learn to weep with others at theirs.

The advice is to go and live like a bird in a cliff face — which is exactly what people did when nothing was left. And the gentleness of the image sits oddly beside the sentence, as though the one pronouncing it is watching a people he does not hate.

Five words for the same thing, piled up: pride, loftiness, pride, arrogance, haughtiness. And then God's own assessment underneath the noise — his boasts are false, his deeds are false. The swagger had nothing behind it, and he had always known.

Then, without warning, the voice breaks. The therefore should introduce a sentence; it introduces tears. The same God who has just catalogued Moab's arrogance and ordered him made drunk now mourns for him by name, and for the men of one particular town.

Moab was famous for vineyards, and the picture is of harvest silenced. Treading grapes was noisy work, done with singing. Now there is shouting in the presses and it is the wrong kind.

It is the LORD who says I have made the wine cease. He is not grieving over something that happened to him. He is grieving over what he has done, and both are true at once, which is as close as the Old Testament comes to explaining the tears of God. The fuller explanation comes in person, when Jesus, who would bear the judgment himself, wept over Jerusalem while he foretold its fall (Luke 19:41-44).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–47 — My Heart Moans Like a Flute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lament deepens, God's heart moaning like a flute (vv. 34-39); there is no escape from terror, pit and snare, and the old song of fire from Heshbon is sung again (vv. 40-46). Then the last line turns everything: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: After forty-six verses of ruin comes one word: Yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. For the waters of Nimrim also have become desolate. And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god. Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished. "For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth. On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD. How it is broken! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! So Moab has become a derision and a horror to all that are around him." For thus says the LORD: "Behold, one shall fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Moab; the cities shall be taken and the strongholds seized. The heart of the warriors of Moab shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains; Moab shall be destroyed and be no longer a people, because he magnified himself against the LORD. Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD. He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I will bring these things upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares the LORD. "In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab, the crown of the sons of tumult. Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity. Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cry runs across the whole map, and the religion goes with it. The high places stop, because there is nobody left to climb them.

Twice more the lament, and now with an instrument: my heart moans for Moab like a flute. The flute was played at funerals. God says his heart makes the sound of a funeral instrument over a pagan nation.

Isaiah had written the same line with a different instrument — my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth (Isa 16:11) — the same town named in both. Two prophets, a century apart, given the same grief.

The mourning rites are the ones we have seen twice already in this book — shaved heads, cut beards, gashed hands (41:5; 47:5). And the vessel image returns one last time: not merely poured out now, but broken... like a vessel for which no one cares.

Three hazards in a row, arranged so that escaping one puts you into the next. It is the picture of a hunt, and it says what the whole chapter has been saying: there is no door out of God's judgment by running faster.

These two verses are a quotation. Centuries earlier, when Israel first came through this territory, the old Amorite victory song ran: For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon... Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! (Num 21:28-29). Jeremiah sings Moab's ancient defeat song back over Moab's final defeat. History rhymes, and God has a long memory for the words.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days. The phrase is the one used of Israel herself (29:14; 30:3). It is spoken over the people of Chemosh, the nation that wagged its head at Jerusalem's funeral, the drunkard in his own vomit.

And it had already begun, quietly, long before. In the years of the judges a Moabite woman had followed her mother-in-law home to Bethlehem and said that Israel's God would be her God; and the neighbourhood women named her son Obed, who was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17). The line that runs to the Messiah has Moab in it, and Matthew names her in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5).

So the closing formula — Thus far is the judgment on Moab — marks a limit in more than one sense. The judgment reaches this far and no further; and the God who wailed over a pagan country while sentencing it had a latter-day mercy in mind for it all along.

How was the promise kept? Moab was subdued by Babylon, probably about 582 BC, and afterwards disappears as a nation, so the promise looks beyond its ruin. Isaiah's oracle on Moab had already pointed to a throne set up in steadfast love in the tent of David (Isa 16:5), and the apostles saw that throne raised up when people from the nations were gathered to David's greater Son (Acts 15:16-17). The Greek translation of Jeremiah, shorter throughout, lacks verses 45-47; the ESV follows the Hebrew, which has them, and the hope they hold is taught in many other places.

48.title: Against Moab
48.overview:
Moab, Israel's close kin and old enemy across the Dead Sea, receives the longest oracle so far. Town after town falls, and Chemosh goes into exile with his priests (vv. 1-10). Moab's deeper trouble is undisturbed comfort, wine never poured from vessel to vessel (vv. 11-20). He is judged for magnifying himself against the LORD and for laughing at Israel's downfall, and then, unexpectedly, the voice pronouncing the sentence breaks into lament (vv. 21-39). There is no escaping by running, yet the last line promises that God will restore Moab's fortunes in the latter days (vv. 40-47).

Why are chapters about Moab and its neighbours in the Bible at all? Jeremiah was appointed a prophet to the nations (1:5, 10), and these oracles were spoken mostly in Judah's hearing. They told God's people that the LORD rules every nation and not only Israel; that the neighbours who mocked them would answer to him, so Judah need neither take revenge nor lean on alliances; and that pride is judged wherever it is found, Judah's included. They also end, again and again, in mercy, which is the first hint of the gospel that would go to all nations (Matt 28:19).
48.theology:
Moab's sins are respectable ones: trust in its own works and treasures, the complacency of a life never disturbed, and the pleasure of watching a neighbour fall (vv. 7, 11, 27). God names all three, and does not flatter Israel by contrast; Bethel stands beside Chemosh (v. 13).

The chapter's deepest note is the grief of the judge. The same God who pronounces the sentence wails over Moab and grieves over what he himself has done (vv. 31-36). And his last word over this pagan enemy is restoration, a mercy already foreshadowed in Ruth the Moabitess, who stands in the line of David and of Christ (v. 47; Ruth 4:17).
48.examples:
It is possible to live a life like wine left on the shelf: never shaken, never poured out, keeping both its strength and its sediment. Moab's comfort was not a sign of God's favour but the reason it never changed. Christians who have been "poured from vessel to vessel" by loss or upheaval can take heart that God's disturbing is often his kindness.

The chapter also warns against the pleasure of seeing someone else humbled. Moab wagged its head at Judah's funeral, and God remembered it, though he had sent Judah's disaster himself.

49.text: <sup>1</sup>Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities?<sup>2</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon is charged with squatting on Gad's inheritance (v. 1), so Israel will dispossess those who dispossessed him and Milcom will go into exile like Chemosh (vv. 2–5). Then, after five verses of ruin: But afterward (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A second national god is carried off with his clergy, and a second nation is given an afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities? Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD. "Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials. Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?' Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives. "But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ammon was Moab's kinsman, descended from Lot's other son, born to his younger daughter and named Ben-ammi (Gen 19:38), and their territory lay east of the Jordan next to Gad's.

The charge is occupation. When Assyria deported the northern tribes, Ammon moved into Gad's towns and stayed. God's questions are those of a landowner: Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? The tribe was gone, but the title deed was not vacant.
