The ESV notes that Milcom, the Ammonite god, may also be read "their king" here and in verse 3. Either reading makes the same point: what took Gad's land was a rival claim to lordship.

The reversal is exact (dispossess those who dispossessed him), and God defends the inheritance of a tribe that had already been carried off for its own sins. His discipline of his people does not transfer their birthright to anyone else.

The same sentence passed on Chemosh one chapter earlier (48:7), word for word in structure. Two national gods, two deportations, both needing their own priests to carry them.

The ESV notes the Hebrew here as "boast of your valleys, your valley flows". What is clear is the confidence: good land, full treasuries, and the question Who will come against me?, which is the sentence every secure nation says just before the answer arrives.

Five verses of judgment, and then afterward. It is the same pattern as Moab's Yet (48:47) and Egypt's (46:26), and it is becoming the signature of this whole section. God's last word to the nations around Israel is not extinction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–22 — Though You Make Your Nest as High as the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom's wisdom fails and her hiding places are opened (vv. 7–11). If the less deserving drank the cup, Edom will not go unpunished (vv. 12–13); though she nests as high as the eagle, God will bring her down, for who can summon him? (vv. 14–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Edom trusts a fortress in a cliff, and God asks who exactly is going to summon him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished? Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him. If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves? But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more. Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me." For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink. For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes." I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle! For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind. The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD. "Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters. As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her. Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea. Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom is Esau, and the rivalry goes back to a womb: Two nations are in your womb... the older shall serve the younger (Gen 25:23). They were famous for shrewdness, and the oracle opens by asking where all that cleverness has gone.

Edom's security was geography: canyons, cliffs and fortresses reached through slot gorges, the region of Petra. I have uncovered his hiding places is the end of that. There is no terrain God does not know.

Then an extraordinary half-verse in the middle of a judgment oracle. To an enemy nation being stripped bare, God says: leave the orphans with me, and let the widows trust me. Even here the character that defends widows and orphans in the law does not switch off.

The deepest sentence in the chapter is about the cup, and its logic runs from the greater to the lesser. The cup is the cup of wrath from chapter 25, which God handed round the nations beginning with Jerusalem (25:15-16). Judah had drunk it, and the phrase those who did not deserve to drink probably has her in view. Compared with Edom's guilt, God's own people were the less deserving party, and they drank anyway. So how shall Edom escape?

And the sentence reaches further than Edom, because there was one who truly did not deserve the cup and drank it to the bottom. In a garden he prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). The argument of verse 12 is the argument of the cross read backwards: if the innocent drank, the guilty cannot plead exemption; and because the innocent drank, the guilty who hide in him need not.

The ESV notes that the clefts of the rock may be read "of Sela", the place name behind Petra. And Obadiah has this passage almost word for word: The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock... Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down (Obad 3-4).

What deceived them was The horror you inspire. Being feared had convinced them they were safe. A reputation for being dangerous is a poor defence against God.

The three questions of verse 19 are the centre of gravity of the whole section: For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? No one is like him, and the second question is the sharpest. To summon is to call someone to court. God asks who is going to issue him a summons, and the silence that follows is the answer to every complaint that his judgments are unfair. There is no higher bench to appeal to. That is not a refusal to hear our questions, for Jeremiah himself brought his complaints to God (12:1). It is a reminder of who sits on the bench.
verseByVerse.note: Teman (v. 7) was a district of Edom named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11) and famous for its wise men; Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite (Job 2:11).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Damascus melts in panic though God calls her the city of my joy (vv. 23-27). Kedar's tents and camels are taken (vv. 28-30), and Hazor, a nation at ease with no gates or bars, becomes a waste (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Walls are no defence, and having no walls at all is no defence either.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet. Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor. How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy? Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad." Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east! Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!' Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you. "Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone. Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. I will scatter to every wind those who cut the corners of their hair, and I will bring their calamity from every side of them, declares the LORD. Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Syria now, and the image is a sea that will not settle. Panic described as water that cannot stop moving is exact: fear has no resting place in it.

The city of my joy. God calls a Gentile capital that. Damascus was ancient and beautiful, and its maker takes pleasure in it even while pronouncing its fall. Anyone who imagines the God of Israel is indifferent to the cities of the nations has not read this verse.

Amos had said the same, naming the same dynasty: I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad (Amos 1:4). The prophets are not improvising.

Now the Arab tribes of the desert; this Hazor is not the old Canaanite city in Galilee but a cluster of desert settlements, which Nebuchadnezzar raided probably about 599 BC. The inventory changes accordingly: not walls and gates but tents, curtains, flocks and camels. God's word reaches the nomads as precisely as the capitals, and it names what they actually own.

And there is the phrase again, Terror on every side!, the words that had been Jeremiah's nickname (20:3, 10) and were pronounced over Egypt (46:5), now shouted after camel herds.

Hazor's defence was that it had nothing worth attacking: no gates or bars, living alone out in the desert where armies do not go.

Set this beside Moab, whose security was that he had never been poured out, and Edom, whose security was a cliff. Here is a people whose security is obscurity. All three fall. There is no arrangement of walls, wealth or remoteness that functions as a hiding place, and the phrase a nation at ease has been a warning throughout these chapters rather than a compliment.

And note which oracles carry no promise of restoration. Egypt, Moab, Ammon and Elam are all given an afterward; Damascus, Kedar and Hazor are not. God does not owe an explanation for the pattern, and the book does not offer one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elam, far east beyond Babylon, has its bow broken and is scattered to the four winds, and God sets his throne there (vv. 34-38). Then the last word: But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets his throne in the farthest country named, and then promises it a future.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come. I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them, and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD. "But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elam lay beyond Babylon, in what is now south-western Iran, one of the farthest nations named in the book, a country most Judeans would never see and had no dealings with.

And their strength is identified precisely: the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. Elamite archers were famous. God names what a nation is actually proud of before he breaks it.

I will set my throne in Elam. Not a garrison or a governor, but a throne, in the most distant capital in the book. The claim is that the LORD of hosts governs there directly, and that its king sits on borrowed furniture.

And the chapter ends with a promise rather than a sentence. After Egypt (46:26), Moab (48:47) and Ammon (49:6), Elam is the fourth nation in these chapters told that judgment is not the end of its story.

And on a day of Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and the crowd heard the mighty works of God each in his own language, Luke's list of the nationalities present begins: Parthians and Medes and Elamites (Acts 2:9). The restoration of Elam, promised through a prophet in a besieged city, turns up as men from Elam hearing the gospel in their own tongue.

49.title: Ammon, Edom, and the Nations Around
49.overview:
Four short oracles sweep round Judah's world. Ammon, which took over Gad's land, will lose it, and its god will go into exile (vv. 1-6). Edom, proud of its wisdom and its cliff fortresses, will be brought down from its eagle's nest, for no one can summon God to court (vv. 7-22). Damascus, the desert tribes of Kedar and Hazor fall in turn (vv. 23-33), and far-off Elam has its famous bow broken (vv. 34-39). Yet Ammon and Elam, like Egypt and Moab before them, are promised restoration.

Why does Judah need oracles about Ammon, Kedar and Elam? These names were the map of her whole world, near neighbours and far-off peoples alike, and the oracles say that no corner of it lay outside the LORD's rule. They also say his last word to many of these nations is mercy, which began to come true when Elamites heard the gospel at Pentecost.
49.theology:
No kind of security works against God, whether walls, wealth, a cliff, a fearsome reputation, or even having no gates at all (vv. 16, 31). He is the only judge, with no higher court to summon him (v. 19). Yet the same God tells a nation being stripped bare to leave its orphans with him (v. 11) and calls a Gentile capital the city of my joy (v. 25).

At the centre stands the cup. If those less deserving drank it, the guilty cannot plead exemption; and because one wholly innocent drank it to the bottom, those who hide in him need not (v. 12; 25:15-16; Matt 26:39).
49.examples:
Edom is the picture of a person whose safety lies in being feared: the sharp tongue, the reputation nobody wants to cross. The horror you inspire was exactly what deceived her. Hazor is the opposite, safe because no one notices her, and she falls too. Neither strength nor obscurity hides anyone from God.

Yet in the middle of Edom's sentence God says, leave your fatherless children with me. Even under judgment, the widow and the orphan can still be placed in his hands.

50.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet:<sup>2</sup>"Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.'<sup>3</sup>"For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away.<sup>4</sup>"In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God.<sup>5</sup>They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.'<sup>6</sup>"My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold.<sup>7</sup>All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.'<sup>8</sup>"Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock.<sup>9</sup>For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed.<sup>10</sup>Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.<sup>11</sup>"Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions,<sup>12</sup>your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.<sup>13</sup>Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds.<sup>14</sup>Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD.<sup>15</sup>Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done.<sup>16</sup>Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land.<sup>17</sup>"Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones.<sup>18</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.<sup>20</sup>In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.<sup>21</sup>"Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you.<sup>22</sup>The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction!<sup>23</sup>How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!<sup>24</sup>I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD.<sup>25</sup>The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her.<sup>27</sup>Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment.<sup>28</sup>"A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple.<sup>29</sup>"Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel.<sup>30</sup>Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you.<sup>32</sup>The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him.<sup>33</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.<sup>34</sup>Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon.<sup>35</sup>"A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men!<sup>36</sup>A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed!<sup>37</sup>A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered!<sup>38</sup>A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols.<sup>39</sup>"Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations.<sup>40</sup>As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her.<sup>41</sup>"Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth.<sup>42</sup>They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon!<sup>43</sup>"The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor.<sup>44</sup>"Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?<sup>45</sup>Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.<sup>46</sup>At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Babylon Is Taken, Bel Is Put to Shame
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The news is to be published everywhere: Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame (v. 2), by a nation Out of the north (v. 3), the phrase that hung over Judah, now turned round. In the middle of it Israel and Judah come home together, weeping and seeking the LORD in an everlasting covenant (vv. 4–5), lost sheep led astray by their shepherds (vv. 6–7), and the call goes out to flee Babylon (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemy from the north gets an enemy from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet: "Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.' "For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away. "In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God. They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.' "My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold. All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.' "Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock. For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed. Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For fifty chapters Babylon has been the instrument. God called Nebuchadnezzar my servant three times, put the yoke on Judah's neck, and told the nations to submit. Now the instrument is the defendant.

Two chapters, a hundred and ten verses, the longest oracle in the book — because the hardest question this prophet faced was whether God had simply changed sides.

The instruction is to publish it and conceal it not. And what falls first is not the walls or the army, but Bel and Merodach, the gods. Isaiah had drawn the same scene: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts (Isa 46:1). Gods that have to be evacuated by pack animal.

Out of the north. That phrase has been a threat since chapter 1: the boiling pot, the enemy from the north, the flood that covered Judah and the Philistines. Now it points at Babylon. The direction of judgment does not belong to Babylon; it belongs to God, and it turns.

In the middle of an oracle against an empire, this: both houses come home together, the northern tribes scattered for more than a century and Judah, in one company. And they come weeping, asking directions: They shall ask the way to Zion. People who had forgotten the road have to be told it, and their faces are turned toward it before their feet arrive. The covenant they ask for is the one promised in chapter 31, an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten, and it is asked for, not imposed. The God who scattered them has made them long for him.

God's diagnosis of the whole tragedy, in two sentences, and he does not begin with the sheep's stupidity. He begins with the shepherds, the kings, priests and prophets of chapter 23, who scattered my flock (23:2).

The sheep are still called my people, and still called lost. Isaiah puts both halves together and adds the remedy: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa 53:6).

The same voice that said build houses and plant gardens in Babylon (29:5) now says leave, and the God who says it is the Redeemer who has broken their captors' grip (v. 34). Obedience is not a fixed posture; it follows the word of God as it moves, and the people who had settled in for seventy years had to be told when the seventy years were up.

John hears that call again over a later Babylon: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Rev 18:4).

When was this fulfilled? It began when exiles of both kingdoms came home under Cyrus, but the everlasting covenant they ask for is the new covenant of 31:31-34, which Hebrews says Christ has brought in (Heb 8:6-13). In him the lost sheep of both houses, and of the nations too, become one flock under one shepherd (John 10:16).
verseByVerse.note: Bel (Marduk) and Merodach are names of Babylon’s chief god.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Hammer Punished, the Flock Restored
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunderers who frolicked over God's heritage will see their mother shamed and Babylon made the last of the nations (vv. 11-13). She is punished because she sinned against the LORD, and must be done to as she has done (vv. 14-16). Israel, the sheep two lions mauled, will be brought back to pasture and its iniquity sought and not found (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Instruments are not exempt. God punishes the hammer he swung.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions, your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds. Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD. Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done. Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land. "Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones. Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria. I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead. In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon is pictured as livestock enjoying itself, a heifer kicking up its heels, stallions neighing. The animal imagery of these oracles is consistently deflating: Egypt a heifer troubled by a fly, Moab wine left on its dregs, Babylon a frolicking herd. And the empire that was first among the nations will be the last of the nations, and the place will be desert.

Here is the ground of the whole chapter, and it answers the question of whether God has changed sides. Babylon is not being punished for defeating Judah; that was God's own doing. She is punished because she has sinned against the LORD, and the measure is do to her as she has done.

An instrument used by God is still accountable for how it behaved in his hand. Babylon went beyond her commission: cruelty, pride, the temple burned, the plundering of God's heritage for pleasure. Being useful to God is not the same as being righteous, and it confers no immunity.

Two empires as two lions over one carcass. Gnawed his bones is what is left when the flesh is gone — the second predator working over what the first left behind.

The precedent is Assyria. That empire had been God's rod against the north, and it fell — Nineveh gone within living memory. Babylon can read its own future in Assyria's ruins, and so can every power that thinks it is the exception.

The sheep get pasture again — named pasture, Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim, Gilead, the good grazing country.

And then a sentence that goes further than any restoration of land. Iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none. Someone will look for the sin and not find it — not because it was small, but because of the last clause: for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant. This is the sins-remembered-no-more of 31:34, stated as a search that comes up empty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The attack goes up against Merathaim and Pekod, "double rebellion" and "punishment" (v. 21). The hammer of the whole earth is broken in a snare Babylon never saw (vv. 22-27); word of vengeance for the temple reaches Zion, for she defied the Holy One of Israel and will not let his people go (vv. 28-33).
verseByVerse.theology: A district named Double Rebellion is caught in a snare it never saw.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you. The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction! How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD. The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans. Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her. Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment. "A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple. "Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you. The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two Babylonian districts, and the ESV explains why these two are named: "Merathaim means double rebellion" and "Pekod means punishment". Real places on the map whose names, heard in Hebrew, spell out the charge and the verdict. The note on devoting also matters — "That is, set apart (devote) as an offering to the Lord (for destruction)" — the old language of holy war, now used against the empire that had carried out God's own judgment.

The hammer of the whole earth. Babylon's own oracle will say it more plainly still: You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces (51:20). A tool, and a tool can be broken by the hand that used it.

You did not know it. The snare was set, sprung and closed while the empire went about its business entirely unaware that anything had happened.

That is how judgment usually arrives on the secure — not as a visible siege but as a position already lost before anyone notices. Belshazzar's feast was going on the night the city fell.

God keeps an armoury, and the weapons in it are nations. The invaders massing on the horizon think they are pursuing their own ambitions; they have been taken out of a store.

Refugees running the other way — out of Babylon toward Zion, carrying news. And the news has a specific object: vengeance for his temple. The burning of that building was not overlooked.

The charge is pride, and the title used is the intimate one: the Holy One of Israel. Babylon had defied not an abstract deity but the God of the people she had plundered.

They refuse to let them go. The phrase belongs to another story, and any Israelite would hear it: a hard-hearted king who would not release God's people, and a God who took them out anyway. Babylon has made herself Egypt, and the next verse is the response.

What of the command to kill and devote them to destruction? The Hebrew word, herem, means to hand something over wholly to God, here for destruction, as in the conquest of Canaan. It is God's sentence on an empire that had crushed nations, carried out by the armies he sent against Babylon: a judgment of that moment, not a pattern for believers, whose King said his servants do not fight for his kingdom (John 18:36). The Judge of all the earth may end a guilty power; no Christian may take up that sword in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Pekod was an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris, known from Assyrian records; Merathaim, "land of bitter waters", was probably a name for southern Babylonia near the Gulf.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their Redeemer is strong (v. 34). Five swords and a drought fall on all that Babylon trusted, for she is mad over idols, and she becomes like Sodom (vv. 35-40). Her king's hands fall helpless, and the questions asked of Edom are asked of Babylon (vv. 41-46).
verseByVerse.theology: The captives do not have a lawyer; they have a Redeemer, and he takes the case himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon. "A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men! A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed! A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered! A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols. "Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations. As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her. "Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon! "The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor. "Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word is Redeemer — the kinsman with the right and the duty to buy back what his relative had lost, the role Jeremiah himself played for a field at Anathoth (32:7). The captives have no standing and no advocate. What they have is a relative with means.

He will surely plead their cause. He does not send a lawyer; he takes the case. Isaiah names him in the same breath: Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts is his name — is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 47:4).

That Redeemer at last became a kinsman in the full sense. The Son of God was born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal 4:4-5), and he shared our flesh and blood to free those held in slavery all their lives (Heb 2:14-15). The captives' relative with means turned out to be the LORD himself, and the price was his own life.

Five swords and a drought, hammered out one after another, and the list is a catalogue of everything Babylon trusted: administration, scholarship, divination, army, cavalry, treasury, and the canal system that made the land fertile.

The diviners get a particular sentence — that they may become fools — and the diagnosis underneath it all is blunt: they are mad over idols. Not merely mistaken: mad.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks in Babylon here. The picture is a ruin with animals in it, measured against the oldest ruin in Scripture — Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24). John sees the same desolation over the last Babylon: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!... a haunt for every unclean bird (Rev 18:2).

The words once used of Jerusalem under siege (6:24), and the labour pains of Edom's warriors (49:22), now fall on Babylon's king: his hands fell helpless. Every empire in this section ends in the same posture.

These are the words spoken over Edom a chapter earlier (49:19), repeated almost without alteration over the superpower. The same three questions do for the greatest nation what they did for the smallest.

I will appoint over her whomever I choose. Within a lifetime the appointment was made, and his name was Cyrus.

So the chapter that began with a banner and a proclamation ends with a sound the whole earth hears. And the point of all of it, for the exiles who first read it, was not the satisfaction of seeing an enemy fall. It was that the God who had used Babylon was not owned by Babylon: that the seventy years had an end written into them, that the shepherds who scattered the flock would answer for it, and that the people asking the way to Zion had a Redeemer strong enough to plead their cause against the hammer of the whole earth.

Did this come true? Babylon surrendered to Cyrus in 539 BC without a battle and stayed inhabited for centuries. The fulfilment came over time: it declined, was damaged by later kings, and became the ruin it is today. Prophecy often speaks of the end as if it were immediate. Revelation takes up Babylon as the name of every proud power that God will bring down (Rev 18).

50.title: Against Babylon
50.overview: The last and longest of the oracles against the nations (chs. 50-51) is spoken against Babylon, the empire God had used against Judah for fifty chapters. The instrument is now the defendant. Her gods are shamed and an enemy comes against her out of the north (vv. 1-3). Woven through the judgment is the homecoming of Israel and Judah together, weeping and seeking an everlasting covenant (vv. 4-20). The hammer of the whole earth is broken in a snare she never saw (vv. 21-33), because the captives' Redeemer is strong and pleads their cause himself (vv. 34-46).
50.theology:
This chapter answers the question the exiles must have asked: had God simply changed sides? He had not. Babylon is judged not for defeating Judah, which was his own doing, but for her pride and cruelty in doing it. Being useful to God confers no immunity, and the direction of judgment belongs to him alone (vv. 3, 14-15, 23).

Through it all runs a promise for the scattered flock. God blames the shepherds before the sheep (v. 6), searches for his people's iniquity and finds none because he has pardoned them (v. 20; 31:34), and stands as their Redeemer, the kinsman who takes their case himself (v. 34).
50.examples:
Some of the strongest powers in history have believed they were the exception, the hammer and never the anvil. Jeremiah tells Babylon to read her future in Nineveh's ruins; she did not, and the city fell while the feast went on.

For the believer, the comfort is personal. Those who have no standing and no advocate are not left to plead their own case. Their Redeemer is strong, and the price of their freedom was his own life.

51.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai,<sup>2</sup>and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land, when they come against her from every side on the day of trouble.<sup>3</sup>Let not the archer bend his bow, and let him not stand up in his armor. Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army.<sup>4</sup>They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets.<sup>5</sup>For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her.<sup>7</sup>Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad.<sup>8</sup>Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed.<sup>9</sup>We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies.<sup>10</sup>The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God.<sup>11</sup>"Sharpen the arrows! Take up the shields! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple.<sup>12</sup>"Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon.<sup>13</sup>O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut.<sup>14</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.<sup>15</sup>"It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens.<sup>16</sup>When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.<sup>17</sup>Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them.<sup>18</sup>They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish.<sup>19</sup>Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.<sup>20</sup>"You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms;<sup>21</sup>with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer;<sup>22</sup>with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman;<sup>23</sup>with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders.<sup>24</sup>"I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD.<sup>25</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain.<sup>26</sup>No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.<sup>27</sup>"Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts.<sup>28</sup>Prepare the nations for war against her, the kings of the Medes, with their governors and deputies, and every land under their dominion.<sup>29</sup>The land trembles and writhes in pain, for the LORD's purposes against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.<sup>30</sup>The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken.<sup>31</sup>One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side;<sup>32</sup>the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic.<sup>33</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come."<sup>34</sup>"Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out.<sup>35</sup>The violence done to me and to my kinsmen be upon Babylon," let the inhabitant of Zion say. "My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say.<sup>36</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry,<sup>37</sup>and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant.<sup>38</sup>"They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs.<sup>39</sup>While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD.<sup>40</sup>I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.<sup>41</sup>"How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!<sup>42</sup>The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves.<sup>43</sup>Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes.<sup>44</sup>And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen.<sup>45</sup>"Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD!<sup>46</sup>Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler.<sup>47</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the images of Babylon; her whole land shall be put to shame, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her.<sup>48</sup>Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD.<sup>49</sup>Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, just as for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth.<sup>50</sup>"You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind:<sup>51</sup>'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.'<sup>52</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan.<sup>53</sup>Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.<sup>54</sup>"A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!<sup>55</sup>For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised,<sup>56</sup>for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay.<sup>57</sup>I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.<sup>58</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire."<sup>59</sup>The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster.<sup>60</sup>Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon.<sup>61</sup>And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words,<sup>62</sup>and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.'<sup>63</sup>When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates,<sup>64</sup>and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'" Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Golden Cup That Made the Earth Drunk
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends a destroyer and winnowers against Babylon (vv. 1–4), for Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God (v. 5). Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand; balm is brought and she is not healed, and the Medes are stirred up as vengeance for his temple (vv. 6–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon was the cup that made the world drunk, held all along in a hand that is now setting it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai, and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land, when they come against her from every side on the day of trouble. Let not the archer bend his bow, and let him not stand up in his armor. Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army. They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets. For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. "Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies. The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God. "Sharpen the arrows! Take up the shields! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple. "Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon. O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut. The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that Leb-kamai is "A code name for Chaldea", a letter-substitution cipher. Why a cipher is used is not certain, since Babylon is named openly in the same verse; it may be wordplay, for read as it stands the name means something like heart of those who rise against me. Either way, Jeremiah is writing about an empire from inside its reach.

And the picture is threshing. Winnowers toss grain into the wind so the chaff blows away; God says he will do that to Babylon and empty her land.

Verse 5 is the pastoral heart of both chapters, and it answers the question the exiles were actually asking. Not: will Babylon fall? But: has God dropped us?

Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God. They had every appearance of being forsaken, with the city gone, the temple burned and the king blinded, and the verse denies it flatly.

This is the faithfulness of God at its most stubborn: he has disciplined them, scattered them and burned his own house, and he has not let go of them for an hour.

An image of terrible beauty. Babylon was a golden cup, genuinely magnificent, and she was in the LORD's hand the whole time. He poured her out for the nations to drink, and the drinking drove them mad.

Empires are intoxicating. Their wealth, art and confidence get into the bloodstream of everyone around them, and the cup was never holding itself up.

And then something unexpected: an attempt at nursing. Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. Somebody fetches medicine for the empire that burned the temple.

We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. The same balm of Gilead offered to Judah (8:22) and denied to Egypt (46:11) is brought to Babylon's bedside, and the verdict is that it did not take. Judgment here is not described as eagerness to destroy, but as a physician's failure declared after the attempt.

The instrument is named a generation before it arrived: the kings of the Medes. Isaiah had said the same — Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them (Isa 13:17) — and Daniel records the night it happened, when Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Dan 5:31).

And the stated motive is a building: the vengeance for his temple. The house Solomon built and the Chaldeans burned is on the charge sheet, which tells you that God does not shrug off what was done to the place where his name was.
verseByVerse.note: Leb-kamai is a code name for Chaldea (ESV note): read with the Hebrew alphabet reversed, it spells the word for Chaldeans.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A creation hymn sets the Maker of the earth against breathless idols (vv. 15–19). Then Babylon is told what she was, my hammer and weapon of war (v. 20), and that she will be repaid for the evil done in Zion and left a burnt mountain (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The tool is told what it was, just before it is put down.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses. Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name. "You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms; with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer; with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman; with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders. "I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain. No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of a war oracle comes a hymn, the same hymn used earlier against the idols of Judah (10:12-13), repeated here against the idols of Babylon.

Three faculties are named: power, wisdom, understanding. And then the weather, described as an operation: mist raised from the ends of the earth, lightning made for the rain, and the wind from his storehouses, as though God keeps weather in a warehouse and brings out what the day requires.

Against that Creator, the craftsman. The contrast is between one who brings forth the wind and one who brings forth a statue, and the fatal lack is named exactly: there is no breath in them. The God who breathed into dust is set beside gods that cannot breathe at all.

The portion of Jacob. Israel's share, her allotted inheritance, is a person, and the sentence turns round and says Israel is his: the tribe of his inheritance. Two parties who have each other as their property.

And the one who formed all things has a name in the New Testament. John says of the Word who became flesh, All things were made through him (John 1:3, 14). The portion of Jacob, the Creator set against breathless idols, is the God who came to his people in Jesus Christ.

Nine times in four verses: with you I break in pieces. It is the rhythm of a hammer, and the list moves from cavalry to civilians to shepherds and ploughmen to the government.

Read as a whole it is God's own account of what Babylon was: You are my hammer and weapon of war. Not a rival kingdom he failed to stop, but an implement he swung.

And a hammer is accountable. For all the evil that they have done in Zion — the tool exceeded its commission, and the repayment will happen before your very eyes, so the exiles will see it.

Babylon sat on a flat plain, so destroying mountain is about stature rather than geology — and the sentence is to be rolled down from the crags and left as a burnt mountain, a slag heap.

Then the detail that finishes it — No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation. Ruined cities were quarries for the next builders. This rubble will not even be worth carting away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Distant nations are summoned against Babylon, and her defence collapses from inside while runners carry the news to the king (vv. 27-33). Zion is given words for what Babylon did to her, and God answers that he will plead her cause, dry up Babylon's waters and give her rulers a feast that ends in endless sleep (vv. 34-40).
verseByVerse.theology: The city is taken while the messengers are still running to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts. Prepare the nations for war against her, the kings of the Medes, with their governors and deputies, and every land under their dominion. The land trembles and writhes in pain, for the LORD's purposes against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant. The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken. One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side; the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come." "Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out. The violence done to me and to my kinsmen be upon Babylon," let the inhabitant of Zion say. "My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say. Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry, and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant. "They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs. While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD. I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three obscure northern peoples are named — Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, from the Armenian highlands — conscripted into the coalition. And the cavalry comes up like bristling locusts: locusts in a bristling swarm (the Hebrew word is uncertain), a cavalry too many to count.

The collapse is from the inside. They have not been beaten in the field — they have ceased fighting and gone indoors, and then their strength has failed. The bars of the gates are broken and the houses are burning.

A brilliant piece of reporting: couriers colliding on the road, each carrying worse news to the palace. By the time the king is told, his city is taken on every side. Anyone who has watched an institution fail will recognise the picture — the messages arriving faster than the leadership can hear them.

Now Zion is given a voice, and it is one of the most physical complaints in Scripture. Six verbs of being eaten: devoured, crushed, emptied, swallowed, and then the last indignity — he has rinsed me out, like a jar licked clean and set aside. The ESV notes that the phrase may be read "Or he has expelled me".

God lets his people say exactly how bad it was. There is no instruction here to be measured about it.

And the answer to that complaint is not a lecture but an advocate: I will plead your cause.

I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry. Babylon lived by water — the Euphrates and its canal network. Isaiah had put the same promise next to a name: God says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers', and says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose' (Isa 44:27-28).

A feast, wine, merriment, and then sleep. Daniel 5 records the night: a banquet, the vessels of the temple used for drinking, writing on the wall, and That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed (Dan 5:30). The cupbearer of the nations was handed a cup of her own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Go Out of the Midst of Her, My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The praise of the whole earth is taken and Bel made to give up what he swallowed (vv. 41-44). God's people are told to go out of her and not to faint at rumours (vv. 45-46); heaven and earth sing, and the escaped are told to remember the LORD and Jerusalem from far away (vv. 47-53).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are told to get out, and to take Jerusalem with them in their minds.

verseByVerse.quote: "How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves. Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes. And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen. "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the images of Babylon; her whole land shall be put to shame, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD. Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, just as for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth. "You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind: 'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.' "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan. Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads Sheshach, "a code name for Babylon" — the same cipher used back in chapter 25, where Babylon drank last from the cup she had carried round (25:26). The code name returns for her funeral.

And the praise of the whole earth is not sarcasm. Babylon was admired everywhere, and the tone here is astonishment rather than gloating.

Bel had swallowed the offerings and tribute of the world, and the temple vessels of Jerusalem with them. God will reach into the idol's mouth and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed — which is exactly what happened when Cyrus counted the bowls back out to a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7-8).

The call to leave comes again, and it rests on verse 5: a people not forsaken by their God is being called home, not driven out. Pastoral care is attached. There will be years of rumour before anything happens — a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year — coups, violence, ruler is against ruler. God tells them in advance not to let their hearts faint at the news cycle.

John hears this same summons over the last Babylon: Come out of her, my people (Rev 18:4).

Creation sings. This is not human vindictiveness but the relief of a world that has been groaning — and the ground given is the dead: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel. The psalmist by the canals had said it in grief, O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed (Ps 137:8), and here God answers him.

Is it right to rejoice when a city falls? The joy here is at the end of oppression and justice for the dead, and it belongs to God's judgment, not to private revenge. Christians still pray for their enemies (Matt 5:44) and leave vengeance with God (Rom 12:19); and they may rejoice, as heaven does in Revelation 19:1-2, when he puts an end to cruelty.

Two instructions for survivors: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind. Faith at a distance, with a city held in the memory — which is how most of God's people have lived ever since, remembering a place they are not in.

The old ambition of Babel, still running: mount up to heaven. Isaiah had put the boast in the first person — I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high — and given the answer: But you are brought down to Sheol (Isa 14:13-15). Height is no defence when the destroyers come from me.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshach is a code name for Babylon (ESV note), formed the same way by reversing the alphabet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God of recompense silences Babylon and levels her broad wall (vv. 54-58). Then comes a last acted sign: Jeremiah sends the written oracle with Seraiah to be read in Babylon and sunk in the Euphrates with a stone, and the book records that the words of Jeremiah end here (vv. 59-64).
verseByVerse.theology: A book weighted with a stone and dropped in a river serves as the closing sermon of Jeremiah's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised, for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire." The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster. Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words, and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.' When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'" Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stilling her mighty voice. A great city is a noise — markets, processions, armies, temple crowds — and God turns the volume off.

The LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. It is one of the plainest statements of the doctrine in Scripture, and it is what makes the rest of the book bearable. A world in which the hammer is never put down is a world without justice.

Babylon's walls were famous across the ancient world; Greek writers said they were wide enough to drive chariots along. They come down.

And the last line is an epitaph for every empire: The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire. Conscripted labour, decades of it, hauling brick for gates that are fuel. Whatever is built without God is built for burning.

Was Babylon really levelled? Not in 539 BC: Cyrus took it with little fighting, and it remained a great city for a time. But over the following centuries it declined until it became the empty mound it is today, as Jeremiah said (50:39-40). Prophecy often shows the end of a long process in a single picture.

(The Greek translation says Seraiah went from Zedekiah, that is, sent by him; either way he travelled on the king's business, probably in 594 or 593 BC.) Seraiah the son of Neriah — Baruch's brother, from the same family, and the quartermaster, a senior official travelling with the king to Babylon. The family that gave Jeremiah his scribe also gave him a courier into the enemy capital.

So the prophet writes it down again — the man whose first scroll was burned and whose second was longer — and sends it a thousand kilometres to be read aloud in the city it condemns. A private reading, probably to nobody but God and one frightened official standing by a river.

And there is the last acted sign recorded in the book, though it was performed years before the stones at Tahpanhes. He had worn a yoke, smashed a flask, buried a loincloth and bought a field. Now, by proxy, a book is weighted with a stone and dropped into the Euphrates, and the words are spoken over the ripples: Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.

Some seven centuries later a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more" (Rev 18:21). The last book of the Bible repeats the gesture of an old man's courier at a riverbank.

Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

Seven words to close forty years. No account of his death, no grave, no vindication scene — he is last seen in Egypt among people who would not hear him, and the book simply stops recording what he said.

And what he said outlasted every power in it. Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, and within a few years his son lost the throne after three months; Babylon is a mound in the desert; and the words thrown into the Euphrates with a stone tied to them float still. The man who asked God why he had ever been born (20:18) wrote the sentence about the law written on the heart and the sins remembered no more, and it is being read this morning in languages that did not exist when he dictated it.
verseByVerse.note: Zedekiah's journey to Babylon in his fourth year is not recorded elsewhere; it may have been to assure Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty after the plotting of chapter 27.

51.title: A Stone in the Euphrates
51.overview:
The oracle against Babylon reaches its climax. God stirs up the Medes against the empire he had held like a golden cup, for his people have not been forsaken by their God (vv. 1-14). A creation hymn sets the Maker of all things against breathless idols, and Babylon is told she was only his hammer (vv. 15-26). Her defence collapses from inside, Zion's complaint is answered by God's promise to plead her cause, and his people are called to leave (vv. 27-53).

The chapter ends with a scene by a river. Jeremiah's written oracle is read aloud in Babylon and thrown into the Euphrates tied to a stone: Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more. With that, the words of Jeremiah end (vv. 54-64).
51.theology:
The exiles' real question was not whether Babylon would fall but whether God had dropped them, and the answer is flat: they have not been forsaken (v. 5). The empire that looked like their master was a cup in his hand and a hammer he swung, accountable for the evil it did beyond its commission (vv. 7, 20, 24).
